knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bayesian Optimization as a Bayesian Sequential-Decision Approach
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the shared Bayesian approach underlying a family of optimization algorithms, rather than defining one particular algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bayesian optimization is an approach to sequential optimization grounded in probability and Bayesian inference. The objective function is treated as an uncertain random function, and prior expectations together with available observations determine a belief about it. This belief takes an active role in the optimization policy by informing the selection of subsequent observations, while optimization also includes decisions about whether to terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayesian optimization is not one particular algorithm, but an approach underlying a family of sequential optimization algorithms. It uses probability and Bayesian inference to maintain beliefs about the unknown objective from prior expectations and available observations. Those beliefs inform where to observe next, while the sequential policy also decides whether to terminate.
assumptions_latex: Observation outcomes are unknown when evaluation decisions are made.
The objective function is represented probabilistically and inferred using prior expectations and available observations.
Optimization proceeds through a sequence of observation and termination decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inferred belief about the objective actively informs the sequential optimization policy, particularly the choice of subsequent observation locations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximization when the objective formula is unavailable and evaluations are prohibitively costly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a domain \(\mathcal X\) and an objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) accessible through queried values \(f(x)\) rather than a known formula, expensive black-box optimization seeks an input \(x^*\in\mathcal X\) satisfying \(f(x^*)\ge f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). Objective evaluations are sufficiently costly that exhaustive search may be intractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expensive black-box optimization seeks an input attaining the largest objective value when the objective formula is unknown, only queried values are observable, and evaluations are too costly for exhaustive search.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R
\text{Access to }f\text{ is through evaluations }f(x)\text{ rather than a known formula.}
\text{Evaluations of }f\text{ are prohibitively costly.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Seek }x^*\in\mathcal X\text{ such that }f(x^*)\ge f(x)\text{ for all }x\in\mathcal X.

children.title: Evaluation-Limited Objectives
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which physical experiments, simulations, or training runs dominate the available budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Limited Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-limited black-box optimization with evaluation cost as the binding resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization problem is evaluation-limited when objective information is obtained through sequential queries \(x_i\in\mathcal X\), query \(i\) costs \(c_i\geq c_{\min}>0\), and the admissible history must satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i\leq B\), where \(B<\infty\). Thus \(N\leq N_B:=\max\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\leq B\}\), with the empty sum defined as zero. The finite bound \(N_B\leq\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor\) constrains attainable objective information independently of the computational cost of fitting a surrogate or optimizing an acquisition function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective is evaluation-limited when a finite cost budget and a positive minimum query cost impose a finite upper bound on the number of black-box queries.
assumptions_latex: The feasible domain is \(\mathcal X\neq\varnothing\).
The total budget is \(B<\infty\), and every evaluation cost satisfies \(c_i\geq c_{\min}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of objective evaluations satisfies \(N\leq N_B\leq\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor\), where \(N_B:=\max\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\leq B\}\).

notation.meaning: Uniform positive lower bound on evaluation cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Cost Does Not Imply Finitely Many Evaluations Without a Positive Cost Floor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the finite-evaluation conclusion in the evaluation-limited definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_i=2^{-i}\) and \(B=1\). Then \(c_i>0\) for every \(i\), but \(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}c_i=1\leq B\). Thus a finite total budget permits infinitely many evaluations when no uniform lower bound \(c_i\geq c_{\min}>0\) is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite budget need not bound the evaluation count when individual costs approach zero.
assumptions_latex: Evaluation costs may depend on the evaluation index.
No positive uniform lower bound on evaluation cost is imposed.

children.title: Objective-Information Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by absent, unreliable, partial, or auxiliary derivative and comparison information.

children.title: Derivative-Free Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives approached without usable derivative observations.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
Only queried function values, possibly corrupted by observation noise, are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The information history contains no queried derivatives of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-free describes the objective-information interface, not the acquisition optimizer.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A black-box objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is derivative-free relative to an evaluation interface when each query at \(x_i\in\mathcal X\) returns only \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\) may be zero, and the history is \(\mathcal D_t=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{t}\). In particular, the interface supplies neither \(\nabla f(x_i)\) nor directional derivatives, even if such derivatives exist mathematically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative-free interface returns objective values but no gradients or directional derivatives at queried points.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Free Objectives

children.title: Derivative-Augmented Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives supported by partial, approximate, or selectively available derivative information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint covariance representation for values and first derivatives of a differentiable Gaussian-process surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), where \(m\) is differentiable and \(k\) has the required mixed derivatives. Then values and mean-square partial derivatives are jointly Gaussian, with \[\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),\partial_{x'_j}f(x'))=\partial_{x'_j}k(x,x'),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_{x_i}f(x),\partial_{x'_j}f(x'))=\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x'_j}k(x,x').\] Exact or Gaussian-noisy derivative observations can therefore be incorporated by augmenting the observation vector and covariance matrix with these derivative blocks and the corresponding noise covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently differentiable Gaussian process jointly models values and derivatives by differentiating its kernel, allowing derivative observations to enter Gaussian conditioning.
assumptions_latex: The mean has the required first derivatives.
The kernel possesses the displayed mixed derivatives and defines the corresponding mean-square derivatives.
Observation noise, if present, is jointly Gaussian with known covariance and independent of the latent process.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (f(x_1),\ldots,\partial_{x_j}f(x'_r),\ldots)\text{ is jointly Gaussian with covariance blocks obtained by differentiating }k.

notation.meaning: Latent mean-square partial derivative of the objective

knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian-Process Conditioning with Derivative Observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact, noisy, partial, directional, or selectively requested first-order objective information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). A derivative-augmented query selects \(x\in\mathcal X\) and directions \(V=(v_1,\ldots,v_q)\), and returns \[Y=f(x)+\varepsilon,\qquad Z_j=D_{v_j}f(x)+\eta_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,q).\] When \(f\) is differentiable, \(D_{v_j}f(x)=v_j^\top\nabla f(x)\). The interface is exact when all errors vanish, coordinate-partial when the directions are selected coordinate vectors, full-gradient when they form the standard basis, and directional for general \(v_j\). The number and directions of requested derivatives may be selected nonanticipatively from the current query and history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative-augmented objective returns a value together with selected exact or noisy directional derivatives; partial derivatives and full gradients are special cases.
assumptions_latex: Each requested directional derivative \(D_{v_j}f(x)\) exists.
Derivative requests are selected without using future observations.
Value and derivative observation errors are included in their respective channels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (Y,Z_1,\ldots,Z_q)\text{ jointly supplies value and selected first-order information about }f\text{ at }x.

notation.meaning: Directional derivative of f at x along v_j

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Augmented Objective Interface

assumptions_latex: The objective \(f:\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at queried points.
Derivative observations may have their own additive errors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The history jointly records value and derivative information about the same objective.

notation.meaning: Observed objective value at the ith query
Observed gradient at the ith query

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order derivative augmentation of a scalar objective on a Euclidean domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable \(f:\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), a derivative-augmented evaluation at \(x_i\) returns \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) and \(g_i=\nabla f(x_i)+\eta_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\in\mathbb R\) and \(\eta_i\in\mathbb R^d\) represent observation errors and may vanish. The resulting information state is \(\mathcal D_t=\{(x_i,y_i,g_i)\}_{i=1}^{t}\), so a surrogate may condition jointly on values and gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative-augmented objective interface supplies function values together with gradients, possibly with separate observation errors.

children.title: Comparison-Augmented Objectives
children.top_down_role: Objectives supplemented by rankings, preferences, or pairwise comparisons.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information identified by pairwise comparisons alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose noiseless comparison data record only whether \(f(x)<f(x')\). For every strictly increasing function \(h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \[f(x)<f(x')\iff h(f(x))<h(f(x')).\] Hence comparison-only data identify the induced ordering of queried alternatives but do not identify objective levels, differences, or a cardinal scale without additional normalization or numerical observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise comparisons are invariant under every strictly increasing transformation, so they identify rankings but not objective levels or differences.
assumptions_latex: Comparisons report only the ordering of objective values.
The transformation \(h\) is strictly increasing on the range of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C(f)=\mathcal C(h\circ f)\text{ for every strictly increasing }h.

notation.meaning: Collection of pairwise order observations induced by f
Strictly increasing transformation of objective values

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinal Invariance and Cardinal Nonidentifiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison augmentation for a latent objective minimized over the design domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(x,x')=1\) mean that \(x\) is reported preferable to \(x'\) for minimizing \(f\). A probit comparison model is \[\mathbb P(C(x,x')=1\mid f)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{f(x')-f(x)}{\tau}\right),\qquad \tau>0.\] Thus a comparison contributes likelihood information about the difference \(f(x')-f(x)\) without revealing either level. Such observations may be used alone or jointly with numerical-value observations under a specified joint conditional model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy preference can be modeled as a probit observation of an objective difference, either alone or alongside numerical evaluations.
assumptions_latex: The latent objective is minimized.
The ordered-pair convention assigns report one to preference for the first argument.
\(\tau>0\) is the comparison-noise scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C(x,x')\text{ informs }f(x')-f(x)\text{ but not either absolute level by itself}.

notation.meaning: Indicator reporting that x is preferred to x-prime.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Pairwise-Comparison Observation Model

assumptions_latex: The latent objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is minimized.
Each comparison concerns an ordered pair of queried alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Comparisons contribute likelihood information about differences \(f(x)-f(x')\), even without revealing either value.

notation.meaning: Indicator that x is preferred to x-prime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise preference observations augment, rather than necessarily replace, numerical evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A comparison-augmented objective supplies binary observations \(C(x,x')\in\{0,1\}\) in addition to any numerical values, with \(C(x,x')=1\) meaning that \(x\) is preferred to \(x'\). A standard noisy representation for minimization is \(\mathbb P(C(x,x')=1\mid f)=\Phi((f(x')-f(x))/\tau)\), where \(\tau>0\) is a comparison-noise scale and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. Hence each comparison informs a latent objective difference without identifying either absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise preferences provide noisy information about objective differences and can augment numerical function evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparison-Augmented Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probit comparison model is plausible and internally consistent, but no inspectable source supports the specific likelihood, sign convention, or augmentation interpretation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp information and direction boundary for binary comparison reports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\{0,1\}\) be a true pairwise ordering and suppose \(\mathbb P(C\neq T\mid T)=\rho\) for both values of \(T\). At \(\rho=1/2\), \(C\) has the same conditional distribution under both orderings and conveys no information about \(T\). For \(\rho>1/2\), the complemented report \(1-C\) has error probability \(1-\rho<1/2\); treating \(C\) as positively reliable reverses its evidential direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric comparison is uninformative at error probability one half and directionally reversed above one half.
assumptions_latex: Comparison errors form a symmetric binary channel.
The orientation of the reported ordering is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Comparison-Channel Reliability Boundary

assumptions_latex: A binary report claims which member of a pair has smaller latent objective value.
Conditional comparison errors are symmetric with probability \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\rho=1/2\) the report is uninformative; for \(\rho>1/2\), treating it as positively reliable reverses its evidential direction.

notation.meaning: Probability that a reported comparison is incorrect

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp reliability boundary for symmetric binary comparison information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\{0,1\}\) be the true ordering of two alternatives and let the auxiliary report satisfy \(\mathbb P(C\neq T\mid T)=\rho\). If \(\rho=1/2\), then \(C\) is independent of \(T\) under the symmetric channel and conveys no ordering information. If \(\rho>1/2\), the complemented report \(1-C\) is more likely correct than \(C\); consequently, a surrogate likelihood that fixes \(\rho<1/2\) assigns evidence in the wrong direction. Positive reliability therefore requires \(0\leq\rho<1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric comparisons lose all information at error probability one half and become directionally misleading above one half.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Information Reliability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric binary-channel boundary is mathematically plausible and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable auxiliary-information source.

children.title: Global Search Geometry Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Continuous, discrete, mixed, and conditional domains where local improvement does not characterize the full task.

children.title: Global Search
children.top_down_role: Search over the full feasible domain when local improvement is insufficient.

assumptions_latex: The feasible domain \(\mathcal X\) is compact.
The objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global consistency is the requirement \(r_t\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Best queried point through time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global search characterized by simple regret rather than local stationarity.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization of \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) on compact \(\mathcal X\), let \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), and after queries \(x_1,\ldots,x_t\) let \(\widehat x_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq i\leq t}f(x_i)\). The simple regret is \(r_t=f(\widehat x_t)-f(x^\star)\). A sequential search is globally consistent when \(r_t\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\); convergence merely to a locally stationary point does not satisfy this criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global search seeks vanishing objective gap to a global minimizer, rather than merely reaching a local stationary point.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Search

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global value certificate from a feasible incumbent and a valid domain-wide lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(U_t=f(\widehat x_t)\) be a feasible incumbent value and let \(L_t\leq f^*:=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\) be a valid global lower bound. Then \(0\leq U_t-f^*\leq U_t-L_t\). Hence \(U_t-L_t\leq\varepsilon\) certifies global \(\varepsilon\)-optimality in objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent is globally near-optimal when its value is close to a valid lower bound over the entire domain.
assumptions_latex: The incumbent is feasible.
The lower bound is valid over the full feasible domain.

notation.meaning: Valid lower bound on the global minimum value.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lower-Bound Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Evaluation Implies Global Value Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method-independent sufficient condition for global simple-regret convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a compact metric space, let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, and let \((x_t)_{t\geq1}\) be dense in \(\mathcal X\). With \(U_t=\min_{1\leq i\leq t}f(x_i)\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), one has \(U_t\downarrow f^*\). Consequently, best-evaluated-point simple regret converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous objective on a compact domain, dense evaluation makes the best observed value converge to the global optimum.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is a compact metric space.
The objective is continuous.
The evaluated sequence is dense in the feasible set.

notation.meaning: Best objective value observed through time t.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Evaluation Implies Global Value Consistency

children.title: Multimodal Search
children.top_down_role: Search across multiple separated promising regions or competing optima.

knowledge_statements.title: Multimodal Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict, separated local minima define the relevant multimodal geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) on a metric space is multimodal if there exist \(k\geq2\) distinct points \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)}\) and pairwise disjoint neighborhoods \(U_1,\ldots,U_k\) such that \(f(x^{(j)})<f(x)\) for every \(x\in U_j\setminus\{x^{(j)}\}\) and every \(j\). These strict local minima need not have equal objective values. A listed local minimizer is global exactly when it attains \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\); any listed local minimizer with a larger value is nonglobal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multimodal objective has at least two separated strict local minima; any that attain the overall minimum are global, while those with larger values are nonglobal.
assumptions_latex: The domain \(\mathcal X\) is a metric space.
The objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is minimized and attains its global minimum when global minimizers are classified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is multimodal when it possesses at least two separated strict local minimizers.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-start coverage of attraction basins belonging to separated modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a deterministic local-search map send every initialization in a measurable basin \(B_j\) to the local minimizer \(x^{(j)}\), and let \(p_j=\nu(B_j)\). For \(m\) independent initializations from \(\nu\), the probability that mode \(j\) is never reached is \((1-p_j)^m\), and \[\mathbb P(\text{some listed mode is missed})\leq\sum_{j=1}^k(1-p_j)^m.\] Thus every listed mode with positive basin probability is discovered with probability tending to one as \(m\to\infty\); a zero-probability basin cannot be discovered by this initialization law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent multistart search misses a basin of probability p with probability (1-p)^m; positive-mass basins are eventually found, whereas zero-mass basins are not.
assumptions_latex: The local-search output is deterministic for each initialization, or its auxiliary randomness is incorporated into the initialization law.
The \(m\) initializations are independent with common distribution \(\nu\).
The listed basins \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) are measurable and finite in number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb P(\exists j\leq k:\,B_j\text{ receives no start})\leq\sum_{j=1}^k(1-p_j)^m.

notation.meaning: Attraction basin of local minimizer j

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Multistart Basin-Coverage Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic niching representation retaining distinct locally optimized candidates at a declared resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\delta>0\). Maintain an archive \(A\) of locally optimized candidates for minimization. For a new candidate \(z\), let \(N_\delta(z)=\{a\in A:d(z,a)\le\delta\}\). If \(N_\delta(z)=\varnothing\), insert \(z\). If \(N_\delta(z)\neq\varnothing\) and \(f(z)<\min_{a\in N_\delta(z)}f(a)\), delete every member of \(N_\delta(z)\) and insert \(z\); otherwise discard \(z\). Starting from \(A=\varnothing\), distinct archive members always satisfy \(d(a,a')>\delta\). Candidates within the declared resolution may intentionally be merged and this archive separation does not certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corrected separation archive keeps representatives more than delta apart, replaces all nearby inferior representatives when necessary, and deliberately merges candidates within its chosen resolution.
assumptions_latex: The search domain has a distance \(d\).
Candidates have comparable objective values.
A deterministic rule resolves equal objective values.

notation.meaning: Archived representatives within distance delta of candidate z.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Preserving Mode Archive

children.title: Structured Search Domains
children.top_down_role: Search respecting discrete, mixed, conditional, or combinatorial organization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for proposals and scores on conditionally encoded domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be an encoding space, \(F\subseteq E\) the valid encodings, and \(\pi:F\to\mathcal D\) the represented-design map. A proposal rule is valid only if it returns elements of \(F\). A surrogate or acquisition \(a:F\to\mathbb R\) is representation-invariant only if \(\pi(e)=\pi(e')\) implies \(a(e)=a(e')\). Otherwise optimization can prefer an invalid encoding or distinguish equivalent encodings for purely representational reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured-domain search must remain feasible and assign identical scores to equivalent encodings of the same design.
assumptions_latex: Valid structured designs may have one or more encodings.
The map \(\pi\) identifies valid encodings representing the same design.

notation.meaning: Set of valid typed or conditional encodings.
Map from valid encodings to represented designs.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility and Encoding-Invariance Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-domain family exposing invalid and duplicate Euclidean encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a design choose \(m\in\{\mathrm{linear},\mathrm{tree}\}\). Tree depth \(d\in\{1,\ldots,D\}\) is active only when \(m=\mathrm{tree}\). The valid domain is \(\mathcal F=\{(\mathrm{linear},\bot)\}\cup\{(\mathrm{tree},d):1\le d\le D\}\). Replacing it by \(\{\mathrm{linear},\mathrm{tree}\}\times(\{\bot\}\cup\{1,\ldots,D\})\) introduces the invalid tree encoding \((\mathrm{tree},\bot)\) and invalid or multiply encoded linear designs \((\mathrm{linear},d)\). Ordinary Cartesian-product search therefore fails to preserve conditional feasibility and design identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating an inactive conditional coordinate as an ordinary product coordinate creates invalid points and duplicate encodings.
assumptions_latex: Depth has semantics only for the tree model.
The symbol \(\bot\) denotes inactivity rather than a numerical depth.
knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-Coordinate Cartesian-Product Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed, mixed, conditional, or combinatorial feasible design space.

Feasibility may couple components or make a component active only under particular values of others. A valid proposal lies in \(\mathcal F\), and any surrogate or acquisition must be well defined on the represented designs rather than rely on an unconstrained Euclidean product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured domain is a feasible combination of typed and possibly conditional components; proposals and models must respect feasibility and design identity.
assumptions_latex: Each component space has a declared semantic type.
The feasible set specifies all coupling and activation constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Search Domain

Feasibility may impose constraints coupling those components.

children.title: Locality Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Landscape regimes where local models or neighborhoods obscure globally relevant alternatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Local Optimality Does Not Certify Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth one-dimensional objective with a strict but nonglobal local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathcal X=[-1,3]\), define \(q(x)=\tfrac34x^2-\tfrac14x^3\) and \(f_\varepsilon(x)=x^2(x-2)^2-\varepsilon q(x)\), where \(0<\varepsilon<16/3\). Then \(q'(0)=q'(2)=0\), so \(f_\varepsilon'(0)=f_\varepsilon'(2)=0\). Moreover, \(f_\varepsilon''(0)=8-3\varepsilon/2>0\) and \(f_\varepsilon''(2)=8+3\varepsilon/2>0\), so both points are strict local minimizers. Nevertheless, \(f_\varepsilon(2)=-\varepsilon<0=f_\varepsilon(0)\), so \(0\) is not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even smooth strict local optimality can coexist with a better remote basin.
assumptions_latex: A method accepts a strict local minimizer without a domain-wide comparison.
The objective is the stated smooth polynomial on the compact interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\text{ is a strict local minimizer but }0\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_\varepsilon(x).

notation.meaning: Smooth objective with unequal strict local minima.
Polynomial tilt preserving stationarity at zero and two.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Local Optimality Does Not Certify Global Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observation-level impossibility for methods confined to a local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[-2,2]\), and choose \(\psi\in C^\infty(\mathcal X;[0,1])\) supported in \((1/2,3/2)\) with \(\psi(1)=1\). For \(M>1\), set \(f_M(x)=x^2-M\psi(x)\). On \((-1/2,1/2)\), \(f_M\) and every derivative equal those of \(x^2\). Hence any method whose queries remain in that neighborhood obtains identical local information from the two objectives, although \(f_M(1)=1-M<f_M(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth objective can be indistinguishable from a quadratic throughout every queried local neighborhood while hiding a better remote basin.
assumptions_latex: All queries remain in \((-1/2,1/2)\).
The available local observations are function values and any finite collection of derivatives at queried points.

notation.meaning: Smooth bump supported away from the local query region.
Objective with a hidden remote basin.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Hidden-Basin Local Indistinguishability

assumptions_latex: Queries are restricted to a neighborhood of the initial point \(0\).
A smooth bump \(\psi\) is supported away from that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Purely local observations cannot distinguish \(f_M\) from \(x^2\), although \(f_M\) has a strictly better point near \(1\).

notation.meaning: Smooth bump supported in the interval one-half to three-halves
Objective with a hidden remote basin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete indistinguishability boundary for methods confined to a local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[-2,2]\), and choose a smooth function \(\psi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]\) supported in \((1/2,3/2)\) with \(\psi(1)=1\). For \(M>1\), define \(f_M(x)=x^2-M\psi(x)\). On \((-1/2,1/2)\), one has \(f_M(x)=x^2\), so any method whose queries remain there receives exactly the same values and derivatives as for \(x^2\) and may return \(0\). Yet \(f_M(1)=1-M<0=f_M(0)\), so \(0\) is not globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth objective can match a simple quadratic locally while hiding a strictly better basin outside every queried neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Locality Failure Boundaries

children.title: Evaluation-Stochasticity Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Observation regimes that change inference, replication, recommendation, and acquisition design.

children.title: Deterministic Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Repeatable objective observations without intrinsic sampling variability.

assumptions_latex: The objective is a fixed function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
Repeated evaluations use the same input and evaluation conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathcal X\), repeated observations satisfy \(Y_1(x)=Y_2(x)=f(x)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Result of the rth repeated evaluation at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determinism concerns repeated objective observations at fixed inputs.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22
1.9 From deterministic to stochastic optimization p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evaluation regime is deterministic when there exists a fixed objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) such that every evaluation at \(x\in\mathcal X\) returns \(Y(x)=f(x)\) almost surely. Equivalently, for any repetitions \(r,s\), \(\mathbb P(Y_r(x)=Y_s(x)=f(x))=1\). Thus repeated evaluations at the same input contain no sampling variation, although numerical approximation may still be treated separately as deterministic error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic evaluation always returns the same fixed objective value when repeated at the same input.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Evaluations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22
1.9 From deterministic to stochastic optimization p. 24

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequence of repeating an exact deterministic evaluation at an observed input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a deterministic evaluation regime, if \(Y_1(x)=f(x)\) has been observed, every exact repetition satisfies \(Y_r(x)=Y_1(x)\) almost surely. Consequently, \(\sigma(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_m(x))=\sigma(Y_1(x))\) modulo null events for every \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once an exact deterministic value is known, repeating it reveals no additional objective-value information.
assumptions_latex: All repetitions use the same input and evaluation conditions.
Evaluations are exact and deterministic.

notation.meaning: The rth exact evaluation at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Replication Is Information-Redundant

children.title: Noisy Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Objective observations perturbed by measurement or numerical noise.

assumptions_latex: The latent target is a fixed function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
Observation errors have conditional mean zero and finite conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated evaluations estimate \(f(x)\), with averaging variance decreasing as \(1/m\) under conditional independence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive unbiased observation noise around a fixed latent objective.

source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A noisy evaluation of a fixed latent objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) has the form \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x)\), where \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon(x)\mid x]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon(x)\mid x)=\sigma^2(x)<\infty\). If \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_m(x)\) are conditionally independent repetitions, then their mean \(\overline Y_m(x)\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[\overline Y_m(x)\mid x]=f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_m(x)\mid x)=\sigma^2(x)/m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noisy evaluations fluctuate around a fixed latent objective, and independent replication reduces the variance of their average.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Evaluations

source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correlated Replication Need Not Eliminate Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the seed's independent-replication variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_r(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_r(x)\), with \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_r(x)\mid x)=\sigma^2(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Corr}(\varepsilon_r(x),\varepsilon_s(x)\mid x)=\rho\in[0,1]\) for \(r\neq s\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_m(x)\mid x)=\sigma^2(x)(\rho+(1-\rho)/m)\), which converges to \(\rho\sigma^2(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive correlation between repeated errors prevents averaging from achieving the independent-replication variance rate.
assumptions_latex: Repeated errors have common finite conditional variance.
Every distinct pair has conditional correlation \(\rho\in[0,1]\).

notation.meaning: Mean of m repeated observations at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Correlated Replication Need Not Eliminate Noise

children.title: Stochastic Evaluations
children.top_down_role: Simulation or sampling outputs with intrinsic random variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-objective formulation of stochastic simulation or experimental outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stochastic evaluation is a realization \(Y=F(x,\xi)\), where \(x\in\mathcal X\) is the decision and \(\xi\) is an exogenous random element. In the expectation formulation, the deterministic optimization target induced by the outcome distribution is \(J(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\), assumed finite, and the problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}J(x)\). Independent repetitions sample the distribution of \(F(x,\xi)\); their randomness is part of the modeled performance system, not merely numerical evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic evaluation samples a random performance outcome, while the expectation formulation optimizes its finite expected value.
assumptions_latex: For each decision \(x\in\mathcal X\), the outcome \(F(x,\xi)\) is integrable.
The exogenous random element \(\xi\) follows a fixed probability law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization target is \(J(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\), while each evaluation samples a random outcome \(F(x,\xi)\).

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Formulating a stochastic optimization problem p. 14

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Formulating a stochastic optimization problem p. 14

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise estimation of the expectation objective from repeated stochastic outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\mathcal X\), and let \(Y_r=F(x,\xi_r)\) be independent and identically distributed with \(\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty\). Then \(\overline Y_m=m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^mY_r\to J(x)=\mathbb E[Y_1]\) almost surely. If additionally \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)=v(x)<\infty\), then \(\mathbb E[\overline Y_m]=J(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_m)=v(x)/m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent stochastic replications consistently estimate expected performance, with inverse-sample variance under finite variance.
assumptions_latex: The decision x is fixed across repetitions.
The outcomes are independent and identically distributed.
The outcome is integrable; the variance identity additionally requires finite variance.

notation.meaning: Mean of m stochastic outcome replications.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency of Independent Stochastic Replication

children.title: Evaluation-Regime Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Consequences of treating repeatability, noise, or stochastic variability under the wrong regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Noise Modeling Can Make Repeated Noisy Data Impossible
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incompatibility created by treating noisy repetitions as deterministic exact observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the fitted regime asserts \(Y_r(x)=f(x)\) almost surely for every repetition. Under the true regime let \(Y_r(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_r\), where \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\) are independent with an atomless nondegenerate distribution. Then \(\mathbb P_0(Y_1(x)\neq Y_2(x))=1\), while the fitted regime assigns probability zero to that event. After unequal repetitions, the exact-observation model assigns zero marginal likelihood to the data, so its ordinary Bayesian posterior update is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating genuinely noisy repetitions as exact can assign zero probability to data that occur almost surely.
assumptions_latex: The assumed observation regime is exact and deterministic.
True repeated errors are independent, nondegenerate, and atomless.

notation.meaning: Probability under the true noisy regime.
Probability under the fitted deterministic regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Noise Modeling Can Make Repeated Noisy Data Impossible

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean-Noise Modeling Can Miss a Nonmean Stochastic Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Target-functional failure when intrinsic outcome variation is represented only through a mean response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let design \(a\) produce \(Y_a=0\) almost surely and design \(b\) produce \(Y_b=-1\) with probability \(0.9\) and \(Y_b=100\) with probability \(0.1\). Then \(\mathbb E[Y_a]=0<9.1=\mathbb E[Y_b]\), whereas the lower quantiles \(Q_{0.9}(Y)=\inf\{y:\mathbb P(Y\le y)\ge0.9\}\) satisfy \(Q_{0.9}(Y_b)=-1<0=Q_{0.9}(Y_a)\). Thus a regime representing designs only by conditional means selects \(a\), while the declared lower-0.9-quantile objective selects \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mean-response noise model can select the wrong design when the declared stochastic objective is a quantile rather than the conditional mean.
assumptions_latex: The declared objective is the lower \(0.9\)-quantile of the outcome law.
The fitted evaluation regime represents each design only through its conditional mean.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic stochastic outcome at design x.

knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Noise Modeling Can Miss a Nonmean Stochastic Objective

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between true and fitted conditional observation laws for a common latent target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\) denote a common latent target with prior \(\Pi\). Conditional on \((x_t,\theta,H_{t-1})\), the true observation law is the kernel \(K_0(\cdot\mid x_t,\theta,H_{t-1})\), while inference uses \(K(\cdot\mid x_t,\theta,H_{t-1})\). Evaluation-regime misspecification occurs when these kernels differ on histories and latent states reached with positive probability under the true joint law. The posterior computed from \((\Pi,K)\) then need not equal the true conditional law generated by \((\Pi,K_0)\), so its uncertainty summaries and acquisition values need not be calibrated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation-regime misspecification uses the wrong conditional observation law for a common latent target, so fitted posterior and acquisition quantities need not be calibrated under the true regime.
assumptions_latex: The design, history, latent, and observation spaces admit the required conditional kernels.
The same latent target and prior are used when comparing the true and fitted observation regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\neq K_0\text{ on a positive-probability reached set}\Longrightarrow \Pi_t^{K}\text{ need not equal }\Pi_t^{K_0}.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation-Regime Misspecification

children.title: Sequential Decision Architecture
children.top_down_role: Organization of beliefs, observations, evaluation choices, horizons, and final recommendations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attached here as the black-box adaptive-learning specialization. The source states the broader architecture for sequential learning and notes that controllable physical states change the state content without changing the transition form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequential adaptive-learning process has state $S^n$, policy decision $x^n=X^\pi(S^n)$, newly observed exogenous information $W^{n+1}$, transition $S^{n+1}=S^M(S^n,x^n,W^{n+1})$, and a performance objective. Its trajectory is $(S^0,X^\pi(S^0),W^1,S^1,X^\pi(S^1),W^2,\ldots)$. In a pure-learning problem, the state may contain only the current belief about the function; more general sequential-decision models may also contain controllable physical state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequential adaptive-learning algorithm can be represented by a state, a policy-selected decision, new information, a transition, and an objective. In pure learning, the state may contain only beliefs about the function; physical-state models use the same transition architecture with richer state content.
assumptions_latex: n=0,1,\ldots
x^n=X^\pi(S^n)

children.title: History-Belief State Interface
children.top_down_role: Representations connecting accumulated evidence to future evaluation decisions.

children.title: Observation Histories
children.top_down_role: Recorded evaluations, metadata, ordering, and contextual information accumulated during search.

assumptions_latex: At stage \(t\), evaluated points and observed responses are measurable random variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The history \(H_t\) contains precisely the ordered information available before choosing \(X_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses ordered point-response histories, with auxiliary recorded data included when present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequential evaluation process, the observation history after \(t\) evaluations is the ordered random element \(H_t=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_t,Y_t))\), with \(H_0=\varnothing\). If evaluations also return known costs, constraints, fidelities, or noise descriptors, these components are included in each observation tuple. The associated information is \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(H_t)\). A nonanticipative next-evaluation rule must select \(X_{t+1}\) using only \(H_t\), equivalently making \(X_{t+1}\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_t\), possibly together with independent randomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An observation history is the ordered record of evaluated points and returned data, generating exactly the information available for the next decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Observation Histories

children.title: Belief-State Representations
children.top_down_role: Decision-relevant summaries of uncertainty after incorporating available evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Belief-State Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior-distribution belief state for a Bayesian sequential evaluation model on standard Borel spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the latent environment \(F\) take values in a standard Borel space with prior law \(\Pi_0\), and let evaluations and observations take values in standard Borel spaces. Given the observation history \(H_t\), define the Bayesian belief state by the regular conditional distribution \(B_t=\mathcal L(F\mid H_t)\). Thus, for every measurable latent event \(A\), \(B_t(A)=P(F\in A\mid H_t)\) almost surely. If the observation model is specified by measurable kernels conditional on \(F\) and the selected evaluation, then a measurable Bayes-update map \(\Phi_t\) may be chosen so that an action \(X_{t+1}=x\) and observation \(Y_{t+1}=y\) give \(B_{t+1}=\Phi_t(B_t,x,y)\) almost surely. The belief may be stored as the full probability measure or by parameters that uniquely determine it, such as the mean and covariance of a Gaussian-process posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian belief state is the regular conditional distribution of the latent environment given the observation history. Under standard measurable-space and observation-kernel assumptions, it admits a measurable recursive update and may be represented by any parameters that uniquely determine the posterior.
assumptions_latex: The latent environment \(F\), evaluation space, and observation space are standard Borel spaces.
The prior law of \(F\) is \(\Pi_0\).
Observations are generated by specified measurable kernels conditional on \(F\) and the selected evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regular conditional distribution \(B_t=\mathcal L(F\mid H_t)\) is a belief-state representation and admits an almost-sure measurable update \(B_{t+1}=\Phi_t(B_t,X_{t+1},Y_{t+1})\).

notation.meaning: Measurable Bayesian update map at stage t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Controlled-Markov Property of the Bayesian Belief
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictive and belief-transition kernels determined by the posterior belief, stage, and next evaluation action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_t=\mathcal L(F\mid H_t)\), and let \(K_t(dy\mid f,x)\) be the observation kernel when latent environment \(f\) is queried at \(x\). Conditional on \((B_t,x)\), the next-observation predictive law is \[P_t(dy\mid B_t,x)=\int K_t(dy\mid f,x)\,B_t(df).\] Together with the measurable update \(B_{t+1}=\Phi_t(B_t,x,Y_{t+1})\), this predictive law induces a controlled transition kernel for \(B_{t+1}\) that depends on the past only through \((t,B_t,x)\). Hence the full posterior is a controlled-Markov information state whenever rewards, feasibility, and terminal losses factor through it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The posterior belief determines the predictive observation law and updated-belief distribution, making it a controlled-Markov information state when all decision quantities factor through it.
assumptions_latex: The regular conditional posterior and measurable Bayes-update map exist.
The observation law is the measurable kernel \(K_t(dy\mid f,x)\).
Rewards, feasibility constraints, and terminal losses depend on history only through the stage and posterior whenever state sufficiency is claimed.

notation.meaning: Stage-t observation kernel conditional on latent environment and query.

knowledge_statements.title: Controlled-Markov Property of the Bayesian Belief

children.title: History-to-State Compression
children.top_down_role: Ways accumulated evidence is reduced to information used by future evaluation decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon factorization criterion for compressing histories without changing the continuation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t=T_t(H_t)\). The compression is exact for a finite-horizon sequential decision model when there are state-indexed feasible-action sets \(\mathcal A_t(s)\), one-step expected losses \(g_t(s,a)\), controlled transition kernels \(Q_t(\cdot\mid s,a)\), and terminal loss \(g_T(s)\) such that, for every relevant history \(h\) with \(T_t(h)=s\), the feasible actions equal \(\mathcal A_t(s)\), the conditional expected one-step loss of action \(a\) equals \(g_t(s,a)\), the conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\) equals \(Q_t(\cdot\mid s,a)\), and the terminal conditional loss equals \(g_T(s)\). A constructive form additionally has a measurable update \(S_{t+1}=U_t(S_t,A_t,Y_{t+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history compression is exact when feasibility, expected losses, controlled next-state laws, and terminal loss all factor through the compressed state, which may be updated recursively.
assumptions_latex: \(T_t\) and any recursive update \(U_t\) are measurable.
The conditional losses and controlled transition laws exist.
The factorization holds for every relevant history and feasible action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_t\mapsto S_t\text{ preserves the controlled continuation model through }(\mathcal A_t,g_t,Q_t,g_T).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Controlled-Markov Compression

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon dynamic-programming consequence of exact controlled-Markov compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under Exact Controlled-Markov Compression, suppose the state and action spaces are standard Borel, losses are measurable and integrable, and each Bellman minimization admits a measurable selector. Then the optimal continuation value after history \(h\) is a function only of \(T_t(h)\), satisfies the Bellman recursion built from \(\mathcal A_t,g_t,Q_t,g_T\), and an optimal policy can be chosen measurable in the current compressed state. Thus restricting from history-dependent policies to state-dependent policies causes no loss of optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the usual finite-horizon measurability and selector assumptions, exact factorization makes the value depend only on the compressed state and permits an optimal state-based policy.
assumptions_latex: The exact factorization in Exact Controlled-Markov Compression holds.
The horizon is finite.
State and action spaces are standard Borel.
Losses are measurable and integrable.
Required Bellman minimizers have measurable selectors.

notation.meaning: Optimal continuation value from history h

knowledge_statements.title: No-Loss State-Policy Reduction

assumptions_latex: A measurable state map \(T_t\) is defined on histories.
Future observation laws and terminal losses are specified for every admissible continuation policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compression \(S_t=T_t(H_t)\) is exact precisely when histories with equal states induce equal conditional continuation laws and losses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact compression relative to future observations and the optimization loss.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Markov Processes with Arbitrary State Space p. 101

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A history-to-state compression is a measurable map \(T_t\) with \(S_t=T_t(H_t)\). It is sufficient for sequential optimization if, whenever \(T_t(h)=T_t(h')\), every admissible continuation policy \(\pi\) has the same conditional joint law of future observations and terminal loss from \(h\) as from \(h'\). Equivalently, there exist state-based transition kernels and loss functions that reproduce all conditional continuation values. Under this condition, optimizing over policies measurable in \(S_t\) loses no value relative to optimizing over policies measurable in the full history \(H_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compressed state is exact when histories mapped to the same state have identical future data and loss distributions under every continuation policy.
knowledge_statements.title: History-to-State Compression

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Markov Processes with Arbitrary State Space p. 101

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed equivalence between equality of all continuation laws and existence of state-based kernels and losses needs a precise controlled-process theorem. Applying the same history-dependent policy at two different histories can itself produce different actions, so the current quantification over continuation policies is not well-defined enough to validate the no-loss conclusion from the cited table-of-contents entry.

children.title: State Sufficiency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where a compressed belief state omits history relevant to subsequent decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: State Sufficiency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes failures of exact value representation and terminal decision sufficiency when a proposed state omits relevant history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t=T_t(H_t)\), and for an admissible continuation policy \(\pi\) let \(V_t^\pi(h)\) denote its conditional expected continuation loss given \(H_t=h\). Exact continuation-value representation by \(S_t\) fails if there exist histories \(h,h'\) with \(T_t(h)=T_t(h')\) and a policy \(\pi\) such that \(V_t^\pi(h)\neq V_t^\pi(h')\). For a terminal-only decision with action set \(\mathcal A\), state-based Bayes optimality fails whenever two such histories have disjoint sets \(\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}E[L(F,a)\mid H_t=h]\) and \(\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}E[L(F,a)\mid H_t=h']\). Hence a summary retaining only sampled locations, posterior means, or incumbent observations can be insufficient when discarded uncertainty, noise, cost, or dependence information changes the relevant conditional values or eliminates every common Bayes-optimal action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed state crosses a sufficiency boundary if it merges histories that cannot share an exact continuation-value representation or, for a terminal decision, have no common Bayes-optimal action.
assumptions_latex: The compressed state is \(S_t=T_t(H_t)\).
For every admissible continuation policy \(\pi\), the conditional expected continuation loss \(V_t^\pi(h)\) is well-defined for relevant histories \(h\).
The terminal action set is \(\mathcal A\), and the conditional risks \(E[L(F,a)\mid H_t=h]\) are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact state sufficiency fails when equal compressed states have unequal continuation values for some admissible policy; terminal decision sufficiency fails when their Bayes-optimal action sets are disjoint.

notation.meaning: Conditional expected continuation loss under policy pi from history h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite terminal-decision example where retaining a query location but discarding its outcome is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\in\{-1,1\}\) have equal prior probabilities and let an evaluation at a fixed location return \(Y=\Theta\) without noise. Define a proposed state that records the location but not \(Y\), so the histories \((x_0,1)\) and \((x_0,-1)\) have the same state. For terminal actions \(a\in\{-1,1\}\) and loss \(L(\Theta,a)=\mathbf 1\{a\neq\Theta\}\), the respective Bayes-optimal action sets are \(\{1\}\) and \(\{-1\}\). The compressed state therefore admits no action optimal for both histories; full-history Bayes risk is zero, whereas every state-only action has prior Bayes risk \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Remembering where an exact observation was made while forgetting its sign merges histories requiring opposite terminal actions.
assumptions_latex: The observation is exact: \(Y=\Theta\).
The state records the query location but not the response.
Terminal loss is zero-one loss.

children.title: Evaluation-Recommendation Policy Interface
children.top_down_role: The separation between selecting information and reporting an optimizer.

children.title: Evaluation Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies selecting observations during the search process.

assumptions_latex: The action space \(\mathcal X\) is measurable.
At stage \(t\), only \(H_t\) and independent policy randomization are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An evaluation policy is a sequence of nonanticipative kernels \(\pi_t(dx\mid H_t)\) governing the next queried point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows deterministic or randomized sequential query rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evaluation policy over horizon \(T\) is a sequence \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_{T-1})\) of stochastic kernels on \(\mathcal X\) such that \(X_{t+1}\mid H_t\sim\pi_t(\cdot\mid H_t)\). Each kernel is measurable in \(H_t\), so the policy is nonanticipative. A deterministic policy is the special case \(X_{t+1}=g_t(H_t)\) for measurable maps \(g_t\). In acquisition-based Bayesian optimization, one such map selects an element of \(\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\alpha_t(x;H_t)\), with a specified measurable tie-breaking rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation policy is a nonanticipative rule, deterministic or randomized, that chooses each next query from the observations available so far.
knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Policies

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the observation-selection component of sequential black-box optimization; the policy may be deterministic or stochastic and adaptive or nonadaptive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An evaluation policy takes the current dataset \(\mathcal D\) as its state and selects a next observation location \(x\in\mathcal X\). A deterministic policy specifies \(x=\operatorname{POLICY}(\mathcal D)\); a stochastic policy specifies a distribution over \(\mathcal X\) conditional on \(\mathcal D\). A nonadaptive policy may ignore the observed outcomes in \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation policy uses the current dataset to select the next observation location. It can be deterministic or random and can either adapt to observed outcomes or ignore them.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D\text{ is the currently available dataset}
\mathcal X\text{ is the objective domain}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\sim\pi(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal D)\text{ on }\mathcal X,\text{ with deterministic policies as degenerate special cases.}

children.title: Terminal Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Rules for reporting a final design after information collection ends.

assumptions_latex: A terminal history \(H_\tau\) is observed at a finite stopping time \(\tau\).
Recommendations belong to a measurable decision set \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A terminal recommendation rule is a measurable map \(\rho:H_\tau\mapsto\widehat x_\tau\in\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the decision returned after evaluation ends.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A terminal recommendation rule is an \(\mathcal F_\tau\)-measurable decision \(\widehat x_\tau=\rho(H_\tau)\in\mathcal A\), issued after evaluations stop at \(\tau\). Given loss \(L(F,a)\), a Bayes terminal rule satisfies \(\rho(H_\tau)\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}E[L(F,a)\mid H_\tau]\), with measurable tie-breaking. For simple regret under minimization, \(L(F,a)=F(a)-\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}F(x)\), so any posterior minimizer of \(E[F(a)\mid H_\tau]\) is Bayes-optimal when the displayed expectations and minimizers exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal recommendation is the measurable decision returned when evaluation stops; under a specified loss it may be chosen to minimize posterior expected loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Recommendations

children.title: Policy-Recommendation Separation
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between locations sampled for information and designs reported for use.

assumptions_latex: An evaluation policy \(\pi\) generates data until \(\tau\).
A recommendation rule \(\rho\) maps the terminal history to a decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((\pi,\rho)\) consists of distinct decision rules and should be optimized jointly for the chosen terminal risk.

notation.meaning: Bayes risk of the policy-rule pair

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates information-gathering actions from the final deployed decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The evaluation policy \(\pi\) determines which information is collected, whereas the terminal rule \(\rho\) determines the deployed decision. Their performance under loss \(L\) is \(R(\pi,\rho)=E_{\pi}[L(F,\rho(H_\tau))]\). For fixed \(\pi\), the Bayes recommendation minimizes conditional terminal risk pointwise in \(H_\tau\); for fixed \(\rho\), evaluation quality depends on how observations affect that terminal decision. Therefore the final recommendation need not equal the last evaluation, the best observed response, or any point selected by the acquisition policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query selection gathers information, while recommendation chooses the deployed decision; these are distinct rules linked only through the chosen terminal risk.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy-Recommendation Separation

children.title: Recommendation Mismatch Risks
children.top_down_role: Cases where the sampling objective does not support the intended terminal decision.

assumptions_latex: The terminal objective is expected loss \(E[L(F,a)\mid H_\tau]\).
A heuristic rule \(\widetilde\rho\) is used instead of a Bayes terminal rule \(\rho^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditional mismatch penalty is nonnegative and equals the posterior-risk gap between \(\widetilde\rho\) and \(\rho^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies terminal loss caused by using a recommendation inconsistent with the declared objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho^*(H_\tau)\in\arg\min_a E[L(F,a)\mid H_\tau]\), and let \(\widetilde\rho\) be the implemented recommendation. The conditional mismatch penalty is \(\Delta(H_\tau)=E[L(F,\widetilde\rho(H_\tau))-L(F,\rho^*(H_\tau))\mid H_\tau]\geq0\). Its expectation is the excess Bayes risk attributable solely to recommendation mismatch under the generated history distribution. Thus returning the last query, a noisy incumbent, or an acquisition maximizer can be suboptimal whenever that rule does not minimize the posterior expected terminal loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recommendation mismatched to the terminal loss incurs a nonnegative posterior-risk gap, even when the preceding evaluation policy gathered useful information.
knowledge_statements.title: Recommendation Mismatch Risks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp equality condition for the posterior-risk mismatch penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminal history \(h\), define \(r_h(a)=\mathbb E[L(F,a)\mid H_\tau=h]\), assume \(r_h^*=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}r_h(a)\) exists, and let \(\widetilde\rho(h)\) be the implemented recommendation. Then \[\Delta(h)=r_h(\widetilde\rho(h))-r_h^*\geq0,\] with \(\Delta(h)=0\) if and only if \(\widetilde\rho(h)\in\arg\min_a r_h(a)\). Consequently, the expected mismatch penalty is zero if and only if the implemented rule selects a Bayes action for almost every generated terminal history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected recommendation-mismatch penalty is zero exactly when the implemented recommendation is Bayes-optimal almost surely.
assumptions_latex: The posterior risks and mismatch penalty are measurable and integrable.
A posterior-risk minimizer exists for almost every generated terminal history.

notation.meaning: Posterior terminal risk of action a at history h.

children.title: Fixed Evaluation Horizons
children.top_down_role: Search conducted under a predetermined number of evaluation opportunities.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Evaluation Horizons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon regime with a predetermined positive evaluation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed evaluation horizon is specified by an integer \(T\geq1\) chosen before the sequential process begins. The evaluation policy selects \(X_{t+1}\) for \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), exactly \(T\) evaluations are completed, and evaluation stops at the deterministic time \(\tau=T\). Any nonanticipative terminal recommendation is \(\mathcal F_T\)-measurable. Because \(T\) is fixed independently of the realized history, observations cannot change the number of evaluations, although they may change all remaining evaluation locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed evaluation horizon, a positive number of evaluations is chosen in advance and cannot change in response to observed outcomes; only the selected locations may adapt.
assumptions_latex: A positive integer evaluation budget \(T\) is fixed before observations are collected.
Exactly one evaluation is completed at each stage.
The terminal recommendation rule is nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stopping time is the deterministic constant \(\tau=T\), independent of the realized history, and the terminal recommendation is \(\mathcal F_T\)-measurable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential optimization under a fixed and known observation-count budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a fixed, known observation budget, the decision horizon \(\tau\) is the known number of observations remaining before termination. Given the current dataset \(\mathcal D\), the decision problem is to select the next evaluation location when exactly \(\tau\) observations remain. Modeling the budget solely by observation count effectively treats every observation as having the same acquisition cost; variable costs and adaptive stopping lie outside this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decision horizon is the known number of evaluations remaining under a fixed observation-count budget. The policy chooses its next location using the current dataset and this horizon. This regime treats evaluations as equally costly and excludes variable-cost and adaptive-stopping decisions.
assumptions_latex: \tau\in\mathbb N\text{ is fixed and known}
\text{termination occurs after exactly }\tau\text{ further observations}
\text{observations are treated as having constant acquisition cost}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau\text{ specifies the finite remaining horizon for the next-location decision.}

children.title: Cost-Constrained Horizons
children.top_down_role: Search governed by heterogeneous evaluation costs or a total expenditure limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Constrained Horizons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget-feasible evaluation horizons with heterogeneous, history-dependent costs and optional early stopping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B>0\), and suppose the cost \(c(x,H_t)\geq0\) of selecting an admissible next action \(x\) is known at stage \(t\). A cost-constrained evaluation regime consists of an evaluation policy and a stopping time \(\tau_B\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^{\tau_B}C_i\leq B\) almost surely, where \(C_{t+1}=c(X_{t+1},H_t)\). On every event \(\{t<\tau_B\}\), the selected next action must satisfy \(c(X_{t+1},H_t)\leq B-\sum_{i=1}^{t}C_i\). The policy may stop voluntarily before exhausting the budget and must stop if no admissible action is affordable. Consequently, \(\tau_B\) may depend on the selected actions and observed history; additional assumptions are needed if almost-sure finiteness is required when zero-cost actions are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-constrained horizon pairs a policy with a stopping time so that every completed evaluation is affordable and total cost never exceeds the budget. Early stopping is allowed, and zero-cost actions require a separate finiteness condition.
assumptions_latex: The total budget satisfies \(B>0\).
For every admissible action \(x\) and history \(H_t\), the known next-evaluation cost \(c(x,H_t)\) is nonnegative.
The evaluation policy and budget stopping time \(\tau_B\) are nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Budget feasibility requires \(\sum_{i=1}^{\tau_B}C_i\leq B\) almost surely and requires every action selected before \(\tau_B\) to cost no more than the remaining budget.

notation.meaning: Known cost of selecting action x after history H_t
Cost of the t-th completed evaluation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation-Count Bound from Positive Query Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed count bound is mathematically sound but canonically owned by Evaluation-Limited Objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a budget-feasible regime has total budget \(B\) and every completed evaluation costs at least \(c_{\min}>0\), then \(\tau_B\leq\lfloor B/c_{\min}\rfloor\) almost surely; zero-cost evaluations invalidate this implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive minimum query cost converts a total budget into a deterministic evaluation-count bound.
assumptions_latex: Budget feasibility holds almost surely.
Every completed evaluation costs at least \(c_{\min}>0\) almost surely.

children.title: Adaptive Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on evolving evidence, opportunity value, or remaining resources.

assumptions_latex: The histories generate a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq0}\).
At each stage, the stop-or-continue decision uses only current information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An adaptive stopping rule is an \((\mathcal F_t)\)-stopping time \(\tau\), equivalently satisfying \(\{\tau=t\}\in\mathcal F_t\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent stopping without anticipation of future evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adaptive stopping rule is a random time \(\tau\) such that \(\{\tau\leq t\}\in\mathcal F_t\) for every \(t\geq0\). Equivalently, there are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable decisions \(D_t\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\tau=\inf\{t:D_t=1\}\). Thus stopping may depend on observed responses, posterior uncertainty, remaining budget, or acquisition value, but not on future observations. At \(\tau\), the algorithm outputs an \(\mathcal F_\tau\)-measurable recommendation; admissibility additionally requires any prescribed almost-sure finiteness or budget constraint on \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive stopping ends evaluation at a history-dependent stopping time whose decision can use current observations but cannot depend on future data.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Stopping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon optimal stopping recursion on a sufficient information state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t\) be sufficient, \(G_t(s)\) the loss from stopping immediately, and \(K_t(s,a,S_{t+1})\) the incremental loss from continuing with action \(a\). For terminal horizon \(T\), define \[V_T(s)=G_T(s),\qquad V_t(s)=\min\left\{G_t(s),\inf_{a\in\mathcal A_t(s)}E[K_t(s,a,S_{t+1})+V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s,A_t=a]\right\}.\] An optimal rule stops where the stopping term is no larger than the continuation term and otherwise uses a minimizing continuation action. Its first entry into the stopping region, truncated at \(T\), is an optimal stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-horizon optimal adaptive stopping compares immediate stopping loss with the best expected continuation loss and stops on first entry into the stopping region.
assumptions_latex: The horizon \(T\) is finite.
\(S_t\) is sufficient for feasible actions, losses, and controlled transitions.
The displayed conditional expectations exist.
Required minimizers and measurable selectors exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau^*=\inf\{t:G_t(S_t)\leq C_t(S_t)\}\wedge T\text{ is optimal, where }C_t\text{ is the Bellman continuation value}.
knowledge_statements.title: Bellman Stop-or-Continue Rule

children.title: Premature-Stop Risks
children.top_down_role: Regimes where uncertain progress or misleading confidence triggers unsuitable termination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regret Lower Bound from Premature Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple-regret consequence of stopping while a separated optimizer remains unevaluated and unrecommended.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(E\) be an event on which a procedure stops without evaluating or recommending \(b\). If under an objective \(f\), \(b\) is uniquely optimal and \(\delta=\inf_{x\ne b}(f(x)-f(b))>0\), then \(r_\tau\ge\delta\) on \(E\), and hence \[\mathbb E_f[r_\tau]\ge\delta\,\mathbb P_f(E).\] Thus a positive probability of such premature stopping precludes zero expected simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stopping with positive probability before evaluating or recommending a separated optimizer yields a proportional positive lower bound on expected simple regret.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb P_f(E)>0\).
The procedure neither evaluates nor recommends \(b\) on \(E\).
\(b\) is uniquely optimal with gap \(\delta>0\).

notation.meaning: Objective gap separating b from all other points.

knowledge_statements.title: Regret Lower Bound from Premature Stopping
Premature-Stop Risks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point Bayesian example quantifying simple-regret risk from stopping before an informative evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{a,b\}\), with \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(b)=-1\) with probability \(p\in(0,1)\), otherwise \(f(b)=1\). Assume \(f(b)\) is independent of observations obtained without evaluating \(b\). Let \(E\) be the event that a stopping rule terminates before evaluating \(b\) and recommends \(a\), and write \(q=\mathbb P(E)\). For minimization, the terminal simple regret \(r_\tau=f(a)-\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\) then satisfies \[\mathbb P(r_\tau=1)\geq \mathbb P(E\cap\{f(b)=-1\})=pq.\] Thus any positive premature-stop probability creates positive probability of missing the optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stopping before an independent, potentially optimal point is evaluated causes positive simple-regret probability proportional to the stopping probability and prior optimality probability.
assumptions_latex: Unevaluated \(f(b)\) is independent of information available on \(E\).

notation.meaning: Event of stopping before evaluating b and recommending a.
Simple regret at the stopping time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but no source is cited for the counterexample. Moreover, independence from observations alone does not imply that E is independent of f(b) when the stopping rule may use additional randomization; the equality P(E intersect {f(b)=-1})=pq requires E to be measurable with respect to information independent of f(b).

children.title: Optimization Utility Families

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dataset utility in sequential Bayesian optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General utility-based formulation of adaptive observation selection under a posterior belief about the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given accumulated data \(\mathcal D\), uncertainty about the objective is represented by a posterior belief \(p(f\mid\mathcal D)\), which need not be Gaussian-process based and induces \(p(y\mid x,\mathcal D)\) for \(x\in\mathcal X\). A utility \(u(\mathcal D)\) orders possible returned datasets. An adaptive policy may use all preceding observations when selecting subsequent locations, with choices guided by their expected improvement in dataset utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequential Bayesian optimization policy uses previous observations to choose new locations. Its posterior belief about the objective induces predictive outcome distributions, while a utility function ranks returned datasets and guides choices by expected utility improvement.

\mathcal D\text{ is the currently observed dataset}
p(f\mid\mathcal D)\text{ is a probabilistic belief, not necessarily a Gaussian process}
p(y\mid x,\mathcal D)\text{ is the induced posterior predictive distribution}
u(\mathcal D)\text{ evaluates the quality of a returned dataset}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Observation locations may be selected adaptively using expected improvements in }u(\mathcal D).
