knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain \(f^\star=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), and let \(\widehat x_\tau\) be the recommendation produced when a sequential policy \(\pi\) stops at \(\tau\). Its terminal solution quality under loss \(\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) is \[Q_\ell(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\ell\!\left(f(\widehat x_\tau),f^\star\right)\right],\] whenever the expectation exists. Smaller \(Q_\ell\) is better. For the excess-value loss \(\ell(u,v)=(u-v)_+\), terminal quality is expected simple regret because \(f(\widehat x_\tau)\geq f^\star\); it depends on the recommendation rule as well as the sampled data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal solution quality is the expected loss comparing the stopped policy's recommendation with the true optimum value.

children.title: Simple Regret
children.top_down_role: Terminal performance viewed through the gap associated with the final recommendation.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal simple regret for minimization, stated pathwise and in Bayesian expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain \(f^\star=\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\). If a sequential optimization policy recommends \(\widehat x_T\in\mathcal X\) after \(T\) evaluations, its simple regret is \[r_T^{\mathrm s}=f(\widehat x_T)-f^\star\geq0.\] Under a prior on \(f\), observation noise, or policy randomization, the Bayesian simple regret is \(\mathbb E[r_T^{\mathrm s}]\), provided it is integrable. Simple regret evaluates only the terminal recommendation; losses incurred by intermediate evaluation points do not enter its definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple regret is the terminal recommendation’s objective gap from the global optimum; its Bayesian version averages this gap over all uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) attains a finite minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
\(f(\widehat x_T)-f^\star\) is integrable when expected regret is used.

children.title: Recommendation Selection Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of terminal assessment on how the reported design is selected.

knowledge_statements.title: Recommendation Selection Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of the terminal decision rule on posterior expected simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D_T\) be the data after \(T\) evaluations and suppose \(f(x)\) is posterior-integrable for every admissible \(x\). Conditional expected simple regret from recommending \(x\) is \[\mathbb E[f(x)-f^\star\mid\mathcal D_T]=\mathbb E[f(x)\mid\mathcal D_T]-\mathbb E[f^\star\mid\mathcal D_T].\] Because the second term is independent of \(x\), every Bayes recommendation for simple regret belongs to \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[f(x)\mid\mathcal D_T].\] Consequently, two policies with identical evaluation data can have different terminal regret solely because they employ different recommendation maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given the same data, posterior-mean minimization is Bayes-optimal for simple regret; another recommendation rule can produce worse terminal quality.
assumptions_latex: Posterior expectations of \(f(x)\) and \(f^\star\) are finite.
The displayed argmin is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noisy Incumbent Selection Can Be Suboptimal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection effect from recommending the smallest observed noisy value instead of minimizing posterior risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization with known values \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(b)=1\). Observe each point once with independent noise equal to \(-2\) or \(2\), each with probability \(1/2\). The smallest-observation rule recommends \(b\) on \(\{Y_a=2,Y_b=-1\}\), an event of probability \(1/4\), and therefore has expected simple regret \(1/4\). The posterior-mean rule always selects \(a\) and has zero simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting the best noisy observation can incur positive terminal regret even when posterior-mean selection is optimal from the same data.
assumptions_latex: The two noises are independent and each equals \(-2\) or \(2\) with probability \(1/2\).
The objective values are known in this diagnostic construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[r^{\mathrm s}(\widehat x_{\mathrm{obs}})]=1/4>0=\mathbb E[r^{\mathrm s}(\widehat x_{\mathrm{PM}})]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction Cost of a Recommendation Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of restricting the terminal recommendation to a smaller admissible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal A\) and define \(V(\mathcal B)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal B}\mathbb E[\ell(a,\Theta)\mid\mathcal D_T]\). Then \[V(\mathcal A_0)-V(\mathcal A)\ge0.\] Equality holds when the restricted class contains a Bayes-optimal action, and more generally exactly when both infima have the same value. Thus an evaluated-point or discrete-candidate restriction can worsen terminal quality without changing the data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the recommendation class cannot improve posterior Bayes risk and may create a positive terminal-quality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal A\).
The displayed conditional-risk infima are finite.

notation.meaning: Optimal posterior risk over class B.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal recommendation under arbitrary loss is a posterior decision problem.

children.title: Terminal-Criterion Misalignment
children.top_down_role: Cases where the reported quality measure does not match the practical terminal objective.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison between a proxy query criterion and the optimized terminal risk induced by each query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\in\mathcal Q\) be a feasible next query, let \(C(q)\) be a proxy criterion to be minimized, and define the optimized terminal risk \[R(q)=\inf_{\rho}\mathbb E\!\left[L(F,\rho(H^q))\right].\] The proxy is terminally aligned if \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\mathcal Q}C(q)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\mathcal Q}R(q).\] It is terminally misaligned if some \(q_C\in\arg\min_q C(q)\) satisfies \(R(q_C)>\inf_qR(q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proxy query criterion is terminally misaligned when one of its optimal queries has strictly greater optimized terminal risk than an available alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(C(q)\) and \(R(q)\) are well-defined for every feasible query.
The proxy minimum is attained; terminal-risk attainment is required only when its argmin is used.

notation.meaning: Proxy criterion assigned to query q.
Optimized expected terminal risk after query q.
Terminal history resulting from query q and its observation.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Criterion Alignment and Misalignment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite correlated-objective example separating expected sampled value from expected terminal simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{a,b,c,d\}\), suppose \(f(a)=0\) is already known, and let \(\Theta\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.1)\). Set \(f(b)=-1\), \(f(c)=2+\Theta\), and set \(f(d)=-5\) when \(\Theta=1\) and \(f(d)=1\) when \(\Theta=0\). One noiseless query remains, with feasible queries \(b\) and \(c\). Expected sampled value favors \(b\), since \(\mathbb E[f(b)]=-1<2.1=\mathbb E[f(c)]\). Querying \(b\) reveals no information about \(\Theta\); the Bayes terminal recommendation is then \(b\), whose expected simple regret is \(0.1\cdot4=0.4\). Querying \(c\) reveals \(\Theta\), after which recommending \(d\) for \(\Theta=1\) and \(b\) for \(\Theta=0\) gives zero simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A poor but informative evaluation can permit perfect terminal selection, while the query with the best immediate value leaves positive expected simple regret.
assumptions_latex: The known value \(f(a)=0\) and the stated joint prior are available before the final query.
The query is noiseless, and the terminal recommendation may be any point in \(\mathcal X\).

notation.meaning: Latent Bernoulli state coupling the values at c and d.
Bayes expected terminal simple regret after querying q.

knowledge_statements.title: Informative but Immediately Inferior Query
Terminal-Criterion Misalignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point example separating one-step sampling loss from terminal simple regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one evaluation, minimization on \(\mathcal X=\{a,b\}\), and \(f(a)=0\). Let \(f(b)=-M\) with probability \(p\) and \(f(b)=1\) otherwise, where \(M>0\) and \(pM<1-p\). Minimizing expected sampled value selects \(a\), because \(\mathbb E[f(b)]=1-p-pM>0=f(a)\). If the terminal recommendation is the best evaluated point, evaluating \(a\) has expected simple regret \(pM\), whereas evaluating \(b\) reveals whether \(a\) or \(b\) is optimal and yields zero simple regret. Hence the sampling criterion and terminal criterion select different actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point with worse expected immediate value can be informative enough to give zero terminal regret, exposing criterion misalignment.
assumptions_latex: An evaluation reveals the selected objective value exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x\mathbb E[f(x)]=\{a\}\), but evaluating \(b\) uniquely minimizes expected terminal simple regret.

notation.meaning: Magnitude of the favorable value at b.
Prior probability that b is optimal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. More importantly, with only one evaluation, evaluating b does not yield zero regret under a rule that recommends the best evaluated point when b=1, unless a is already an admissible known baseline. The information state and recommendation rule must be corrected and sourced before the claimed separation is reliable.

children.title: Cumulative Reward-Regret Duality
children.top_down_role: Criteria that value every evaluation made during search.

children.title: Cumulative Reward
children.top_down_role: Utility assigned to outcomes obtained throughout the evaluation sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative Reward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon reward accumulated by an adaptive sequential policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an adaptive policy choose \(X_t\in\mathcal X\) using information available before round \(t\), and let \(Y_t\) be the integrable reward observed at that round. The pathwise cumulative reward through horizon \(T\in\mathbb N\) is \[G_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_t.\] Its expected cumulative reward is \(J_T(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_T]\). When \(\mathbb E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]=r(x)\), the tower property gives \(J_T(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r(X_t)]\). A cumulative-reward objective selects a policy maximizing \(J_T(\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative reward sums rewards obtained at every evaluation; its expected value is the sequential policy’s finite-horizon performance criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\).
Each \(Y_t\) is integrable.

notation.meaning: Expected cumulative reward of policy pi.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministically weighted finite-horizon cumulative reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integrable rewards \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_T\) and deterministic weights \(w_t\ge0\), define \[G_T^w=\sum_{t=1}^T w_tY_t,\qquad J_T^w(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_T^w].\] Ordinary cumulative reward uses \(w_t=1\); geometric discounting uses \(w_t=\gamma^{t-1}\), \(\gamma\in[0,1]\). If \(\mathbb E[Y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},X_t]=r(X_t)\), then \(J_T^w(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi[\sum_{t=1}^T w_tr(X_t)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted cumulative reward includes ordinary and geometrically discounted finite-horizon reward as special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
\(w_t\ge0\) is deterministic.
Every \(w_tY_t\) is integrable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Step Acquisition Induced by Cumulative Reward
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected one-step marginal utility under the cumulative sum of observed rewards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
u(\mathcal D)=\sum_i y_i,
\]
then the marginal utility contributed by a measurement at \(x\) is its observed value \(y\), and hence
\[
\alpha(x;\mathcal D)=\mathbb E[y\mid x,\mathcal D].
\]
Under additive observation noise having conditional mean zero, this becomes
\[
\alpha(x;\mathcal D)=\mu_{\mathcal D}(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For cumulative observed reward, the one-step acquisition is the posterior predictive mean of the next observation. With conditionally zero-mean additive noise, it equals the posterior mean of the latent objective.
assumptions_latex: u(\mathcal D)=\sum_i y_i
y=f(x)+\eta
\mathbb E[\eta\mid x,\mathcal D]=0\text{ for the reduction to }\mu_{\mathcal D}(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(x;\mathcal D)=\mathbb E[y\mid x,\mathcal D],\qquad \alpha(x;\mathcal D)=\mu_{\mathcal D}(x)\text{ under conditionally zero-mean additive noise}

children.title: Cumulative Regret
children.top_down_role: Opportunity loss accumulated across evaluations during search.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparator formulation distinguishing fixed-action and dynamic-oracle benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given round-dependent mean rewards \(r_t\), selected actions \(X_t\), and benchmarks \(b_t\), define \[R_T(b)=\sum_{t=1}^T(b_t-r_t(X_t)).\] The best-fixed-action convention takes one \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_x\sum_{s=1}^T r_s(x)\) and \(b_t=r_t(x^\star)\); the dynamic-oracle convention takes \(b_t=\max_x r_t(x)\). Whenever both are defined, \(R_T^{\mathrm{dyn}}\ge R_T^{\mathrm{fixed}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative regret depends on its comparator; best-fixed and time-varying oracle benchmarks generally yield different values.
assumptions_latex: All displayed rewards are finite.
The required maxima are attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparator-Relative Cumulative Regret

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between noisy realized regret and mean-reward pseudo-regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y_t=r(X_t)+\varepsilon_t\) and \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},X_t]=0\). Relative to \(r^\star\), define \(\widetilde R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T(r^\star-Y_t)\) and \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T(r^\star-r(X_t))\). Then \[\widetilde R_T=R_T-\sum_{t=1}^T\varepsilon_t,\qquad \mathbb E[\widetilde R_T]=\mathbb E[R_T],\] when integrable. Unlike pseudo-regret, realized regret can be negative on a sample path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Realized regret equals pseudo-regret minus accumulated noise; they agree in expectation under conditionally mean-zero noise but not pathwise.
assumptions_latex: \(X_t\) is selected before observing \(Y_t\).
\(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},X_t]=0\).
All displayed terms are integrable.
knowledge_statements.title: Realized Regret and Pseudo-Regret Distinction
Cumulative Regret
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon pseudo-regret relative to the best fixed action in expected reward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be the mean-reward function and assume \(r^\star=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}r(x)\) is finite and attained. For actions \(X_1,\ldots,X_T\), the cumulative pseudo-regret is \[R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(r^\star-r(X_t)\bigr)\geq0.\] For a randomized adaptive policy \(\pi\), expected cumulative regret is \(\mathbb E_\pi[R_T]\), provided it is finite. Unlike simple regret, cumulative regret charges every suboptimal evaluation, including evaluations undertaken primarily to acquire information for later decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative regret sums each evaluation’s mean-reward gap from the best action, thereby charging exploratory as well as exploitative decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(r^\star=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}r(x)\) exists and is finite.
\(R_T\) is integrable when expected regret is used.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudo-regret definition is standard and internally correct, but the cited locator concerns average-reward dynamic programming and is not sufficiently specific evidence for finite-horizon cumulative pseudo-regret relative to the best fixed action. A regret-specific section or theorem is required.

children.title: Reward-Regret Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Conditions and conventions governing comparison between the two cumulative criteria.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which reward and regret cease to induce identical policy rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identity \(R_T=Tr^\star-G_T^r\) yields identical policy orderings when compared policies share the same deterministic horizon \(T\), benchmark \(r^\star\), and mean-reward convention. If horizons or benchmarks vary by policy, the affine offset is no longer common. If \(Y_t=r(X_t)+\varepsilon_t\), then \[\sum_{t=1}^T(r^\star-Y_t)=R_T-\sum_{t=1}^T\varepsilon_t,\] so pathwise equivalence with pseudo-regret also fails unless the accumulated noise is common or zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reward and pseudo-regret are exact affine equivalents only under a common horizon, common benchmark, and consistent mean-reward convention.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark and horizon are defined for every compared policy.
The noise decomposition is used only when all terms are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{A common }(T,r^\star)\text{ and mean-reward convention give the policy-independent affine offset.}\)
review_flags: wording corrected so sufficient common-offset conditions are not mislabeled individually necessary in every degenerate problem
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of Exact Reward-Regret Equivalence
Reward-Regret Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence between expected cumulative mean reward and cumulative pseudo-regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r^\star=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}r(x)<\infty\), and define the cumulative mean reward \(G_T^r=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r(X_t)\) and cumulative pseudo-regret \(R_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r^\star-r(X_t))\). Then, pathwise, \[R_T=Tr^\star-G_T^r.\] Consequently \(\mathbb E_\pi[R_T]=Tr^\star-\mathbb E_\pi[G_T^r]\) whenever either side is finite. For a fixed horizon and common benchmark \(r^\star\), maximizing expected cumulative mean reward is therefore equivalent to minimizing expected cumulative pseudo-regret, with identical policy orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed horizon, cumulative pseudo-regret equals optimal benchmark reward minus cumulative mean reward, so their policy rankings are reversed exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\) and \(r^\star<\infty\).
The relevant expectations exist.

notation.meaning: Cumulative mean reward along the selected actions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine identity is mathematically correct and duality is the appropriate content kind. However, the average-reward dynamic-programming locator is not specific evidence for the stated cumulative pseudo-regret correspondence and identical policy ordering, so a regret-specific source is required.

children.title: Pathwise Utility Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tensions between productive evaluations, information gathering, and terminal performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Pathwise Utility Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial ordering and scalarization of cumulative and terminal losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate each realized policy path with the loss pair \((R_T,r_T^{\mathrm s})\), comprising cumulative and simple regret. Path \(A\) dominates path \(B\) only if both coordinates for \(A\) are no larger and at least one is smaller. Otherwise their ranking requires a preference parameter. For example, pairs \((1,0)\) and \((0.8,0.4)\) are incomparable. Under scalar loss \[L_\lambda=\lambda R_T+(1-\lambda)r_T^{\mathrm s},\qquad \lambda\in[0,1],\] the first pair is preferred when \(\lambda<2/3\), the second when \(\lambda>2/3\), and they tie at \(\lambda=2/3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative and terminal regret can rank paths oppositely; a scalar preference weight resolves the tradeoff but changes which path is preferred.
assumptions_latex: \(R_T\ge0\), \(r_T^{\mathrm s}\ge0\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The loss pairs \((1,0)\) and \((0.8,0.4)\) reverse order at \(\lambda=2/3\).

source_refs.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Sums Need Not Recover Every Pareto-Efficient Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of linear scalarization for nonconvex attainable loss sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\subset\mathbb R^2\) be the attainable set of cumulative-terminal loss pairs. Every minimizer of \(\lambda u+(1-\lambda)v\), \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), is Pareto efficient, but a Pareto-efficient point need not minimize any such weighted sum when \(\mathcal L\) is nonconvex. For example, \((0,1),(0.6,0.6),(1,0)\) are all Pareto efficient, yet \((0.6,0.6)\) is never a weighted-sum minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear weights recover only supported Pareto points; a nonconvex tradeoff set can contain efficient compromises selected by no weight.
assumptions_latex: Both loss coordinates are minimized.
\(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Sums Need Not Recover Every Pareto-Efficient Path

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-constraint representation complementary to weighted scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((R_T,r_T^{\mathrm s})\in\mathcal L\), consider \[\min R_T\quad\text{subject to}\quad r_T^{\mathrm s}\le\varepsilon.\] Every attained solution is weakly Pareto efficient. Moreover, every Pareto-efficient point \((R^\star,r^\star)\) solves this problem for \(\varepsilon=r^\star\), provided the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard bound on terminal loss can recover efficient compromises, including nonsupported points missed by weighted sums.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinates are minimized.
The constrained minimum is attained.
review_flags: weak rather than strong Pareto efficiency asserted for arbitrary minimizers
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Scalarization of Pathwise Tradeoffs

children.title: Information-Gain Utility
children.top_down_role: Criteria centered on uncertainty about an optimizer, optimum value, level set, or latent function.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Gain Utility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step conditional mutual information about a designated latent optimization target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be a posterior-random target, such as an optimizer, optimum value, level set, or latent function, and let \(Y_x\) denote the prospective observation at \(x\in\mathcal X\). Given current data \(\mathcal D_t\), the information-gain utility of evaluating \(x\) is \[\alpha_t^{\mathrm{IG}}(x)=I(Z;Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t).\] When the conditional entropies are finite, \(\alpha_t^{\mathrm{IG}}(x)=H(Z\mid\mathcal D_t)-\mathbb E[H(Z\mid\mathcal D_t,Y_x)\mid\mathcal D_t]\). A greedy information policy chooses any maximizer of \(\alpha_t^{\mathrm{IG}}\), optionally after incorporating evaluation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Information-gain utility is the expected posterior uncertainty reduction about a chosen optimization target produced by one prospective observation.
assumptions_latex: The conditional mutual information \(I(Z;Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t)\) is well-defined.
Entropy identities are used only when the displayed entropies are finite.

source_refs.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

source_witnesses.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information about a latent function need not equal information about a derived optimization target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Z=g(F)\) is a measurable function of a latent object \(F\), conditional data processing gives \[I(Z;Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t)\le I(F;Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t).\] The inequality can be strict, and maximizing the right-hand side need not maximize the left-hand side. Information-gain acquisitions are therefore interchangeable only when their declared targets coincide or an additional equivalence is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Learning the whole function can rank evaluations differently from learning its optimizer, optimum value, or another derived target.
assumptions_latex: \(Z=g(F)\) measurably.
The relevant conditional mutual informations are well-defined.

notation.meaning: Latent function or richer latent object.

knowledge_statements.title: Target Dependence of Information Utility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Chain Rule for Information Utility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of batch or adaptive information gain into conditional increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For observations \(Y_{1:T}\), \[I(Z;Y_{1:T}\mid\mathcal D_0)=\sum_{t=1}^T I(Z;Y_t\mid\mathcal D_0,Y_{1:t-1}).\] Under an adaptive policy whose action at round \(t\) is measurable with respect to the preceding history, expected total information is the expected sum of these one-step conditional increments. Conditional independence is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Batch information gain decomposes exactly into successive posterior information increments, including under adaptive sampling.
assumptions_latex: All conditional mutual informations are well-defined.
Adaptive actions are measurable with respect to the preceding history.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Chain Rule for Information Utility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed form for information about a Gaussian latent quantity from a noisy linear observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Conditioned on \(\mathcal D_t\), let \(Z\) be Gaussian with covariance \(\Sigma_Z\), and let \(Y=AZ+\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\varepsilon)\) is independent and \(\Sigma_\varepsilon\succ0\). Then \[I(Z;Y\mid\mathcal D_t)=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I+\Sigma_\varepsilon^{-1/2}A\Sigma_ZA^\top\Sigma_\varepsilon^{-1/2}\right).\] For a scalar observation with latent variance \(s^2\) and noise variance \(\sigma^2\), this is \(\tfrac12\log(1+s^2/\sigma^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linear Gaussian observation, information gain is a log-determinant signal-to-noise quantity.
assumptions_latex: The conditional linear-Gaussian model holds.
\(\Sigma_\varepsilon\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Observation Information Formula

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior-divergence representation of one-step information utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When regular conditional distributions exist and the divergence is well-defined, \[I(Z;Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t)=\mathbb E_{Y_x\mid\mathcal D_t}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(P_{Z\mid\mathcal D_t,Y_x}\,\|\,P_{Z\mid\mathcal D_t}\bigr)\right].\] Hence information gain is zero exactly when \(Z\) and \(Y_x\) are conditionally independent, up to null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Information gain equals the expected KL divergence from the current target posterior to the updated posterior.
assumptions_latex: Regular conditional distributions exist.
The displayed divergence and expectation are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected-KL Representation of Information Gain

children.title: Cost-Risk Utility Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Criteria coupling decision value to heterogeneous costs or risk preferences.

children.title: Cost-Sensitive Utility
children.top_down_role: Decision value adjusted for heterogeneous evaluation expenditures or resource use.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Sensitive Utility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian utility balancing terminal benefit against total evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let policy \(\pi\) stop at \(\tau\), produce terminal benefit \(B(\widehat x_\tau,f)\), and incur nonnegative evaluation cost \(c_t\) at round \(t\). For tradeoff parameter \(\lambda\ge0\), its cost-sensitive utility is \[U_\lambda(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[B(\widehat x_\tau,f)-\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t\right],\] whenever the terms are integrable. Maximizing \(U_\lambda\) is the Lagrangian form of trading terminal performance against expected total cost. Increasing \(\lambda\) weakly penalizes every policy in proportion to its expected cost, although optimal policies need not vary continuously with \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost-sensitive utility subtracts a weighted total evaluation cost from expected terminal benefit, making the cost-quality preference explicit.
assumptions_latex: \(c_t\ge0\) and \(\lambda\ge0\).
Terminal benefit and stopped total cost are integrable.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 A Simple Modeling Framework for Dynamic Programs p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Budget Constraint and Cost-Penalty Dual Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian relation between a hard expected-cost budget and penalized utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[P(b)=\sup_{\pi}\{V(\pi):C(\pi)\leq b\}.\] For every \(\lambda\geq0\), weak duality gives \[P(b)\leq \lambda b+\sup_{\pi}\{V(\pi)-\lambda C(\pi)\}.\] Therefore \(\inf_{\lambda\geq0}[\lambda b+\sup_\pi(V(\pi)-\lambda C(\pi))]\) is an upper bound on the hard-budget optimum. Equality and recovery of a budget-optimal policy require additional convexification and constraint-qualification conditions; they do not follow from the cost-sensitive definition alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalized cost-sensitive utility is the Lagrangian dual of a hard expected-cost budget; it always gives a weak-dual bound, while exact equivalence needs additional convexity and regularity.
assumptions_latex: The problem maximizes expected terminal benefit.
The expected-cost constraint is \(C(\pi)\leq b\).
The multiplier satisfies \(\lambda\geq0\), and the displayed suprema are well defined in the extended-real sense.

notation.meaning: Optimal benefit under expected-cost budget b

knowledge_statements.title: Budget Constraint and Cost-Penalty Dual Form

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity of Optimal Cost Under Its Price
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparative statics of the cost penalty in cost-sensitive utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each policy \(\pi\), write \(V(\pi)=\mathbb E[B(\widehat x_\tau,f)]\) and \(C(\pi)=\mathbb E[\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}c_t]\). Let \(\pi_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\pi}\{V(\pi)-\lambda_iC(\pi)\}\) for \(0\leq\lambda_1<\lambda_2\), with finite selected values. Then \[C(\pi_2)\leq C(\pi_1),\qquad V(\pi_2)\leq V(\pi_1).\] Thus increasing the evaluation price selects an optimizer with weakly lower expected cost and weakly lower unpenalized terminal benefit, although the selected policy may jump when ties change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As the cost penalty increases, an optimal policy's expected evaluation cost and unpenalized terminal benefit weakly decrease, though the selected policy may jump.
assumptions_latex: Both penalized optimization problems attain finite maxima.
The compared policies are selected from the same feasible policy class.
Expected benefit and expected total cost are finite for the selected policies.

notation.meaning: Expected terminal benefit of policy pi
Expected total evaluation cost of policy pi
Policy optimal at cost price lambda_i

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity of Optimal Cost Under Its Price

children.title: Risk-Sensitive Utility
children.top_down_role: Decision value adjusted for aversion to uncertainty, downside, or undesirable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential certainty-equivalent utility for a policy-induced loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a random loss \(L_\pi\) and \(\theta>0\) with \(\mathbb E[e^{\theta L_\pi}]<\infty\), define \[\rho_\theta^{\mathrm{ent}}(L_\pi)=\frac1\theta\log\mathbb E[e^{\theta L_\pi}],\qquad U_\theta^{\mathrm{ent}}(\pi)=-\rho_\theta^{\mathrm{ent}}(L_\pi).\] This risk measure is monotone and translation equivariant, and \(\rho_\theta^{\mathrm{ent}}(L_\pi)\ge\mathbb E[L_\pi]\). If exponential moments are finite on a neighborhood of zero, then \(\rho_\theta^{\mathrm{ent}}(L_\pi)\to\mathbb E[L_\pi]\) as \(\theta\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropic utility penalizes losses through an exponential certainty equivalent and approaches expected-loss utility as risk aversion vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[e^{\theta L_\pi}]<\infty\).
The risk-neutral limit additionally requires finite exponential moments on a neighborhood of zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Risk-Sensitive Utility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean-Variance Utility Is Not Monotone in General
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural limitation of mean-variance risk adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mean-variance loss functional \(\rho_\gamma(L)=\mathbb E[L]+\gamma\operatorname{Var}(L)\), \(\gamma>0\), need not be monotone under almost-sure loss ordering. Let \(L_1\equiv1\) and let \(L_2\) equal zero or one with equal probability. Then \(L_2\le L_1\) almost surely, but \(\rho_\gamma(L_2)=1/2+\gamma/4>1=\rho_\gamma(L_1)\) whenever \(\gamma>2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-variance adjustment can rank an everywhere smaller loss as worse, so it is not a monotone risk measure without restrictions.
assumptions_latex: The compared losses are square-integrable.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Variance Utility Is Not Monotone in General
Risk-Sensitive Utility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CVaR-based utility for policies exposed to upper-tail optimization loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_\pi\) be an integrable loss generated by sequential policy \(\pi\), including terminal error and any accumulated costs. For confidence level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \[\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L_\pi)=\inf_{\eta\in\mathbb R}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(L_\pi-\eta)_+]\right\}.\] The corresponding risk-sensitive utility is \(U_\alpha^{\mathrm{risk}}(\pi)=-\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(L_\pi)\). Maximizing this utility minimizes upper-tail loss rather than merely mean loss. The parameter \(\alpha\) specifies the tail emphasis and must be fixed when policies are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CVaR risk-sensitive utility ranks policies by their upper-tail loss, penalizing adverse outcomes that an expectation-only criterion can obscure.
assumptions_latex: \(L_\pi\) is integrable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The CVaR representation and induced negative-CVaR utility are mathematically standard and the definition role fits the leaf. However, the cited introductory stochastic-optimization section is not a sufficiently specific locator for the CVaR variational formula or its upper-tail interpretation; a risk-measure section, theorem, or page is required.

children.title: Cost-Risk Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between resource efficiency and exposure to uncertain outcomes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-based representation of the cost-risk frontier, including unsupported Pareto points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For attainable pairs \(\mathcal Y=\{(C_D(a),R_D(a)):a\in\mathcal A\}\), consider \[\min_{a\in\mathcal A}R_D(a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad C_D(a)\leq\varepsilon.\] This epsilon-constraint formulation does not require convexity of \(\mathcal Y\). If \(a^\star\) is Pareto efficient for simultaneous minimization of cost and risk, then with \(\varepsilon=C_D(a^\star)\), the action \(a^\star\) solves this problem. Thus varying \(\varepsilon\) can recover efficient points that no weighted sum supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraining cost and minimizing risk can represent efficient points on a nonconvex cost-risk frontier that weighted sums miss.
assumptions_latex: The same admissible action set \(\mathcal A\) and the same cost and risk criteria are used throughout.
Pareto efficiency means that no admissible action weakly improves both criteria and strictly improves at least one.
The stated epsilon-constraint minimum is interpreted with all its minimizers.

notation.meaning: Cost limit in the epsilon-constraint formulation

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Constraint Cost-Risk Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonconvex attainable set showing the limitation of positive weighted sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Y=\{(0,2),(1,1.1),(2,0)\}\), with both coordinates minimized. The point \((1,1.1)\) is Pareto efficient but is not a minimizer of \(w_Cy_C+w_Ry_R\) for any \(w_C,w_R>0\). It is, however, the unique solution of minimizing risk over \(\mathcal Y\) subject to cost at most \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-point nonconvex frontier has an efficient middle point that no positive weighted sum selects, although an epsilon cost constraint selects it.
assumptions_latex: Both coordinates are minimized.
The attainable set is exactly \(\mathcal Y=\{(0,2),(1,1.1),(2,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Efficient Cost-Risk Point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier relation between an epsilon cost constraint and penalized cost-risk scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p(\varepsilon)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}\{R(a):C(a)\leq\varepsilon\},\] the Lagrange dual value is \[d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{\mu\geq0}\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}\bigl(R(a)+\mu(C(a)-\varepsilon)\bigr),\] and weak duality gives \(d(\varepsilon)\leq p(\varepsilon)\). If \(\mathcal A\) is convex, \(C\) and \(R\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, the primal optimum is attained, and a relative-interior Slater point satisfies \(C(\bar a)<\varepsilon\), then strong duality holds and an optimal multiplier \(\mu^\star\geq0\) exists. A primal-dual optimum satisfies primal feasibility, minimization of \(R+\mu^\star C\), and \(\mu^\star(C(a^\star)-\varepsilon)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost limit always has a weak Lagrange dual; under convexity, closedness, attainment, and Slater feasibility, an optimal multiplier yields an equivalent penalized cost-risk problem with complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is convex.
\(C\) and \(R\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on \(\mathcal A\).
The constrained optimum is attained.
Some \(\bar a\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal A)\) satisfies \(C(\bar a)<\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Optimal risk under cost limit epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Limit Lagrange Duality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted scalarization of two simultaneously minimized posterior criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For admissible actions \(a\in\mathcal A\), finite posterior cost \(C_D(a)\), posterior risk \(R_D(a)\), and weights \(w_C,w_R\geq0\) not both zero, define \[a_w\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in\mathcal A}\{w_CC_D(a)+w_RR_D(a)\}.\] If \(w_C,w_R>0\), every minimizer is Pareto efficient. Without convexity of the attainable upper image, varying positive weights need not recover every Pareto-efficient pair; it recovers only supported efficient points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weights scalarize cost and risk and select Pareto-efficient actions, but weighted sums can miss unsupported points of a nonconvex frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\), and the displayed minimum is attained.
\(C_D\) and \(R_D\) are finite on \(\mathcal A\).
Both criteria are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w_C,w_R>0\implies a_w\text{ is Pareto efficient; completeness of weighted-sum recovery requires suitable convexity of the attainable upper image}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Cost-Risk Scalarization
Cost-Risk Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted scalarization of posterior evaluation cost and decision risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the admissible actions at history \(D\). For posterior expected cost \(C_D(a)\), posterior risk \(R_D(a)\), and preference weight \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), define \[U_{D,\lambda}(a)=-(1-\lambda)C_D(a)-\lambda R_D(a),\qquad a_\lambda\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal A}U_{D,\lambda}(a).\] Equivalently, \(a_\lambda\) minimizes \((1-\lambda)C_D(a)+\lambda R_D(a)\). Every selected action is weakly Pareto efficient whenever both weights are positive; varying \(\lambda\) recovers only supported points of a nonconvex cost-risk frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preference weight scalarizes posterior cost and risk. Positive weights select Pareto-efficient actions, but weighted sums can miss unsupported points on a nonconvex frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\), and the displayed argmax is attained.
\(C_D,R_D:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\) are finite.
\(\lambda\in[0,1]\).

notation.meaning: posterior expected cost of action a

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted multiobjective scalarization and its supported-frontier limitation are standard
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted scalarization, positive-weight Pareto-efficiency claim, and supported-frontier limitation are mathematically standard and fit the representation container, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Preference Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Consequences of utility choices that poorly reflect actual cost or risk priorities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on inferring a cost-risk weight from an observed optimal choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L_\lambda(a)=(1-\lambda)C(a)+\lambda R(a)\), define \[\Lambda(a)=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:a\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{b\in\mathcal A}L_\lambda(b)\}.\] Observing that \(a\) is optimal identifies the weight only up to \(\Lambda(a)\). If this set contains distinct weights, the weight is not point-identified; if one action minimizes both \(C\) and \(R\), its compatibility set can equal \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An observed optimal action generally identifies a set of compatible preferences rather than a unique cost-risk weight.
assumptions_latex: The decision maker minimizes the displayed scalarization.
The observer knows \(C\) and \(R\) and observes only an optimal action.

notation.meaning: Weights for which a is optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Preference Nonidentifiability from Optimal Actions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic decision-regret bound for an erroneous linear cost-risk weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_\lambda(a)=C(a)+\lambda D(a)\), where \(D(a)=R(a)-C(a)\), and let \(a_\theta\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in\mathcal A}L_\theta(a)\). If \(|D(a)|\le M\) for every \(a\), then \[0\le L_\lambda(a_{\widehat\lambda})-L_\lambda(a_\lambda)\le |\lambda-\widehat\lambda|\,|D(a_{\widehat\lambda})-D(a_\lambda)|\le2M|\lambda-\widehat\lambda|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded cost-risk contrasts, preference-misspecification regret is Lipschitz in the weight error; no uniform bound follows without control of those contrasts.
assumptions_latex: Both displayed minimizers exist.
\(C,R:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\).
\(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}|R(a)-C(a)|\le M<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Sensitivity to Preference-Weight Error
Preference Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision loss caused by using incorrect cost-risk preference weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the true loss be \(L_\lambda(a)=(1-\lambda)C_D(a)+\lambda R_D(a)\), but let the policy select \(a_{\widehat\lambda}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in\mathcal A}L_{\widehat\lambda}(a)\). Its preference-misspecification regret is \[\Delta_D(\lambda,\widehat\lambda)=L_\lambda(a_{\widehat\lambda})-\min_{a\in\mathcal A}L_\lambda(a)\geq0.\] Misspecification can reverse the decision: for actions with \((C_D(a_1),R_D(a_1))=(0,1)\) and \((C_D(a_2),R_D(a_2))=(1,0)\), the preferred action changes when the deployed and true weights lie on opposite sides of \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the wrong cost-risk weight creates nonnegative decision regret and may reverse the selected action, even with perfectly known costs and risks.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\), and both displayed minima are attained.
\(C_D\) and \(R_D\) are finite real-valued functions.
\(\lambda,\widehat\lambda\in[0,1]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: regret is the true scalarized-loss gap and the two-action reversal is directly checkable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regret definition and two-action reversal example are correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the record has no inspectable source supporting this preference-misspecification formulation.

children.title: Observation-Economy Initialization System
children.top_down_role: Design choices that create the initial data set and govern the allocation of costly observation channels.

children.title: Space-Filling Initial Designs
children.top_down_role: Latin-hypercube, maximin, low-discrepancy, and hybrid designs for initial domain coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Space-Filling Initial Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite initial designs characterized by geometric coverage, discrepancy, or marginal stratification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty compact domain and let \(X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset\mathcal X\) contain \(n\) distinct points. Its fill distance and separation distance are \[h(X_n,\mathcal X)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{1\le i\le n}\lVert x-x_i\rVert,\qquad q(X_n)=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert.\] Space-filling designs seek small \(h\), large \(q\), or low discrepancy relative to a specified reference measure. A maximin design maximizes \(q\) over a specified feasible design class. When each coordinate has a specified continuous marginal distribution, a Latin-hypercube design places exactly one transformed coordinate value in each of the \(n\) equal-probability strata for every coordinate. Hybrid designs combine two or more coverage criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Space-filling initial designs use fill distance, separation, discrepancy, or marginal stratification to cover a domain. Latin-hypercube stratification is defined relative to specified coordinate marginals, and hybrid designs combine coverage criteria.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and compact.
\(n\geq2\), and the points of \(X_n\) are distinct.
Any discrepancy criterion has a specified reference measure, and Latin-hypercube stratification has specified continuous coordinate marginals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n\) is assessed using \(h(X_n,\mathcal X)\), \(q(X_n)\), a specified discrepancy, coordinatewise stratification, or a stated combination of these criteria.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latin-Hypercube Stratification Need Not Ensure Multivariate Filling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of coordinatewise stratification as a joint-domain coverage criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\ge1\), the design \[X_n=\left\{\left(\frac{i-1/2}{n},\frac{i-1/2}{n}\right):i=1,\ldots,n\right\}\subset[0,1]^2\] is a Latin-hypercube design because each coordinate occupies every equal-width stratum exactly once. Nevertheless all points lie on the diagonal, and at \((0,1)\), \[\min_{x_i\in X_n}\|(0,1)-x_i\|_2\ge\frac1{\sqrt2}.\] Thus \(h(X_n,[0,1]^2)\ge1/\sqrt2\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid Latin hypercube can remain on one diagonal and leave a fixed-size uncovered region as its size grows.
assumptions_latex: The reference domain is \([0,1]^2\).
Latin-hypercube strata are the n equal intervals in each coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Latin-Hypercube Stratification Need Not Ensure Multivariate Filling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical axis-aligned discrepancy criterion for initial designs on a unit cube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset[0,1]^d\), its star discrepancy is \[D_n^*(X_n)=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^d}\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{x_i\in[0,u)\}-\prod_{j=1}^d u_j\right|,\] where \([0,u)=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j)\). A sequence \((X_n)\) is low-discrepancy in the asymptotic sense when \(D_n^*(X_n)\to0\), with any stronger claimed rate stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Star discrepancy measures the largest error between empirical and uniform mass over anchored axis-aligned boxes; low-discrepancy sequences make this error vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(X_n\subset[0,1]^d\).
The reference measure is uniform Lebesgue measure.
The anchored boxes are \([0,u)\).

notation.meaning: star discrepancy of the n-point design
axis-aligned box anchored at the origin

knowledge_statements.title: Star-Discrepancy Low-Discrepancy Designs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric maximin-style construction of a finite space-filling initial design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a compact metric space. Start with any \(x_1\in\mathcal X\), and for \(j=2,\ldots,n\) choose \[x_j\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{1\le i<j}d(x,x_i).\] If \(h(X_n)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\min_{x_i\in X_n}d(x,x_i)\) and \(h_n^*=\inf_{|Z|=n}h(Z)\), then \(h(X_n)\le2h_n^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially adding a farthest point produces an n-point design whose covering radius is at most twice optimal.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a nonempty compact metric space.
Each farthest-point maximizer is selected exactly.

notation.meaning: covering radius of the greedy design
smallest covering radius attainable by an n-point design

review_flags: Commonly called the farthest-first metric k-center two-approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Farthest-Point Covering Guarantee

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-free initial or augmented designs for surrogate training; the claimed predictive benefit is motivation rather than a guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model-free space-filling design of run size \(n\) is a set \(D=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subseteq[0,1]^m\) whose points are spread across the input domain without reference to a specified response model. Latin hypercube sampling targets uniform dispersion probabilistically, whereas maximin design seeks dispersion through relative distances. If an initial design \(D\) of size \(n\) is fixed, \(n'\) new locations may be selected so that the augmented design of size \(n+n'\) respects, or at least does not substantially violate, the chosen space-filling criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model-free space-filling design consists of n points spread across the unit m-dimensional hypercube without using a specified response model. Latin hypercube sampling targets uniform dispersion probabilistically, while maximin design uses relative distances. A fixed design of size n may be augmented with n-prime new points while seeking to preserve the selected space-filling criterion.
assumptions_latex: m,n\in\mathbb{N}
D\subseteq[0,1]^m
|D|=n
\text{the inputs are coded to }[0,1]^m\text{ unless otherwise stated}
n'\in\mathbb{N}_0\quad\text{when augmentation is considered}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ provides model-free geometric domain coverage, and an augmentation seeks }|D_{\mathrm{aug}}|=n+n'\text{ without substantially violating the chosen space-filling criterion}

children.title: Knowledge-Seeded Initialization Family
children.top_down_role: Initialization from historical observations, incumbent designs, or related optimization tasks.

children.title: Historical Prior Data
children.top_down_role: Initialization using observations collected before the current optimization campaign.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Same-task observations collected before the current optimization campaign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Historical prior data are records \(D_H=\{(x_i,y_i,z_i)\}_{i=1}^m\) collected before the current campaign, where \(z_i\) records context and measurement metadata needed to interpret the likelihood. They may be pooled as current-task observations only when their domain, response definition, measurement process, and relevant operating context are compatible; otherwise an explicit discrepancy model is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Historical prior data are pre-campaign same-task observations with metadata sufficient to assess compatibility with the current task.
assumptions_latex: Every reused record has a defined current-domain representation.
Available metadata suffice to specify or reject its current-task likelihood contribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_H\) is directly poolable only under current-task observational compatibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Historical Prior Data

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchangeable Pooling of Compatible Historical Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior equivalence of compatible historical and current observations under a common likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If historical data \(D_H\) and current data \(D_0\) are conditionally independent given \((f,\theta)\) and use the same specified observation model, then \[p(f,\theta\mid D_H,D_0)\propto p(f,\theta)p(D_H\mid f,\theta)p(D_0\mid f,\theta).\] The posterior is therefore invariant to labeling compatible records as historical or current; their effect depends on their inputs, responses, noise, and metadata rather than collection time alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible historical and current observations pool exchangeably under a common observation model and conditional independence.
assumptions_latex: \(D_H\perp D_0\mid(f,\theta)\).
Both datasets use the specified common likelihood.
The posterior is proper.
knowledge_statements.title: Exchangeable Pooling of Compatible Historical Data

children.title: Expert-Selected Designs
children.top_down_role: Initial designs supplied through domain expertise or operational judgment.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ex ante initialization using feasible locations supplied through domain or operational judgment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An expert-selected initial design is a finite feasible set \(X_0\subseteq\mathcal X\) chosen using expert information before observing the current-campaign responses generated at its points. Expert rankings, scores, exclusions, or mandatory points may determine \(X_0\). The optimizer evaluates its previously unevaluated members and conditions the initial surrogate on the resulting observations; later response-dependent proposals are not part of this initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Experts specify a feasible initial set before its current responses are observed, after which its evaluations initialize the surrogate.
assumptions_latex: \(X_0\subseteq\mathcal X\) is finite and feasible.
Selection does not use the current responses subsequently generated at \(X_0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Expert-Selected Initial Design

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Automatic Coverage from Expert-Only Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of a global-coverage guarantee for an arbitrary expert-selected set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X_0\subsetneq\mathcal X\) and no structural restriction forces an optimizer into \(X_0\), there exists an objective \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) whose unique minimizer lies in \(\mathcal X\setminus X_0\). Hence expert selection alone does not certify global coverage or optimality; such protection requires a separate coverage condition or later evaluations outside \(X_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary expert-only initial set need not contain or cover the global optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(X_0\) is a proper subset of \(\mathcal X\).
No objective-class assumption confines the optimizer to \(X_0\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Automatic Coverage from Expert-Only Initialization
Expert-Selected Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained initial-design selection from expert scores and geometric coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{z_1,ldots,z_M\}\subset\mathcal X\) be expert-proposed points with scores \(s:P\to\mathbb R\), and let \(n\leq M\). Choose the initial design by \[X_n\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{X\subseteq P,\,|X|=n}\left\{\alpha\sum_{x\in X}s(x)+(1-\alpha)\min_{x\ne x'\in X}\lVert x-x'\rVert\right\},\] where \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) is fixed in advance. Evaluate the objective at every point in \(X_n\), fit the initial surrogate to those observations, and return the resulting posterior state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select expert-proposed points by balancing expert scores against pairwise separation, evaluate them, and fit the initial surrogate.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d\) is finite with \(|P|=M\geq n\geq2\).
\(s(x)\) is finite for every \(x\in P\).
\(\alpha\in[0,1]\) is fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n\subseteq P\), \(|X_n|=n\), and \(X_n\) maximizes the stated score-coverage criterion.
review_flags: no supplied locator supports this particular score-separation formulation
formula is a precise candidate operationalization rather than a canonical algorithm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The score-separation optimization is a plausible operationalization but not a canonical expert-selected-design algorithm, and no source supports it. The candidate-set expression also contains the malformed text “z_1,ldots,z_M”.

children.title: Incumbent Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Initialization around an existing design, solution, or operating configuration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization that includes or concentrates new evaluations around a prior feasible design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a prior feasible design \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\in\mathcal X\), an incumbent warm start constructs \(X_0\) either to include \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) or to place a declared subset in \(B(x^{\mathrm{inc}},r)\cap\mathcal X\). A stored incumbent response may be reused only when observationally compatible; otherwise the location is reevaluated. Location reuse does not certify that the incumbent remains optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent warm start includes a previous feasible design or samples near it, reusing its old response only when compatible.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) is feasible for the current task.
The neighborhood and initial local allocation are chosen before observing their new responses.
knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Warm Start

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Only Warm Starts Lack Global Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global-search limitation of initialization confined to an incumbent neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X_0\subseteq B(x^{\mathrm{inc}},r)\cap\mathcal X\) and that neighborhood is a proper subset of \(\mathcal X\), then, absent an assumption locating every optimizer inside it, there exists an objective uniquely minimized outside the neighborhood. Consequently a local-only incumbent warm start supplies neither a global-coverage nor a global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling only near a prior incumbent cannot guarantee global coverage or continued optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(B(x^{\mathrm{inc}},r)\cap\mathcal X\subsetneq\mathcal X\).
No objective-class assumption confines the optimizer to that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Only Warm Starts Lack Global Coverage
Incumbent Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization around a previously best feasible point while retaining global coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a previous incumbent \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\in\mathcal X\), radius \(r>0\), initial budget \(n\), and local fraction \(\rho\in[0,1]\), let \(n_L=\lfloor\rho n\rfloor\). Construct \(X_L\subseteq\mathcal X\cap B(x^{\mathrm{inc}},r)\) with \(|X_L|=n_L\) and \(X_G\subseteq\mathcal X\) with \(|X_G|=n-n_L\), each by a specified space-filling rule, and remove duplicates. Evaluate unevaluated points in \(X_L\cup X_G\), include the incumbent observation when valid, fit the surrogate, and output its initial posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate part of the initial design near a valid previous incumbent and the remainder globally, then evaluate, deduplicate, and fit the surrogate.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\in\mathcal X\subsetb R^d\) is feasible for the current task.
The incumbent response is reused only when its observation semantics remain valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_0=X_L\cup X_G\) combines local incumbent-centered and global coverage points.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mixed local-global initialization formalizes incumbent warm starting while preserving coverage
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-global warm-start construction is plausible but source-dependent and not established as a canonical algorithm. The assumption contains the invalid command “\subsetb”.

children.title: Cross-Task Warm Starts
children.top_down_role: Initialization from related optimization tasks, environments, or historical campaigns.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Target initialization by conditioning a joint task model on related source-task observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let task \(0\) be the target and let \(D_s\) contain observations from task \(s\). Specify compatible input and response mappings and a proper joint surrogate for \((f_0,\ldots,f_S)\). Condition it on \(D_0,\ldots,D_S\), form the marginal target posterior \(p(f_0\mid D_0,\ldots,D_S)\), and initialize the target acquisition policy from that posterior. For a separable multitask Gaussian process, one admissible covariance is \[k((x,t),(x',s))=k_X(x,x')k_T(t,s),\] with positive-semidefinite kernels \(k_X\) and \(k_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map related tasks into a joint surrogate, condition on source and target observations, and initialize target acquisition from the target marginal posterior.
assumptions_latex: Task input and response mappings are specified.
The joint observation model and posterior are proper.
The modeled cross-task dependence is identifiable to the extent required for prediction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(f_0\mid D_0,\ldots,D_S)\) is the warm-start target posterior.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Surrogate Cross-Task Warm Start

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion determining whether Gaussian source observations affect target predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If target latent values \(f_0(X_*)\), target observations \(Y_0\), and source observations \(Y_S\) are jointly Gaussian, the source-dependent correction to the target posterior mean is \[\operatorname{Cov}(f_0(X_*),Y_S\mid Y_0)\operatorname{Var}(Y_S\mid Y_0)^{-1}\bigl(Y_S-\mathbb E[Y_S\mid Y_0]\bigr).\] Therefore conditional cross-covariance zero implies that source observations do not change the target posterior. In the separable model, \(k_T(0,s)=0\) for every source task is a sufficient no-transfer condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian source data influence the target posterior only through conditional cross-task covariance; zero task covariance gives no transfer.
assumptions_latex: The stated joint Gaussian conditional distribution exists.

children.title: Prior-Data Shift Risks
children.top_down_role: Cases where inherited evidence is incompatible with the current objective or domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ignored, decision-relevant mismatch between inherited records and the current optimization task.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let historical records follow \(P_H(dx,dy,dz)\) and current records follow \(P_0(dx,dy,dz)\). Prior-data shift is a consequential difference between these laws that is ignored when inherited data initialize the current surrogate. It includes domain or support shift in \(x\), response or concept shift in \(P(y\mid x,z)\), measurement or noise shift, and context-mixture shift. A change only in \(P(x,z)\) need not be harmful when the conditional observation law is correctly modeled on the required support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prior-data shift is an ignored, decision-relevant mismatch in historical and current input, response, context, or measurement laws.
assumptions_latex: Historical and current record semantics permit comparison.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Persistent Bias from Unmodeled Response Shift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-transfer boundary when growing historical data identify the wrong response surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose historical responses satisfy \(Y_H=f_0(X)+b(X)+\varepsilon_H\), whereas current responses satisfy \(Y_0=f_0(X)+\varepsilon_0\), with \(b\not\equiv0\). If an estimator trained on increasing historical data consistently estimates the historical conditional mean while the fitted model incorrectly imposes \(b\equiv0\), then its historical-data limit is \(f_0+b\), not \(f_0\). More shifted historical data therefore need not remove current-task bias; compatible current data or an identifiable discrepancy model is required to distinguish \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing shifted historical data can reinforce, rather than remove, bias toward the historical response surface.
assumptions_latex: Historical sampling identifies \(f_0+b\) on a decision-relevant region.

Prior-Data Shift Risks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative transfer when historical and current observation laws differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose historical responses satisfy \(y=f_H(x)+\varepsilon\), whereas the current task satisfies \(y=f_0(x)+\varepsilon\). If a noiseless surrogate pools both tasks as though \(f_H=f_0\), then incompatible historical duplicates can force erroneous interpolation. Concretely, at some \(x_0\), let historical data contain \((x_0,0)\) while \(f_0(x_0)=1\). Any interpolating pooled predictor constrained to the historical value has \(\widehat f(x_0)=0\), hence absolute target error \(|\widehat f(x_0)-f_0(x_0)|=1\), even with zero historical observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pooling shifted historical data as current-task data can force an interpolating surrogate to be confidently wrong, producing negative transfer even without observation noise.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate treats historical and current responses as observations of one noiseless function.
There exists \(x_0\) with \(f_H(x_0)\neq f_0(x_0)\).
The pooled surrogate interpolates the historical response at \(x_0\).

children.title: Replication Allocation
children.top_down_role: Budgeting repeated evaluations at previously observed locations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Replication Precision and Diminishing Variance Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent repeated observations at one fixed location with finite noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y_{ij}=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_{ij}\), where conditional on \(f(x_i)\) the errors are independent, have mean zero, and have variance \(\sigma_i^2<\infty\). For \(r\ge1\), the replicate mean \(\bar Y_{i,r}=r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^rY_{ij}\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[\bar Y_{i,r}\mid f(x_i)]=f(x_i),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{i,r}\mid f(x_i))=\frac{\sigma_i^2}{r}.\] Adding replicate \(r+1\) reduces this conditional variance by \(\sigma_i^2/[r(r+1)]\), a strictly decreasing marginal reduction when \(\sigma_i^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent replication leaves the site mean unbiased, reduces its noise variance as one over the replicate count, and has diminishing marginal variance benefit.
assumptions_latex: The replicate errors at \(x_i\) are conditionally independent.
\(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{ij}\mid f(x_i)]=0\).
\(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij}\mid f(x_i))=\sigma_i^2<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Replication Precision and Diminishing Variance Reduction
Replication Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential allocation of repeated noisy measurements by value per unit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At history \(D\), let \(r_i\geq1\) observations already exist at sampled location \(x_i\), and let a further replicate cost \(c_i>0\). For terminal loss \(L(D)\), define the one-step replication value \[V_i(D)=L(D)-\mathbb E\!\left[L\!\left(D\cup\{(x_i,Y_i^{\mathrm{new}})\}\right)\mid D\right].\] Choose \(i^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i V_i(D)/c_i\) when the maximum is positive and affordable; observe the new response, update the surrogate noise and latent-function posterior, and repeat until no positive affordable value remains or the replication budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate the sampled location with greatest positive expected loss reduction per unit cost, updating the surrogate after each observation.
assumptions_latex: Conditional predictive laws for new replicates are defined at every sampled location.
\(c_i>0\), and the remaining budget is known.

knowledge_statements.title: New-Location Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential selection of an unevaluated location by acquisition value per cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_D\subsetb R^d\) be the locations already observed, let \(a_D(x)\geq0\) be the posterior value of sampling \(x\), and let \(c(x)>0\) be its evaluation cost. Select \[x^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in\mathcal X\setminus X_D}\frac{a_D(x)}{c(x)}.\] If the maximum is positive and affordable, evaluate at \(x^\star\), augment \(D\), refit or update the surrogate, and repeat. Stop when the budget is exhausted, the feasible unevaluated set is empty, or no candidate has positive value; output the final recommended design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the affordable unevaluated location with greatest acquisition value per cost, update the surrogate, and stop when budget or positive value is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^d\), and the displayed argmax is attained.
\(a_D(x)\geq0\) and \(c(x)>0\) on unevaluated candidates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior Variance at a New Noiseless Gaussian-Process Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rejected from this allocation leaf because it is a general Gaussian-process posterior-uncertainty property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), let \(X_n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be distinct noiselessly observed locations, and let \(K_n=[k(x_i,x_j)]\) be nonsingular. For a candidate \(x\), \[s_n^2(x)=k(x,x)-k(x,X_n)K_n^{-1}k(X_n,x).\] Then \(s_n^2(x_i)=0\) for every observed location. If the augmented Gram matrix on \(X_n\cup\{x\}\) is positive definite, then \(s_n^2(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With noiseless GP observations, variance is zero at existing sites and positive at a new site when the augmented kernel matrix is positive definite.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has Gaussian-process covariance \(k\).
Observations at \(X_n\) are noiseless.

children.title: Derivative-Channel Allocation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step allocation over function and derivative measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A(D)\) contain affordable, model-valid actions \((x,j)\), where \(j=0\) denotes a function observation and \(j\ge1\) a derivative observation. Define \[\Delta_{x,j}(D)=\mathbb E[V(D\oplus((x,j),Y_j(x)))\mid D]-V(D).\] Select a maximizer of \(\Delta_{x,j}(D)-\lambda q_{x,j}\), or of \(\Delta_{x,j}(D)/q_{x,j}\) under an explicitly fractional one-step convention, obtain the measurement, and update the joint function-derivative posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare affordable function and derivative measurements by expected terminal-value gain and cost, then update their joint posterior.
assumptions_latex: Each action in \(\mathcal A(D)\) has positive cost and a defined observation law.
The expected gains are finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Aware Derivative-Channel Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a claimed derivative measurement is not a valid observation channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative action is inadmissible when the physical interface does not supply the claimed derivative, the latent process lacks the corresponding mean-square derivative, or the differentiated kernel and noise blocks do not define a valid joint covariance. Such an action must be excluded from \(\mathcal A(D)\). A finite difference is instead a linear combination of function observations and is not an exact derivative observation without an explicit approximation-error model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivative allocation requires an available derivative and a valid differentiable covariance model; finite differences are not exact derivative channels by default.
assumptions_latex: The proposed channel is interpreted as a derivative of the modeled latent objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Invalid or unavailable derivative actions must be excluded from \(\mathcal A(D)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative Observations as Gaussian Linear Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint Gaussian-process representation needed to value derivative measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) possess the required mean-square derivatives, and let \(Y_j(x)=\partial_j f(x)+\varepsilon_j\). Function and derivative observations are jointly Gaussian with \[\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),\partial_{j'}f(x'))=\partial_{x'_{j'}}k(x,x'),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_jf(x),\partial_{j'}f(x'))=\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x'_{j'}}k(x,x').\] Adding the specified channel-noise covariance yields the observation covariance used for conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivative measurements are linear Gaussian-process observations whose covariance blocks are obtained by differentiating the kernel.
assumptions_latex: The mean and kernel possess the derivatives required by the selected channels.
The resulting mean-square derivatives exist.
Derivative-channel noise has a specified positive-semidefinite covariance.

Given history \(D\), channel cost \(c_j(x)>0\), and terminal loss \(L\), define \[V_j(x;D)=L(D)-\mathbb E[L(D\cup\{(x,j,Y_{x,j})\})\mid D].\] Select an affordable \((x^star,j^\star)\) maximizing \(V_j(x;D)/c_j(x)\), observe that channel, condition jointly using the function-derivative covariance, and stop when no positive affordable value remains or the budget is exhausted.

children.title: Fidelity-Channel Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocating evaluations across accuracy, resolution, or simulation-fidelity levels.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Target Value from a Conditionally Uninformative Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient boundary under which a fidelity observation cannot improve a target-fidelity Bayesian decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta_H\) denote the target-fidelity quantity governing terminal loss, let \(D\) be the current data, and let \(Y_{x,s}\) be a prospective observation. If \(Y_{x,s}\perp\!\!\!\perp\Theta_H\mid D\), then the posterior law of \(\Theta_H\) is unchanged almost surely after observing \(Y_{x,s}\). Consequently, for any finite Bayes terminal loss depending on the data only through that posterior, the one-step value \(V_s(x;D)\) equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fidelity observation conditionally independent of the target quantity cannot change its posterior and has zero one-step target decision value.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_{x,s}\perp\!\!\!\perp\Theta_H\mid D\).
Terminal Bayes loss is finite and depends on observations through the posterior law of \(\Theta_H\).

notation.meaning: target-fidelity latent quantity relevant to the terminal decision
