children.title: Channel-Value Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparative value of replication, new locations, derivatives, fidelities, or auxiliary sources.

knowledge_statements.title: Channel-Value Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step allocation among heterogeneous observation channels under a resource price.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a finite set of feasible observation channels. For posterior information state \(D\), channel \(c\in\mathcal C\) has cost \(q_c>0\), random outcome \(Y_c\), updated state \(D\oplus(c,Y_c)\), and terminal decision value \(V(D)\). Define \(\Delta_c(D)=\mathbb E[V(D\oplus(c,Y_c))\mid D]-V(D)\). Given resource price \(\lambda\ge 0\), a myopic value-cost allocation selects any \[c^\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\mathcal C}\{\Delta_c(D)-\lambda q_c\}.\] Under a fractional budget convention, it instead maximizes \(\Delta_c(D)/q_c\). Thus replication, new-location, derivative, and fidelity observations are comparable only through their posterior expected decision value and commensurate costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate the next observation channel by comparing its expected improvement in terminal decision value with its cost, using net value or value per unit cost.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is finite and each \(q_c>0\).
The conditional expectations defining \(\Delta_c(D)\) are finite.

notation.meaning: expected incremental terminal value of channel c

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Value per Cost Need Not Be Budget-Optimal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of repeated myopic ratio selection with indivisible actions and a finite budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the budget be \(B=3\), and let two once-available actions have \((q_a,\Delta_a)=(2,3)\) and \((q_b,\Delta_b)=(3,4)\). Since \(3/2>4/3\), the ratio rule selects \(a\), obtains value \(3\), and leaves insufficient budget for \(b\). Selecting \(b\) obtains value \(4\). Therefore the one-step value-per-cost rule does not generally solve the finite-budget nonmyopic allocation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The highest-ratio indivisible action can consume budget that would have supported a larger total-value action.
assumptions_latex: Actions are indivisible and each is available at most once.
The displayed gains are deterministic and additive.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Value per Cost Need Not Be Budget-Optimal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of a channel that is no more valuable and no cheaper than another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At information state \(D\), suppose \(\Delta_1(D)\ge\Delta_2(D)\) and \(q_1\le q_2\), with at least one strict inequality. Then channel \(2\) cannot strictly maximize \(\Delta_c(D)-\lambda q_c\) for any \(\lambda\ge0\). If additionally \(\Delta_2(D)\ge0\), it also cannot strictly maximize \(\Delta_c(D)/q_c\). Thus a value-cost dominated channel may be removed from a one-step choice set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A channel providing no more expected value at no lower cost is never the unique best one-step net-value or nonnegative value-per-cost choice.

children.title: Prior Mean Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Prior Mean Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic mean component of a real-valued Gaussian-process surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input set and let \(f\) be a real-valued Gaussian process. Its prior mean function is the deterministic map \(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) defined by \[m(x)=\mathbb E[f(x)],\qquad x\in\mathcal X.\] A parametric mean structure has the form \(m_\beta(x)=h(x)^\top\beta\), where \(h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p\) is fixed and \(\beta\in\mathbb R^p\); the constant-mean and zero-mean specifications correspond respectively to \(h(x)=1\) and \(m(x)=0\). The centered latent field \(f-m\) has zero prior mean and carries the covariance structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The GP prior mean is a deterministic trend, often zero, constant, or linear in prescribed basis functions; covariance models the centered residual field.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)\) is integrable for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).

notation.meaning: fixed vector of trend basis functions

This choice encodes the assumption that the objective's expected behavior is an affine function of its input features.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Role of the Gaussian-process prior mean
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the GP prior mean, its translation effect on sample paths, and its role in posterior prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(\mu,K)\), \(\mu(x)=\mathbb E[f(x)]\). The process \(f\) has the same sample-path distribution as the centered process \(f-\mu\) shifted pointwise by \(\mu\). Consequently, Gaussian processes with the same covariance function differ in their sample paths only by their deterministic mean functions. If \(\mathbf y\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf m,\mathbf C)\), \(\kappa(x)=\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf y,f(x))\), and \(\mathbf C\) is invertible, then \(\mu_{\mathcal D}(x)=\mu(x)+\kappa(x)^\top\mathbf C^{-1}(\mathbf y-\mathbf m)\). Thus, when \(\kappa(x)\approx\mathbf0\), \(\mu_{\mathcal D}(x)\approx\mu(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The GP mean is the expected function value. With covariance fixed, changing the deterministic mean translates sample paths pointwise. After conditioning, the prior mean enters the posterior-mean formula, and it dominates where the prediction is nearly uncorrelated with the observations.

\mathbf y\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf m,\mathbf C)

knowledge_statements.title: Prior Latent-Field Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of a latent Gaussian-process prior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input set, \(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be symmetric and positive semidefinite. The notation \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\) means that for every \(n\ge1\) and \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal X\), \[(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))^\top\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K_{XX}),\] where \((m_X)_i=m(x_i)\) and \((K_{XX})_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\). Equivalently, \(f(x)=m(x)+z(x)\) with \(z\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,k)\). This latent field is distinct from observation noise added by the data model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A latent GP is completely specified by a mean and positive-semidefinite covariance kernel through all of its finite-dimensional Gaussian distributions.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Predictive Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional mean of a GP latent value under Gaussian observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), and observe \(y=f_X+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\) independent of \(f\). If \(K_{XX}+\Sigma\) is invertible, then the conditional location of the latent value at \(x\in\mathcal X\) is \[\mu_D(x)=\mathbb E[f(x)\mid y]=m(x)+k_{xX}(K_{XX}+\Sigma)^{-1}(y-m_X).\] For prediction of a future zero-mean noisy response, the conditional location is also \(\mu_D(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The posterior predictive mean equals the prior mean plus a covariance-weighted correction formed from observed residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\).
Observation noise is independent Gaussian with covariance \(\Sigma\).
\(K_{XX}+\Sigma\) is invertible.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interpolation by the GP posterior location and its observation-noise boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Predictive Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional covariance of latent GP values under Gaussian observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the Gaussian-process observation model \(y=f_X+\varepsilon\), with \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), independent \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\), and invertible \(K_{XX}+\Sigma\), the posterior latent covariance is \[k_D(x,x')=k(x,x')-k_{xX}(K_{XX}+\Sigma)^{-1}k_{Xx'}.\] Hence \(\operatorname{Var}(f(x)\mid y)=k_D(x,x)\). If a future response is \(Y(x)=f(x)+\varepsilon_x\), where \(\varepsilon_x\) is independent with variance \(\tau^2(x)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y(x)\mid y)=k_D(x,x)+\tau^2(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior latent uncertainty is prior covariance minus the covariance explained by data; future observation variance additionally includes new measurement noise.
assumptions_latex: The latent process and observation noise are jointly Gaussian and independent.
\(K_{XX}+\Sigma\) is invertible.
Future noise is conditionally independent of existing data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero uncertainty after exact observations versus residual uncertainty after noisy observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Sigma=0\), training sites are distinct, and \(K_{XX}\) is invertible, then \(k_D(x_i,x_i)=0\) at every observed site. With observation noise, latent uncertainty generally remains positive. For a single site with prior variance \(v>0\) and one independent observation with variance \(\tau^2>0\), \[\operatorname{Var}(f(x)\mid Y(x))=v-\frac{v^2}{v+\tau^2}=\frac{v\tau^2}{v+\tau^2}>0.\] Future observation variance additionally includes fresh noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact observations eliminate latent variance at their sites, while noisy observations generally leave positive latent uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: Covariance matrices are nonsingular where inverses are used.
The noisy single-site example has \(v>0\) and \(\tau^2>0\).

notation.meaning: Prior latent variance at the observed site.

knowledge_statements.title: Observed-Site Latent Variance Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one covariance update and monotonicity after one additional noisy observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given current posterior covariance \(k_D\), suppose one additionally observes \(Y(z)=f(z)+\epsilon_z\) with independent variance \(\tau^2(z)\). If \(k_D(z,z)+\tau^2(z)>0\), then \[k_{D\cup z}(x,x')=k_D(x,x')-\frac{k_D(x,z)k_D(z,x')}{k_D(z,z)+\tau^2(z)}.\] Consequently, \[0\le k_{D\cup z}(x,x)=k_D(x,x)-\frac{k_D(x,z)^2}{k_D(z,z)+\tau^2(z)}\le k_D(x,x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One more Gaussian observation subtracts a rank-one positive-semidefinite term and cannot increase latent pointwise posterior variance.
assumptions_latex: Current and prospective latent values are jointly Gaussian conditional on existing data.
Prospective noise is independent with known nonnegative variance.

notation.meaning: Posterior latent covariance after observing at z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchical Gaussian-process regression and the nugget contribution distinguishing latent-function uncertainty from noisy-response predictive uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\mid X_n\sim\mathcal N_n(0,\tau^2C_n)\) and \(Y_n\mid F,X_n\sim\mathcal N_n(F,g\tau^2I_n)\), with training correlation matrix \(K_n=C_n+gI_n\). Conditional on \(F\), the observations are independent. The posterior predictions of \(f(x)\) and the noisy response \(Y(x)\) have the same mean, while their fitted variances satisfy \[\breve\sigma^2(x)=\widehat\tau^2\left(1-k_n(x)^\top K_n^{-1}k_n(x)\right),\qquad \sigma_Y^2(x)=\breve\sigma^2(x)+\widehat\tau^2\widehat g.\] The nugget is omitted only from the predicted latent-response variance contribution; it remains in \(K_n\) used for conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A GP prior is placed on an unobserved latent function, and observations are conditionally independent noisy measurements of it. Latent-function and noisy-response predictions have the same posterior mean, but response prediction additionally includes the nugget variance. The nugget remains in the training covariance inversion when latent uncertainty is calculated.

knowledge_statements.title: Prior-to-Posterior Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sensitivity of GP prediction to prior mean and observed responses with fixed covariance parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(k\), \(X\), and \(\Sigma\), and write \(A=(K_{XX}+\Sigma)^{-1}\). If the response vector changes by \(\delta y\) while the prior mean is fixed, then \[\delta\mu_D(x)=k_{xX}A\,\delta y.\] If the prior mean changes from \(m\) to \(m+\delta m\) while observations remain fixed, then \[\delta\mu_D(x)=\delta m(x)-k_{xX}A\,\delta m_X.\] The posterior covariance \(k_D\) is unchanged by either perturbation. Consequently, response and mean sensitivity are linear for fixed kernel and noise parameters, whereas refitting those parameters introduces additional nonlinear sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With covariance parameters fixed, posterior means respond linearly to data and prior-mean perturbations, while posterior covariance does not depend on observed values or the mean.
assumptions_latex: \(K_{XX}+\Sigma\) is invertible.
Kernel, inputs, and noise covariance remain fixed during perturbation.

notation.meaning: prior-mean perturbation evaluated at training inputs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary radial family interpolating between exponential and squared-exponential covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha\le2\), \(\ell>0\), and \(\sigma^2>0\), \[k_\alpha(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\|x-x'\|}{\ell}\right)^\alpha\right].\] It is stationary and isotropic. The cases \(\alpha=1\) and \(\alpha=2\) are respectively exponential and, up to length-scale convention, squared-exponential covariance. For \(0<\alpha<2\), the associated field lacks a first mean-square derivative; \(\alpha=2\) yields mean-square derivatives of every order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinitely smooth stationary family obtained by mixing squared-exponential length scales.

It is mean-square differentiable to every order, decays polynomially in distance, and converges pointwise to the squared-exponential kernel as \(a\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rational-quadratic kernel mixes squared-exponential scales, remains infinitely smooth, and has heavier correlation tails.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matérn smoothness parameter and sample-path regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity interpretation of the Matérn covariance family and its squared-exponential limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v>0\), the unit-length-scale, unit-output-scale Matérn covariance is \(K_{\mathrm M}(d;v)=\frac{2^{1-v}}{\Gamma(v)}(\sqrt{2v}d)^vK_v(\sqrt{2v}d)\), where \(d=|x-x'|\) and \(K_v\) is the modified Bessel function of the second kind. A centered Gaussian process with this covariance has sample paths that are \(\lceil v\rceil-1\) times continuously differentiable. For noninteger \(v\), the covariance belongs to \(\mathcal C^{\alpha,\beta}\), where \(\alpha=\lfloor2v\rfloor\) and \(\beta=2v-\lfloor2v\rfloor\), and the final sample-path derivative is expected to be \((v-\lfloor v\rfloor)\)-Hölder continuous. As \(v\to\infty\), the covariance converges to the squared-exponential covariance, representing the infinitely differentiable limiting regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Matérn parameter v continuously controls Gaussian-process sample-path smoothness. Paths have ceil(v)−1 continuous derivatives, with fractional Hölder regularity refining this count for noninteger v; the squared-exponential covariance is the infinitely smooth limit.
assumptions_latex: f\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,K_{\mathrm M})
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ has }\lceil v\rceil-1\text{ continuously differentiable sample paths, and }K_{\mathrm M}(\cdot;v)\to K_{\mathrm{SE}}\text{ as }v\to\infty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity and isotropy of covariance functions on Euclidean input spaces, with the corresponding process-stationarity distinctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A covariance function is stationary if \(k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\kappa(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')\), and isotropic if \(k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\varphi(\!\left\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\right\|\!)\). Stationarity implies invariance under simultaneous translations, while isotropy implies invariance under simultaneous rigid motions. A process with constant mean and translation-invariant covariance is weakly stationary; it is strictly stationary if all finite-dimensional distributions are translation invariant. A valid covariance function must be positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary covariance function depends only on the difference between its inputs, whereas an isotropic covariance function depends only on their distance. These properties give translation invariance and rigid-motion invariance, respectively. Constant mean with stationary covariance defines weak stationarity; strict stationarity requires translation invariance of all finite-dimensional distributions. Covariance functions must also be positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'\in\mathbb{R}^D
k:\mathbb{R}^D\times\mathbb{R}^D\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is a valid covariance function}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square continuity of a second-order random field under the centered or constant-mean convention, including the stationary reduction and the sample-path failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a second-order random field on \(\mathbb{R}^D\) with constant mean and covariance function \(k\). The field is mean-square continuous at \(\mathbf{x}_*\) if, for every sequence \(\mathbf{x}_j\to\mathbf{x}_*\), \(\mathbb{E}|f(\mathbf{x}_j)-f(\mathbf{x}_*)|^2\to0\). This holds if and only if \(k\) is continuous at \((\mathbf{x}_*,\mathbf{x}_*)\). If \(k\) is stationary, the condition reduces to continuity of the lag covariance at \(\mathbf{0}\). Mean-square continuity does not in general imply sample-path continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a second-order random field with constant mean, mean-square continuity at a point means that the expected squared increment tends to zero along every sequence approaching that point. It is equivalent to covariance continuity at the corresponding diagonal point. For a stationary covariance function, it is enough to check continuity at zero lag. Mean-square continuity does not guarantee continuous sample paths.

\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{x})]\text{ is constant}
k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\operatorname{Cov}(f(\mathbf{x}),f(\mathbf{x}'))
\mathbf{x}_j\to\mathbf{x}_*

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, spectrum, mean-square smoothness, infinite divisibility, and Gaussian-feature representation of the squared-exponential family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\ell>0\), the squared-exponential covariance function is \[k_{\mathrm{SE}}(r)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^2}{2\ell^2}\right).\] In \(D\) dimensions its spectral density is \[S(\mathbf s)=(2\pi\ell^2)^{D/2}\exp\!\left(-2\pi^2\ell^2\|\mathbf s\|^2\right).\] The kernel is infinitely differentiable, and the associated Gaussian process has mean-square derivatives of every order. Moreover, \(k_{\mathrm{SE}}(r)^t\) is a valid kernel for every \(t>0\), equal to an SE kernel with length scale \(\ell/\sqrt t\). For \(\phi_c(x)=\exp(-(x-c)^2/(2\ell^2))\), \[\sigma_p^2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi_c(x_p)\phi_c(x_q)\,dc=\sqrt\pi\ell\sigma_p^2\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_p-x_q)^2}{2(\sqrt2\ell)^2}\right),\] which is an SE covariance with length scale \(\sqrt2\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared-exponential kernel has a characteristic length scale, a Gaussian spectrum, and infinite differentiability, so its Gaussian process is mean-square differentiable to every order. Every positive power remains an SE kernel, and a continuum of Gaussian basis functions yields another SE covariance with a rescaled length scale.

D\in\mathbb N

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An anisotropic squared-exponential kernel with coordinate-specific length scales and an overall variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $r=x-x'\in\mathbb R^D$, $\sigma^2>0$, and $\Sigma\succ0$. The ARD kernel is $\mathcal K(r;\Sigma,\sigma^2)=\sigma^2\exp(-\tfrac12r^\top\Sigma^{-1}r)$. If $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\ell_1^2,\ldots,\ell_D^2)$ with $\ell_d>0$, then $\mathcal K(r;\ell,\sigma^2)=\sigma^2\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_{d=1}^D r_d^2/\ell_d^2)$. In the limiting case $\ell_d\to\infty$, dependence on coordinate $d$ vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ARD kernel generalizes the RBF kernel using a Mahalanobis distance or a separate length scale for each coordinate. Taking one length scale to infinity makes the kernel ignore that coordinate.

knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Length Scales
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned anisotropic deformation of a stationary radial kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inputs \(x,x'\in\mathbb R^d\), positive coordinate length scales \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d\) define the anisotropic squared distance \[r_\ell^2(x,x')=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{(x_j-x'_j)^2}{\ell_j^2}.\] If \(\kappa:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) generates a valid isotropic stationary kernel, then \(k_\ell(x,x')=\kappa(r_\ell(x,x'))\) is its axis-aligned anisotropic form. A smaller \(\ell_j\) produces faster prior correlation decay under changes in coordinate \(j\), while a larger \(\ell_j\) produces slower decay, conditional on the input scaling and the remaining kernel parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anisotropic kernels rescale each coordinate separately; short length scales encode rapid variation and long length scales encode slow variation.
assumptions_latex: \(x,x'\in\mathbb R^d\) and every \(\ell_j>0\).
\(\kappa(\lVert x-x'\rVert)\) is a positive-semidefinite kernel.

children.title: Automatic Relevance Weighting
children.top_down_role: Dimension-specific weighting used to represent differing input influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Automatic Relevance Weighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate relevance represented by learned inverse squared length scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an axis-aligned stationary kernel, let finite positive length scales \(\ell_j>0\) define relevance weights \(w_j=\ell_j^{-2}>0\) and \[r_w^2(x,x')=\sum_{j=1}^d w_j(x_j-x'_j)^2.\] Automatic relevance determination estimates \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_d)\), equivalently the finite length scales \(\ell\), from data by a specified procedure such as marginal-likelihood maximization or posterior inference. Extending the parameter space by continuity permits \(w_j=0\), corresponding to the limiting convention \(\ell_j=\infty\). Conditional on documented input scaling and a fixed kernel form, large \(w_j\) permits rapid covariance change along coordinate \(j\), while \(w_j=0\) removes that coordinate from the kernel distance. These weights express model-dependent prior-predictive relevance and do not by themselves establish causal or global functional importance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automatic relevance determination learns coordinatewise inverse squared length scales; under the extended boundary convention, a zero weight corresponds to infinite length scale and suppresses that coordinate, but the resulting relevance is model-dependent rather than causal.
assumptions_latex: Inputs have fixed, documented scaling.
The stationary kernel depends on inputs through \(r_w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_j=\ell_j^{-2}\) for finite \(\ell_j>0\), with the continuous extension \(w_j=0\) making the kernel invariant to coordinate \(j\)

notation.meaning: kernel relevance weight for coordinate j
coordinatewise length scale, with infinity allowed only as a limiting convention

knowledge_statements.title: Grouped Relevance Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared kernel relevance parameters for a prescribed partition of input coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{G_1,\ldots,G_M\}\) be a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A grouped relevance metric assigns one weight \(w_g\ge0\) to every group and defines \[r_G^2(x,x')=\sum_{g=1}^M w_g\sum_{j\in G_g}(x_j-x'_j)^2.\] A stationary radial profile \(\kappa\) then gives \(k_G(x,x')=\kappa(r_G(x,x'))\). Coordinates in the same group share a relevance weight, reducing the number of metric parameters from \(d\) to \(M\). If \(w_g=0\), the covariance is invariant to simultaneous or separate changes in coordinates belonging to \(G_g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grouped relevance ties the length-scale or relevance parameter across predefined coordinate groups, reducing dimension and suppressing an entire group when its weight is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(G_1,\ldots,G_M\) form a disjoint partition of the input coordinates.
Each group weight satisfies \(w_g\ge0\).

notation.meaning: shared relevance weight for group g

knowledge_statements.title: Relevance Identifiability Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact non-identifiability caused by absent coordinate variation in the design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider observations at \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) under an anisotropic kernel \(k_w(x,x')=\kappa(\sum_{j=1}^d w_j(x_j-x'_j)^2)\). If some coordinate \(j\) is constant on the design, so that \(x_{ij}=a\) for every \(i\), then every entry of \(K_{XX}(w)\) is independent of \(w_j\). Consequently, with all other model quantities fixed, the Gaussian marginal likelihood and posterior for training-point latent values contain no information distinguishing values of \(w_j\). More generally, collinear or weakly varying coordinates can yield confounded or weakly identified relevance weights; estimated length scales therefore need not uniquely represent variable importance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate that never varies in the design has an unidentifiable relevance weight; collinearity and limited variation similarly weaken relevance interpretation.
assumptions_latex: The likelihood depends on \(w_j\) only through the training covariance matrix.
Coordinate \(j\) is constant across all training inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{XX}(w)\) and the marginal likelihood are invariant under changes of \(w_j\)

constant observed value of coordinate j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-design certificate for nonidentifiability of anisotropic relevance weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For training inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), form the pairwise squared-difference matrix \(D\) whose row indexed by \((i,j)\) has entries \(D_{(i,j),r}=(x_{ir}-x_{jr})^2\). Under \(k_w(x,x')=\kappa(\sum_{r=1}^d w_r(x_r-x'_r)^2)\), if \(z\ne0\) satisfies \(Dz=0\), then every feasible pair \(w,w+tz\in\mathbb R_+^d\) produces the same weighted distances and hence the same training Gram matrix. With all other model quantities fixed, the Gaussian marginal likelihood cannot distinguish those weight vectors. A constant coordinate gives a zero column of \(D\); two coordinates differing by a constant give identical columns and identify only the sum of their weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero null vector of the design's pairwise squared-difference matrix certifies that distinct relevance weights produce the same training covariance.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite kernels formed by summing component kernels on selected coordinate subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input set and let \(k_r:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), for \(r=1,\ldots,R\), be positive-semidefinite kernels. For coefficients \(a_r\ge0\), their additive composition is \[k(x,x')=\sum_{r=1}^R a_r k_r(x,x').\] This \(k\) is positive semidefinite and therefore a valid covariance kernel. If each component depends only on a coordinate subset \(G_r\), the corresponding latent representation may be written \(f(x)=m(x)+\sum_{r=1}^R f_r(x_{G_r})\), where independent \(f_r\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,a_rk_r)\). Its covariance is exactly the displayed additive kernel; interaction effects absent from all components are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative sum of valid kernels is valid and represents a sum of independent latent components, possibly attached to different coordinate subsets.
assumptions_latex: Each \(k_r\) is positive semidefinite.
Each coefficient \(a_r\ge0\).
Latent components are independent for the stated process representation.

notation.meaning: coordinate subset used by component r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-space characterization of a finite positive weighted sum kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k=\sum_{r=1}^R a_rk_r\) with \(a_r>0\), and let \(\mathcal H_r\) be the RKHS of \(k_r\). The RKHS of \(k\) consists of functions admitting a decomposition \(f=\sum_{r=1}^R f_r\) with \(f_r\in\mathcal H_r\), and its squared norm is \[\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}^2=\inf_{f=\sum_r f_r}\sum_{r=1}^R\frac{\|f_r\|_{\mathcal H_r}^2}{a_r}.\] The decomposition need not be unique when component spaces overlap; the infimum gives the minimum weighted norm among valid decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The RKHS of a positive weighted sum kernel is the sum of the component RKHSs, with norm given by the least-cost weighted component decomposition.
assumptions_latex: Each \(k_r\) is positive semidefinite with RKHS \(\mathcal H_r\).
Each \(a_r>0\).
\(R<\infty\).

children.title: Interaction Kernels

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tensor-product interaction centered against reference measures so lower-order marginal effects vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\mathcal X_j,\mu_j)\), \(j\in S\), be probability spaces and let \(k_j\) be positive-semidefinite kernels for which the displayed integrals exist. Define
\[
\widetilde k_j(s,t)=k_j(s,t)-\int k_j(s,u)\,d\mu_j(u)-\int k_j(v,t)\,d\mu_j(v)+\iint k_j(v,u)\,d\mu_j(v)d\mu_j(u).
\]
Then
\[
k_S(x,x')=\prod_{j\in S}\widetilde k_j(x_j,x'_j)
\]
is positive semidefinite and satisfies \(\int k_S(x,x')\,d\mu_j(x_j)=0=\int k_S(x,x')\,d\mu_j(x'_j)\) for every \(j\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centering every factor before multiplication produces a valid interaction kernel whose marginal average vanishes in each participating coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\mu_j\) is a probability measure.
Each \(k_j\) is positive semidefinite and the displayed integrals are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_S\) is positive semidefinite and centered in every coordinate in \(S\).

notation.meaning: Pure interaction kernel over coordinate set S.

knowledge_statements.title: Centered Pure-Interaction Kernel
Interaction Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product construction for joint effects across coordinate groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathcal X_j\), let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) satisfy \(|S|\ge 2\), and let each \(k_j:\mathcal X_j^2\to\mathbb R\) be positive semidefinite. The interaction component indexed by \(S\) is
\[
k_S(x,x')=\prod_{j\in S}k_j(x_j,x'_j).
\]
The Schur product theorem implies that \(k_S\) is positive semidefinite. A compositional covariance may therefore include \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}\tau_S^2k_S\) with \(\tau_S^2\ge0\); terms with \(|S|\ge2\) encode covariance that depends jointly on multiple coordinate groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying positive-semidefinite kernels on distinct coordinate groups yields a valid kernel representing their joint interaction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathcal X_j\).
\(k_j\) is positive semidefinite for every \(j\in S\).
\(\tau_S^2\ge0\) for every included interaction.

notation.meaning: Product interaction kernel indexed by S.

children.title: Periodic Kernel Components
children.top_down_role: Components representing recurring variation over relevant coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fourier Characterization of Stationary Periodic Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral representation of continuous real stationary covariance kernels on a one-dimensional periodic domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p>0\) and let \(\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and \(p\)-periodic. The kernel \(k(x,x')=\psi(x-x')\) is positive semidefinite if and only if
\[
\psi(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n e^{2\pi i nt/p},\qquad c_n\ge0,\quad c_{-n}=c_n,\quad \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n<\infty.
\]
Equivalently, \(\psi(t)=c_0+2\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\cos(2\pi nt/p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous stationary periodic kernel is exactly a nonnegative summable mixture of integer Fourier harmonics.
assumptions_latex: \(\psi\) is real-valued, continuous, and \(p\)-periodic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k(x,x')=\psi(x-x')\) is positive semidefinite exactly when its Fourier coefficients are nonnegative and summable.
knowledge_statements.title: Fourier Characterization of Stationary Periodic Kernels
Periodic Kernel Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard one-dimensional periodic component induced by a circular embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For period \(p>0\), length scale \(\ell>0\), and variance \(\sigma^2\ge0\), embed \(x\in\mathbb R\) as \(u_p(x)=(\cos(2\pi x/p),\sin(2\pi x/p))\). Pulling back the squared-exponential kernel on \(\mathbb R^2\) gives
\[
k_{\mathrm{per}}(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp\!\left[-\frac{2\sin^2(\pi(x-x')/p)}{\ell^2}\right].
\]
This kernel is positive semidefinite and satisfies \(k_{\mathrm{per}}(x+mp,x')=k_{\mathrm{per}}(x,x')\) for every \(m\in\mathbb Z\), with the analogous identity in its second argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared-exponential kernel pulled back through a circular embedding is positive semidefinite and exactly periodic with period p.
assumptions_latex: \(x,x'\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathrm{per}}\) is positive semidefinite and \(p\)-periodic in each argument.

notation.meaning: Length scale on the circular embedding.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The circular pullback formula, positive-semidefiniteness claim, and periodicity claim are consistent, and representation fits the container, but the record has no cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-separation kernels representing exactly repeating covariance structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\in\mathbb R\), \(\ell>0\), and \(p>0\), the periodic kernel is \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm{per}}(r;\ell,p)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{2}{\ell^2}\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi r}{p}\right)\right]\). A related kernel is \(\mathcal K_{\cos}(r;p)=\cos(2\pi r/p)\). Both are periodic in their separation argument: \(\mathcal K(r+p)=\mathcal K(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The periodic kernel captures repeating structure with period p through a sinusoidal separation. The related cosine kernel is also periodic with period p.
assumptions_latex: r\in\mathbb R
\ell>0

children.title: Hierarchical Kernel Composition
children.top_down_role: Nested or layered combinations of kernel components.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Kernel Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-structured construction using positive-semidefinite closure operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite rooted tree whose leaves carry positive-semidefinite kernels on a common input set \(\mathcal X\). Assign each internal node either a nonnegative weighted-sum rule \(k_v=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}a_{vc}k_c\), where \(a_{vc}\ge0\), or a product rule \(k_v=\prod_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}k_c\). Recursively evaluating from the leaves to the root defines \(k_T=k_{\operatorname{root}(T)}\). Closure under nonnegative sums and pointwise products ensures that every intermediate \(k_v\), and hence \(k_T\), is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite tree of kernels remains valid when every internal node combines its children by nonnegative sums or pointwise products.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite rooted tree.
Every leaf kernel is positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal X\).
Every sum coefficient satisfies \(a_{vc}\ge0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite tree construction correctly uses positive-semidefinite closure operations, and representation fits the leaf, but no authoritative compositional-kernel locator is supplied.

children.title: Composition Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Cases where imposed decompositions omit important dependence or create unsupported complexity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsupported compositional complexity caused by proportional kernel components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a composite kernel contains two proportional components, \(k(x,x')=a_1k_1(x,x')+a_2k_2(x,x')+k_0(x,x')\), with \(k_2=c\,k_1\) for some \(c>0\). Then \[k=(a_1+ca_2)k_1+k_0.\] Hence the covariance and Gaussian marginal likelihood depend on \((a_1,a_2)\) only through \(a_1+ca_2\). The separate component amplitudes are not identifiable, so interpreting or selecting both components as distinct structure is unsupported without additional constraints or information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proportional kernel components create redundant complexity: data identify only their combined amplitude, not the individual component weights.
assumptions_latex: The likelihood depends on component amplitudes through the composite covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-Component Nonidentifiability
Composition Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of purely additive kernels to represent genuine interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathcal X=[-1,1]^2\), every function of the additive form \(g(x_1,x_2)=g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)\) has zero rectangular contrast:
\[
g(a,c)-g(a,d)-g(b,c)+g(b,d)=0.
\]
For the interaction function \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\), the same contrast equals \((a-b)(c-d)\), which is nonzero whenever \(a\ne b\) and \(c\ne d\). Consequently, an additive-kernel model whose support is restricted to additive functions cannot represent \(f\) exactly; interaction components or another richer composition are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Purely additive kernel models cannot exactly represent a product interaction, as witnessed by its nonzero rectangular contrast.
assumptions_latex: The model class contains only functions \(g_1(x_1)+g_2(x_2)\).
\(a\ne b\) and \(c\ne d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1x_2\) does not belong to the purely additive function class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rectangular-contrast example correctly exposes the failure of a purely additive function class, and failure_boundary is the correct role, but the record lacks an inspectable source locator supporting this misspecification claim.

children.title: Nonstationary Kernels
children.top_down_role: Covariance structures permitting location-dependent regularity, scale, or variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance nonstationarity on a Euclidean input domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). A covariance kernel \(k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is stationary when there exists a function \(\kappa\) on \(\mathcal X-\mathcal X\) such that \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) for all \(x,x'\in\mathcal X\). It is nonstationary when no such \(\kappa\) exists. Thus its covariance may depend on absolute location as well as displacement; in particular, spatially varying marginal variance \(k(x,x)\) is sufficient, though not necessary, to establish nonstationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A kernel is nonstationary when its covariance cannot be expressed solely as a function of input displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\).
\(k\) is a positive-semidefinite covariance kernel on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is nonstationary exactly when no \(\kappa\) satisfies \(k(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) for all input pairs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite Gaussian covariance with a location-dependent local scale matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Sigma(x)\) be symmetric positive definite for every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(\sigma(x)\ge0\), and set \(M(x,x')=(\Sigma(x)+\Sigma(x'))/2\). Then
\[
k(x,x')=\sigma(x)\sigma(x')\frac{|\Sigma(x)|^{1/4}|\Sigma(x')|^{1/4}}{|M(x,x')|^{1/2}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac12(x-x')^\top M(x,x')^{-1}(x-x')\right]
\]
is positive semidefinite. Constant \(\Sigma\) and \(\sigma\) recover a stationary anisotropic Gaussian kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A determinant-corrected Gaussian kernel with input-dependent positive-definite scale matrices is valid and generalizes the stationary anisotropic Gaussian kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma(x)\) is symmetric positive definite for every input.
\(\sigma(x)\ge0\) for every input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed spatially varying Gaussian covariance is positive semidefinite.

notation.meaning: Average of the two local scale matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonstationary covariance obtained by spatial modulation of a valid base kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k_0\) be positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal X\) and let \(a:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\). Then
\[
k(x,x')=a(x)a(x')k_0(x,x')
\]
is positive semidefinite. If \(k_0(x,x)=c>0\) is constant and \(|a(x)|\) is nonconstant, then \(k(x,x)=c a(x)^2\) varies with location, so \(k\) is nonstationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided input-dependent amplitude modulation preserves kernel validity and yields nonstationarity whenever marginal variance varies.
assumptions_latex: \(k_0\) is positive semidefinite.
\(a\) is real-valued.
For the nonstationarity conclusion, \(k_0(x,x)=c>0\) and \(|a|\) is nonconstant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is positive semidefinite and is nonstationary under the stated diagonal-variation condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Amplitude-Modulated Nonstationary Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid normalized nonstationary covariance with positive input-dependent coordinate length scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary functions \(\ell_d:\mathbb R^D\to(0,\infty)\),
\[
k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\prod_{d=1}^D\left(\frac{2\ell_d(\mathbf{x})\ell_d(\mathbf{x}')}{\ell_d^2(\mathbf{x})+\ell_d^2(\mathbf{x}')}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\sum_{d=1}^D\frac{(x_d-x_d')^2}{\ell_d^2(\mathbf{x})+\ell_d^2(\mathbf{x}')}\right)
\]
is a valid covariance function and satisfies \(k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x})=1\). By contrast, directly replacing constant length scales in a general anisotropic covariance by input-dependent functions does not generally preserve validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gibbs construction gives a valid normalized nonstationary covariance for arbitrary positive input-dependent coordinate length scales. Naive input-dependent substitution into an anisotropic kernel is not generally valid.
assumptions_latex: D\in\mathbb N
\ell_d(\mathbf{x})>0\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^D,\ d=1,\ldots,D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is a valid covariance function and }k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x})=1\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positive-definite matrix field transforms a dimension-universally valid isotropic covariance into a valid nonstationary covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k_S\) be a stationary isotropic covariance valid on \(\mathbb R^m\) for every \(m\ge1\). For a matrix field \(\Sigma(\mathbf{x})\succ0\), set \(\Sigma_i=\Sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)\) and
\[
Q_{ij}=(\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j)^\top\left(\frac{\Sigma_i+\Sigma_j}{2}\right)^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j).
\]
Then
\[
k_{NS}(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)=2^{D/2}|\Sigma_i|^{1/4}|\Sigma_j|^{1/4}|\Sigma_i+\Sigma_j|^{-1/2}k_S(\sqrt{Q_{ij}})
\]
is a valid covariance function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary isotropic covariance valid in every Euclidean dimension can be transformed into a valid location-adaptive covariance using a positive-definite matrix field, a corresponding quadratic distance, and determinant normalization.
assumptions_latex: D\in\mathbb N
k_S\text{ is stationary and isotropic and valid on }\mathbb R^m\text{ for every }m\ge1
\Sigma(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb R^{D\times D}\text{ is positive definite for every }\mathbf{x}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_{NS}\text{ is a valid covariance function, generally nonstationary when }\Sigma\text{ varies with }\mathbf{x}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inputs in a domain $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, a kernel $K$ is stationary if there is a function $\kappa$ such that \[K(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\] for all $x,x'\in\mathcal X$. A nonstationary kernel relaxes this translation-invariance requirement, allowing similarity to depend on the locations themselves rather than only on their displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary kernel depends on two inputs only through their displacement. A nonstationary kernel permits covariance or similarity to vary with absolute location.

x,x'\in\mathcal X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian basis functions with Gaussian-distributed centers induce a modulated squared-exponential covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{u})=\exp(-\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{u}\|^2/(2\sigma_g^2))\) and \(\mathbf{u}\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf0,\sigma_u^2I)\). Then
\[
k_G(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')=\left(\frac{\sigma_e}{\sigma_u}\right)^d e^{-\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x}/(2\sigma_m^2)}e^{-\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|^2/(2\sigma_s^2)}e^{-\mathbf{x}'^\top\mathbf{x}'/(2\sigma_m^2)},
\]
where \(\sigma_e^{-2}=2\sigma_g^{-2}+\sigma_u^{-2}\), \(\sigma_s^2=2\sigma_g^2+\sigma_g^4/\sigma_u^2\), and \(\sigma_m^2=2\sigma_u^2+\sigma_g^2\). It is generally nonstationary for finite \(\sigma_u^2\). As \(\sigma_u^2\to\infty\), with amplitude scaled appropriately, it approaches a covariance proportional to \(\exp(-\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|^2/(4\sigma_g^2))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian basis functions with isotropic Gaussian-distributed centers induce a squared-exponential covariance modulated by Gaussian decay envelopes in both inputs. It is generally nonstationary, with a stationary squared-exponential limit under appropriate amplitude scaling.
assumptions_latex: d\in\mathbb N
\sigma_g^2>0
\sigma_u^2>0
\mathbf{u}\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf0,\sigma_u^2I)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_G\text{ has the displayed modulated squared-exponential form and converges, up to appropriate amplitude scaling, to }\exp(-\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|^2/(4\sigma_g^2)).

children.title: Input-Warped Kernels
children.top_down_role: Kernel structures operating on transformed input geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear Warping Need Not Produce Nonstationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nonlinearity alone to certify a nonstationary pullback kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w(x)=(\cos x,\sin x)\) and let \(k_0(z,z')=\sigma^2\exp(-\|z-z'\|^2/(2\ell^2))\). Although \(w\) is nonlinear,
\[
k_w(x,x')=k_0(w(x),w(x'))=\sigma^2\exp\!\left[-\frac{1-\cos(x-x')}{\ell^2}\right],
\]
which depends only on \(x-x'\) and is therefore stationary on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear circular warp of a stationary squared-exponential kernel produces a stationary periodic pullback, so nonlinearity alone does not imply nonstationarity.
assumptions_latex: The base kernel is squared exponential on \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonlinear warp \(w(x)=(\cos x,\sin x)\) yields a stationary periodic kernel.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Warping Need Not Produce Nonstationarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinitesimal geometry induced by a differentiable warp under a squared-exponential base kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(w:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^q\) be differentiable, and define
\[
k_w(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w(x)-w(x')\|^2}{2\ell^2}\right).
\]
For every interior \(x\) and \(h\to0\),
\[
\|w(x+h)-w(x)\|^2=h^\top J_w(x)^\top J_w(x)h+o(\|h\|^2).
\]
Thus the induced local metric is \(G(x)=J_w(x)^\top J_w(x)/\ell^2\). If \(G(x)\) varies with \(x\), then \(k_w\) is not displacement-stationary on an open set containing that variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable warp induces a local kernel metric through its Jacobian; spatial variation of that metric certifies nonstationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(w\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of the points considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local metric is \(G(x)=J_w(x)^\top J_w(x)/\ell^2\), and variation of \(G\) is sufficient for nonstationarity.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the warp at x.
Squared-exponential kernel pulled back through w.

knowledge_statements.title: Warp-Induced Local Metric
Input-Warped Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonstationary covariance obtained by pulling back a base kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z\) be any map and let \(k_0:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) be positive semidefinite. The input-warped kernel is
\[
k_w(x,x')=k_0(w(x),w(x')).
\]
For every finite collection \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal X\), its Gram matrix equals the Gram matrix of \(k_0\) at \(w(x_1),\ldots,w(x_n)\), so \(k_w\) is positive semidefinite. Even when \(k_0\) is stationary on \(\mathcal Z\), a nonlinear warp generally makes \(k_w\) nonstationary on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing both kernel arguments with an input warp preserves positive semidefiniteness and can produce spatially varying covariance.
assumptions_latex: \(w:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z\) is a map.
\(k_0\) is positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal Z\).

notation.meaning: Base kernel on the warped space.
Pulled-back kernel on the original space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{A_r\}_{r=1}^R\) be a disjoint partition of \(\mathcal X\), and for each \(r\) let \(k_r:A_r\times A_r\to\mathbb R\) be positive semidefinite. Define the hard-partition kernel by
\[
k_{\mathrm{part}}(x,x')=
\begin{cases}
k_r(x,x'), & x,x'\in A_r\text{ for some }r,\\
0, & x\text{ and }x'\text{ belong to distinct regions}.
\end{cases}
\]
For every finite input collection, ordering the inputs by region makes the Gram matrix block diagonal with positive-semidefinite diagonal blocks. Hence \(k_{\mathrm{part}}\) is positive semidefinite. It assigns zero covariance across distinct regions while permitting region-specific covariance parameters or kernel families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard-partition kernel uses a regional kernel when both inputs lie in the same region and zero covariance otherwise, yielding a positive-semidefinite block-diagonal covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Partitioned Kernels

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regional Posterior Separability of Hard Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise Gaussian-process inference under a fixed hard partition and independent regional covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider Gaussian-process regression with the hard-partition kernel \(k_{\mathrm{part}}\), independent observation noise, fixed mean and hyperparameters, and training inputs grouped by regions \(A_1,\ldots,A_R\). The training covariance plus noise is block diagonal. For \(x_*\in A_r\), its covariance with observations outside \(A_r\) is zero; consequently its posterior mean and variance depend only on observations in \(A_r\) and the r-th covariance block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed hard partitions and independent noise, prediction in one region is separated from observations in every other region.
assumptions_latex: The hard partition and regional kernels are fixed.
Observation noise is independent across observations.
Mean and covariance hyperparameters are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(x_*\in A_r\), posterior summaries use only observations and the covariance block associated with \(A_r\).
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Posterior Separability of Hard Partitions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overlapping regional covariance formed from valid local kernels and input-dependent gates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k_r\) be positive-semidefinite kernels on \(\mathcal X\) and let \(g_r:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), \(r=1,\ldots,R\). Then
\[
k_{\mathrm{gate}}(x,x')=\sum_{r=1}^R g_r(x)g_r(x')k_r(x,x')
\]
is positive semidefinite. Region-indicator gates recover a hard-partition kernel; overlapping or smoothly varying gates permit shared covariance across soft regional boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gating regional kernels in both arguments and summing yields a valid soft-partition kernel; indicator gates recover the hard partition.
assumptions_latex: \(R<\infty\).
Every \(k_r\) is positive semidefinite.
Every \(g_r\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k_{\mathrm{gate}}\) is positive semidefinite, with hard partitioning as an indicator-gate special case.
knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Partition Gated Kernel

children.title: Cross-Partition Continuity
children.top_down_role: Continuity and dependence behavior at boundaries between modeled regions.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a second-order process with mean \(m\) and covariance \(k\).
\(b\) is a boundary point shared by two partition regions.
Sequences may approach \(b\) from either adjacent region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is mean-square continuous at \(b\) if and only if \((m(x_n)-m(b))^2+k(x_n,x_n)+k(b,b)-2k(x_n,b)\to0\) for every sequence \(x_n\to b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square continuity condition at boundaries between kernel regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be a second-order process with mean function \(m\) and covariance kernel \(k\), and let \(b\) lie on a boundary shared by two partition regions. Cross-partition mean-square continuity at \(b\) holds exactly when, for every sequence \(x_n\to b\) approaching from either adjacent region,
\[
(m(x_n)-m(b))^2+k(x_n,x_n)+k(b,b)-2k(x_n,b)\longrightarrow0.
\]
This expression equals \(\mathbb E[(f(x_n)-f(b))^2]\). For a hard-partition kernel, an approach from a region distinct from the one containing \(b\) has zero cross-region covariance, so continuity requires the remaining mean and marginal-variance terms to vanish in the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitioned process is mean-square continuous across a boundary exactly when the second moment of its boundary increment, including both mean and covariance terms, tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Partition Continuity

children.title: Nonstationarity Identifiability
children.top_down_role: Limits on distinguishing genuine spatial variation from noise or sparse coverage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observational equivalence of latent covariance and noise decompositions on a fixed finite design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be fixed and suppose
\[
y\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K_k(X,X)+\Sigma_\varepsilon).
\]
If two model pairs \((k_1,\Sigma_{\varepsilon,1})\) and \((k_2,\Sigma_{\varepsilon,2})\) have the same mean and satisfy
\[
K_{k_1}(X,X)+\Sigma_{\varepsilon,1}=K_{k_2}(X,X)+\Sigma_{\varepsilon,2},
\]
then they induce exactly the same data distribution and marginal likelihood. Thus off-design nonstationarity and any allocation of observed covariance between spatially varying latent signal and noise are not identifiable on that design without restrictions, additional observations, replication, or prior information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite design, models with the same total observation covariance are indistinguishable even when they allocate variation differently between a nonstationary latent kernel and noise.
assumptions_latex: The observation design \(X\) is fixed and finite.
The compared Gaussian models use the same mean vector.
Each total covariance matrix is valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality of total design covariance implies identical data distributions and likelihoods.

notation.meaning: Latent-kernel Gram matrix on the design.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Design Signal–Noise Nonidentifiability
Nonstationarity Identifiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale confounding between a warp and its stationary base kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\mathcal X=\mathbb R\), the warp \(w_a(x)=ax\) with \(a>0\), and a squared-exponential base kernel with length scale \(\ell>0\). The induced covariance is
\[
k_{a,\ell}(x,x')=\sigma^2\exp\!\left[-\frac{a^2(x-x')^2}{2\ell^2}\right].
\]
For every \(c>0\), \(k_{ca,c\ell}=k_{a,\ell}\). Hence observations governed only through this covariance can identify the ratio \(a/\ell\), but cannot separately identify the warp scale and base-kernel length scale without a normalization, constraint, or informative prior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warp scale and base-kernel length scale are not separately identifiable when the covariance depends only on their ratio.
assumptions_latex: The likelihood depends on \(a\) and \(\ell\) only through \(k_{a,\ell}\).

notation.meaning: Linear input warp with scale a.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling invariance correctly demonstrates nonidentifiability of the warp scale and base-kernel length scale under the stated covariance-only likelihood, and failure_boundary fits the leaf, but no authoritative identifiability locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for selecting covariance-function structures and setting their hyperparameters in Gaussian-process models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a Gaussian-process model, model selection comprises both discrete choices among covariance-function families and the setting of continuous covariance-function hyperparameters. Selecting a covariance function together with its parameters is called training the Gaussian process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Gaussian-process model, model selection includes choosing among covariance-function families and setting their continuous hyperparameters. Selecting the covariance function and its parameters is called training the Gaussian process.
assumptions_latex: \text{The Gaussian-process specification admits choices of covariance-function family and covariance hyperparameters.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Both covariance-family choice and covariance-hyperparameter setting are model selection; their joint selection is Gaussian-process training.}

children.title: Marginal-Likelihood Fitting
children.top_down_role: Point-oriented surrogate fitting based on integrated data likelihood.

assumptions_latex: \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) is modeled with zero mean or has been centered using a fixed known mean.
\(C_\theta\) is positive definite for every admissible \(\theta\).
A constrained optimization method, stopping tolerance, and iteration limit are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact marginal-likelihood fit is any \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta)\); a terminated numerical run returns an approximation to such a fit.

notation.meaning: Observation covariance including any noise term.
Numerical approximation returned by the optimizer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical-Bayes fitting of Gaussian-process covariance hyperparameters for a zero-mean or fixed-mean model.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) have zero mean, or let \(y\) denote observations centered using a fixed known mean, and let \(C_\theta\) be positive definite for every \(\theta\) in an admissible set \(\Theta\). Define
\[
L(\theta)=\tfrac12 y^\top C_\theta^{-1}y+\tfrac12\log|C_\theta|+\tfrac n2\log(2\pi).
\]
Marginal-likelihood fitting seeks any \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta)\). Starting from an admissible \(\theta^{(0)}\), apply a constrained numerical optimizer, using derivatives when available, until its prescribed tolerance or iteration limit is reached, and return the resulting numerical estimate \(\widetilde\theta\). Use \(C_{\widetilde\theta}\) for plug-in Gaussian-process prediction. A parametric mean with unknown coefficients requires a correspondingly profiled, jointly optimized, or integrated likelihood criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a zero-mean or fixed-mean Gaussian process, fit covariance hyperparameters by numerically minimizing the negative Gaussian log marginal likelihood; a terminated optimizer returns an approximation rather than a guaranteed global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Likelihood Fitting

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative and interior stationarity condition for Gaussian negative log marginal likelihood with a fixed mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(\theta)=\tfrac12y^\top C_\theta^{-1}y+\tfrac12\log|C_\theta|+\tfrac n2\log(2\pi)\), \(C_j=\partial C_\theta/\partial\theta_j\), and \(\alpha=C_\theta^{-1}y\). Then \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_j}=\frac12\operatorname{tr}\!\left[(C_\theta^{-1}-\alpha\alpha^\top)C_j\right].\] An interior differentiable minimizer satisfies these score equations for every free coordinate; a boundary minimizer need not have zero ordinary gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gaussian negative log marginal-likelihood gradient is a trace involving the inverse covariance and fitted quadratic term; zero gradient is necessary only at an interior differentiable fit.
assumptions_latex: \(C_\theta\) is positive definite and differentiable at \(\theta\).
The mean is fixed and independent of \(\theta\).

notation.meaning: Covariance derivative with respect to coordinate \(j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Likelihood Score

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Profile Likelihood with a Linear Mean
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary Gaussian covariance fitting after profiling an unknown linear trend, distinguished from restricted likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\sim N(H\beta,C_\theta)\), define \[\widehat\beta_\theta=(H^\top C_\theta^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top C_\theta^{-1}y.\] Profiling the ordinary likelihood over \(\beta\) gives \[L_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta)=\tfrac12(y-H\widehat\beta_\theta)^\top C_\theta^{-1}(y-H\widehat\beta_\theta)+\tfrac12\log|C_\theta|+\tfrac n2\log(2\pi).\] Unlike REML, this criterion has no \(\tfrac12\log|H^\top C_\theta^{-1}H|\) adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unknown linear mean can be profiled by generalized least squares from the ordinary likelihood; the resulting covariance criterion is not REML.
assumptions_latex: \(C_\theta\succ0\).
\(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) has rank \(p<n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\theta L_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta)\) is an ordinary profiled-likelihood covariance fit.
knowledge_statements.title: Profile Likelihood with a Linear Mean

children.title: Restricted-Likelihood Fitting
children.top_down_role: Likelihood treatment separating covariance fitting from specified trend effects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of REML through Gaussian contrasts that eliminate a linear mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\sim N(H\beta,C_\theta)\), where \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) has rank \(p<n\). Choose \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-p)}\) with full column rank and \(A^\top H=0\). Then \[z=A^\top y\sim N(0,A^\top C_\theta A),\] so its likelihood is free of \(\beta\). Maximizing this contrast likelihood over \(\theta\) gives the restricted-likelihood estimator. Different admissible contrast bases change the restricted log likelihood only by a constant independent of \(\theta\), hence give the same optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: REML is Gaussian likelihood applied to full-rank error contrasts that annihilate the linear mean; its covariance fit is invariant to the chosen contrast basis.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) has rank \(p<n\).
\(C_\theta\succ0\).
\(A\) has rank \(n-p\) and satisfies \(A^\top H=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_\theta p(A^\top y\mid\theta)\) is invariant to the admissible error-contrast basis.

notation.meaning: Full-rank error-contrast basis annihilating the mean design.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Contrast Representation of Restricted Likelihood
Restricted-Likelihood Fitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: REML covariance fitting after accounting for a linear mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), a full-column-rank matrix \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\), and positive-definite \(C_\theta\), define \(P_\theta=C_\theta^{-1}-C_\theta^{-1}H(H^\top C_\theta^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top C_\theta^{-1}\). Initialize admissible \(\theta^{(0)}\), then minimize
\[
L_R(\theta)=\tfrac12\!\left(\log|C_\theta|+\log|H^\top C_\theta^{-1}H|+y^\top P_\theta y+(n-p)\log(2\pi)\right)
\]
until a prescribed tolerance or iteration limit is reached. Return an attained minimizer \(\widehat\theta_R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: REML fits covariance parameters by optimizing the likelihood of residual contrasts after removing the linear mean effects.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) has rank \(p<n\).
\(C_\theta\) is positive definite.
A stopping tolerance or iteration limit is specified.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The REML criterion and generalized residual-forming matrix are internally consistent under the stated rank and positive-definiteness assumptions, and algorithm fits the terminal container. No specific authoritative REML source locator is supplied, so the formula cannot yet be accepted as sourced candidate-review knowledge.

children.title: Posterior Parameter Inference
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty-aware treatment of surrogate parameters after observing data.

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Parameter Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully Bayesian inference and prediction over surrogate parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) parameterize a surrogate likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\), and let \(p(\theta)\) be a proper prior with finite evidence \(0<p(y)<\infty\). The parameter posterior and integrated predictive distribution are
\[
p(\theta\mid y)=\frac{p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{\int_\Theta p(y\mid\vartheta)p(\vartheta)\,d\vartheta},\qquad
p(f_*\mid y)=\int_\Theta p(f_*\mid y,\theta)p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta.
\]
Thus prediction averages conditional surrogate predictions over parameter uncertainty rather than conditioning on a single fitted value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian surrogate inference combines likelihood and prior, then averages predictions over the resulting parameter posterior.
assumptions_latex: \(p(\theta)\) is a proper prior on \(\Theta\).
\(0<\int_\Theta p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Latent or predictive quantity at target inputs.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-based approximation of predictions integrated over surrogate parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given retained draws \(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}\), approximate the integrated predictive law by \[\widehat p_S(\cdot\mid y)=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S p(\cdot\mid y,\theta^{(s)}).\] For any posterior-integrable predictive functional \(h\), iid posterior draws, or an ergodic Markov chain with invariant law \(p(\theta\mid y)\), give \[\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S\mathbb E[h(Z)\mid y,\theta^{(s)}]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[h(Z)\mid y]\] almost surely. A finite or unconverged run is only approximate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average conditional predictions over posterior parameter draws; iid or ergodic sampling consistently estimates integrable predictive expectations.
assumptions_latex: The retained draws are iid from \(p(\theta\mid y)\), or form an ergodic chain with that invariant law.
The predictive functional is posterior-integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^{-1}\sum_s\mathbb E[h(Z)\mid y,\theta^{(s)}]\to\mathbb E[h(Z)\mid y]\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: Number of retained posterior parameter draws.

knowledge_statements.title: Monte Carlo Posterior Predictive Integration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of conditional process uncertainty from surrogate-parameter uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar predictive quantity \(Z\), whenever the relevant moments exist, \[\mathbb E[Z\mid y]=\mathbb E_{\theta\mid y}[\mathbb E(Z\mid y,\theta)],\] \[\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid y)=\mathbb E_{\theta\mid y}[\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid y,\theta)]+\operatorname{Var}_{\theta\mid y}(\mathbb E[Z\mid y,\theta]).\] The second nonnegative term represents parameter uncertainty and is absent from single-parameter plug-in prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian predictive variance equals average conditional variance plus variance caused by posterior uncertainty about surrogate parameters.
assumptions_latex: The required conditional first and second moments are posterior-integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid y)=\mathbb E_{\theta\mid y}[\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid y,\theta)]+\operatorname{Var}_{\theta\mid y}(\mathbb E[Z\mid y,\theta])\).
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Predictive Moment Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayesian updating of surrogate-model parameters or hyperparameters from observed inputs and responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations $\mathcal D=(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$, a prior density $p(\boldsymbol\theta)$, and likelihood $p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)$, the posterior distribution satisfies
\[
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto p(\boldsymbol\theta)\,p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given observed inputs and responses, the posterior distribution over model parameters is proportional to the prior multiplied by the likelihood of the observed responses.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal D=(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)
p(\boldsymbol\theta)\text{ is a prior density}
p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)\text{ is the likelihood of the observations}
0<\int p(\boldsymbol\theta)p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)\,d\boldsymbol\theta<\infty

children.title: Fitting-Regime Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation in fitted surrogates across likelihood-oriented or posterior-oriented treatments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient certificate that a fitting-regime perturbation preserves a unique acquisition choice on a finite candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be finite, let \(x_r\) uniquely maximize \(a_r\), and define \[\gamma_r=a_r(x_r)-\max_{x\in\mathcal C\setminus\{x_r\}}a_r(x)>0.\] If \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal C}|a_s(x)-a_r(x)|<\gamma_r/2\), then \(x_r\) is also the unique maximizer of \(a_s\) on \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fitting-regime change preserves a finite-set acquisition maximizer when the uniform acquisition perturbation is less than half the reference decision margin.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is finite.
\(a_r\) has a unique maximizer \(x_r\).
\(\sup_{x\in\mathcal C}|a_s(x)-a_r(x)|<\gamma_r/2\).

notation.meaning: gap between the best and second-best reference acquisition values

knowledge_statements.title: Acquisition-Decision Stability Margin

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision Instability Without an Acquisition Margin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for converting small acquisition discrepancies into stable decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathcal C=\{u,v\}\), let \(a_r(u)=0\), \(a_r(v)=-\varepsilon/2\), \(a_s(u)=0\), and \(a_s(v)=\varepsilon/2\). Then \(\|a_r-a_s\|_\infty=\varepsilon\), but the unique maximizer changes from \(u\) to \(v\). Since \(\varepsilon>0\) can be arbitrarily small, no positive universal discrepancy threshold guarantees decision invariance without a margin or another stability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small uniform acquisition changes can flip the selected point when the reference decision margin is arbitrarily small.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Instability Without an Acquisition Margin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-preserving comparison of posterior summaries produced by two parameter-inference regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let regimes \(r\) and \(s\), fitted to the same data on \(\mathcal X\), produce posterior mean \(\mu_j\), predictive standard deviation \(\sigma_j\), and acquisition \(a_j\). Define \[S_{r,s}=\left(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\mu_r(x)-\mu_s(x)|,\ \sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\sigma_r(x)-\sigma_s(x)|,\ \sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|a_r(x)-a_s(x)|\right).\] Each coordinate retains its own units. A scalar score requires declared positive normalization scales and an aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare fitting regimes by separate worst-case discrepancies in mean, uncertainty, and acquisition, combining them only after declaring scales and an aggregation rule.
assumptions_latex: Both regimes use the same data, domain, predictive target, and acquisition convention.
The displayed suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{r,s}\) is a componentwise, unit-preserving sensitivity profile.

notation.meaning: predictive standard deviation under regime j

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Fitting-Regime Discrepancy Profile
Fitting-Regime Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how alternative surrogate-parameter fitting regimes change GP predictions and acquisition values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let fitting regimes \(r\) and \(s\) produce parameter estimates \(\widehat\theta_r\) and \(\widehat\theta_s\) from the same data \(D\). For their GP posterior means, variances, and acquisition functions, define \[\Delta_{r,s}(D)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\left(|\mu_r(x)-\mu_s(x)|+|v_r(x)-v_s(x)|+|a_r(x)-a_s(x)|\right).\] The fitted surrogate-acquisition architecture is regime-sensitive on \(D\) precisely when \(\Delta_{r,s}(D)>0\). If each acquisition maximizer is unique, decision sensitivity is additionally measured by \(d(\arg\max_x a_r(x),\arg\max_x a_s(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fitting-regime sensitivity is the maximum predictive and acquisition discrepancy induced by fitting the same surrogate under two parameter-inference regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(\mathcal X\) are fixed across regimes.
The displayed suprema are finite.
Acquisition-maximizer distance is used only when both maximizers are unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{r,s}(D)>0\) certifies sensitivity to the fitting regime.

notation.meaning: surrogate parameters fitted under regime r
posterior predictive variance under regime r
