children.top_down_role: Comparison and automated search across competing surrogate structures.

children.title: Candidate Model Selection
children.top_down_role: Comparison among a specified collection of competing surrogate structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive selection from a prespecified finite family of fitted surrogate structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M=\{M_1,\ldots,M_K\}\) be nonempty and finite. Fit each candidate under a fixed fitting convention, compute a finite comparable score \(S(M_k;D)\) oriented so that larger is better, and return \[\widehat M\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{M_k\in\mathcal M}S(M_k;D),\] using a declared tie rule when necessary. The fitted score table certifies optimality only within \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit and score every model in a fixed finite candidate family, then return a score maximizer under a declared tie rule.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le K<\infty\).
Every candidate can be fitted and assigned a finite comparable score.
Score orientation, fitting conventions, and tie rule are fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Candidate Score Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of finite-candidate selection on the declared comparison family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(\mathcal M\), define \(S^*(\mathcal M)=\max_{M\in\mathcal M}S(M;D)\). If \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal M'\), then \[S^*(\mathcal M')\ge S^*(\mathcal M).\] The selected model is therefore optimal only relative to its declared family. Enlarging that family can change the winner, and a larger in-sample selection score does not by itself imply smaller out-of-sample predictive risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-candidate winner is optimal only within its declared family; adding candidates cannot reduce the best score but need not improve predictive performance.
assumptions_latex: The same oriented score and fitting convention are used for both families.
\(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal M'\) are nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^*(\mathcal M')\ge S^*(\mathcal M)\), without a general corresponding ordering of predictive risks.

notation.meaning: Best attained score in candidate family \(\mathcal M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Set Relativity
Candidate Model Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-candidate selection of a GP covariance, mean, or noise structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input data \(D\), a finite candidate family \(\mathcal M=\{M_1,\ldots,M_K\}\), and a criterion \(S(M;D)\) oriented so that larger values are preferred. For each \(M_k\), fit its admissible parameters \(\widehat\theta_k\), compute \(S_k=S(M_k,\widehat\theta_k;D)\), and return \[\widehat M\in\arg\max_{M_k\in\mathcal M}S_k.\] If the argmax is not unique, apply a declared deterministic tie rule, such as choosing the candidate of smallest dimension. The selected predictive law is \(p(\,cdot\mid D,\widehat M,\widehat\theta_{\widehat M})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit every candidate surrogate structure, compare them using a common oriented score, and return a score maximizer under a declared tie rule.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le K<\infty\).
Every candidate admits a fitted parameter value and a finite comparable score.
The score orientation and tie rule are fixed before selection.

notation.meaning: finite family of candidate surrogate structures
model-selection score, with larger values preferred

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative finite-model-selection source is required. The score is introduced as S(M;D) but evaluated with an additional parameter argument, and the predictive-law expression uses literal “cdot” rather than \(\cdot\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: MAP selection within a specified surrogate-model family, including its equivalence to maximum-likelihood selection under a positive flat prior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observed inputs and responses $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ and a candidate domain $\Theta$ of model hyperparameters, a maximum-a-posteriori selection satisfies
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}p(\boldsymbol\theta)\,p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta).
\]
If the prior is a positive constant on $\Theta$, then the MAP and maximum-likelihood argmax sets coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A MAP model maximizes the product of the model prior and the data likelihood over the candidate hyperparameters. If the prior is positive and flat throughout the candidate domain, MAP and maximum-likelihood selection have the same maximizers.
assumptions_latex: (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\text{ are the observed inputs and responses.}
\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta\text{ indexes the specified candidate surrogate-model family.}
p(\boldsymbol\theta)\text{ and }p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)\text{ are defined on }\Theta.
p(\boldsymbol\theta)\equiv c>0\text{ on }\Theta\text{ for the MAP--MLE equivalence.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}p(\boldsymbol\theta)p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta),\qquad p(\boldsymbol\theta)\equiv c>0\implies \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}p(\boldsymbol\theta)p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta).

children.title: Automated Structure Search
children.top_down_role: Exploration of kernel, trend, interaction, or partition structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic score-improving traversal of a finite admissible surrogate-structure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M\) be finite, let \(N(M)\subseteq\mathfrak M\) be a finite neighborhood, and let \(S(M;D)\) be evaluated under fixed fitting and tie conventions. Starting from \(M^{(0)}\), repeatedly move to a neighbor with strictly larger score, retaining the highest-scoring visited structure. Stop when no neighbor strictly improves the score or a declared budget is exhausted. Without budget exhaustion, strict improvement implies finite termination at a neighborhood-wise score maximizer; the returned structure need not maximize the score over all of \(\mathfrak M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite neighborhood search repeatedly accepts score-improving structures and terminates at a local score optimum unless its budget ends first; it has no general global guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak M\) is finite and nonempty.
Generated neighbors are admissible.
Fitting, scoring, and tie conventions remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unbudgeted strict-improvement run terminates after finitely many accepted moves at \(\widehat M\) satisfying \(S(\widehat M;D)\ge S(M;D)\) for every \(M\in N(\widehat M)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Neighborhood Structure Search

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global score-optimality certificate for automated search over a finite structure space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M\) be nonempty and finite. Evaluating every \(M\in\mathfrak M\) and returning \(\widehat M\) with \[S(\widehat M;D)=\max_{M\in\mathfrak M}S(M;D)\] certifies global score optimality over \(\mathfrak M\). If only \(\mathcal V\subsetneq\mathfrak M\) is visited, best-visited status certifies optimality only over \(\mathcal V\), unless valid upper bounds establish \(\sup_{M\notin\mathcal V}S(M;D)\le S(\widehat M;D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration certifies global score optimality over a finite structure space; partial search requires valid bounds on every unvisited structure or certifies only best-visited status.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak M\) is finite and nonempty.
Scores use a common deterministic fitting and comparison convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete enumeration, or domination of all unvisited score upper bounds, certifies \(\widehat M\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{M\in\mathfrak M}S(M;D)\).

notation.meaning: Set of visited and scored structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Structure-Search Certificate
Automated Structure Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete search over admissible GP structures generated by a model grammar or neighborhood operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input data \(D\), an admissible structure set \(\mathfrak M\), a neighborhood map \(N:\mathfrak M\to2^{\mathfrak M}\), score \(S\), and initial structure \(M^{(0)}\). At iteration \(t\), fit and score every unvisited member of \(N(M^{(t)})\), then set \[M^{(t+1)}\in\arg\max_{M\in N(M^{(t)})\cup\{M^{(t)}\}}S(M;D).\] Stop when no neighbor strictly improves the score, a budget \(B\) is exhausted, or another prespecified stopping condition holds. Return the highest-scoring visited structure and its fitted predictive distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automated structure search repeatedly generates, fits, and scores neighboring surrogate structures, returning the best visited model when improvement or budget ends.
assumptions_latex: \(M^{(0)}\in\mathfrak M\).
Each generated neighborhood is finite and contains only admissible structures.
Score comparisons use a fixed fitting and tie-breaking convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output maximizes \(S(M;D)\) over the visited structures, but need not maximize it over all of \(\mathfrak M\).

notation.meaning: search space of admissible surrogate structures
structures reachable from M in one search step

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the container, but this particular neighborhood-search procedure and its stopping and return guarantees lack a cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grammar-Generated Space of Compositional Kernel Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a candidate language for automated covariance-kernel structure search and notes the exhaustive-search limitation of partition-indexed additive alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B\) be a collection of covariance kernels on a common input domain. A language of candidate kernel-structure expressions is generated by the context-free grammar \[K\to B\quad(B\in\mathcal B),\qquad K\to K+K,\qquad K\to KK,\qquad K\to (K),\] where juxtaposition denotes pointwise multiplication and parentheses provide grouping. Closure of covariance kernels under addition and pointwise multiplication ensures that every generated expression represents a covariance kernel. Coordinate-specific base kernels can thereby generate additive and interaction structures. Alternatively, additive model structures may be indexed by partitions of the input variables; although expressive, this class has so many partitions in high dimensions that exhaustive search is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from covariance kernels on a common input domain, a context-free grammar recursively forms candidate kernel expressions using addition, pointwise multiplication, and parentheses. These operations preserve covariance-kernel validity and can generate additive and interaction structures. A partition-indexed additive search space is also expressive, but exhaustive search becomes infeasible as the number of variable partitions grows rapidly.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal B\text{ is a collection of valid covariance kernels on a common input domain.}
\text{The grammar interprets addition and multiplication as kernel addition and pointwise multiplication, respectively.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lang}\!\left(K\to B\ (B\in\mathcal B),\ K\to K+K,\ K\to KK,\ K\to(K)\right)\text{ is a recursively generated candidate language whose expressions represent valid compositional covariance kernels.}

children.title: Selection-Criterion Families
children.top_down_role: Predictive, evidence-based, or complexity-sensitive criteria for comparing structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretive boundary separating predictive, complexity-penalized, and evidence-based selection targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection criterion must be interpreted according to the target it estimates or approximates. Under their respective regularity conditions, AIC-type criteria target expected predictive discrepancy, BIC-type criteria provide a large-sample evidence approximation, cross-validation estimates performance for its declared split and loss, and marginal likelihood averages likelihood under the within-model prior. These criteria can rank the same surrogate structures differently; rankings cannot be transferred between families without assumptions linking their targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AIC, BIC, cross-validation, and marginal likelihood target different quantities and can legitimately rank surrogate structures differently.
assumptions_latex: Each criterion has a declared orientation, loss, data-reuse convention, and parameter-count convention where applicable.
Any asymptotic interpretation is restricted to models satisfying that criterion's regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Criterion rankings are target-specific and are not generally interchangeable across families.
knowledge_statements.title: Criterion Alignment Principle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bayes Factors and Posterior Model Odds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evidence-based comparison of two surrogate structures with explicit model priors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For models \(M_i,M_j\) with finite positive marginal likelihoods, \[BF_{ij}=\frac{p(D\mid M_i)}{p(D\mid M_j)},\qquad \frac{p(M_i\mid D)}{p(M_j\mid D)}=BF_{ij}\frac{p(M_i)}{p(M_j)}.\] Marginal likelihood alone ranks models when their model prior probabilities are equal; posterior model odds additionally incorporate prior odds. A Bayes factor is not defined when a required marginal likelihood is undefined, as can occur with an improper within-model prior whose arbitrary normalizing constant does not cancel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayes factor is a marginal-likelihood ratio; posterior model odds multiply it by prior odds, and improper within-model priors can make the comparison undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(0<p(D\mid M_i),p(D\mid M_j)<\infty\).
Within-model priors are proper, or arbitrary constants provably cancel.
Model prior probabilities are positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Bayes Factors and Posterior Model Odds
Selection-Criterion Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical score representations for likelihood-, penalty-, and predictive-validation-based surrogate selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(M\) with maximized log likelihood \(\ell_M\), parameter count \(d_M\), sample size \(n\), and held-out predictive densities \(p_M(y_i\mid D_{-i})\), standard minimization criteria include \[\operatorname{AIC}(M)=-2\ell_M+2d_M,\qquad \operatorname{BIC}(M)=-2\ell_M+d_M\log n,\] and the predictive log-loss \[\operatorname{CV}(M)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log p_M(y_i\mid D_{-i}).\] Bayesian selection instead compares marginal likelihoods \(p(D\mid M)=\int p(D\mid\theta,M)p(\theta\mid M)\,d\theta\). Criteria from different families are not numerically interchangeable without an explicit orientation and scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common selection families compare fitted likelihood with complexity penalties, held-out predictive loss, or likelihood integrated over parameter priors.
assumptions_latex: All candidate likelihoods refer to the same observed data.
\(d_M\) counts the parameters used by the chosen AIC or BIC convention.
Each Bayesian candidate has a proper marginal likelihood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model selection minimizes \(\operatorname{AIC}\), \(\operatorname{BIC}\), or \(\operatorname{CV}\), or maximizes \(p(D\mid M)\), according to the declared family.

notation.meaning: maximized log likelihood under model M
effective parameter count under the selected convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The criterion formulas are standard and the representation kind fits, but no inspectable source supports them or the conventions governing \(d_M\), likelihood comparability, and cross-validation loss.

children.title: Selection Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of preferred structures to limited data, noise, or candidate-set choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal counterexample showing that deterministic tie-breaking does not create score robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(S(M_1;D)=S(M_2;D)\) at the maximum and a deterministic tie rule selects \(M_1\). For every \(\delta>0\), let \[\widetilde S(M_1;D)=S(M_1;D),\qquad \widetilde S(M_2;D)=S(M_2;D)+\delta.\] This sup-norm perturbation of size \(\delta\) selects \(M_2\). Thus a tie-broken exact score tie has zero positive robustness radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an exact score tie, an arbitrarily small perturbation can reverse a deterministic tie-broken selection.
assumptions_latex: Two candidates attain the same maximal unperturbed score.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tie-broken selection has robustness radius zero under uniform score perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Tie Instability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical diagnostic for sensitivity of a selected surrogate structure to a declared data-perturbation law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D^{*(1)},\ldots,D^{*(B)}\) be resampled or otherwise prespecified perturbations of \(D\). Apply the complete fitting, scoring, and tie-breaking procedure to each and define \[\widehat\pi_k=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B\mathbf1\{\widehat M(D^{*(b)})=M_k\}.\] The vector \((\widehat\pi_1,\ldots,\widehat\pi_K)\) is the empirical selection distribution. Concentration indicates stability under the chosen perturbation law; dispersion indicates instability. These frequencies are not posterior model probabilities unless the perturbation construction explicitly gives them that interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated refitting under declared data perturbations yields selection frequencies; dispersion diagnoses instability but does not automatically represent posterior model uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: Every perturbation uses the same candidate family, fitting rules, score, and tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\pi_k\) estimates the selection probability of \(M_k\) under the declared perturbation law.
knowledge_statements.title: Resampling Selection Stability
Selection Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Score-gap boundary governing robustness of finite-candidate model selection to criterion perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_{(1)}\) and \(M_{(2)}\) have the largest and second-largest unperturbed scores, with gap \(g=S(M_{(1)})-S(M_{(2)})\ge0\). Suppose perturbed scores satisfy \(|\widetilde S(M)-S(M)|\le\varepsilon\) for every candidate. If \(g>2\varepsilon\), then \(M_{(1)}\) remains the unique maximizer of \(\widetilde S\). If \(g\le2\varepsilon\), admissible perturbations can make \(M_{(2)}\) tie or outrank \(M_{(1)}\). Thus \(g=2\varepsilon\) is the sharp worst-case stability boundary for uniformly bounded score perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected model is robust to uniformly bounded score errors exactly beyond the sharp two-error score-gap threshold.
assumptions_latex: The candidate family is finite.
\(M_{(1)}\) is the unique unperturbed maximizer.
Every score perturbation has magnitude at most \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g>2\varepsilon\) guarantees unchanged selection; \(g\le2\varepsilon\) permits a selection reversal or tie.

notation.meaning: gap between the two largest unperturbed scores

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sharp \(2\varepsilon\) perturbation boundary is mathematically coherent and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but the nontrivial claim has no cited evidence.

children.title: Bayesian Model-Uncertainty Synthesis
children.top_down_role: Propagation of uncertainty over parameters and model structures.

children.title: Model Averaging
children.top_down_role: Prediction combined across competing surrogate structures or fitted alternatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixture Prediction Is Not Parameter Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of replacing a predictive mixture by prediction at an averaged parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonlinear parameter-to-law map \(\theta\mapsto P_\theta\), generally \[\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_{\theta_k}\ne P_{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k\theta_k}.\] For example, equal weights on \(P_{-a}=\mathcal N(-a,\sigma^2)\) and \(P_a=\mathcal N(a,\sigma^2)\) produce a two-component mixture, whereas prediction at the averaged mean is \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\); the laws differ for \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging predictive distributions is generally not equivalent to inserting an averaged parameter into one model.
assumptions_latex: The candidate predictive laws share a common measurable response space.
In the example, \(a>0\) and \(\sigma^2>0\).

notation.meaning: predictive law indexed by parameter θ

knowledge_statements.title: Mixture Prediction Is Not Parameter Averaging

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Within-model and between-model moment decomposition for a finite predictive mixture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For mixture weights \(w_k\), component means \(\mu_k\), and component variances \(v_k\), \[\mu=\sum_{k=1}^K w_k\mu_k,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sum_{k=1}^K w_kv_k+\sum_{k=1}^K w_k(\mu_k-\mu)^2.\] The second term vanishes exactly when all positive-weight component means coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite predictive mixture averages component means, while its variance is average within-model variance plus between-model mean disagreement.
assumptions_latex: \(w_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k w_k=1\).
Every positive-weight component has a finite second moment.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Averaged Predictive Moments

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational sampling representation of a finite model-averaged predictive distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\) lie in the \(K\)-simplex and let \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) be component predictive laws. Draw \(J\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(w_1,\ldots,w_K)\), then draw \(Y\sim P_J\) conditionally on \(J\). The marginal law is \[P_w=\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_k.\] Independent repetitions therefore sample exactly from the predictive mixture.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a model according to its averaging weight and then sample from that model to obtain an exact draw from the predictive mixture.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_k\) is a probability law on the common response space.
Sampling kernels for the component laws are available.

notation.meaning: Random index of the selected predictive component.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Mixture Predictive Sampler

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise logarithmic-score comparison with randomized component use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If component predictive densities \(p_k\) share a dominating measure and \(p_w=\sum_kw_kp_k\), then for every \(y\), in the extended-real convention, \[-\log p_w(y)\le\sum_kw_k[-\log p_k(y)].\] Equality holds when all positive-weight component densities have the same value at \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixture's logarithmic loss is no worse pointwise than the weighted average loss from randomly choosing a component.
assumptions_latex: All component laws have densities with respect to one dominating measure.
The weights form a probability vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Score Advantage of Mixture Prediction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite predictive mixture and posterior-probability weighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For candidate models \(M_1,\ldots,M_K\), proper predictive laws \(P_k(\cdot)=P(y_*\in\cdot\mid x,D,M_k)\), priors \(\pi_k\), and finite marginal likelihoods, \[P_w=\sum_{k=1}^Kw_kP_k,\qquad w_k=p(M_k\mid D)=\frac{\pi_kp(D\mid M_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K\pi_jp(D\mid M_j)}.\] The denominator must be finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayesian model averaging forms a finite predictive mixture weighted by normalized posterior model probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le K<\infty\).
Each component predictive law is proper.
The posterior-weight normalizer is finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Bayesian Model-Averaged Predictive Law
Model Averaging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior predictive mixture over a finite collection of surrogate models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M=\{M_1,\ldots,M_K\}\) be mutually indexed surrogate models with posterior probabilities \(w_k=p(M_k\mid D)\). Their model-averaged predictive distribution at \(x\) is \[p(y_*\mid x,D)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\,p(y_*\mid x,D,M_k),\qquad w_k\ge0,\quad\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k=1.\] If model priors \(\pi_k\) and marginal likelihoods exist, then \(w_k=\pi_kp(D\mid M_k)/\sum_j\pi_jp(D\mid M_j)\). Consequently, predictive uncertainty includes both within-model uncertainty and between-model disagreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model averaging forms the predictive law as a posterior-probability-weighted mixture of candidate-model predictive distributions.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le K<\infty\).
Each candidate defines a proper posterior predictive distribution.
The model priors and marginal likelihoods yield a positive finite normalizing constant.

notation.meaning: future response at the query x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite Bayesian model-averaging representation is precise and locally appropriate, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior-weighted averaging over multiple model structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayesian averaging over a discrete collection of surrogate-model structures with structure-specific hyperparameter spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathcal M_i\}\) be a discrete collection of candidate model structures, with structure-conditional hyperparameters \(\theta\), and let \(p(\theta,\mathcal M)=\Pr(\mathcal M)p(\theta\mid\mathcal M)\). Then \(p(\theta,\mathcal M\mid\mathcal D)=\Pr(\mathcal M\mid\mathcal D)p(\theta\mid\mathcal D,\mathcal M)\), where \(\Pr(\mathcal M\mid\mathcal D)\propto \Pr(\mathcal M)p(y\mid x,\mathcal M)\) and \(p(y\mid x,\mathcal M)=\int p(y\mid x,\theta,\mathcal M)p(\theta\mid\mathcal M)\,d\theta\). The model-marginal posterior is \(p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\sum_i\Pr(\mathcal M_i\mid\mathcal D)p(f\mid\mathcal D,\mathcal M_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For discrete competing model structures, each potentially having its own hyperparameter space, the posterior probability of a structure is proportional to its prior probability times its hyperparameter-integrated marginal likelihood. Model averaging mixes the structure-conditional posteriors using these posterior structure probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \{\mathcal M_i\}\text{ is a discrete collection of candidate model structures.}
\theta\text{ is interpreted conditionally on }\mathcal M\text{ and may have structure-dependent dimension.}
p(\theta,\mathcal M)=\Pr(\mathcal M)p(\theta\mid\mathcal M).
p(y\mid x,\mathcal M)=\int p(y\mid x,\theta,\mathcal M)p(\theta\mid\mathcal M)\,d\theta\text{ exists.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\mathcal M\mid\mathcal D)\propto\Pr(\mathcal M)p(y\mid x,\mathcal M),\qquad p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\sum_i\Pr(\mathcal M_i\mid\mathcal D)p(f\mid\mathcal D,\mathcal M_i).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-marginal objective posterior and predictive distribution obtained by integrating posterior uncertainty in objective- and observation-model hyperparameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observed data \(\mathcal D\), Bayesian model averaging marginalizes the objective-model hyperparameters \(\boldsymbol\theta\): \[p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\int p(f\mid\mathcal D,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol\theta.\] Marginalizing both \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and the observation-model hyperparameters \(\phi\) gives \[p(y\mid x,\mathcal D)=\iint p(y\mid x,\phi,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\phi\mid x,\mathcal D,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,\mathrm d\phi\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol\theta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayesian model averaging forms model-marginal objective and predictive distributions by integrating model-conditional distributions over the posterior uncertainty in the objective- and observation-model hyperparameters.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is the observed data.
\(\boldsymbol\theta\) and \(\phi\) denote the hyperparameters of the objective and observation models, respectively.
The displayed conditional distributions and marginalization integrals are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\int p(f\mid\mathcal D,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol\theta,\qquad p(y\mid x,\mathcal D)=\iint p(y\mid x,\phi,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\phi\mid x,\mathcal D,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,\mathrm d\phi\,\mathrm d\boldsymbol\theta.

children.title: Fully Bayesian Parameter Prediction
children.top_down_role: Prediction propagating posterior uncertainty over surrogate parameters.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monte Carlo approximation of a parameter-integrated predictive law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Draw \(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}\) independently from \(p(\theta\mid D,M)\) and form \[\widehat P_S=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S P_{\theta^{(s)}},\qquad P_\theta(\cdot)=p(y_*\in\cdot\mid x,D,M,\theta).\] For every bounded measurable \(h\), \[\int h\,d\widehat P_S\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathbb E[h(y_*)\mid D,M].\] An analogous conclusion holds for posterior samples satisfying an applicable ergodic theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average conditional predictive laws over posterior parameter draws; bounded predictive summaries converge almost surely under independent sampling, with an ergodic analogue for valid MCMC output.
assumptions_latex: The posterior draws are independent for the displayed convergence statement.
\(h\) is bounded and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int h\,d\widehat P_S\to\mathbb E[h(y_*)\mid D,M]\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: conditional predictive law at parameter θ

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior-Draw Predictive Mixture

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parameter-Integrated Prediction Need Not Be Gaussian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of Gaussian closure after integrating uncertain parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y_*\mid\theta,D,M\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,v_\theta)\). The integrated law \(\int\mathcal N(\mu_\theta,v_\theta)p(d\theta\mid D,M)\) is generally a Gaussian mixture rather than a Gaussian distribution. For example, if \(v_\theta=\sigma^2\) and \(\mu_\theta\in\{-a,a\}\) with probabilities \(1/2,1/2\), then for \(a>0\) the predictive law \(\tfrac12\mathcal N(-a,\sigma^2)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(a,\sigma^2)\) is not a single Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating Gaussian conditional predictions over uncertain parameters generally produces a non-Gaussian mixture.
assumptions_latex: The conditional predictive distributions are Gaussian and measurable in \(\theta\).
The parameter posterior is proper.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Integrated Prediction Need Not Be Gaussian

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-induced dependence in joint fully Bayesian prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a future-response vector \(Y_*\), let \(\mu_\theta=\mathbb E[Y_*\mid D,M,\theta]\) and \(V_\theta=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_*\mid D,M,\theta)\). If second moments exist, \[\operatorname{Cov}(Y_*\mid D,M)=\mathbb E_\theta[V_\theta]+\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(\mu_\theta).\] Shared parameter uncertainty can therefore induce cross-query dependence even when a corresponding conditional covariance entry vanishes for every \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint predictive covariance is average conditional covariance plus covariance of the parameter-conditional means.
assumptions_latex: The parameter posterior is proper.
The joint predictive second moment is finite.
The conditional moments are measurable.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiquery Total-Covariance Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction under one fixed structure with surrogate parameters marginalized rather than plugged in.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed structure \(M\), data \(D\), query \(x\), and parameter posterior \(p(d\theta\mid D,M)\), \[P(\,dy_*\mid x,D,M)=\int P_\theta(\,dy_*\mid x,D,M)\,p(d\theta\mid D,M).\] If the required moments exist, \[\mathbb E[y_*\mid D,M]=\mathbb E_\theta[\mu_\theta],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(y_*\mid D,M)=\mathbb E_\theta[v_\theta]+\operatorname{Var}_\theta(\mu_\theta).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian parameter prediction averages conditional predictive laws and includes between-parameter variation in its variance.
assumptions_latex: The parameter posterior is proper.
The conditional predictive kernel is measurable in \(\theta\).
The displayed moments are finite.

notation.meaning: Predictive law conditional on the surrogate parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Integrated Posterior Prediction
Fully Bayesian Parameter Prediction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: GP prediction obtained by integrating covariance, mean, and noise parameters rather than plugging in estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed surrogate structure \(M\), parameter \(\theta\), data \(D\), and query \(x\), fully Bayesian prediction is \[p(y_*\mid x,D,M)=\int p(y_*\mid x,D,M,\theta)\,p(\theta\mid D,M)\,d\theta.\] When the required moments exist, \[\mathbb E[y_*\mid D,M]=\mathbb E_{\theta\mid D,M}[\mu_\theta(x)],\] \[\operatorname{Var}(y_*\mid D,M)=\mathbb E_{\theta\mid D,M}[v_\theta(x)]+\operatorname{Var}_{\theta\mid D,M}(\mu_\theta(x)).\] The second term is parameter-uncertainty variance and is absent from a plug-in predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian prediction integrates conditional GP predictions over the parameter posterior and adds parameter-induced variation to predictive uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: \(p(\theta\mid D,M)\) is proper.
Each conditional predictive law is measurable in \(\theta\).
The displayed first and second moments are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Predictive variance equals expected conditional variance plus variance of the conditional predictive mean.

notation.meaning: surrogate covariance, mean, and noise parameters

children.title: Fully Bayesian Structure Prediction
children.top_down_role: Prediction propagating uncertainty over model structures or representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of Bayesian structure averaging to structures in prior support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any structure \(M\) in a countable candidate family, \(p(M)=0\) implies \(p(M\mid D)=0\) whenever the posterior is defined. Thus marginalization over the declared family propagates uncertainty within its prior support but cannot recover an omitted structure assigned zero prior mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bayesian structure averaging cannot recover a structure excluded from prior support.
assumptions_latex: The structure posterior is well defined.
\(M\) belongs to the countable candidate family.
knowledge_statements.title: Excluded-Structure Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictive uncertainty decomposition under structure and structure-specific parameter uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_{M,\theta}=\mathbb E[y_*\mid D,M,\theta]\) and \(v_{M,\theta}=\operatorname{Var}(y_*\mid D,M,\theta)\). When second moments exist, \[\operatorname{Var}(y_*\mid D)=\mathbb E_M\mathbb E_{\theta\mid M}[v_{M,\theta}]+\mathbb E_M\operatorname{Var}_{\theta\mid M}(\mu_{M,\theta})+\operatorname{Var}_M\!\left(\mathbb E_{\theta\mid M}[\mu_{M,\theta}]\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predictive variance separates into conditional variance, within-structure parameter uncertainty, and between-structure disagreement.
assumptions_latex: The joint posterior over \((M,\theta_M)\) is proper.
The predictive second moment is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Predictive variance is the sum of conditional, within-structure parameter, and between-structure components.

notation.meaning: conditional predictive mean under structure M and parameters θ
conditional predictive variance under structure M and parameters θ

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Structure-and-Parameter Variance Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sampling representation for a posterior predictive law marginalized over structures and their parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given data \(D\), draw \(M^{(s)}\sim p(M\mid D)\), then \(\theta^{(s)}\sim p(\theta_{M^{(s)}}\mid D,M^{(s)})\), and finally \(y_*^{(s)}\sim p(y_*\mid x,D,M^{(s)},\theta^{(s)})\). Each resulting \(y_*^{(s)}\) has the fully structure-integrated posterior predictive law. Independent repetitions give ordinary Monte Carlo estimates of integrable predictive summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a structure, its parameters, and then a response to obtain an exact draw from the fully structure-integrated predictive distribution.
assumptions_latex: The structure posterior and every selected structure-specific parameter posterior are proper.
The relevant conditional distributions admit sampling kernels.
For Monte Carlo estimation, the predictive summary is integrable.

notation.meaning: Posterior draw of a surrogate structure.
Parameter draw conditional on the sampled structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Ancestral Structure-Integrated Predictive Sampling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Posterior Structure Odds and Bayes Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise form of posterior evidence for competing structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For structures \(M_i,M_j\) with positive prior probabilities and finite positive marginal likelihoods, \[\frac{p(M_i\mid D)}{p(M_j\mid D)}=\frac{p(M_i)}{p(M_j)}\frac{p(D\mid M_i)}{p(D\mid M_j)}.\] The marginal-likelihood ratio is a Bayes factor, not itself a posterior probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior structure odds equal prior odds multiplied by the Bayes factor.
assumptions_latex: Both structures have positive prior probability.
Both marginal likelihoods are finite and positive.
The common structure posterior is defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Structure Odds and Bayes Factors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable-structure prediction marginalized over structures and their structure-specific parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a countable family \(\mathcal M\), \[P(dy_*\mid x,D)=\sum_{M\in\mathcal M}p(M\mid D)\int P(dy_*\mid x,D,M,\theta_M)p(d\theta_M\mid D,M),\] where \[p(M\mid D)=\frac{p(M)p(D\mid M)}{\sum_{M'\in\mathcal M}p(M')p(D\mid M')}.\] Thus prediction marginalizes both structure and structure-specific parameter uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian structure prediction averages parameter-integrated predictive laws using normalized posterior structure probabilities.
assumptions_latex: The posterior normalizing constant is finite and positive.
Each selected structure-specific posterior and predictive kernel is proper.
The countable mixture is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(dy_*\mid x,D)=\sum_Mp(M\mid D)\int P(dy_*\mid x,D,M,\theta_M)p(d\theta_M\mid D,M).

notation.meaning: Countable family of candidate surrogate structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Structure-and-Parameter Posterior Prediction
Fully Bayesian Structure Prediction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction marginalized jointly over discrete surrogate structure and structure-specific parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a countable structure family \(\mathcal M\), fully Bayesian structure prediction is \[p(y_*\mid x,D)=\sum_{M\in\mathcal M}p(M\mid D)\int p(y_*\mid x,D,M,\theta_M)p(\theta_M\mid D,M)\,d\theta_M.\] The posterior structure weights satisfy \[p(M\mid D)=\frac{p(M)p(D\mid M)}{\sum_{M'\in\mathcal M}p(M')p(D\mid M')}.\] Thus neither a single structure nor a single parameter estimate is selected for prediction; both uncertainty levels are marginalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fully Bayesian structure prediction averages parameter-integrated predictive laws over posterior uncertainty in the surrogate structure.
assumptions_latex: The structure posterior has a positive finite normalizing constant.
Every structure-specific parameter posterior and predictive law is proper.
The mixture is measurable and convergent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The predictive distribution marginalizes jointly over \(M\) and \(\theta_M\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint marginalization over countable structures and structure-specific parameters is coherent and fits the representation container, but it has no cited source.

children.title: Averaging-Weight Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of predictive uncertainty on weighting choices or poorly supported alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition under which changing averaging weights leaves the predictive law unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For component probability measures \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) and simplex weights \(w,\widetilde w\), \[P_w=P_{\widetilde w}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_{k=1}^K(w_k-\widetilde w_k)P_k=0\] as a finite signed measure. Consequently, distinct weights can produce the same predictive law when the component measures are affinely dependent; if they are affinely independent, equality of the mixtures implies \(w=\widetilde w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weight change is predictively invisible exactly when its signed combination of component laws vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) are probability measures on a common measurable space.
\(w\) and \(\widetilde w\) belong to the probability simplex.

notation.meaning: signed measure induced by the weight perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Predictive Invariance Under Weight Perturbation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Universal Bounds for Averaging-Weight Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case distributional and bounded-summary sensitivity with fixed component laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_w=\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_k\) and \(P_{\widetilde w}=\sum_{k=1}^K\widetilde w_kP_k\), where \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\). Then \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_w,P_{\widetilde w})\le\tfrac12\|w-\widetilde w\|_1.\] For every measurable \(h\) satisfying \(|h|\le B\), \[|\mathbb E_{P_w}h-\mathbb E_{P_{\widetilde w}}h|\le B\|w-\widetilde w\|_1.\] These constants are attainable for mutually singular components and suitable perturbations or test functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With components fixed, predictive total variation and bounded summaries are Lipschitz in the mixture weights, with sharp worst-case constants.
assumptions_latex: All component laws are probability measures on a common measurable space.
Both weight vectors lie in the probability simplex.
\(|h|\le B<\infty\) for the expectation bound.

notation.meaning: Total-variation distance under the supremum-over-events convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Universal Bounds for Averaging-Weight Perturbations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Component-Aware Transport Bound for Weight Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity bound accounting for similarity among mixture components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma(w,\widetilde w)\) be the couplings with row sums \(w\) and column sums \(\widetilde w\). Then \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_w,P_{\widetilde w})\le\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(w,\widetilde w)}\sum_{i,j}\gamma_{ij}d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_i,P_j).\] The bound vanishes when all displaced weight can be coupled between identical component laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transporting weight between similar components can give a tighter sensitivity bound than the universal L1 bound.
assumptions_latex: All component laws share one measurable space.
Both weight vectors are probability vectors.

notation.meaning: Set of couplings of the two weight vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Aware Transport Bound for Weight Perturbations
Averaging-Weight Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case predictive sensitivity of a finite mixture to perturbations of its model weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_w=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_kP_k\) and \(P_{\widetilde w}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widetilde w_kP_k\) share component predictive laws but have probability weights \(w\) and \(\widetilde w\). Then \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_w,P_{\widetilde w})\le\frac12\lVert w-\widetilde w\rVert_1.\] Moreover, for any measurable \(h\) with \(|h|\le B\), \[\left|\mathbb E_{P_w}h-\mathbb E_{P_{\widetilde w}}h\right|\le B\lVert w-\widetilde w\rVert_1.\] Hence posterior predictive conclusions are Lipschitz-sensitive to averaging weights, although the realized discrepancy can be smaller when component predictions overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing mixture weights perturbs the predictive distribution by at most half their L1 distance and bounded predictive summaries proportionally.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) are probability measures on one measurable space.
\(w\) and \(\widetilde w\) lie in the probability simplex.
The test function satisfies \(|h|\le B<\infty\).

notation.meaning: L1 norm on the weight vector

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both mixture-sensitivity inequalities are mathematically correct under the stated total-variation convention, but the nontrivial bounds require an inspectable source.

children.title: Gaussian-Process Formulations
children.top_down_role: Probabilistic latent-function formulations used for surrogate prediction and uncertainty representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian-Process Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-space formulation of a Gaussian-process surrogate with Gaussian observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is a Gaussian process with mean \(m\) and kernel \(k\), written \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\), when every finite vector \((f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))^\top\) is multivariate normal with mean \((m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_n))^\top\) and covariance entries \(k(x_i,x_j)\). With observations \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) and independent \(\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\), the data covariance is \(K+\sigma^2I\), where \(K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian process is a random function whose every finite evaluation vector is jointly Gaussian, commonly paired with independent Gaussian observation noise.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal X\).
\(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
Observation noise is independent of \(f\).

notation.meaning: kernel Gram matrix at observed inputs

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional construction and characterization of a finite-rank Gaussian process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p\), \(w\sim\mathcal N(\mu_w,\Sigma_w)\), and \(f(x)=m_0(x)+\phi(x)^\top w\). Then \(f\) is a Gaussian process with \[m(x)=m_0(x)+\phi(x)^\top\mu_w,\qquad k(x,x')=\phi(x)^\top\Sigma_w\phi(x').\] Conversely, a Gaussian process with mean \(m\) and covariance factorization \(k(x,x')=\phi(x)^\top\Sigma_w\phi(x')\) has the same finite-dimensional laws as \(m(x)+\phi(x)^\top u\), where \(u\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_w)\). For a design of \(n>p\) points, its noiseless Gram matrix has rank at most \(p\) and is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian linear feature model is a finite-rank GP, and every finitely factorized GP covariance has an equivalent Gaussian weight-space representation.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi(x)\in\mathbb R^p\).
\(\Sigma_w\succeq0\).
The converse assumes the displayed finite-rank covariance factorization.

notation.meaning: noiseless Gram matrix on a finite design

children.title: Kriging Formulations
children.top_down_role: Spatial-prediction formulations emphasizing trend, covariance, interpolation, and prediction error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpolation by noise-free kriging and its failure under an observation nugget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At distinct design sites with a strictly positive-definite covariance matrix and no observation nugget, simple, ordinary, or universal kriging reproduces each observed response and has zero latent kriging variance there. If a positive observation-noise covariance is included while predicting the latent field, the weights use \(K+\Sigma\), so exact interpolation and zero latent variance at observed sites generally no longer hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise-free kriging interpolates its data, whereas an observation nugget generally produces smoothing.
assumptions_latex: Design sites are distinct and the noise-free covariance matrix is positive definite.
Trend-unbiasedness constraints are feasible for ordinary or universal kriging.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Kriging Interpolation and Nugget Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best linear unbiased prediction with an unknown constant mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Y=\beta\mathbf1+Z\), where \(\beta\) is fixed and unknown, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z)=C\succ0\), and \(c_*\) is the target cross-covariance. Ordinary kriging minimizes \(C_{**}-2\lambda^\top c_*+\lambda^\top C\lambda\) subject to \(\mathbf1^\top\lambda=1\). Its weights solve \[\begin{pmatrix}C&\mathbf1\\ \mathbf1^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\eta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_*\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] When this system is nonsingular, the predictor is the unique BLUP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary kriging constrains weights to sum to one so prediction remains unbiased for an unknown constant mean.
assumptions_latex: The mean is an unknown constant.
\(C\) is positive definite.
The augmented kriging system is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary-Kriging System

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best linear prediction when the trend is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=m_X+Z\) with known trend \(m_X\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z)=C\succ0\), target trend \(m_*\), and cross-covariance \(c_*\). Among affine predictors \(m_*+\lambda^\top(Y-m_X)\), simple kriging uniquely minimizes mean-squared prediction error at \(\lambda=C^{-1}c_*\). Hence \[\widehat Y_*^{\mathrm{SK}}=m_*+c_*^\top C^{-1}(Y-m_X),\qquad \operatorname{MSPE}=C_{**}-c_*^\top C^{-1}c_*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a known trend, simple kriging uses covariance-inverse weights and has Schur-complement prediction error.
assumptions_latex: The trend is known.
\(C\) is positive definite.
Second moments follow the stated covariance model.
knowledge_statements.title: Simple-Kriging Predictor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form minimized mean-squared prediction error for ordinary kriging with an unknown constant mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the ordinary-kriging assumptions with \(C\succ0\), the minimized prediction-error variance is \[\sigma_{\mathrm{OK}}^2(x_*)=C_{**}-c_*^\top C^{-1}c_*+\frac{(1-\mathbf1^\top C^{-1}c_*)^2}{\mathbf1^\top C^{-1}\mathbf1}.\] The final nonnegative term is the additional error associated with the unknown constant mean and vanishes when \(\mathbf1^\top C^{-1}c_*=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary-kriging error equals simple-kriging error plus a nonnegative correction associated with the unknown constant mean.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is positive definite.
The residual covariance model has finite second moments.
The target and observations share one fixed unknown constant mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary-Kriging Prediction-Error Variance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Reproduction of the Kriging Trend Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproduction property induced by universal-kriging unbiasedness constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If observations contain only a trend \(Y=F\beta\) and kriging weights satisfy \(F^\top\lambda=f_*\), then \[\lambda^\top Y=f_*^\top\beta.\] Thus every trend in the declared basis span is reproduced exactly whenever the constraint is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal-kriging unbiasedness constraints exactly reproduce every function in the declared trend space.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=F\beta\) contains no residual or observation error.
\(F^\top\lambda=f_*\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Reproduction of the Kriging Trend Space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-trend-basis best linear unbiased prediction and prediction-error variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=F\beta+Z\), with \(C=\operatorname{Cov}(Z)\succ0\), full-column-rank \(F\), target basis vector \(f_*\), target cross-covariance \(c_*\), and residual variance \(C_{**}\). Universal-kriging weights solve \[\begin{pmatrix}C&F\\F^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\nu\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_*\\f_*\end{pmatrix}.\] Equivalently they minimize prediction-error variance subject to \(F^\top\lambda=f_*\). Writing \(A=F^\top C^{-1}F\), the minimized variance is \[C_{**}-c_*^\top C^{-1}c_*+(f_*-F^\top C^{-1}c_*)^\top A^{-1}(f_*-F^\top C^{-1}c_*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal kriging is the unique minimum-variance linear predictor unbiased for every trend in a finite basis.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is positive definite.
\(F\) has full column rank.
Trend coefficients are fixed and unknown.
The stated second moments are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat Y_*=\lambda^\top Y\text{ is the unique BLUP subject to }F^\top\lambda=f_*.

notation.meaning: Trend-basis vector at the prediction site.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Kriging BLUP and Block System
Kriging Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal-kriging predictor as the minimum-variance linear unbiased predictor under a covariance model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let observations satisfy \(Y=F\beta+Z\), where \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z)=C\), and let \(f_*\) and \(c_*\) denote the trend vector and covariance vector at \(x_*\). A linear predictor \(\widehat Y_* =\lambda^\top Y\) is unbiased for every \(\beta\) exactly when \(F^\top\lambda=f_*\). Universal kriging chooses \[\lambda_*\in\arg\min_{\lambda:\,F^\top\lambda=f_*}\left(C_{**}-2\lambda^\top c_*+\lambda^\top C\lambda\right).\] When \(C\) is positive definite and the constraint is feasible, this yields the unique best linear unbiased predictor and its minimized mean-squared prediction error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal kriging minimizes prediction variance among linear predictors satisfying the trend-unbiasedness constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is positive definite.
\(F^\top\lambda=f_*\) is feasible.
The trend coefficients \(\beta\) are fixed and unknown.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat Y_*=\lambda_*^\top Y\) is the unique best linear unbiased predictor at \(x_*\).

notation.meaning: covariance between observed residuals and the target residual

children.title: Formulation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections and convention differences between Gaussian-process and kriging viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for an unknown linear trend under a flat prior, complementing the deferred known-mean simple-kriging correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\mid\beta\sim\mathcal N(F\beta,C)\), where \(C\succ0\), and let a latent target \(z_*\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Cov}(y,z_*)=c_*\), \(\mathbb E[z_*\mid\beta]=h_*^\top\beta\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(z_*\mid\beta)=k_{**}\). If \(F\) has full column rank, then under the improper flat prior \(p(\beta)\propto1\), the GP posterior mean is the universal-kriging predictor \[\widehat z_*=h_*^\top\widehat\beta+c_*^\top C^{-1}(y-F\widehat\beta),\qquad \widehat\beta=(F^\top C^{-1}F)^{-1}F^\top C^{-1}y.\] Its posterior variance equals the universal-kriging mean-squared prediction error, \[k_{**}-c_*^\top C^{-1}c_*+(h_*-F^\top C^{-1}c_*)^\top(F^\top C^{-1}F)^{-1}(h_*-F^\top C^{-1}c_*).\] Ordinary kriging is the constant-trend case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating an unknown linear GP trend under a flat prior yields the universal-kriging predictor and prediction-error variance; a constant trend yields ordinary kriging.
assumptions_latex: \(C\succ0\).
\(\operatorname{rank}(F)\) equals the number of trend coefficients.
\(p(\beta)\propto1\).
The GP and kriging formulations use identical covariance, noise, trend, and target conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Kriging and Gaussian-Process Correspondence
Formulation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of simple-kriging prediction and conditional Gaussian-process prediction with known mean and covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\), observe \(y=f_X+\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)\), and set \(C=K+\Sigma\). For a target latent value \(f_*=f(x_*)\), define \(c_*=k(X,x_*)\). The GP conditional mean and variance are \[m(x_*)+c_*^\top C^{-1}(y-m_X),\qquad k(x_*,x_*)-c_*^\top C^{-1}c_*.\] These equal, respectively, the simple-kriging best linear predictor and its mean-squared prediction error under the same known mean and covariance specification. Thus the two formulations differ in interpretation, not in their predictor or uncertainty formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With identical known mean, covariance, and noise, GP conditioning and simple kriging produce the same predictor and prediction-error variance.
assumptions_latex: The GP mean and covariance parameters are known.
\(C=K+\Sigma\) is positive definite.
The kriging and GP formulations use the same target and covariance convention.

children.title: Exact Observations
children.top_down_role: Deterministic evaluations treated as directly revealing the latent response.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency Requirement for Repeated Exact Inputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for repeated noiseless observations of a single-valued latent function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(y_i=f(x_i)\), repeated observations at the same input must agree: \[x_i=x_j\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_i=y_j.\] Unequal repeated values cannot all satisfy a single-valued exact-observation model. Equal duplicates are redundant and produce duplicate rows in an unaggregated noiseless Gram matrix, making it singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated exact observations at one input must agree; unequal repeats contradict the exact model, while equal unaggregated repeats make the noiseless Gram matrix singular.
assumptions_latex: The latent response \(f\) is single-valued.
Observations contain no error term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=x_j\) requires \(y_i=y_j\); otherwise the exact-observation equations are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Requirement for Repeated Exact Inputs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Variance Reduction under Exact Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior covariance ordering for noiseless Gaussian-process observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact observations at \(X\) with nonsingular Gram matrix \(K\), Gaussian conditioning at a finite query set gives \[K_{**\mid X}=K_{**}-K_{*X}K^{-1}K_{X*}\preceq K_{**}.\] If another exact observation is added and the enlarged Gram matrix remains nonsingular, then \[K_{**\mid X\cup\{x_{n+1}\}}\preceq K_{**\mid X}.\] These covariance reductions depend on observation locations, not observed numerical values. Variance is zero at sampled sites and can also vanish elsewhere when the queried Gaussian variable lies in the linear span of the observed variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact Gaussian conditioning reduces covariance in positive-semidefinite order; additional exact data cannot increase it, and the covariance reduction is independent of observed values.
assumptions_latex: The required finite Gaussian conditioning operations are well defined.
The original and enlarged exact-observation Gram matrices are nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Conditional covariance at query sites after exact observations at \(X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Variance Reduction under Exact Conditioning

assumptions_latex: \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) on an input set \(\mathcal X\).
The distinct design sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal X\) have nonsingular Gram matrix \(K=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^n\).

notation.meaning: Prior covariance vector between a query and the design sites.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noiseless scalar Gaussian-process observations with an invertible design Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Observations are exact when \(y_i=f(x_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), with no observation-error term. Writing \(m_X=(m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_n))^\top\), the conditional process has mean and covariance
\[
m_n(x)=m(x)+k_x^\top K^{-1}(y-m_X),\qquad k_n(x,x')=k(x,x')-k_x^\top K^{-1}k_{x'}.
\]
Consequently, conditioning interpolates every datum and eliminates posterior uncertainty at each sampled site: \(m_n(x_i)=y_i\) and \(k_n(x_i,x_i)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact observations equal latent function values. A nonsingular noiseless Gaussian-process posterior interpolates all data and has zero posterior variance at every sampled site.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Observations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and noiseless interpolation formulas fit the leaf and are mathematically coherent, but no inspectable citation supports them.

children.title: Homoscedastic Observations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Replication Reduction under Homoscedastic Gaussian Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency and effective variance of replicated observations at one input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y_j=f(x)+\varepsilon_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,r\), with \(\varepsilon_j\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) and known \(\sigma^2\), then the likelihood for \(f(x)\) depends on the replicates only through \(\bar Y\), and \(\bar Y\mid f(x)\sim\mathcal N(f(x),\sigma^2/r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The replicate mean is sufficient for the latent value and has noise variance divided by the replicate count.
assumptions_latex: Errors are conditionally independent Gaussian variables with common known variance \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Replication Reduction under Homoscedastic Gaussian Noise

assumptions_latex: \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) on \(\mathcal X\).
Observation errors are independent of \(f\) and of one another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data covariance is \(K+\sigma^2I_n\), so every site has the same observation-noise variance \(\sigma^2\).

notation.meaning: Observed responses at the design sites.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent additive Gaussian noise with input-independent variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Observations are homoscedastic when
\[
y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
\]
for a single constant \(\sigma^2\geq0\). Conditional on the design sites, \(y\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K+\sigma^2I_n)\). For \(\sigma^2>0\), the latent posterior mean is \(m(x)+k_x^\top(K+\sigma^2I_n)^{-1}(y-m_X)\), while the predictive variance of a new noisy response equals the latent posterior variance plus \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homoscedastic observations add independent Gaussian errors having one common variance at every input; noisy-response prediction includes that same variance.

children.title: Nugget Interpretation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interpretations of small-scale variation as measurement noise, numerical error, or regularization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance decomposition and interpretation-dependent prediction targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and let \(\eta(x)\) be independent zero-mean variation with \(\operatorname{Cov}(\eta(x),\eta(x'))=\tau^2\mathbf1\{x=x'\}\). Then \(h(x)=g(x)+\eta(x)\) has covariance \(k_h(x,x')=k(x,x')+\tau^2\mathbf1\{x=x'\}\). Prediction of \(g(x_*)\) excludes a new nugget term, whereas prediction of a new \(h(x_*)\) includes it. Pure numerical jitter changes neither stochastic target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic nugget is independent small-scale variation added to a smooth process; its inclusion in predictive variance depends on the target, whereas numerical jitter changes no stochastic target.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(\eta\) are independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Latent-Process and Stochastic-Nugget Decomposition

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a positive-semidefinite covariance matrix and \(\tau^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only the noise interpretation adds \(\tau^2\) to the variance of a future observed response; numerical jitter does not alter the stated data-generating model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard distinction between statistical nugget and computational jitter
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes observational, microscale, and purely numerical uses of a diagonal nugget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The same matrix replacement \(K\mapsto K+\tau^2I_n\) has distinct regimes. In an observation-noise regime, \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\tau^2\). In a microscale regime, \(\tau^2\) represents unresolved variation independent across distinct sites. In a numerical-jitter regime, \(\tau^2\) is introduced only to stabilize factorization of \(K\). The first two regimes change the stochastic model; numerical jitter does not justify adding \(\tau^2\) to the modeled variance of a future physical observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal nugget may represent measurement noise, unresolved microscale variation, or numerical stabilization; these interpretations have different predictive consequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Nugget Interpretation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle appropriately distinguishes statistical nuggets from numerical jitter, but these interpretation and prediction claims require an inspectable specialized source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spurious Smoothing under a Positive Noise Assumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by imposing positive observation noise on exact evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\), \(K\succ0\), and \(y_i=f_0(x_i)\), while inference fixes \(\sigma^2>0\). Then \(m_n(X)=m_X+K(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}(y-m_X)\) and \(K_n(X,X)=K-K(K+\sigma^2I)^{-1}K\succ0\). Thus the fitted latent posterior generally neither interpolates the exact data nor has zero variance at their sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating exact values as noisy causes unnecessary smoothing and residual uncertainty at observed sites.
assumptions_latex: \(K\succ0\).
\(\sigma^2>0\) is fixed in the fitted model.
The observations are exact latent values.

notation.meaning: Fitted posterior covariance of the latent response.

assumptions_latex: True data satisfy \(y_i=f_0(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)>0\).
A fitted Gaussian-process model instead imposes \(y_i=f(x_i)\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fitted posterior satisfies \(m_n(x_i)=y_i\) and \(k_n(x_i,x_i)=0\), although \(y_i\neq f_0(x_i)\) with positive probability.

notation.meaning: Posterior mean and covariance under the misspecified exact model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by fitting a noiseless interpolator to genuinely noisy evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y_i=f_0(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where independent errors satisfy \(\mathbb P(\varepsilon_i\neq0)>0\), but inference uses an exact-observation Gaussian process with nonsingular \(K\). Then \(m_n(x_i)=y_i\) and \(k_n(x_i,x_i)=0\). Thus the fitted model is certain about a noisy realization rather than the latent value \(f_0(x_i)\). Moreover, two unequal responses assigned to the same input cannot both be exact values of a single-valued function, exposing the misspecification directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating noisy evaluations as exact forces interpolation and zero uncertainty at sampled sites; unequal replicates at one site directly contradict the fitted model.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and stated consequences of fitting a noiseless model to noisy data are coherent, but no source supports the misspecification claim.

children.title: Replicated Evaluation Summaries
children.top_down_role: Location-level response and variability summaries derived from repeated evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scope in which the site mean, sample variance, and count preserve the replication likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{ir_i}\) are iid \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,v_i)\), then
\[
L_i(\mu_i,v_i;y_i)=(2\pi v_i)^{-r_i/2}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(r_i-1)S_i^2+r_i(\bar Y_i-\mu_i)^2}{2v_i}\right].
\]
Hence \((\bar Y_i,S_i^2,r_i)\) is sufficient for \((\mu_i,v_i)\). If \(v_i\) is known, \(\bar Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,v_i/r_i)\) is sufficient for \(\mu_i\). For a general non-Gaussian replication family, these moment summaries need not be sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under iid Gaussian replication, the site mean, sample variance, and count preserve the likelihood; this sufficiency generally fails outside the Gaussian family.
assumptions_latex: Y_{ij}\mid x_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu_i,v_i)
r_i\ge2
v_i>0
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Replication Factorization and Sufficiency

assumptions_latex: At site \(x_i\), replications \(Y_{ij}=\mu(x_i)+\epsilon_{ij}\) are conditionally independent for \(j=1,\ldots,r_i\).
\(\mathbb E(\epsilon_{ij}\mid x_i)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{ij}\mid x_i)=v(x_i)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E(\bar Y_i\mid x_i)=\mu(x_i)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_i\mid x_i)=v(x_i)/r_i\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary independent-replication mean and variance identities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sitewise sufficient summaries for independent finite-variance simulation replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each site \(x_i\), summarize \(r_i\geq2\) independent evaluations by
\[
\bar Y_i=\frac1{r_i}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}Y_{ij},\qquad S_i^2=\frac1{r_i-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}(Y_{ij}-\bar Y_i)^2.
\]
Then \(\bar Y_i\) is unbiased for \(\mu(x_i)\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_i\mid x_i)=v(x_i)/r_i\), and \(S_i^2\) is unbiased for \(v(x_i)\). Under conditionally Gaussian replication noise, \(\bar Y_i\) and \(S_i^2\) are conditionally independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicates yield a site mean with variance reduced by the replication count and an unbiased within-site estimator of intrinsic simulation variance.
knowledge_statements.title: Replicated Evaluation Summaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The moment identities and Gaussian independence statement are standard, but the scope note's description of these summaries as sufficient under merely finite-variance noise is not generally justified, and no source is cited.

children.title: Stochastic Kriging Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Kriging representations incorporating intrinsic simulation or sampling variability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional assumptions required to interpret stochastic-kriging moments as a full posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The stochastic-kriging linear predictor and its mean-squared prediction error depend only on the specified first and second moments and remain BLUP quantities without Gaussian errors. They equal a conditional posterior mean and covariance, with a Gaussian predictive law, only when the latent process and site-mean errors are jointly Gaussian. For example, Gaussian errors and variance-matched standardized Student-\(t_\nu\) errors with \(\nu>2\) can produce the same BLUP covariance inputs but different predictive tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second moments suffice for the stochastic-kriging BLUP, but a Gaussian posterior interpretation requires joint Gaussianity; covariance-matched non-Gaussian errors have different tails.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E(\bar Y)=m_X
\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y)=K+D
\operatorname{Cov}(\mu(x),\bar Y)=k_x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{BLUP validity is second-order, whereas Gaussian posterior validity requires joint Gaussianity}.

notation.meaning: Cross-covariance between the target response and site means.

knowledge_statements.title: BLUP–Posterior Interpretation Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of positive intrinsic noise and increasing replication on stochastic-kriging behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With known intrinsic variances \(v_i>0\), let \(D(r)=\operatorname{diag}(v_i/r_i)\). For finite replication, the latent-response predictor generally does not interpolate \(\bar Y_i\), and its latent prediction variance at \(x_i\) need not vanish. If every \(r_i\to\infty\), then \(D(r)\to0\); when \(K\succ0\), the stochastic-kriging mean and covariance formulas converge algebraically to their noise-free kriging counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite replication yields smoothing rather than interpolation; as all replication counts diverge, stochastic kriging approaches noise-free kriging.
assumptions_latex: v_i>0
D(r)=\operatorname{diag}(v_i/r_i)
K\succ0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(r)\to0\text{ as }\min_i r_i\to\infty,\text{ yielding the noise-free kriging limit}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unknown linear trend with known process and intrinsic-noise covariance parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu(x)=h(x)^\top\beta+Z(x)\), let \(Z\) have covariance kernel \(k\), and set \(C=K+D\). For \(H=(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))^\top\), assume \(C\succ0\) and \(H^\top C^{-1}H\) is nonsingular. Then
\[
\widehat\beta=(H^\top C^{-1}H)^{-1}H^\top C^{-1}\bar Y,
\]
\[
\widehat\mu(x)=h(x)^\top\widehat\beta+k_x^\top C^{-1}(\bar Y-H\widehat\beta).
\]
This is the best linear unbiased predictor among predictors linear in \(\bar Y\) under the stated second-moment model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal stochastic kriging combines generalized least squares for an unknown trend with covariance-weighted prediction of the residual process.
assumptions_latex: \mu(x)=h(x)^\top\beta+Z(x)
\operatorname{Cov}(Z_X)=K
\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y-\mu_X)=D
C=K+D\succ0
H^\top C^{-1}H\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.title: Universal Stochastic-Kriging Predictor

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) and \(\bar Y_i=\mu(x_i)+\eta_i\).
The errors \(\eta_i\) are independent with known variances \(v_i/r_i\) and are independent of \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioning replaces the usual homoscedastic noise matrix by \(D=\operatorname{diag}(v_i/r_i)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian stochastic kriging with known sitewise intrinsic variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar Y=(\bar Y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_n)^\top\), \(m_X=(m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_n))^\top\), and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(v_i/r_i)\). The stochastic-kriging posterior for the latent mean response has
\[
m_n(x)=m(x)+k_x^\top(K+D)^{-1}(\bar Y-m_X),
\]
\[
k_n(x,x')=k(x,x')-k_x^\top(K+D)^{-1}k_{x'}.
\]
Hence replication enters through the reduced observation variances \(v_i/r_i\), allowing distinct precision at different sites.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic kriging conditions a Gaussian-process mean surface on replicated site means whose heterogeneous noise variances are intrinsic variances divided by replication counts.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Kriging Surrogates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stochastic-kriging representation fits the leaf, but the displayed Gaussian posterior formulas require Gaussian sample-mean errors, whereas the formal assumptions specify only independence and known variances. An authoritative source is also absent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential kriging with noise-adjusted expected improvement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-domain kriging representation and a sequential expected-improvement criterion adjusted for experimental noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For continuous $x\in\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, represent the response surface by
$$\mu(x)=\sum_{f\in\mathcal F}\theta_f\phi_f(x)+Z(x)+\varepsilon,$$
where
$$\operatorname{Cov}(Z(x),Z(x'))=\beta\exp\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i(x_i-x_i')^2\right).$$
Let $\bar Y^n(x)$ and $\sigma^n(x)$ denote the kriging predictive mean and standard deviation after $n$ observations. Define $u^n(x)=-(\bar Y^n(x)+\sigma^n(x))$ and choose
$$x^{**}\in\arg\max_{x\in\{x^1,\ldots,x^n\}}u^n(x).$$
With $\Delta_n(x)=\bar Y^n(x^{**})-\bar Y^n(x)$, the stated noise-adjusted expected improvement is
$${\mathbb E}^n I(x)=\left[\Delta_n(x)\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_n(x)}{\sigma^n(x)}\right)+\sigma^n(x)\phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_n(x)}{\sigma^n(x)}\right)\right]\left(1-\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2,n}(x)+\sigma_\varepsilon^2}}\right).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kriging combines a fitted feature-based trend, a spatially correlated residual process, and experimental noise. Sequential sampling may use analytically evaluated expected improvement multiplied by a factor that discounts uncertainty attributable to experimental noise.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d
\operatorname{Cov}(Z(x),Z(x'))=\beta\exp\!\left(-\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i(x_i-x_i')^2\right)
\beta\ge 0,\quad \alpha_i\ge 0
\sigma^n(x)>0
x^{**}\in\arg\max_{x\in\{x^1,\ldots,x^n\}}[-(\bar Y^n(x)+\sigma^n(x))]
