children.title: Intrinsic-Variance Estimation
children.top_down_role: Estimation of location-dependent sampling variability from replicated outputs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sampling Distribution and Precision of Sample Variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-replication uncertainty of the intrinsic-variance estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For iid Gaussian replications with variance \(v_i\),
\[
\frac{(r_i-1)S_i^2}{v_i}\sim\chi^2_{r_i-1},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(S_i^2\mid x_i)=\frac{2v_i^2}{r_i-1}.
\]
More generally, for iid replications with fourth central moment \(\mu_{4,i}<\infty\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}(S_i^2\mid x_i)=\frac1{r_i}\left(\mu_{4,i}-\frac{r_i-3}{r_i-1}v_i^2\right).
\]
If the fourth central moment is infinite, \(S_i^2\) need not have finite variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Gaussian replication, sample variance has an exact scaled chi-square law; generally its precision depends on the fourth moment and may be arbitrarily poor or infinite.
assumptions_latex: Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{ir_i}\text{ are iid conditional on }x_i
r_i\ge2
v_i=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid x_i)<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{(r_i-1)S_i^2}{v_i}\sim\chi^2_{r_i-1}\text{ under Gaussian replication, with the displayed general variance formula when }\mu_{4,i}<\infty.

notation.meaning: Fourth central moment of a replication at site i.

assumptions_latex: At site \(x_i\), \(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{ir_i}\) are conditionally independent and identically distributed.
\(r_i\geq2\) and \(v(x_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid x_i)<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased sitewise variance estimation from independent replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\widehat v_i=S_i^2=\frac1{r_i-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}(Y_{ij}-\bar Y_i)^2.
\]
For conditionally independent and identically distributed replications with finite variance, \(\mathbb E(S_i^2\mid x_i)=v(x_i)\). Therefore \(S_i^2/r_i\) estimates the sampling variance of \(\bar Y_i\). If replication counts are small, \(S_i^2\) may be highly variable; smoothing or a separate positive variance model changes the estimator and must be represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The within-site sample variance unbiasedly estimates intrinsic simulation variance, and dividing it by replication count estimates the variance of the site mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Variance Estimation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The estimator and unbiasedness property are correctly scoped to iid finite-variance replications and fit the leaf, but no citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Sparse-Replication Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits arising when replication is insufficient to characterize intrinsic variance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision boundary when intrinsic variance is estimated from only a few Gaussian replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under iid Gaussian replication,
\[
\frac{(r_i-1)S_i^2}{v_i}\sim\chi^2_{r_i-1},\qquad \frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S_i^2\mid x_i)}}{v_i}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{r_i-1}}.
\]
Thus \(r_i=2\) supplies one variance degree of freedom and relative standard deviation \(\sqrt2\). The relative uncertainty vanishes only as \(r_i\to\infty\); treating \(S_i^2/r_i\) as known when \(r_i\) is small ignores material variance-estimation uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With few replications, the plug-in intrinsic-variance estimate is extremely noisy; its relative uncertainty disappears only as replication grows without bound.
assumptions_latex: Y_{ij}\mid x_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal N(\mu_i,v_i)
r_i\ge2
v_i>0

assumptions_latex: Each distinct design site has only one evaluation, so \(r_i=1\).
The intrinsic variances \(v(x_i)\) are otherwise unknown.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No within-site estimator \(S_i^2\) exists, so the diagonal covariance \(D=\operatorname{diag}(v(x_i)/r_i)\) is not identifiable from replication summaries alone.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sample variance is undefined with one observation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability boundary for sitewise intrinsic variance without replication or structural pooling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(r_i=1\), the statistic \(S_i^2=(r_i-1)^{-1}\sum_j(Y_{ij}-\bar Y_i)^2\) is undefined and supplies no sitewise estimate of \(v(x_i)\). Consequently, stochastic kriging cannot construct \(D=\operatorname{diag}(v(x_i)/r_i)\) from within-site replication summaries alone. Estimation then requires additional structure, such as known noise variances, replicated sites, parametric variance restrictions, or borrowing information across inputs; without such structure, local mean variation and observation variation cannot be separated empirically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one evaluation per site, within-site variance is unavailable; intrinsic noise requires known variances, replication, or a variance model that pools information.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Replication Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary at one replication per site is precisely qualified by the absence of additional structure, but its stochastic-kriging identifiability interpretation lacks a supporting source.

assumptions_latex: \(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) and \(k_m:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The latent response mean is represented by \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k_m)\), with observations centered conditionally at \(f(x)\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process representation of the latent conditional mean in a heteroscedastic observation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A latent mean process is a random function \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k_m)\) and
\[
\mathbb E(Y\mid x,f,g)=f(x),
\]
where \(g\) denotes any latent variance process. Thus every finite vector \((f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n))^\top\) is multivariate normal with mean \((m(x_1),\ldots,m(x_n))^\top\) and covariance \((k_m(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^n\). The process represents uncertainty about the conditional response mean, not observation noise itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A latent mean process is a Gaussian-process random function that supplies the conditional center of a heteroscedastic observation model.
knowledge_statements.title: Latent Mean Processes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition cleanly separates the latent conditional-mean process from observation noise and fits the leaf, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Latent Variance Processes
children.top_down_role: Surrogate representations for input-dependent observation variability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconjugacy of the Gaussian Log-Variance Process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy boundary for latent log-variance inference under Gaussian observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Y_i\mid f_i,g_i\sim\mathcal N(f_i,e^{g_i})\), residuals \(r_i=y_i-f_i\), and \(g_X\sim\mathcal N(q_X,K_v)\) with \(K_v\succ0\),
\[
p(g_X\mid f_X,y_X)\propto\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(g_X-q_X)^\top K_v^{-1}(g_X-q_X)-\tfrac12\sum_i\{g_i+r_i^2e^{-g_i}\}\right].
\]
The nonquadratic terms \(r_i^2e^{-g_i}\) make this posterior non-Gaussian in general, so exact Gaussian-process conjugacy is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential variance link produces a non-Gaussian posterior over log variance, requiring explicit approximation or integration for inference.
assumptions_latex: Y_i\mid f_i,g_i\sim\mathcal N(f_i,e^{g_i})
g_X\sim\mathcal N(q_X,K_v)
K_v\succ0
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconjugacy of the Gaussian Log-Variance Process

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prior moments induced by the exponential link.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(g\sim\mathcal{GP}(q,k_v)\) and \(v(x)=\exp(g(x))\), then
\[
\mathbb E[v(x)]=\exp\!\left(q(x)+\tfrac12k_v(x,x)\right),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(v(x),v(x'))=\mathbb E[v(x)]\mathbb E[v(x')]\left(\exp(k_v(x,x'))-1\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponentiating a Gaussian log-variance process gives a lognormal positive field with explicit moments and a variance-induced mean shift.
assumptions_latex: g\sim\mathcal{GP}(q,k_v)
v(x)=\exp(g(x))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[v(x)]=e^{q(x)+k_v(x,x)/2}\text{ and the displayed lognormal covariance identity holds}.

notation.meaning: Mean function of the log-variance process.
Covariance kernel of the log-variance process.

assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)\) is a fixed positive link.
\(g\sim\mathcal{GP}(q,k_v)\) on \(\mathcal X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-link construction of an input-dependent latent observation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A latent variance process consists of \(g\sim\mathcal{GP}(q,k_v)\) together with a fixed link \(h:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)\). It defines
\[
v(x)=h(g(x))=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x,f,g).
\]
A common log-variance specification is \(h(t)=\exp(t)\), giving \(\log v(x)=g(x)\). Positivity follows from the range of \(h\), while \(k_v\) controls how information about noise magnitude is shared across inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A latent Gaussian process transformed by a positive link, commonly the exponential, represents input-dependent observation variance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-link latent variance-process definition is coherent and appropriately scoped, but no authoritative source or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latent Gaussian-process representation of heteroscedastic variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input-dependent observation variances at replicated unique design sites, including positivity and full-observation-level failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the unique design sites \(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n\), let \(A_n=\operatorname{Diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) and introduce one latent variance quantity per site, collected in \(\Delta_n\), with \[\Delta_n\sim\mathcal N_n\!\left(0,\nu_{(\delta)}K_{(\delta)}\right),\qquad K_{(\delta)}=C_{(\delta)}+g_{(\delta)}A_n^{-1}.\] The smoothed sitewise noise parameters are \[\Lambda_n=C_{(\delta)}K_{(\delta)}^{-1}\Delta_n.\] When \(g_{(\delta)}=0\) and \(C_{(\delta)}\) is invertible, \(\Lambda_n=\Delta_n\), so the smoothed values interpolate the latents. The untransformed Gaussian construction can produce negative latent or smoothed variance values; positivity can instead be imposed by thresholding or by modeling log variances and exponentiating. Introducing latents at all \(N\) observations rather than only the \(n\) unique sites creates identifiability and numerical-stability challenges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign one latent variance quantity to each unique replicated design site and smooth the latents with a second Gaussian process. A zero variance-process nugget yields interpolation when the correlation matrix is invertible. Because an untransformed Gaussian model can produce negative variances, positivity requires thresholding or a log-variance formulation. Using one latent per raw observation instead of per unique site creates identifiability and numerical-stability problems.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n\) are the unique design sites, with replication counts \(a_i\geq 1\).
\(A_n=\operatorname{Diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), \(g_{(\delta)}\geq 0\), \(\nu_{(\delta)}>0\), and \(K_{(\delta)}=C_{(\delta)}+g_{(\delta)}A_n^{-1}\) is invertible.
For the interpolation conclusion, \(g_{(\delta)}=0\) and \(C_{(\delta)}\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda_n=C_{(\delta)}K_{(\delta)}^{-1}\Delta_n\) defines smoothed input-dependent noise parameters, with \(g_{(\delta)}=0\Rightarrow\Lambda_n=\Delta_n\) under invertibility; positivity needs thresholding or a log-variance transformation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-design Schur-complement test and process-level validity requirement for a joint mean–log-variance Gaussian process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a common finite design, let
\[
\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}K_f&K_{fg}\\K_{fg}^{\top}&K_g\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If \(K_f\succ0\), then
\[
\Sigma\succeq0\iff K_g-K_{fg}^{\top}K_f^{-1}K_{fg}\succeq0.
\]
A proposed block kernel defines a joint process only if the corresponding block Gram matrix is positive semidefinite for every finite choice of inputs; validity on one design alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-kernel is admissible only when every finite block Gram matrix is positive semidefinite; on a fixed design this is equivalent to the stated Schur-complement condition.
assumptions_latex: K_f\succ0
K_g=K_g^\top
\Sigma=\Sigma^\top
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Covariance Admissibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional law induced by a valid jointly Gaussian mean–variance coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
\begin{pmatrix}f_X\\g_X\end{pmatrix}\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}m_X\\q_X\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}K_f&K_{fg}\\K_{fg}^{\top}&K_g\end{pmatrix}\right),\qquad K_f\succ0,
\]
then
\[
g_X\mid f_X\sim\mathcal N\!\left(q_X+K_{fg}^{\top}K_f^{-1}(f_X-m_X),K_g-K_{fg}^{\top}K_f^{-1}K_{fg}\right).
\]
Thus nonzero cross-covariance induces conditional borrowing between response level and log variance. If \(k_{fg}(x,x')=0\) for every input pair, the jointly Gaussian processes are independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint Gaussian coupling shifts the conditional log-variance field according to latent response values through the cross-covariance.
assumptions_latex: (f_X,g_X)\text{ is jointly Gaussian}
K_f\succ0
\Sigma\succeq0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_X\mid f_X\text{ has the displayed Gaussian conditional law}.

assumptions_latex: The pair \((f,g)\) is a jointly Gaussian process on \(\mathcal X\).
Conditional on \((f,g)\), observations are independent with \(Y_i\mid f,g\sim\mathcal N(f(x_i),\exp(g(x_i)))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mean-variance dependence is encoded by the cross-covariance kernel \(k_{fg}(x,x')=\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),g(x'))\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-Gaussian coupling of latent mean and log-variance processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any finite design, represent the latent vectors by
\[
\begin{pmatrix}f_X\\g_X\end{pmatrix}\sim\mathcal N\left(\begin{pmatrix}m_X\\q_X\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}K_f&K_{fg}\\K_{fg}^\top&K_g\end{pmatrix}\right),
\]
where the block covariance is positive semidefinite. Conditional observations satisfy \(Y_i\mid f,g\sim\mathcal N(f(x_i),\exp(g(x_i)))\). The model is uncoupled exactly when \(K_{fg}=0\), which for jointly Gaussian processes makes \(f_X\) and \(g_X\) independent; nonzero \(K_{fg}\) permits response level and noise magnitude to vary dependently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid joint Gaussian-process block covariance couples latent mean and log-variance; zero cross-covariance gives prior independence.

children.title: Coupling Identifiability Limits
children.top_down_role: Regimes where data cannot reliably distinguish mean variation from variance variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order nonidentifiability of an unrestricted latent covariance and diagonal intrinsic-noise covariance from unreplicated Gaussian observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_X=f_X+\varepsilon_X\), where \(f_X\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K_f)\), \(\varepsilon_X\sim\mathcal N(0,D)\), \(f_X\perp\!\!\perp\varepsilon_X\), and \(D\) is diagonal. Then \(Y_X\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K_f+D)\). If a nonzero diagonal matrix \(A\) satisfies \(K_f+A\succeq0\) and \(D-A\succeq0\), the distinct decompositions \((K_f,D)\) and \((K_f+A,D-A)\) induce the same observation law. Thus unreplicated data identify at most the covariance sum unless kernel restrictions, known noise, replication, or other structure fixes the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unreplicated Gaussian observations can reveal only the sum of latent and intrinsic-noise covariance, so admissible diagonal variance can be transferred between the components without changing the observation law.
assumptions_latex: f_X\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K_f)
\varepsilon_X\sim\mathcal N(0,D)
f_X\perp\!\!\perp\varepsilon_X
D\text{ is diagonal}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (K_f,D)\text{ is not identifiable whenever a nonzero admissible diagonal transfer }A\text{ exists}.

notation.meaning: Finite-design covariance of the latent response process.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Design Signal–Noise Covariance Confounding

assumptions_latex: At distinct sites, only one Gaussian observation \(y_i\) is available.
The latent values \(f_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i=g(x_i)\) are unrestricted at the observed sites.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observation likelihood alone does not identify separate mean and variance surfaces and is unbounded along \(f_i=y_i\), \(g_i\to-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Likelihood-level nonidentifiability with unreplicated data and unrestricted latent site values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Y_i\mid f_i,g_i\sim\mathcal N(f_i,\exp(g_i))\), the sitewise log-likelihood, up to an additive constant, is
\[
\ell_i(f_i,g_i)=-\frac12\left[g_i+(y_i-f_i)^2\exp(-g_i)\right].
\]
Setting \(f_i=y_i\) and sending \(g_i\to-\infty\) gives \(\ell_i\to+\infty\). Hence one unrestricted mean value and one unrestricted variance value cannot be identified from a single response at each site. Replication, informative priors, smoothness restrictions, or parametric coupling is required to regularize the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one response per site and unrestricted latent values, mean and variance are not separately likelihood-identifiable; the Gaussian likelihood can diverge at zero residual and vanishing variance.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Identifiability Limits

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within-site differences cancel the latent mean and identify intrinsic variance at the population level.

\mathbb E(\varepsilon_{ij}\mid x_i)=0

children.title: Replication-versus-Exploration Design
children.top_down_role: Sequential allocation between variance estimation and new-location exploration.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information losses caused by excluding either action class from a heteroscedastic sequential design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A policy restricted to replication cannot learn the latent response or noise behavior at unsampled locations. Conversely, if every sampled input is new and the observation model permits unrestricted location-dependent mean and noise variance, one response per input cannot separately identify those two local quantities without structural pooling or external variance information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication alone cannot explore new regions, while one observation per new site cannot nonparametrically separate a local mean from local noise variance.
assumptions_latex: The domain contains unsampled locations.
Both the latent response and observation variance may vary with location.
No exact external noise-variance information is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Neither replication-only nor unrestricted one-observation-per-site exploration is universally information-sufficient.}
knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Replication and Pure-Exploration Boundaries
Replication-versus-Exploration Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step allocation rule for a noisy surrogate with location-dependent observation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given data \(D_t\), evaluated locations \(R_t\), candidate set \(X_t\), and a posterior utility \(U(D)\), compute \(V_t(x)=\mathbb E[U(D_t\cup\{(x,Y_x)\})-U(D_t)\mid D_t]\). Define the best replication and exploration values by \(V_t^{\mathrm{rep}}=\max_{x\in R_t}V_t(x)\) and \(V_t^{\mathrm{new}}=\max_{x\in X_t\setminus R_t}V_t(x)\). Sample a maximizer from the class having larger value, update both the latent-response and noise-variance posteriors, and repeat until the evaluation budget is exhausted; output the prescribed posterior decision, such as the minimizer of the posterior mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each step, compare the expected posterior utility of replicating an evaluated location with that of sampling a new location, then choose the better action.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_x\) has a specified posterior predictive distribution conditional on \(D_t\).
The one-step expectations and maxima defining \(V_t^{\mathrm{rep}}\) and \(V_t^{\mathrm{new}}\) exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in X_t}V_t(x)\), classified as replication when \(x_{t+1}\in R_t\) and exploration otherwise.

children.title: Non-Gaussian Value Observations
children.top_down_role: Discrete, heavy-tailed, bounded, or otherwise non-Gaussian response observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for valid direct-value likelihood selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fitted direct-value likelihood is incompatible with the true law if it assigns zero probability to an observable set having positive true probability. Also, the assertion \(g(\mathbb E[Y_i\mid f])=f(x_i)\) is distinct from asserting that \(f(x_i)\) is a location parameter; interchanging them generally changes the likelihood and posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The likelihood must match the value support, and a linked mean must not be confused with a location parameter.
assumptions_latex: True and fitted conditional laws share a measurable observation space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_0(Y\in A\mid f)>0=P_\theta(Y\in A\mid f)\Rightarrow\text{likelihood misspecification}.
knowledge_statements.title: Support and Link Misspecification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior form under a non-Gaussian value likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f_X\sim\mathcal N(m_X,K)\) and positive likelihood factors \(p_i(y_i\mid f_i)\), \(p(f_X\mid y)\propto\exp[-\tfrac12(f_X-m_X)^\top K^{-1}(f_X-m_X)]\prod_i p_i(y_i\mid f_i)\). This posterior is Gaussian exactly when the summed log-likelihood is affine-quadratic in \(f_X\); otherwise Gaussian conditioning formulas are not exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely nonquadratic value likelihood destroys the usual closed-form Gaussian-process update.
assumptions_latex: \(K\succ0\).
Likelihood factors are positive on the relevant support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \log p(f_X\mid y)\text{ is quadratic iff the posterior is Gaussian.}

notation.meaning: Latent response vector at observed inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Gaussian Conjugacy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative direct-value likelihoods indexed by a latent response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Representative direct-value models include \(Y_i\mid f\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(e^{f(x_i)})\) or \(\operatorname{NegBin}(\mu=e^{f(x_i)},\kappa)\) for counts, \(Y_i\mid f\sim t_\nu(f(x_i),s)\) for heavy-tailed real values, and \(Y_i\mid f\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi)\), \(\mu_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(f(x_i))\), for values in \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count, heavy-tailed, and bounded values require likelihoods with matching support, link, and dispersion.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa,\nu,s,\phi>0\), subject to each family's parameter restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(y_{1:n}\mid f)=\prod_i p_i(y_i\mid f(x_i))\text{ with family-specific support.}
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Non-Gaussian Value Likelihoods
Non-Gaussian Value Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized likelihood model for direct, nonnormally distributed evaluations of a latent response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be a latent response. A non-Gaussian value-observation model specifies observations \(Y_i\) at inputs \(x_i\in X\) through conditional laws \(Y_i\mid f,\theta\sim P_\theta(\cdot\mid f(x_i))\), conditionally independent across \(i\), where \(P_\theta(\cdot\mid z)\) is not a Gaussian location family in the observed value. Its likelihood is \(p(y_{1:n}\mid f,\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(y_i\mid f(x_i))\), interpreted as a density or probability mass function relative to an appropriate dominating measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Observed values follow a specified non-Gaussian likelihood whose parameter depends on the latent response at each queried input.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is measurable.
Each \(P_\theta(\cdot\mid z)\) is a probability law on the observation space.

notation.meaning: non-Gaussian observation law at latent value z

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and generalized non-Gaussian likelihood formulation fit the leaf, but no source is supplied for the model class, conditional-independence convention, or exclusion of Gaussian location families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Factored non-Gaussian information for Gaussian-process inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of non-Gaussian value observations, possibly augmented by hard or soft constraints, for variables jointly Gaussian with a latent function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((f,\mathbf y)\) be jointly Gaussian with mean \((\mu,\mathbf m)\) and block covariance \(\begin{bmatrix}K&\kappa^\top\\\kappa&\mathbf C\end{bmatrix}\). If information \(\mathcal D\) about \(\mathbf y\) is encoded by \(t(\mathbf y)=\prod_i t_i(\mathbf y)\), whose factors may represent likelihood terms and hard or soft constraints, then \(p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\propto\mathcal N(\mathbf y;\mathbf m,\mathbf C)\prod_i t_i(\mathbf y)\), and \(p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\int p(f\mid\mathbf y)p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\,d\mathbf y\). A non-Gaussian posterior on \(\mathbf y\) usually makes this induced posterior analytically intractable, although \(p(f\mid\mathbf y)\) is Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-Gaussian observations and associated constraints can be encoded as factored local functions multiplying the Gaussian prior on jointly modeled variables. Integrating the conditional Gaussian process against the resulting posterior yields the latent-function posterior, which is usually analytically intractable when the variable posterior is non-Gaussian.
assumptions_latex: (f,\mathbf y)\text{ is jointly Gaussian with mean }(\mu,\mathbf m)\text{ and block covariance }\begin{bmatrix}K&\kappa^\top\\\kappa&\mathbf C\end{bmatrix}.
t(\mathbf y)=\prod_i t_i(\mathbf y)\text{ encodes the information }\mathcal D\text{ through likelihood and/or constraint factors}.
p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\text{ is non-Gaussian for the stated intractability boundary}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\propto\mathcal N(\mathbf y;\mathbf m,\mathbf C)\prod_i t_i(\mathbf y),\qquad p(f\mid\mathcal D)=\int p(f\mid\mathbf y)p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\,d\mathbf y,\text{ and this integral is usually analytically intractable when }p(\mathbf y\mid\mathcal D)\text{ is non-Gaussian}.

children.title: Censored Observations
children.top_down_role: Responses reported only through limits, thresholds, intervals, or detection boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which the reporting mechanism may be ignored.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i\) denote the censoring mechanism and \(O_i\) the reported interval event for latent \(Z_i\). The interval-probability likelihood alone is valid only when the conditional law of \(C_i\), given modeled observed information, contributes no additional factor depending on \(f\) or the hidden value within the interval. Otherwise omitting \(p(C_i\mid Z_i,f)\) generally misspecifies the likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value-dependent censoring must be modeled; an interval-only likelihood requires a noninformative reporting mechanism.
assumptions_latex: A joint data-generating law for \((Z_i,C_i)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(O_i,C_i\mid f)\not\propto p(O_i\mid f)\text{ in general under informative censoring.}
knowledge_statements.title: Informative-Censoring Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided and interval likelihoods for a Gaussian latent measurement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Z_i\mid f\sim\mathcal N(f(x_i),\sigma_i^2)\), then \(L_i<Z_i\le U_i\) contributes \(\Phi((U_i-f(x_i))/\sigma_i)-\Phi((L_i-f(x_i))/\sigma_i)\). Right censoring \(Z_i>c\) contributes \(1-\Phi((c-f(x_i))/\sigma_i)\), and left censoring \(Z_i\le c\) contributes \(\Phi((c-f(x_i))/\sigma_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian interval and one-sided censoring likelihoods are normal-CDF differences or tails.
assumptions_latex: \(\sigma_i>0\).
The censoring event and endpoints are observed.
knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Censoring Likelihoods
Censored Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Likelihood contribution when a latent noisy value is observed only within a censoring interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_i\mid f\) have conditional distribution function \(F_i(\cdot\mid f(x_i))\). A censored observation reports an interval \([L_i,U_i]\), with endpoints allowed to be infinite, asserting \(L_i<Z_i\le U_i\). Its likelihood contribution is \(F_i(U_i\mid f(x_i))-F_i(L_i\mid f(x_i))\). Right censoring at \(c\) uses \((L_i,U_i)=(c,\infty)\); left censoring uses \((L_i,U_i)=(-\infty,c)\). Exact continuous observations instead contribute the corresponding conditional density.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A censored datum contributes the probability that its unobserved noisy value lies in the reported interval, including one-sided intervals.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i(\cdot\mid f(x_i))\) is a conditional distribution function.
Censoring endpoints and censoring type are observed.

notation.meaning: conditional distribution function of the latent value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative censoring-likelihood source is required. The reported interval is denoted [L_i,U_i] while the event and CDF difference correspond to (L_i,U_i]; this endpoint convention should be made consistent once the source is fixed.

children.title: Ordinal Observations
children.top_down_role: Ordered categorical feedback without direct cardinal response values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Likelihood invariances requiring threshold or latent-scale normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing \(f(x)\) by \(f(x)+a\) and every finite threshold \(\tau_k\) by \(\tau_k+a\) leaves all ordinal probabilities unchanged. If the error distribution has unknown scale \(s\), scaling \(f\), all finite thresholds, and \(s\) by the same \(c>0\) also leaves them unchanged. Absolute location therefore requires a constraint, and latent scale requires a fixed link scale or equivalent normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinal labels identify score position relative to thresholds, not unrestricted absolute location or scale.
assumptions_latex: Thresholds and latent scores are jointly estimated.
For scale invariance, the error family is closed under positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinal Location and Scale Identifiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity induced by increasing latent score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the cumulative threshold model, \(\Pr(Y_i\le k\mid f(x_i)=z)=G(\tau_k-z)\). Hence if \(z_2>z_1\), then \(G(\tau_k-z_2)\le G(\tau_k-z_1)\) for every \(k\), so the ordinal response at \(z_2\) first-order stochastically dominates that at \(z_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing the latent score shifts the ordinal-label distribution upward.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is nondecreasing.
Thresholds are ordered.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Ordering of Ordinal Labels
Ordinal Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-category likelihood induced by thresholds on a latent noisy score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix ordered labels \(1<\cdots<K\), thresholds \(-\infty=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=\infty\), and a strictly increasing distribution function \(G\). An ordinal observation at \(x_i\) is generated by a latent score \(f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(G\) the distribution function of \(\varepsilon_i\), and \(Y_i=k\) exactly when \(\tau_{k-1}<f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\le\tau_k\). Consequently, \(\Pr(Y_i=k\mid f)=G(\tau_k-f(x_i))-G(\tau_{k-1}-f(x_i))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordinal label indicates which ordered threshold interval contains a noisy latent response, yielding a difference-of-cumulative-probabilities likelihood.
assumptions_latex: \(K\ge2\) and the thresholds are strictly ordered.
The score errors are conditionally independent with distribution function \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and threshold likelihood fit ordinal observations and are internally coherent, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Preference Observations
children.top_down_role: Pairwise or ranking feedback expressing relative desirability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Utility-level identifiability determined by comparison connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the undirected graph of evaluated alternatives and observed comparisons. A likelihood depending only on edge differences \(f(u)-f(v)\) is invariant under a separate additive constant on each connected component. Relative utility levels across all vertices therefore require graph connectivity, and even then one global additive normalization remains necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise data identify utilities only within connected comparison components and always leave an additive level free.
assumptions_latex: The likelihood depends on utilities only through observed edge differences.

notation.meaning: Oriented incidence matrix of the comparison graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparison-Graph Identifiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two failures of unregularized or deterministic preference models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an unregularized logistic difference likelihood, if one utility direction strictly orders every observed winning edge, scaling it drives all fitted winning probabilities toward one and a finite maximizer need not exist. Separately, deterministic preferences induced by a scalar utility cannot realize every edge of a directed cycle; positive likelihood for such cycles requires observation noise or a model allowing intransitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separable comparisons can eliminate a finite unregularized optimum, while deterministic scalar utility cannot realize directed cycles.
assumptions_latex: The separation claim uses an unregularized logistic likelihood.
The cycle claim assumes deterministic preferences induced by scalar utility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Separation may destroy finite attainment; deterministic scalar utility excludes directed cycles.}
knowledge_statements.title: Separation and Deterministic-Cycle Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical random-utility links for binary comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U(x)=f(x)+\epsilon_x\) and report \(x\succ x'\) when \(U(x)>U(x')\). If the error difference is Gaussian with standard deviation \(s\), then \(\Pr(x\succ x'\mid f)=\Phi((f(x)-f(x'))/s)\). If it is logistic with scale \(s\), then this probability is \(\{1+\exp[-(f(x)-f(x'))/s]\}^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian and logistic random-utility differences yield probit and logistic preference likelihoods.
assumptions_latex: Comparison errors are conditionally independent when likelihood factors are multiplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Probit and Logistic Preference Links
Preference Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise-comparison likelihood determined by latent utility differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be a latent utility and let \(G:\mathbb R\to(0,1)\) be an increasing link satisfying \(G(-z)=1-G(z)\). For a queried pair \((x_i,x_i')\), define \(Y_i=1\) when the observation prefers \(x_i\) to \(x_i'\). The pairwise preference model is \(\Pr(Y_i=1\mid f)=G(f(x_i)-f(x_i'))\), with comparisons conditionally independent given \(f\). Thus only utility differences, not an additive level of \(f\), are identified by the likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary comparison is modeled through an increasing link applied to the difference between the two alternatives' latent utilities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is increasing and satisfies \(G(-z)=1-G(z)\).
Comparisons are conditionally independent given \(f\).

notation.meaning: latent utility difference for comparison i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and pairwise-difference likelihood fit the leaf, but an authoritative source is absent. The conclusion additionally uses y_i without explicitly declaring y_i in {0,1}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for label noise in the preference-based Bayesian-optimization setting of the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{In preference-based Bayesian optimization, observations are called noisy when the observed labels are suspected to be corrupted by noise.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In preference-based Bayesian optimization, observations are called noisy when the observed labels are suspected to be corrupted by noise.

children.title: Approximation-Regime Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of approximate inference under sparse, imbalanced, or weakly informative feedback.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: What an evidence lower bound certifies and what it does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For normalized \(q\) with finite terms, \(\log p(y)=\mathcal L(q)+\operatorname{KL}(q\Vert p(\cdot\mid y))\), where \(\mathcal L(q)=\mathbb E_q[\log p(y,z)-\log q(z)]\). Hence the ELBO certifies a lower bound on log evidence and its gap is reverse KL, but its value alone does not bound posterior moments, tails, or acquisition error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ELBO certifies a log-evidence lower bound, not posterior or acquisition accuracy by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is normalized and the displayed quantities are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: ELBO Certificate Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Boundary of Exact Gaussian Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary for Gaussian posterior approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With a nonsingular Gaussian prior for \(z\) and likelihood \(L(z)>0\), the posterior is multivariate Gaussian if and only if \(\log L(z)\) is affine-quadratic in \(z\), up to an additive constant, on the posterior support. Thus Laplace inference is exact for a quadratic full log posterior; a genuinely nonquadratic generalized-feedback likelihood generally produces a non-Gaussian posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian inference is exact at the affine-quadratic likelihood boundary; genuinely nonquadratic feedback generally requires approximation.
assumptions_latex: The prior covariance is nonsingular.
\(L(z)>0\) on the relevant support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(z\mid y)\text{ is Gaussian}\iff \log L(z)=c+a^\top z-\tfrac12z^\top Bz.

notation.meaning: Generalized-feedback likelihood as a function of the latent vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Boundary of Exact Gaussian Inference

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Curvature Does Not Certify Global Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of mode-and-Hessian information to determine tails or remote modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist smooth proper densities with the same mode and identical log-density value, gradient, and Hessian at that mode but arbitrarily different tail probabilities or variances. Consequently a Laplace approximation based only on local mode and curvature cannot certify tails, variance, or absence of separated mass without global assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching local mode and curvature does not determine global posterior tails, variance, or remote mass.
assumptions_latex: The compared densities are smooth and proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Local second-order agreement does not imply global distributional accuracy.}
knowledge_statements.title: Local Curvature Does Not Certify Global Accuracy
Approximation-Regime Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of Gaussian Laplace approximations for generalized-feedback posteriors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For latent vector \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) with log posterior \(\ell(z)\), the Laplace approximation \(N(\hat z,H^{-1})\) is defined locally only when \(\hat z\) is a finite interior maximizer and \(H=-\nabla^2\ell(\hat z)\) is positive definite. It does not represent distinct separated modes. A concrete failure occurs for an unregularized logistic preference likelihood with perfectly separable comparisons: along a separating direction \(v\), \(\ell(cv)\) increases toward its supremum as \(c\to\infty\), so no finite mode or invertible local covariance exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laplace inference requires a finite, locally regular mode and cannot capture separated modes; separable unregularized logistic comparisons can eliminate the finite mode entirely.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\) is twice differentiable near any proposed mode.
The stated logistic example has no proper prior or other coercive regularizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If no finite \(\hat z\) with \(-\nabla^2\ell(\hat z)\succ0\) exists, the standard Laplace Gaussian approximation is undefined.

notation.meaning: posterior mode used by the Laplace approximation
negative Hessian of the log posterior at the mode

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, but the regular-mode conditions, multimodality limitation, and separable-logistic example require cited support. No source is provided.

children.title: Linear-Functional Observation Family
children.top_down_role: Surrogates augmented by gradients, integrals, averages, and related linear information.

children.title: Gradient Observations
children.top_down_role: First-order derivative information supplied at selected inputs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which an exact mean-square gradient channel is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mean-square partial derivative \(\partial_jf(x)\) requires the corresponding covariance difference-quotient limit to exist finitely; when kernel differentiation is justified, its variance is \(\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x'_j}k(x,x')|_{x'=x}\). If that finite limit does not exist, the prior does not define an exact finite-variance derivative observation at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A kernel without the required finite mixed covariance derivative cannot support an exact mean-square gradient observation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a Gaussian process with covariance kernel \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_{x_j}\partial_{x'_j}k(x,x')|_{x'=x}\ \text{undefined or nonfinite}\implies \partial_jf(x)\ \text{is not defined as a finite-variance mean-square observation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient-Kernel-Smoothness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional and coordinate specializations of gradient observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional derivatives are linear combinations of gradient components, with covariances obtained by directional kernel differentiation.
assumptions_latex: The required first and mixed second kernel derivatives exist.
The corresponding mean-square derivatives exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional-Derivative Observations
Gradient Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process conditioning with noisy first-derivative functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\) on an open set \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\), with \(m\) differentiable and \(k\) continuously differentiable once in each argument. For observations \(Y_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}f(x_i)+\varepsilon_{ij}\), jointly Gaussian noise gives a joint Gaussian model with \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),Y_{ij})=\partial_{x_i,j}k(x,x_i)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{r\ell})=\partial_{x_i,j}\partial_{x_r,\ell}k(x_i,x_r)+\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{ij},\varepsilon_{r\ell})\). Conditioning this joint law yields the gradient-informed surrogate posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient data enter a Gaussian process as linear derivative functionals, with cross-covariances obtained by differentiating the kernel.
assumptions_latex: The stated kernel derivatives exist and are continuous.
Derivative observations exist in mean square.
Observation noise is jointly Gaussian and independent of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f(x),Y_{11},\ldots,Y_{nd})\) is jointly Gaussian with covariance blocks obtained by differentiating \(k\).

notation.meaning: j-th mean-square partial derivative of f
noisy j-th gradient component at input i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and differentiated-kernel covariance construction fit gradient observations, but no authoritative Gaussian-process derivative-observation source is cited.

children.title: Higher-Order Derivative Observations
children.top_down_role: Curvature or higher-order differential information supplied at selected inputs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel regularity required for derivative observations of prescribed orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To jointly model \(D^\alpha f(x)\) and \(D^\beta f(x')\), the mixed kernel derivative \(D_x^\alpha D_{x'}^\beta k(x,x')\) must exist finitely at the required pairs and represent the corresponding mean-square covariance limit. In particular, covariance between two order-\(p\) derivative observations requires \(p\) derivatives in each kernel argument, totaling mixed order \(2p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two order-p derivative observations require the corresponding p-by-p mixed kernel derivative; without it, the exact channel is undefined.
assumptions_latex: Derivative observations are interpreted in the mean-square sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_x^\alpha D_{x'}^\beta k(x,x')\ \text{undefined or nonfinite}\implies \operatorname{Cov}(D^\alpha f(x),D^\beta f(x'))\ \text{is undefined}.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Order Smoothness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order specialization of the multi-index representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H_{ab}(x)=\partial_a\partial_bf(x)\), commuting mixed derivatives give \(H_{ab}(x)=H_{ba}(x)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{Cov}(H_{ab}(x),f(z))=\partial_{x_a}\partial_{x_b}k(x,z)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(H_{ab}(x),H_{cd}(z))=\partial_{x_a}\partial_{x_b}\partial_{z_c}\partial_{z_d}k(x,z)\). Thus a symmetric Hessian has \(d(d+1)/2\) distinct entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hessian observations use second and fourth kernel derivatives, and symmetry reduces the number of distinct entries.
assumptions_latex: The required mean-square second derivatives and fourth mixed kernel derivatives exist.
Mixed second derivatives commute.
knowledge_statements.title: Hessian Observation Blocks
Higher-Order Derivative Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process covariance representation for arbitrary finite derivative functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\) on an open subset of \(\mathbb R^d\). For multi-indices \(\alpha_i\), suppose the mean-square derivatives \(D^{\alpha_i}f(x_i)\) exist, and observe \(Y_i=D^{\alpha_i}f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\). Then the observations and function values are jointly Gaussian, with \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),Y_i)=D_{x_i}^{\alpha_i}k(x,x_i)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=D_{x_i}^{\alpha_i}D_{x_j}^{\alpha_j}k(x_i,x_j)+\Sigma_{ij}\). These differentiated covariance blocks determine the conditioned surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher derivatives are linear Gaussian-process observations whose covariance matrices are obtained by applying the corresponding derivatives to the kernel.
assumptions_latex: All displayed mixed kernel derivatives exist and define the required mean-square derivatives.
\(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) is independent of \(f\), with \(\Sigma\succeq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and multi-index covariance formulas fit higher-order derivative observations, but the mean-square differentiability and joint-Gaussian claims lack a cited source.

children.title: Integral Observations
children.top_down_role: Aggregate response information expressed through integration over regions or measures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when the kernel-induced second moment of an integral channel is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted integral \(L_wf=\int w(u)f(u)\,d\mu(u)\) is not defined as a finite-variance mean-square observation when the associated covariance integral \(\iint w(u)k(u,v)w(v)\,d\mu(u)d\mu(v)\) does not exist finitely. Formal kernel integration alone cannot then create a valid Gaussian observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the kernel-weight covariance integral is not finite, the proposed weighted integral is not a finite-variance Gaussian-process observation.
assumptions_latex: The integral is intended as a mean-square random variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegrable Functional Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linearity and Superposition of Integral Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic closure of admissible weighted-integral observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For admissible weights \(w_1,w_2\) and scalars \(a,b\), \(L_{aw_1+bw_2}f=aL_{w_1}f+bL_{w_2}f\). Observation means and value-integral cross-covariances are linear in the weight, while integral-integral covariance is bilinear in its two weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted-integral channels superpose linearly, and their covariance is bilinear in the weights.
assumptions_latex: All involved weighted integrals exist in mean square.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearity and Superposition of Integral Channels
Integral Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process representation of noisy weighted-integral measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\) on \(X\), and let \(L_i f=\int_X w_i(u)f(u)\,d\mu(u)\) be well-defined mean-square integrals. For \(Y_i=L_i f+\varepsilon_i\), independent Gaussian noise implies joint Gaussianity and \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),Y_i)=\int_X k(x,u)w_i(u)\,d\mu(u)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=\int_X\!\int_X w_i(u)k(u,v)w_j(v)\,d\mu(u)d\mu(v)+\Sigma_{ij}\). Conditioning these covariance blocks yields the posterior process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted integral is a linear Gaussian-process observation; its covariances are the corresponding single and double integrals of the kernel.
assumptions_latex: The weights and kernel satisfy the integrability conditions needed for the displayed mean-square integrals.
\(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) is independent of \(f\), with \(\Sigma\succeq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and linear-functional covariance formulas fit integral observations, but no authoritative source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Average-Response Observations
children.top_down_role: Linear summaries representing local, temporal, or population averages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale error caused by treating an integral as an average response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\mu(A)<\infty\), let \(I_Af=\int_A f\,d\mu\) and \(L_Af=I_Af/\mu(A)\). Modeling one channel as the other without the known normalization scales its mean and every cross-covariance incorrectly whenever \(\mu(A)\ne1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Confusing an integral with an average introduces a region-mass scaling error.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mu(A)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unnormalized-Average Mismatch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-region specialization and limiting relation to point observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\mu(A)<\infty\), \(L_Af=\mu(A)^{-1}\int_A f(u)\,d\mu(u)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),L_Af)=\mu(A)^{-1}\int_A k(x,u)\,d\mu(u)\). If probability measures \(P_n\) defining the averages converge weakly to \(\delta_{x_0}\) and \(k(x,\cdot)\) is bounded and continuous on their relevant support, then \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),\int f\,dP_n)\to k(x,x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regional average is a normalized integral, and concentrating averages recover point-observation cross-covariances under kernel continuity.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mu(A)<\infty\).
The displayed kernel integrals exist.
For the limit, \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_{x_0}\) and \(k(x,\cdot)\) is bounded and continuous on the relevant support.

notation.meaning: probability measure defining the nth average

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Average and Point Limit
Average-Response Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized regional or distributional averages as linear surrogate observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(m,k)\), and let \(P_i\) be a known probability measure on \(X\). An average-response observation has the form \(Y_i=\int_X f(u)\,P_i(du)+\varepsilon_i\). Whenever the integrals exist in mean square, \(Y_i\) is Gaussian and \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(x),Y_i)=\int_X k(x,u)\,P_i(du)\), while \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=\int_X\!\int_X k(u,v)\,P_i(du)P_j(dv)+\Sigma_{ij}\). Point observations are recovered when \(P_i\) is a Dirac measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An average response integrates the latent function against a probability measure, with covariance obtained by averaging the kernel over one or two arguments.
assumptions_latex: The kernel is integrable with respect to each required product measure.
\(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) is independent of \(f\), with \(\Sigma\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: probability measure defining the i-th averaging region or distribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and probability-measure averaging formulas fit the leaf, including the Dirac-measure specialization, but the claims have no cited source.

children.title: Auxiliary-Channel Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits between value observations and derivative or functional information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary created by linearly redundant noiseless auxiliary functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_1f,\ldots,L_nf\) be jointly Gaussian linear observations. If \(a\ne0\) satisfies \(\sum_i a_iL_if=0\) almost surely and \(a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a=0\), then \(a^{\mathsf T}(K_L+\Sigma)a=0\), so the observation covariance is singular. Ordinary inverse-based conditioning is then unavailable; redundant-channel removal, positive noise in that direction, or singular-Gaussian conditioning may be used instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact noiseless linear redundancy makes the auxiliary observation covariance singular.
assumptions_latex: Every \(L_if\) exists in mean square.
\(K_L\) and \(\Sigma\) are the latent-channel and noise covariance matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_i a_iL_if=0\ \text{a.s.},\ a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a=0\implies a^{\mathsf T}(K_L+\Sigma)a=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant-Channel Singularity
Auxiliary-Channel Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for combining heterogeneous linear observation channels in one surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have covariance kernel \(k\), and let \(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be value, derivative, integral, or average-response functionals defined in mean square. The auxiliary channels are covariance-consistent precisely when every pair \((L_i,L_j)\) acts on \(k\), the matrix \(K_L=[L_i^{(1)}L_j^{(2)}k]_{i,j=1}^n\) is finite and positive semidefinite, and the noise covariance \(\Sigma\) is positive semidefinite. Then \(K_L+\Sigma\) is a valid joint observation covariance; if it is positive definite, ordinary Gaussian conditioning is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heterogeneous observation channels are jointly valid when all induced kernel covariances exist and both the induced covariance and noise covariance are positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: Each \(L_i f\) exists in mean square.
The noise is independent of \(f\) and has covariance \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_L\succeq0\) and \(\Sigma\succeq0\) imply \(K_L+\Sigma\succeq0\); if \(K_L+\Sigma\succ0\), its Gaussian conditioning equations are nonsingular.

notation.meaning: functionals applied to the first and second kernel arguments
induced covariance matrix across observation channels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits auxiliary-channel consistency, but no source supports the asserted necessary-and-sufficient characterization. Moreover, positive semidefiniteness is automatic when the L_i f are genuinely defined as joint mean-square random variables, so the intended status of this condition needs source-backed clarification.

children.title: Alternative Surrogate Families
children.top_down_role: Non-Gaussian-process models offering different interpolation, regularity, scaling, or domain capabilities.

children.title: Classical Response-Surface Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Low-order and basis-expansion surrogates inherited from classical response-surface methodology.

children.title: Linear Surrogate Models
children.top_down_role: Low-order surrogate representations based on linear predictor structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Surrogate Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional response surface linear in fixed basis coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given fixed features \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^p\), a linear surrogate represents the latent response as \(f_\beta(x)=\phi(x)^\top\beta\). With observations \(y=\Phi\beta+\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), and prior \(\beta\sim N(b_0,B_0)\), where \(B_0\succ0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\), the posterior is \(N(b_n,B_n)\), with \(B_n=(B_0^{-1}+\Phi^\top\Sigma^{-1}\Phi)^{-1}\) and \(b_n=B_n(B_0^{-1}b_0+\Phi^\top\Sigma^{-1}y)\). The predictive latent response is Gaussian with mean \(\phi(x)^\top b_n\) and variance \(\phi(x)^\top B_n\phi(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear surrogate combines fixed features with unknown coefficients; under Gaussian noise and a Gaussian prior, coefficient and predictive posteriors are Gaussian.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^p\) is fixed and known.
\(B_0\succ0\) and \(\Sigma\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta\mid y\sim N(b_n,B_n)\) and \(f_\beta(x)\mid y\sim N(\phi(x)^\top b_n,\phi(x)^\top B_n\phi(x))\).

notation.meaning: design matrix with rows equal to feature vectors

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization characterization of the Gaussian posterior mode for a fixed-feature linear surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed's Gaussian model, the posterior mean \(b_n\) is also the unique posterior mode and satisfies \[b_n=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p}\left\{(y-\Phi\beta)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(y-\Phi\beta)+(\beta-b_0)^\top B_0^{-1}(\beta-b_0)\right\}.\] If \(\Sigma=\sigma^2I\), \(b_0=0\), and \(B_0=(\sigma^2/\lambda)I\), this becomes ridge regression: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_\beta\{\|y-\Phi\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gaussian linear-surrogate posterior mean and mode equal a generalized penalized least-squares solution, with isotropic choices yielding ridge regression.
assumptions_latex: \(y\mid\beta\sim N(\Phi\beta,\Sigma)\).
\(\beta\sim N(b_0,B_0)\).
\(\Sigma\succ0\) and \(B_0\succ0\).

notation.meaning: quadratic form v transpose M v

knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Linear MAP–Penalized Least-Squares Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-linear surrogate representation and pseudoinverse least-squares fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given data $\{(\mathbf{x}^{(j)},y_j)\}_{j=1}^m$, form the design matrix $X$ with rows $(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^\top$. The linear surrogate $\widehat f(\mathbf{x})=\boldsymbol\theta^\top\mathbf{x}$ is fitted by $\min_{\boldsymbol\theta}\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\theta\|_2^2$, and $\boldsymbol\theta=X^+\mathbf y$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate-linear surrogate is fitted by least squares. The pseudoinverse returns the unique minimum-norm least-squares coefficient vector, even when the design matrix is rank deficient.
assumptions_latex: m\ge 1
\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in\mathbb R^n
X_{j:}=(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^\top
\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m

source_evidence.locator: Surrogate Models / 14.3. Basis Functions / Definition 14.3-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Surrogate Least-Squares Fit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear surrogate representation and least-squares fitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine surrogate models on an n-dimensional design space, their augmented-coordinate representation, and the sample and rank requirements for unique fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear surrogate has the form \(\widehat f(x)=w_0+w^\top x\). Defining \(\widetilde x=(1,x^\top)^\top\) and \(\theta=(w_0,w^\top)^\top\) gives \(\widehat f(x)=\theta^\top\widetilde x\). For sampled responses \(y\), fitting solves \(\min_\theta\|y-\widetilde X\theta\|_2^2\), where row \(i\) of \(\widetilde X\) is \(\widetilde x^{(i)\top}\). At least \(n+1\) samples are necessary for an unambiguous fit; uniqueness additionally requires \(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde X)=n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear surrogate is affine in the design variables. Prepending an intercept coordinate gives a single linear parameterization fitted by least squares. An unambiguous fit needs at least n+1 samples and full column rank of the augmented design matrix.
assumptions_latex: x^{(i)}\in\mathbb R^n\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
y\in\mathbb R^m
\widetilde X_{i,:}=(1,(x^{(i)})^\top)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f(x)=\theta^\top\widetilde x,\qquad \theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u}\|y-\widetilde Xu\|_2^2;\quad \text{unique fitting requires }\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde X)=n+1\text{, hence }m\ge n+1.

source_evidence.locator: Surrogate Models / 14.2. Linear Models / Definition 14.2-extra-1

children.title: Polynomial Surrogate Models
children.top_down_role: Basis-expansion surrogates using polynomial terms of selected degree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressive-limit result for unrestricted polynomial order, distinct from finite-order estimation tradeoffs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) be compact. For every \(f\in C(K)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a multivariate polynomial \(p\) such that \[\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-p(x)|<\varepsilon.\] Thus restrictions of multivariate polynomials are dense in \(C(K)\) under the uniform norm. This existence result supplies neither a finite-degree rate nor stable estimation from a specified design.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomials uniformly approximate every continuous function on a compact Euclidean set, but this gives no finite-degree rate or statistical stability guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) is compact.
\(f:K\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Approximation on Compact Domains
Polynomial Surrogate Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-degree polynomial regression surrogate on a finite-dimensional continuous design domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(p\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and define \(\mathcal{A}_p=\{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_0^d:|\alpha|_1\le p\}\). A polynomial surrogate of total degree at most \(p\) is a function \[\widehat f_p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}_p}\beta_\alpha x^\alpha,\qquad x^\alpha=\prod_{j=1}^d x_j^{\alpha_j}.\] Given observations \((x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\), ordinary least squares chooses \(\widehat\beta\in\arg\min_{\beta}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\widehat f_p(x_i;\beta))^2\). The number of coefficients is \(|\mathcal{A}_p|=\binom{d+p}{p}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-p polynomial surrogate fits observed responses using every monomial whose total degree is at most p; its coefficient count grows combinatorially with dimension and degree.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\)
\(p\in\mathbb{N}_0\)
\((x_i,y_i)\in D\times\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\)

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Response-Surface Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order response-surface representations with least-squares coefficient estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For coded inputs \(x\in D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), a classical second-order response surface has the representation \[\widehat f(x)=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^d\beta_jx_j+\sum_{j=1}^d\beta_{jj}x_j^2+\sum_{1\le j<k\le d}\beta_{jk}x_jx_k.\] Omitting all quadratic and interaction terms gives the first-order model. For a design matrix \(X\) formed from the displayed basis and response vector \(y\), coefficients minimize \(\|y-X\beta\|_2^2\); if \(X\) has full column rank, the unique estimate is \(\widehat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical response surface is a fitted first- or second-order polynomial in coded factors, including linear, pure-quadratic, and pairwise-interaction effects.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\)
\(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\) is the response-surface design matrix
\(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=q\), then \(\widehat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) uniquely defines the fitted surface.

children.title: Basis-Order Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Predictive consequences of low-order approximation versus richer basis expansion.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Order Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias–variance and identifiability tradeoff induced by increasing polynomial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For total-degree polynomial spaces \(V_p\subset V_{p+1}\) on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), empirical least-squares residuals satisfy \[\min_{g\in V_{p+1}}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2\le \min_{g\in V_p}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2.\] However, the parameter count increases from \(q_p=\binom{d+p}{p}\) to \(q_{p+1}=\binom{d+p+1}{p+1}\). Unregularized unique estimation requires the corresponding design matrix to have rank \(q_p\), hence \(n\ge q_p\). Thus increasing order cannot worsen training fit but increases data requirements and may amplify estimation variance or numerical ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher polynomial order weakly improves training fit but increases coefficient count, rank requirements, variance risk, and numerical sensitivity.
assumptions_latex: \(V_p\) is the total-degree polynomial space of order \(p\)
\((x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n\subset D\times\mathbb{R}\)
Coefficients are fitted by unregularized least squares
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Training error is nonincreasing in \(p\), while unique estimation requires \(n\ge\binom{d+p}{p}\) and full column rank.

children.title: Extrapolation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regions where fitted low-order surfaces become unreliable beyond supported design coverage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp deterministic amplification outside a supported one-dimensional interval for degree-bounded polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h\) be a real polynomial of degree at most \(p\) with \(\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|h(x)|\le\varepsilon\). For every \(|x_\star|>1\), \[|h(x_\star)|\le\varepsilon|T_p(x_\star)|,\] where \(T_p\) is the degree-\(p\) Chebyshev polynomial. The bound is sharp, being attained by \(h=\pm\varepsilon T_p\). Moreover, \(|T_p(x_\star)|=\cosh(p\operatorname{arcosh}|x_\star|)\), so worst-case amplification grows exponentially in \(p\) for fixed \(|x_\star|>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-bounded polynomial that is uniformly small on the supported interval can be exponentially larger outside it, with Chebyshev polynomials attaining the sharp bound.
assumptions_latex: \(h\in\mathbb R[x]\) and \(\deg h\le p\).
\(\|h\|_{L^\infty([-1,1])}\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind of degree p
prediction point outside the supported interval

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Chebyshev Extrapolation Amplification
Extrapolation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-identifiability of polynomial behavior outside the sampled design region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let distinct sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}\) be observed, let \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}\), and choose \(x_\star\notin[a,b]\). If a polynomial \(g\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) satisfies \(g(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\), then for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\), the polynomial \[g_M(x)=g(x)+M\prod_{i=1}^n(x-x_i)\] has the same fitted values at all sampled sites. Because \(\prod_{i=1}^n(x_\star-x_i)\ne0\), the values \(g_M(x_\star)\) are unbounded as \(|M|\to\infty\). Consequently, interpolation at the sampled sites alone supplies no finite deterministic bound on polynomial extrapolation at \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial interpolants can agree at every sampled point while taking arbitrarily different values at an exterior point, so sampled interpolation alone cannot certify polynomial extrapolation.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) are distinct points in \([a,b]\)
\(x_\star\notin[a,b]\)
\(g\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) and \(g(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\)

notation.meaning: data-equivalent polynomial perturbation of an interpolant

children.title: Radial-Basis Surrogates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise native-space error bound for strictly positive-definite kernel interpolation without a polynomial tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be strictly positive definite with native Hilbert space \(\mathcal H_k\), let \(K\) be its matrix on distinct sites \(X\), and define \(P_X(x)^2=k(x,x)-k_X(x)^\top K^{-1}k_X(x)\). For the kernel interpolant \(s_Xf\) of \(f\in\mathcal H_k\), \(|f(x)-s_Xf(x)|\le P_X(x)\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\), with \(P_X(x_i)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kernel power function gives a pointwise RBF interpolation-error certificate when a native-space norm bound is available.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is strictly positive definite on the distinct sites.
\(f\in\mathcal H_k\).
The interpolant uses the same kernel and no polynomial augmentation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense RBF Fit and Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct dense-system complexity for an augmented RBF surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(n\) centers and \(q\) polynomial terms, dense direct factorization of the \((n+q)\times(n+q)\) augmented system costs \(O((n+q)^3)\) arithmetic and \(O((n+q)^2)\) storage. Once coefficients are available, evaluating a globally supported expansion costs \(O(n+q)\) per point when individual basis evaluations have constant cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense augmented RBF fit is cubic in system dimension, quadratic in storage, and linear per global prediction.
assumptions_latex: The augmented matrix is treated as dense.
A conventional direct factorization is used.
Individual basis evaluations have constant cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense RBF Fit and Evaluation Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solvability theorem for augmented RBF interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi\) be strictly conditionally positive definite of order \(m\), let \(P\) evaluate a basis of \(\Pi_{m-1}\) at distinct centers, and suppose the centers are \(\Pi_{m-1}\)-unisolvent. Then \(\begin{pmatrix}\Phi&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\) is nonsingular. Hence every data vector has a unique coefficient pair satisfying interpolation and \(P^\top\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly conditionally positive-definite radial kernel and polynomial-unisolvent centers make the augmented RBF system uniquely solvable.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is strictly conditionally positive definite of order \(m\).
Centers are distinct and \(\Pi_{m-1}\)-unisolvent.
\(P\) evaluates a basis of \(\Pi_{m-1}\).

notation.meaning: polynomial space associated with the CPD order

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Conditional-Positive-Definite Uniqueness
Radial-Basis Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial-kernel interpolant with a polynomial tail and side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given distinct centers \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a radial-basis surrogate has the form \[s(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\phi(\|x-x_i\|_2)+\sum_{j=1}^q\gamma_jp_j(x).\] For observations \(y_i\), interpolation imposes \(s(x_i)=y_i\), and conditional positive-definiteness is handled by \(P^\top\lambda=0\), where \(P_{ij}=p_j(x_i)\). Thus \((\lambda,\gamma)\) solves \[\begin{pmatrix}\Phi&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\\\gamma\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}y\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Phi_{ik}=\phi(\|x_i-x_k\|_2).\] Uniqueness holds when this block matrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An RBF surrogate combines radial kernels centered at observations with an optional polynomial tail; interpolation reduces to a constrained block linear system.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^d\) are distinct
\(\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) is an admissible radial kernel
The block interpolation matrix is nonsingular
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique solution \((\lambda,\gamma)\) defines an interpolant satisfying \(s(x_i)=y_i\).
