children.title: Spline Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Piecewise smooth surrogate representations controlled by knots or basis structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction cost resulting from compact basis support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a degree-\(p\) B-spline representation, at most \(p+1\) basis functions are nonzero at a query point away from endpoint conventions. Locating the knot span among \(M\) basis functions costs \(O(\log M)\) by binary search, and standard de Boor evaluation then costs \(O(p^2)\) arithmetic using local coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After locating the knot interval, spline prediction uses only local coefficients and standard evaluation is quadratic in degree.
assumptions_latex: A degree-\(p\) B-spline representation and knot vector are stored.
Binary search locates the knot span.
Standard de Boor evaluation is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Local B-Spline Evaluation Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity boundary at a repeated interior knot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a degree-\(p\) spline, an interior knot of multiplicity \(r\le p+1\) guarantees continuity through derivative order \(p-r\) and generally no higher. Thus a simple knot gives \(C^{p-1}\) continuity, while multiplicity \(p+1\) permits a jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing an interior knot's multiplicity lowers the continuity guaranteed there.
assumptions_latex: The spline degree is \(p\).
The interior knot has multiplicity \(1\le r\le p+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\le p:\ s\in C^{p-r}\text{ at the knot in general};\qquad r=p+1:\text{a jump is permitted}.
knowledge_statements.title: Knot Multiplicity and Smoothness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional matrix representation of quadratic penalized spline fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_{ij}=B_j(x_i)\), let \(\Omega\succeq0\), and suppose \(B^\top B+\lambda\Omega\) is nonsingular. Minimizing \(\|y-B\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\beta^\top\Omega\beta\) gives \(\widehat\beta=(B^\top B+\lambda\Omega)^{-1}B^\top y\) and \(\widehat y=S_\lambda y\), where \(S_\lambda=B(B^\top B+\lambda\Omega)^{-1}B^\top\). For this linear smoother, \(\operatorname{tr}(S_\lambda)\) is its effective degrees of freedom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic penalized spline is a linear smoother whose smoothing-matrix trace measures effective flexibility.
assumptions_latex: The spline basis and quadratic penalty are fixed.
\(\Omega\succeq0\).
\(B^\top B+\lambda\Omega\) is nonsingular.
Squared-error fitting is used.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalized-Spline Linear-Smoother Form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-support representation of a univariate spline surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid nondecreasing knot vector and degree \(p\), the associated B-splines \(B_{1,p},\ldots,B_{M,p}\) form a basis of the corresponding spline space. Hence each spline has unique coefficients \(s(x)=\sum_{j=1}^M\beta_jB_{j,p}(x)\). The basis functions are nonnegative, locally supported, and form a partition of unity on the modeled knot interval under the standard endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every spline in a fixed knot space has unique B-spline coefficients, with nonnegative locally supported basis functions summing to one.
assumptions_latex: A valid nondecreasing knot vector and degree \(p\) are fixed.
The standard endpoint convention is used on the modeled interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s=\sum_{j=1}^M\beta_jB_{j,p}\text{ uniquely, with local support and }\sum_jB_{j,p}(x)=1.
knowledge_statements.title: B-Spline Basis Representation
Spline Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate smoothing spline defined by penalized least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a<x_1<\cdots<x_n<b\), responses \(y_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\lambda\ge0\). A cubic smoothing-spline surrogate is any minimizer over functions \(g\) with absolutely continuous first derivative and square-integrable second derivative of \[J_\lambda(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2+\lambda\int_a^b(g''(t))^2\,dt.\] For \(\lambda>0\), the fitted values are uniquely determined, and the minimizer is a natural cubic spline with knots among \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), satisfying \(g''(a)=g''(b)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cubic smoothing spline balances squared data misfit against integrated squared curvature; its minimizer is a natural cubic spline with data-site knots.
assumptions_latex: \(a<x_1<\cdots<x_n<b\)
\(y_i\in\mathbb{R}\)
\(\lambda>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizer of \(J_\lambda\) is a natural cubic spline with knots among the observation sites.

children.title: Interpolating Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Surrogates constrained to reproduce deterministic observations at sampled locations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lebesgue-constant characterization of value-perturbation amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I_Xy(x)=\sum_{j=1}^ny_j\ell_j(x)\), define \(\Lambda_X(x)=\sum_{j=1}^n|\ell_j(x)|\) and \(\Lambda_X=\sup_{x\in D}\Lambda_X(x)\). If \(\Lambda_X<\infty\), then \(\|I_Xy-I_X\widetilde y\|_{\infty,D}\le\Lambda_X\|y-\widetilde y\|_\infty\). Moreover, \(\Lambda_X\) is the operator norm from data \(\ell_\infty\) to function \(L_\infty(D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lebesgue constant is the worst-case amplification factor for perturbations in interpolated data values.
assumptions_latex: A cardinal representation exists on \(D\).
\(\Lambda_X<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation Operator Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility boundary for exact single-valued interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_i=x_j\) but \(y_i\ne y_j\), no single-valued function \(s:D\to\mathbb R\) can satisfy all interpolation constraints. If \(x_i=x_j\) and \(y_i=y_j\), the duplicate constraint is redundant, although a coefficient system retaining both rows may be singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conflicting responses at one input make exact interpolation impossible; matching duplicates are redundant and can still cause algebraic singularity.
assumptions_latex: The surrogate is a single-valued real function.
At least two observations share an input.
knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Repeated-Site Data

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representation of a uniquely solvable linear interpolation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an \(n\)-dimensional linear trial space admits a unique interpolant at distinct sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) for every data vector. Let \(\ell_j\) interpolate the coordinate vector \(e_j\), so \(\ell_j(x_i)=\delta_{ij}\). Then the interpolant to \(y\) is \(I_Xy=\sum_{j=1}^ny_j\ell_j\). Conversely, cardinal functions lying in the trial space and spanning it give interpolation for every data vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniquely solvable linear interpolation problem is equivalently represented by cardinal functions that equal one at one site and zero at the others.
assumptions_latex: The trial space is linear and has dimension \(n\).
Evaluation at the \(n\) distinct sites is bijective.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinal-Basis Representation
Interpolating Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-data surrogate defined through interpolation constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty set, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in D\) be distinct, and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}\). For a prescribed function class \(\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^D\), an interpolating surrogate is a function \(s\in\mathcal{H}\) satisfying \[s(x_i)=y_i\qquad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,n.\] If evaluation is represented by an invertible square matrix \(K\) and \(s(x)=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jk_j(x)\), then interpolation is equivalent to \(Kc=y\) and determines the unique coefficient vector \(c=K^{-1}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interpolating surrogate belongs to a chosen function class and exactly matches every observed response; uniqueness depends on invertibility of its evaluation system.
assumptions_latex: \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in D\) are distinct
\(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb{R}\)
\(\mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^D\) is prescribed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) interpolates the data exactly; when \(K\) is invertible, its coefficient vector is uniquely \(K^{-1}y\).

children.title: Interpolation-Smoothing Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Choices between exact data reproduction and robustness to irregular or uncertain observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of zero training residual to certify latent-response accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) and let \(s(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). Then \(s(x_i)-f(x_i)=\varepsilon_i\), so \(\|s-f\|_{\infty,D}\ge\max_i|\varepsilon_i|\). Thus exact training fit reproduces every realized observation error at its site.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact interpolant reproduces observation noise at sampled sites, so zero training residual does not certify latent-function accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\).
The surrogate exactly interpolates all observations.
At least one \(\varepsilon_i\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Noise Replication by Exact Interpolation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: External Selection of the Smoothing Level
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between a penalty path and selection of its tuning parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ordering of residual and roughness along \(g_\lambda\in\arg\min_g\{R(g)+\lambda\Omega(g)\}\) does not identify a universally optimal \(\lambda\). Selection requires an additional target and criterion, such as validation loss, cross-validation, generalized cross-validation under an appropriate linear-smoother model, or a specified probabilistic evidence criterion; different criteria may select different values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A penalized objective generates a tradeoff path but does not choose its own smoothing level.
assumptions_latex: More than one smoothing level is admissible.
No external risk, validation rule, or probabilistic model has fixed \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Monotonicity of }R(g_\lambda)\text{ and }\Omega(g_\lambda)\text{ alone does not determine an optimal }\lambda.
knowledge_statements.title: External Selection of the Smoothing Level

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lexicographic Endpoint Limits of Penalized Smoothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small- and large-penalty limits on a compact admissible class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be compact, let \(R,\Omega:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)\) be lower semicontinuous, and choose \(g_\lambda\in\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal H}\{R(g)+\lambda\Omega(g)\}\). Every cluster point as \(\lambda\downarrow0\) minimizes \(R\) and, among minimizers of \(R\), minimizes \(\Omega\). Every cluster point as \(\lambda\to\infty\) minimizes \(\Omega\) and, among minimizers of \(\Omega\), minimizes \(R\). Uniqueness of the corresponding lexicographic minimizer yields convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing penalty prioritizes residual then roughness; diverging penalty prioritizes roughness then residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is compact.
\(R\) and \(\Omega\) are nonnegative and lower semicontinuous.
A minimizer is selected for each \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lexicographic Endpoint Limits of Penalized Smoothing
Interpolation-Smoothing Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual–roughness tradeoff in penalized smooth surrogate fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(g)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-g(x_i))^2\) and let \(\Omega(g)\ge0\) measure roughness on a common function class \(\mathcal{H}\). For \(\lambda>0\), choose \(g_\lambda\in\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal{H}}\{R(g)+\lambda\Omega(g)\}\). If \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\) and minimizers exist, optimality implies \[\Omega(g_{\lambda_2})\le\Omega(g_{\lambda_1}),\qquad R(g_{\lambda_1})\le R(g_{\lambda_2}).\] Hence increasing the smoothing penalty selects a no-rougher fit at the cost of no-smaller training residual. Exact interpolation is recovered only when a zero-residual solution is selected, commonly at the zero-penalty boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing a roughness penalty makes the selected surrogate no rougher but makes its training residual no smaller, formalizing the interpolation–smoothing tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: \(R(g)\ge0\) and \(\Omega(g)\ge0\) on \(\mathcal{H}\)
Minimizers exist for \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\)
\(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2\)

children.title: Geometric Conditioning Limits
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity to clustered designs, poor coverage, or unstable basis geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary caused by an unsampled open region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a finite design \(X\subset D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) omits a nonempty open set \(U\subset D\), then a nonzero continuous function \(b\) can be supported in \(U\). Consequently \(f\) and \(f+b\) agree on \(X\) but differ in \(U\). Without a specified regularity class and norm bound excluding such perturbations, the observations cannot certify uniform accuracy on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsampled open region permits continuous objectives that agree at every observation but differ inside the region.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subset D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and open.
\(U\cap X=\varnothing\).
The admissible class permits a nonzero continuous perturbation supported in \(U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill Distance, Separation Radius, and Mesh Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical geometric quantities distinguishing coverage from crowding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite design \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset D\), define \(h_{X,D}=\sup_{x\in D}\min_i\|x-x_i\|_2\), \(q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), and, when \(q_X>0\), \(\rho_{X,D}=h_{X,D}/q_X\). Fill distance measures the largest coverage hole, separation measures closest-pair crowding, and mesh ratio measures their imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill distance measures coverage, separation measures crowding, and their ratio measures design nonuniformity.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and contains at least two sites.
\(D\) is nonempty.
Sites are distinct when \(\rho_{X,D}\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_{X,D}\text{ measures coverage},\quad q_X\text{ measures separation},\quad \rho_{X,D}=h_{X,D}/q_X.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill Distance, Separation Radius, and Mesh Ratio

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singularity of augmented interpolation caused by deficient center geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_{ij}=p_j(x_i)\) evaluate \(q\) polynomial-tail basis functions. If \(\operatorname{rank}(P)<q\), then the augmented matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}\Phi&P\\P^\top&0\end{pmatrix}\) is singular for every \(\Phi\). Thus full polynomial unisolvency is necessary for unique solvability of the augmented interpolation system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the sites do not identify every polynomial-tail coefficient, the augmented interpolation system is singular regardless of its radial-kernel block.
assumptions_latex: The interpolant includes polynomial basis functions \(p_1,\ldots,p_q\).
Their evaluation matrix \(P\) is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Unisolvency Failure
Geometric Conditioning Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel interpolation becomes ill-conditioned as distinct design sites coalesce.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k(x,z)=\phi(\|x-z\|_2)\) be a continuous strictly positive-definite kernel with \(\phi(0)>0\). For distinct sites \(x_1^{(m)},\ldots,x_n^{(m)}\), let \(K_m=(k(x_i^{(m)},x_j^{(m)}))_{ij}\). Suppose two sites coalesce, \(\|x_1^{(m)}-x_2^{(m)}\|_2\to0\), while all sites remain in a bounded set. With \(v=(1,-1,0,\ldots,0)^\top\), continuity gives \(v^\top K_mv\to0\), so \(\lambda_{\min}(K_m)\to0\). Since \(\lambda_{\max}(K_m)\ge\phi(0)\), \(\kappa_2(K_m)\to\infty\). Thus arbitrarily close sites impose an intrinsic numerical conditioning limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When two kernel centers approach each other, their matrix rows become nearly identical, the smallest eigenvalue vanishes, and the interpolation system becomes arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: \(k(x,z)=\phi(\|x-z\|_2)\) is continuous and strictly positive definite
Two distinct sites coalesce while the designs remain bounded
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Rayleigh-quotient argument for coalescing kernel centers
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coalescing-site conditioning claim is mathematically consistent for strictly positive-definite kernel matrices, but no source with a specific locator supports this failure boundary.

children.title: Recursive Partition Surrogate Family
children.top_down_role: Partition-based models suited to discontinuities, mixed variables, and nonstationarity.

children.title: Tree Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Single-tree predictive representations based on recursive domain subdivision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested subtree selection for a fixed grown regression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subtree \(T\) of a finite grown tree \(T_0\), let \(C_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|\mathcal L(T)|\), with additive terminal-node loss \(R(T)\). Repeatedly prune all branches attaining the smallest effective loss increase per removed leaf. With consistent treatment of ties, the resulting nested sequence contains a smallest minimizer of \(C_\alpha\) over subtrees of \(T_0\) for every \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakest-link pruning produces a nested sequence containing an optimal cost-complexity subtree for every penalty level.
assumptions_latex: \(T_0\) is finite.
Loss is additive over terminal nodes.
Candidates are subtrees obtained by branch pruning.
Simultaneous weakest links or an equivalent consistent tie rule are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\alpha\ge0,\ \text{the pruning sequence contains a minimizer of }C_\alpha\text{ over subtrees of }T_0.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakest-Link Cost-Complexity Pruning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical recursive squared-error construction of a single regression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node containing indices \(I\), each admissible split \(s\) produces nonempty children \(I_L(s),I_R(s)\). Define \(Q(s)=\sum_{i\in I_L(s)}(y_i-\bar y_L)^2+\sum_{i\in I_R(s)}(y_i-\bar y_R)^2\). Select a minimizer of \(Q\), recurse while the stopping rule permits, and assign each terminal node its sample mean. This is locally greedy and need not produce a globally loss-minimizing tree of a prescribed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression tree greedily minimizes immediate within-child squared error, recurses, and predicts leaf means; the resulting full tree need not be globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: Every admissible split produces two nonempty child samples.
Squared-error leaf loss is used.
Tie-breaking and stopping rules are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat s\in\arg\min_sQ(s)\text{ at each expanded node, without global final-tree optimality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Regression-Tree Growing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation and storage complexity of an explicitly stored binary tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fitted binary tree of depth \(h\), one prediction follows one root-to-leaf path and uses at most \(h\) internal-node tests plus a leaf lookup. Hence prediction time is \(O(h)\) and storage is \(O(|T|)\). A balanced tree with \(L\) leaves has \(h=O(\log L)\), whereas an unbalanced tree may have \(h=\Theta(L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-tree prediction is logarithmic in leaf count when balanced but can be linear when the tree is highly unbalanced.
assumptions_latex: Each internal-node test has constant cost.
The tree is stored explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Tree Prediction Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of a deterministic single-tree fit for uncertainty-dependent acquisition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic regression tree with fixed leaf values determines a point predictor \(\widehat f(x)\) but, by itself, determines neither a predictive distribution nor a predictive variance. These require an added observation model, posterior construction, resampling distribution, conformal method, or other uncertainty specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single deterministic tree supplies point predictions but no canonical predictive uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: Only one deterministic fitted tree and its leaf values are specified.
No probabilistic, resampling, or conformal construction is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f(x)\text{ alone does not identify a predictive law or variance.}
knowledge_statements.title: No Intrinsic Predictive Distribution
Tree Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant regression surrogate induced by recursive binary partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) and let a finite binary tree recursively partition \(D\) by tests \(x_{j(v)}\le t_v\) at internal nodes \(v\). Its leaves define pairwise-disjoint regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) whose union is \(D\). A regression-tree surrogate is \[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L\mu_\ell\mathbf{1}\{x\in R_\ell\}.\] Under squared-error fitting with nonempty leaves, \(\mu_\ell=|I_\ell|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_\ell}y_i\), where \(I_\ell=\{i:x_i\in R_\ell\}\). Thus prediction is constant within each terminal partition cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression-tree surrogate recursively partitions the design space and predicts each terminal cell’s mean observed response.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\)
The finite tree induces a partition \((R_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) of \(D\)
Every fitted leaf contains at least one observation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f(x)=\mu_\ell\) for \(x\in R_\ell\), with \(\mu_\ell\) equal to the leaf sample mean under squared loss.

notation.meaning: indices of observations in leaf l

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard regression-tree partition representation under squared loss
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise-constant tree representation and leaf-mean estimate under squared loss fit the container, but no inspectable source is provided.

children.title: Forest Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Aggregated tree representations used for flexible prediction and empirical uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Refinement Piecewise Constancy of Regression Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric structure of forests whose constituent regression trees have constant leaf predictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each regression tree \(T_b\) is constant on every leaf of a finite partition \(\mathcal P_b\). The forest mean \(\widehat f_B=B^{-1}\sum_{b=1}^BT_b\) is constant on every nonempty cell of the common refinement \[\mathcal P=\left\{\bigcap_{b=1}^B R_b:R_b\in\mathcal P_b\right\}.\] Consequently, wherever the cells have ordinary interiors, the classical gradient of \(\widehat f_B\) is zero in those interiors and may fail to exist at their boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression forest is piecewise constant on the common refinement of its tree leaves, with zero interior gradients and possible jumps at boundaries.
assumptions_latex: Each constituent regression tree has finitely many leaves and a constant prediction on each leaf.
The forest prediction is the arithmetic mean of the tree predictions.

notation.meaning: common refinement of all tree partitions

review_flags: Removed the builder's acquisition-optimization prescription because that algorithmic consequence is owned outside the forest representation leaf.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Refinement Piecewise Constancy of Regression Forests
Forest Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ensemble surrogate formed by averaging randomized regression trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_B:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be regression-tree predictors constructed from randomized resamples, randomized feature selection, or both. A forest surrogate is the ensemble average \[\widehat f_B(x)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^BT_b(x).\] Treating the construction randomness as random variables and fixing \(x\), identically distributed trees with variance \(\sigma_T^2(x)\) and common pairwise correlation \(\rho(x)\) satisfy \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_B(x))=\sigma_T^2(x)\left(\rho(x)+\frac{1-\rho(x)}{B}\right).\] Averaging therefore reduces the uncorrelated variance component, while correlated tree variation remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forest averages randomized tree predictors; averaging reduces the trees’ uncorrelated variance component but cannot remove their shared correlated variation.
assumptions_latex: \(T_1(x),\ldots,T_B(x)\) have finite second moments
The tree predictions are identically distributed at fixed \(x\)
Distinct tree predictions have common correlation \(\rho(x)\)

notation.meaning: variance of one randomized tree prediction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard ensemble-average representation and equicorrelated variance identity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ensemble representation and equicorrelated variance identity are correct under the stated common-variance and common-correlation model, but they lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Partition Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Region-specific predictive models organized by explicit or latent domain partitions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compatibility condition for gluing continuous regional predictors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^L C_\ell\) be a finite closed cover and let \(g_\ell:C_\ell\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. There exists a continuous \(s:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(s|_{C_\ell}=g_\ell\) for every \(\ell\) if and only if \(g_\ell(x)=g_m(x)\) for every \(x\in C_\ell\cap C_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous regional predictors glue into a continuous global surrogate exactly when they agree wherever their closed regions overlap, including shared boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \((C_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) is a finite closed cover of \(D\).
Each \(g_\ell\) is continuous on \(C_\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists s\in C(D)\ \forall\ell\;s|_{C_\ell}=g_\ell\iff g_\ell=g_m\text{ on every }C_\ell\cap C_m.

notation.meaning: closed regional cell or cell closure

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Compatibility Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-support requirement for independently fitted regional components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a hard-partition cell \(R_\ell\) contains no observation and its regional model is neither linked to other cells nor identified by a prior, constraint, or penalty, then the empirical criterion is invariant to that regional component. Predictions within \(R_\ell\) are consequently unidentified by the observed data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty region has no data-identified local predictor unless information is supplied through sharing, constraints, regularization, or a prior.
assumptions_latex: No observation lies in \(R_\ell\).
The regional component has no identifying cross-cell link, prior, constraint, or penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_\ell\text{ is not identified by the empirical data criterion.}
knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Cell Identifiability Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separable Fitting on a Fixed Hard Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of additive empirical-risk fitting across fixed cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed partition \((R_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\), suppose \(J(g_1,\ldots,g_L)=\sum_{\ell=1}^LJ_\ell(g_\ell)\) and the admissible set is \(\prod_{\ell=1}^L\mathcal G_\ell\). If every regional argmin is nonempty, then \(\arg\min J=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\arg\min_{g_\ell\in\mathcal G_\ell}J_\ell(g_\ell)\). Shared parameters, coupling constraints, or cross-cell penalties invalidate this decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed partition and no cross-region coupling, fitting decomposes into independent regional problems.
assumptions_latex: The partition is fixed during fitting.
The objective is additive by cell.
The admissible model set is a Cartesian product.
Every regional minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Fitting on a Fixed Hard Partition
Partition Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General local-model surrogate assembled over a finite design-space partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be partitioned into pairwise-disjoint measurable cells \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) with \(D=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^L R_\ell\). Given predictors \(g_\ell:D\to\mathbb{R}\), the associated hard-partition surrogate is \[s(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L g_\ell(x)\mathbf{1}\{x\in R_\ell\}.\] More generally, weights \(w_\ell:D\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell(x)=1\) for every \(x\in D\) define the soft-partition surrogate \[s_w(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell(x)g_\ell(x).\] The hard form permits discontinuities at cell boundaries, whereas the soft form blends the predictor values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition surrogate either selects a local predictor according to the point's partition cell or blends predictors using nonnegative weights that sum to one.
assumptions_latex: \((R_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) is a finite measurable partition of \(D\)
\(g_\ell:D\to\mathbb{R}\) for every \(\ell=1,\ldots,L\)
\(w_\ell(x)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{\ell=1}^Lw_\ell(x)=1\) for every \(x\in D\) when soft weights are used
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hard representation selects one predictor according to the unique cell containing \(x\), while the soft representation is a convex combination of predictor values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard hard and soft partition-of-domain representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned tree partitions with independently fitted regional predictive models, including their computational and continuity consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\) recursively partition \(\mathcal X\) by axis-aligned binary splits into leaves \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal T}\). Assign an independent predictive model to each leaf \(\eta\), and define \(\widehat y(x)\) using the model in the unique leaf \(\eta(x)\) containing \(x\). Conditional independence between leaves makes the globally reordered covariance matrix block diagonal. Region-specific processes or hyperparameters permit nonstationary behavior and reduce inference to smaller local matrix decompositions, but predictions need not be continuous across partition boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursive axis-aligned tree assigns each input to one leaf and uses that leaf's independently fitted predictive model. Independence gives block-diagonal covariance and cheaper local computations while allowing region-specific, nonstationary behavior, but continuity across leaf boundaries is not guaranteed.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is a binary recursive partition of \(\mathcal X\) with leaves \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal T}\).
Each \(x\in\mathcal X\) belongs to a unique leaf \(\eta(x)\).
Leaf predictive models are conditionally independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat y(x)=\widehat y_{\eta(x)}(x),\quad K_{\mathcal T}\text{ is block diagonal up to permutation, while boundary continuity is not guaranteed.}

children.title: Mixed-Variable Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Partition structures accommodating continuous, categorical, or conditional inputs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Numeric Encoding Distorts Nominal Splits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing why unordered categories require subset splits rather than order-dependent thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nominal levels \(\{a,b,c\}\), encode them as \(e(a)=0,e(b)=1,e(c)=2\). The threshold split \(e(x)\leq1/2\) separates \(\{a\}\) from \(\{b,c\}\). Under the equally valid relabeling \(e'(a)=1,e'(b)=0,e'(c)=2\), the same numeric threshold separates \(\{b\}\) from \(\{a,c\}\). Thus thresholding an arbitrary numeric encoding is not invariant to category relabeling and does not define an intrinsic nominal partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numeric threshold splits on nominal category codes change when the codes are permuted, imposing an artificial order.
assumptions_latex: The categories are nominal and have no intrinsic ordering.
The splitting rule treats their numeric codes as ordered values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Numeric-threshold partitions of nominal levels are not invariant under relabeling.}

notation.meaning: two numeric encodings of the same nominal levels

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Numeric Encoding Distorts Nominal Splits

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity conditions for recursive partitions on hierarchical spaces containing inactive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_j(x_{-j})\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether coordinate \(x_j\) is active. A valid hierarchical partition must distinguish the inactive subset \(\{x\in R:A_j(x_{-j})=0\}\) before applying value-based splits of \(x_j\), or apply such splits only within a cell where \(A_j=1\) throughout. Points with the same active configuration that differ only in an inactive coordinate must remain in the same predictive cell unless a declared inactive-value state has independent semantics. Thus arbitrary placeholders for inactive coordinates cannot change the represented prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditionally active variables may be value-split only on active points, and irrelevant inactive placeholders must not alter cell membership or prediction.
assumptions_latex: Each conditional coordinate has a declared activation rule determined by other coordinates.
Inactive coordinate values have no semantic effect unless an explicit inactive state is modeled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_j(x_{-j})=0,\ x_{-j}=x'_{-j}\Rightarrow C(x)=C(x')\ \text{when }x,x'\text{ differ only in inactive }x_j.
review_flags: Revised to permit an explicit inactive branch before splitting the active subset; the builder's active-throughout-parent rule was unnecessarily restrictive.
knowledge_statements.title: Partitions with Conditionally Active Variables
Mixed-Variable Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Axis-aligned recursive partitions for continuous, ordinal, and categorical Bayesian-optimization inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the search space be \(\mathcal X=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathcal X_j\), where each coordinate domain is continuous, ordinal, or categorical. A mixed-variable recursive partition is a finite rooted tree whose root represents \(\mathcal X\) and whose internal node representing \(R\subseteq\mathcal X\) is split on one coordinate \(j\): by \(x_j\le t\) versus \(x_j>t\) for ordered domains, or by \(x_j\in A\) versus \(x_j\notin A\) for categorical domains, with nonempty children. Its leaves form pairwise-disjoint cells \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) satisfying \(\mathcal X=\bigcup_{\ell=1}^L R_\ell\); a partition surrogate assigns a local predictive distribution to each cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-variable partition recursively splits ordered coordinates at thresholds and categorical coordinates by level subsets, producing disjoint cells with local predictive models.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathcal X_j\) has finitely many coordinates.
Every categorical split uses a nonempty proper subset of the levels present in its parent cell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{R_\ell\}_{\ell=1}^L\) is a disjoint partition of \(\mathcal X\) supporting cellwise prediction.

notation.meaning: leaf cell of the recursive partition
subset defining one branch of a categorical split

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recursive mixed-variable partition definition is standard, but supplied locators do not specifically support it

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent, properly delimited, and fits the mixed-variable partitioning leaf, but no inspectable source supports the specialized construction.

children.title: Partition Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of predictions or uncertainty to sparse data near changing partition boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient local certificate for stability of finite score-maximizing split selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite and suppose \(|q_s(D)-q_s(D_0)|\le L_s d(D,D_0)\) locally. If \(s^*\) uniquely maximizes \(q_s(D_0)\) with gap \(\Delta=q_{s^*}(D_0)-\max_{s\ne s^*}q_s(D_0)>0\), then \(s^*\) remains the unique maximizer whenever \(d(D,D_0)<\Delta/(L_{s^*}+\max_{s\ne s^*}L_s)\), interpreting a zero denominator as an unbounded certified radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive best-versus-second-best score margin and local score-sensitivity bounds certify a neighborhood in which the selected split cannot change.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
Each \(q_s\) satisfies the stated local Lipschitz bound at \(D_0\).
The maximizing split at \(D_0\) has positive gap \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s^*\text{ is the unique maximizing split throughout the certified neighborhood.}

notation.meaning: score of candidate split s on dataset D

knowledge_statements.title: Split-Margin Stability Certificate
Partition Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of data-selected recursive partitions near competing empirical split optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a metric space of datasets, and let \(T(D)\) select a score-maximizing root split from a finite candidate set using a fixed tie-breaking rule. Suppose distinct splits \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) tie for the maximum score at \(D_0\), and every neighborhood of \(D_0\) contains a dataset where \(s_1\) is the uniquely maximizing split and a dataset where \(s_2\) is the uniquely maximizing split. Then there are sequences \(D_n\to D_0\) and \(D'_n\to D_0\) for which the selected root splits are respectively \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), so the selected-root-split map is not locally constant at \(D_0\). If, at some query \(x\), the corresponding surrogate predictions converge along these sequences to distinct limits, then the prediction map is discontinuous at \(D_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a tie between competing globally optimal splits, arbitrarily small data changes can select different root partitions. Prediction discontinuity follows when the associated predictions approach different limits.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is a metric space and the candidate split set is finite.
\(T(D)\) maximizes the empirical split score using a fixed tie-breaking rule.
Distinct splits \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) tie for the maximum at \(D_0\) and occur as unique maximizers arbitrarily near \(D_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected-root-split map is not locally constant at \(D_0\); if the resulting predictions have distinct sequential limits at some \(x\), the prediction map is discontinuous there.

notation.meaning: dataset at which the competing splits tie

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: instability of finite argmax selection near alternating unique maximizers

children.title: Neural Uncertainty Surrogate Family
children.top_down_role: Neural predictive models with posterior or ensemble-based uncertainty representations.

children.title: Bayesian Neural Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Neural predictive models carrying posterior uncertainty over parameters or functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Bayesian Neural Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior predictive neural-network surrogate for noisy black-box observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \(D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), a Bayesian neural surrogate specifies a neural conditional model \(p(y\mid x,w)\), a prior \(p(w)\), and posterior \(p(w\mid D)\propto p(w)\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i\mid x_i,w)\). Its surrogate prediction at \(x\) is the posterior predictive distribution \[p(y\mid x,D)=\int p(y\mid x,w)p(w\mid D)\,dw.\] For scalar responses, posterior predictive mean and variance may be supplied to an acquisition rule; the variance combines variability across posterior weights with conditional observation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian neural surrogate integrates neural-network predictions over a posterior distribution on weights, yielding a predictive distribution for acquisition decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) is conditionally independent given \(w\).
The posterior predictive integral exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(y\mid x,D)\) is the surrogate predictive distribution used by Bayesian optimization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Likelihood-power and full-posterior temperature transformations for Bayesian neural inference, retained here as a neural-surrogate specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(\boldsymbol\theta)=p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\theta)\). The \(\alpha\)-tempered posterior and temperature-\(T\) posterior are respectively
\[
p_{\mathrm{temp}}(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto L(\boldsymbol\theta)^\alpha p_{\mathrm{temp}}(\boldsymbol\theta),
\qquad
p_T(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto \left[L(\boldsymbol\theta)p_{\mathrm{cold}}(\boldsymbol\theta)\right]^{1/T}.
\]
The latter is cold when \(T<1\). If \(p_{\mathrm{cold}}=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{cold}}^2I)\), then the same normalized target is obtained by setting
\[
\alpha=1/T,\qquad p_{\mathrm{temp}}=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{temp}}^2I),\qquad
\sigma_{\mathrm{temp}}^2=T\sigma_{\mathrm{cold}}^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Likelihood tempering raises only the likelihood to a power, whereas a temperature posterior raises both likelihood and prior to power 1/T; temperatures below one are cold. With an isotropic Gaussian prior, the cold target is equivalent to likelihood tempering with alpha equal to 1/T after multiplying the prior variance by T.
assumptions_latex: L(\boldsymbol\theta)=p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\theta)
\alpha>0
p_{\mathrm{cold}}(\boldsymbol\theta)=\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{cold}}^2I)\text{ for the equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_T\equiv p_{\mathrm{temp}}\text{ after normalization when }\alpha=1/T\text{ and }\sigma_{\mathrm{temp}}^2=T\sigma_{\mathrm{cold}}^2

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayesian model averaging for a neural predictive model; within this node it is a surrogate-model specialization of a more general Bayesian-inference representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given data \(\mathcal D\), prior \(p(\boldsymbol\theta)\), likelihood \(p(\mathcal D\mid\boldsymbol\theta)\), and conditional predictive model \(p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)\),
\[
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto p(\boldsymbol\theta)p(\mathcal D\mid\boldsymbol\theta),\qquad
p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\mathcal D)=\int p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,d\boldsymbol\theta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian neural predictive model averages predictions over the posterior distribution of its parameters instead of retaining only one fitted parameter setting.
assumptions_latex: p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto p(\boldsymbol\theta)p(\mathcal D\mid\boldsymbol\theta)
p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)\text{ is the conditional predictive model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\mathcal D)=\int p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta)p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\,d\boldsymbol\theta

children.title: Deep Ensemble Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Collections of neural predictors used to represent predictive diversity.

knowledge_statements.title: Deep Ensemble Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-mixture predictive representation for independently trained neural networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\ge2\) neural predictors be trained from distinct initializations, data resamples, or randomized optimization paths, with member predictive distributions \(p_m(y\mid x)\). The deep-ensemble surrogate is the equally weighted mixture \[p_{\mathrm{ens}}(y\mid x)=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M p_m(y\mid x).\] If member \(m\) has mean \(\mu_m(x)\) and variance \(v_m(x)\), then \[\mu_{\mathrm{ens}}(x)=\frac1M\sum_m\mu_m(x),\qquad v_{\mathrm{ens}}(x)=\frac1M\sum_m\bigl(v_m(x)+\mu_m(x)^2\bigr)-\mu_{\mathrm{ens}}(x)^2.\] The second expression includes within-member and between-member uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deep ensemble represents uncertainty by mixing predictions from randomized neural models; total variance combines within-model variance and disagreement among models.
assumptions_latex: \(M\ge2\) and every member predictive distribution has a finite second moment.
Mixture weights are \(1/M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ensemble predictive law is \(p_{\mathrm{ens}}\), with mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{ens}}\) and variance \(v_{\mathrm{ens}}\) as displayed.

notation.meaning: predictive distribution of ensemble member m

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-mixture representation and moment decomposition are correct and the representation kind fits, but no authoritative deep-ensemble source with a locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A mixture-of-point-masses representation for multiple fitted neural predictors; within this node it is used as a surrogate specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(M\) fitted neural models with MAP estimates \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_1,\ldots,\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_M\), a deep ensemble approximates the parameter posterior by
\[
p(\boldsymbol\theta\mid\mathcal D)\approx \frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\delta\!\left(\boldsymbol\theta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_m\right).
\]
The members may be diversified through initialization, hyperparameters, architecture, or an explicit functional-repulsion term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deep ensemble represents the posterior by an equally weighted mixture of point masses at the fitted MAP parameters of multiple neural models. Diverse members can capture distinct predictive functions rather than only a local neighborhood of one fitted mode.
assumptions_latex: M\in\mathbb N
\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_m\text{ is the MAP estimate for fitted ensemble member }m

children.title: Approximate Posterior Neural Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Neural uncertainty representations based on tractable posterior approximations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Posterior Fitting by the ELBO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical variational construction of a tractable neural weight posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For prior \(p(w)\), likelihood \(p(D\mid w)\), and variational family \(\mathcal Q=\{q_\phi\}\), define \[\operatorname{ELBO}(\phi)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi}[\log p(D\mid W)]-\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi\|p(W)).\] Whenever the quantities are finite, \[\log p(D)=\operatorname{ELBO}(\phi)+\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi\|p(W\mid D)).\] Therefore increasing the ELBO decreases reverse KL by the same amount, and \(\sup_\phi\operatorname{ELBO}(\phi)=\log p(D)-\inf_\phi\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi\|p(W\mid D))\). A positive infimum is an irreducible variational-family gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variational neural surrogates fit a tractable weight distribution by maximizing the evidence lower bound, equivalently minimizing reverse KL within the selected family.
assumptions_latex: \(0<p(D)=\int p(D\mid w)p(w)\,dw<\infty\).
The required absolute-continuity conditions hold.
The displayed expectations and divergences are finite.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational Posterior Fitting by the ELBO

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampling-error rate for predictive summaries under a fitted approximate posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W_1,\ldots,W_S\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim q_\phi\), and suppose \(v_x=\operatorname{Var}_{q_\phi}(g_x(W))<\infty\). Then \(\widehat\mu_S(x)=S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^Sg_x(W_s)\) is unbiased for \(\widetilde\mu(x)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi}[g_x(W)]\), and \[\mathbb E[(\widehat\mu_S(x)-\widetilde\mu(x))^2]=\frac{v_x}{S}.\] Thus its root-mean-square integration error is \(\sqrt{v_x/S}\). This does not bound error from replacing \(p(w\mid D)\) by \(q_\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent approximate-posterior prediction averages have inverse-square-root Monte Carlo error but do not reduce posterior-approximation bias.
assumptions_latex: \(W_1,\ldots,W_S\) are independent draws from \(q_\phi\).
\(g_x(W)\) has finite variance under \(q_\phi\).

notation.meaning: predictive quantity at input x and weights W

knowledge_statements.title: Monte Carlo Predictive-Expectation Error

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of a neural weight-posterior approximation bound to the posterior predictive distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_D\) and \(Q_D\) be exact and approximate posterior laws of \(W\), and let \(K_x(w,\cdot)=p(\cdot\mid x,w)\) be the predictive Markov kernel. Then \[\|P_DK_x-Q_DK_x\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\|P_D-Q_D\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.\] Hence a certified weight-posterior total-variation error bounds predictive-event probability errors at each fixed input; the inequality supplies no guarantee when the posterior discrepancy itself is uncertified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying the same neural likelihood to exact and approximate weight posteriors cannot increase their total-variation discrepancy.
assumptions_latex: \(P_D\) and \(Q_D\) are probability measures on the same parameter space.
\(K_x\) is a Markov kernel from parameters to outcomes.
knowledge_statements.title: Predictive Total-Variation Contraction
Approximate Posterior Neural Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational or sampling approximation to a Bayesian neural posterior predictive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_\phi(w)\) approximate the intractable neural posterior \(p(w\mid D)\). The approximate posterior surrogate is \[\widetilde p(y\mid x,D)=\int p(y\mid x,w)q_\phi(w)\,dw.\] With draws \(w^{(1)},\ldots,w^{(S)}\) from \(q_\phi\), it is represented computationally by \[\widetilde p_S(y\mid x,D)=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S p(y\mid x,w^{(s)}).\] For integrable test functions, independent sampling gives convergence of mixture expectations to expectations under \(\widetilde p\) as \(S\to\infty\); this removes Monte Carlo error but not posterior-approximation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate posterior neural surrogate replaces the exact weight posterior by a tractable distribution and averages predictions over samples from it.
assumptions_latex: \(q_\phi\) is a probability distribution on the neural parameter space.
The predictive quantities being averaged are integrable under \(q_\phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde p_S\) approximates \(\widetilde p\), while any discrepancy between \(q_\phi\) and \(p(w\mid D)\) remains.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: approximate posterior predictive and Monte Carlo mixture

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The approximate posterior predictive and Monte Carlo representation are precise and correctly distinguish sampling error from posterior-approximation error, but they lack an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo dropout predictive approximation and fixed-rate failure boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Test-time Bernoulli dropout as an approximate neural posterior-prediction method; here retained only as a surrogate specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s=1,\ldots,S\), independently sample a dropout mask with dropout probability \(p\), apply it to the fitted neural network to obtain \(\boldsymbol\theta^s\), and use
\[
p(y\mid\mathbf x,\mathcal D)\approx \frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S p(y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta^s).
\]
The associated posterior approximation is degenerate, with parameter components represented by point masses at zero and at fitted values. If a positive dropout probability remains fixed as the data size tends to infinity, this approximation does not converge to the limiting point mass at the maximum-likelihood estimate. Optimizing the dropout probability can remove this fixed-rate pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monte Carlo dropout keeps dropout active at test time, samples multiple masks, and averages the resulting predictive distributions. Its degenerate posterior approximation is inconsistent when a positive dropout rate stays fixed as the dataset grows; optimizing that rate can fix this particular pathology.
assumptions_latex: S\in\mathbb N
\boldsymbol\theta^s\text{ is obtained by independently sampled Bernoulli dropout applied to a fitted neural network}
p>0\text{ remains fixed as the sample size tends to infinity for the inconsistency conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(y\mid\mathbf x,\mathcal D)\approx S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^S p(y\mid\mathbf x,\boldsymbol\theta^s),\qquad p>0\text{ fixed}\implies q_n\not\to\delta_{\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}}

children.title: Ensemble Calibration
children.top_down_role: Assessment of whether ensemble spread reflects predictive error across the search domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample certificate for marginal calibration error on an independent deployment-distributed validation sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For i.i.d. validation PIT values \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) with CDF \(H\), let \(\widehat H_n(u)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{U_i\leq u\}\) and \(d_n=\sup_{u\in[0,1]}|\widehat H_n(u)-u|\). The Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz inequality implies that, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), \[\sup_{u\in[0,1]}|H(u)-u|\leq d_n+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent validation PIT values give a uniform finite-sample upper bound on marginal PIT miscalibration.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are i.i.d. from the deployment PIT distribution.

notation.meaning: empirical Kolmogorov distance from the uniform CDF

review_flags: Certifies marginal calibration only under the validation distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Held-Out PIT Calibration Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calibration condition requiring the predictive CDF to equal the response law conditional on the modeled input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_X\) be the predictive CDF for scalar \(Y\). It is input-conditionally distribution-calibrated when, for every continuity point \(y\), \[P(Y\leq y\mid X)=F_X(y)\quad\text{almost surely}.\] With continuous conditional distributions this condition implies \(F_X(Y)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), whereas marginal PIT uniformity alone does not imply the conditional equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input-conditional calibration requires the announced predictive distribution to equal the response distribution at each input, a stronger requirement than marginal PIT uniformity.
assumptions_latex: \(F_X\) is a measurable predictive CDF.
Regular conditional response laws given \(X\) exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(Y\leq y\mid X)=F_X(y)\ \text{a.s.},\quad\text{implying marginal PIT calibration under continuity.}

notation.meaning: ensemble predictive CDF at the random input

review_flags: Corrected from forecast-conditional calibration so that the stated implication and subgroup counterexample use the same conditioning variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Input-Conditional Distribution Calibration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal PIT Calibration Does Not Imply Input-Conditional Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit mixture counterexample separating marginal PIT uniformity from input-conditional reliability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), let every forecast be \(F_x(y)=y\) on \([0,1]\), and let the true conditional densities be \(f_0(y)=2y\) and \(f_1(y)=2(1-y)\). The marginal density of \(Y\) is \((f_0+f_1)/2=1\), so \(U=F_X(Y)=Y\) is uniform. Nevertheless, \(P(Y\leq y\mid X=0)=y^2\neq y\) and \(P(Y\leq y\mid X=1)=2y-y^2\neq y\) for \(0<y<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oppositely miscalibrated input groups can cancel, yielding a uniform marginal PIT while every group forecast is wrong.
assumptions_latex: The two input groups have equal deployment probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal PIT Calibration Does Not Imply Input-Conditional Calibration
Ensemble Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal predictive calibration condition for ensemble distribution forecasts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_x\) be the ensemble predictive cumulative distribution for a scalar response \(Y\), and suppose \((X,Y)\) follows the deployment distribution. The ensemble is marginally probabilistically calibrated when the randomized probability integral transform \[U=F_X(Y^-)+V\bigl(F_X(Y)-F_X(Y^-)\bigr),\qquad V\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1),\] is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\), with \(V\) independent of \((X,Y)\). For continuous predictive distributions this reduces to \(F_X(Y)\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\). This condition concerns distributional calibration, not merely agreement of predictive means or variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ensemble is marginally calibrated when its randomized probability integral transform is uniform under the deployment distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(F_x\) is a valid cumulative distribution function for every \(x\).
\(V\) is independent of \((X,Y)\) and uniform on \([0,1]\).

notation.meaning: ensemble predictive cumulative distribution at input x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The randomized probability-integral-transform condition is coherent and appropriate as a marginal distributional calibration condition, but no calibration reference with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Limits
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty failures for candidates unlike the data supporting model training.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Ensemble Disagreement Does Not Certify OOD Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of between-member spread as an extrapolative reliability certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a point \(x_\star\) outside the training-input support and suppose every ensemble member predicts \(T_m(x_\star)=0\). The between-member variance is then zero. For any \(K>0\), a data-generating law agreeing with the observed-data law on the training support but satisfying \(Y(x_\star)=K\) has absolute ensemble-mean error \(K\) at \(x_\star\). Thus zero ensemble disagreement is compatible with arbitrarily large OOD error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All ensemble members can extrapolate identically and incorrectly, so zero OOD disagreement is not an accuracy certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(x_\star\) lies outside the support of the training inputs.
The admissible data-generating laws are unrestricted at \(x_\star\) after their behavior on the observed support is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Ensemble Disagreement Does Not Certify OOD Accuracy
Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-identifiability of neural predictive uncertainty outside observed support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the training-input distribution be supported on \(S\subsetneq\mathcal X\), and let \(x_\star\notin S\). If two data-generating laws \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) induce the same joint law of observations on \(S\) but different conditional laws of \(Y\) at \(x_\star\), then no surrogate procedure using only the training data can distinguish \(P_0\) from \(P_1\). Hence no distribution-free guarantee can require its predictive distribution or uncertainty at \(x_\star\) to be correct under both laws. Reliable out-of-distribution uncertainty therefore requires additional structural assumptions, representative data, or external information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Training data cannot identify predictive uncertainty outside their support when observationally identical data-generating laws disagree there.
assumptions_latex: Training inputs lie in \(S\subsetneq\mathcal X\) almost surely.
\(P_0\) and \(P_1\) agree on observed data over \(S\) but disagree at \(x_\star\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No data-only surrogate has universally valid predictive uncertainty at \(x_\star\) over a class containing both \(P_0\) and \(P_1\).
