children.title: Asymmetric Distributional Surrogate Family
children.top_down_role: Models centered on promising-region densities, conditional quantiles, or asymmetric predictive targets.

children.title: Density-Ratio Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models contrasting candidate density across promising and nonpromising outcome regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support and Calibration Failure of Density Ratios
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where ratio rankings are undefined or unstable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(x)=0<\ell(x)\), then \(\ell(x)/g(x)=+\infty\); if \(g(x)=\ell(x)=0\), the ratio is undefined. For classifier odds, \(d[\eta/(1-\eta)]/d\eta=(1-\eta)^{-2}\), so calibration errors are strongly amplified as \(\eta\uparrow1\). Stable numerical ranking therefore requires suitable support handling and calibration or regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support mismatch makes density ratios infinite or undefined, and classifier-odds ratios are highly calibration-sensitive near probability one.
assumptions_latex: The ratio is constructed from class-conditional densities or classifier odds.
knowledge_statements.title: Support and Calibration Failure of Density Ratios

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability property when only candidate ranking is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiplying numerator and denominator densities by the same finite positive pointwise factor leaves their ratio unchanged, and any strictly increasing transform of the ratio preserves its ordering. Consequently normalized class-conditional densities are unnecessary when the policy uses only an argmax of the ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common positive factors and increasing transformations preserve density-ratio rankings.
assumptions_latex: The common factor is finite and strictly positive on the candidate domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Ratio Ranking Invariance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifier-odds representation of the promising-to-nonpromising density ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With promising label \(Z\in\{0,1\}\), \(\gamma=P(Z=1)\), and \(\eta(x)=P(Z=1\mid X=x)\), Bayes' rule gives \(p(x\mid Z=1)/p(x\mid Z=0)=((1-\gamma)/\gamma)(\eta(x)/(1-\eta(x)))\) wherever denominators are positive. A calibrated probabilistic classifier can therefore estimate the density ratio without separately estimating both class-conditional densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The good-to-bad input-density ratio equals posterior class odds times a prior-odds correction.
assumptions_latex: Both class-conditional laws are dominated by a common measure.
\(0<\eta(x)<1\) at the evaluated point.
knowledge_statements.title: Class-Probability Odds and Density-Ratio Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population target and empirical fitting rule for estimating the promising-to-nonpromising input-density ratio through probabilistic classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given labeled observations \((X_i,Z_i)\), where \(Z_i=\mathbf 1\{Y_i\leq\tau\}\), fit \(\eta:\mathcal X\to(0,1)\) by minimizing empirical logarithmic loss \[\widehat L(\eta)=-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left[Z_i\log\eta(X_i)+(1-Z_i)\log(1-\eta(X_i))\right].\] At every point where \(0<P(Z=1\mid X=x)<1\), population logarithmic risk is uniquely minimized by \(\eta^*(x)=P(Z=1\mid X=x)\). With \(\gamma=P(Z=1)\), the corresponding ratio is \[r(x)=\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma}\frac{\eta^*(x)}{1-\eta^*(x)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-loss classification of threshold-induced labels estimates promising probability, which prior-odds correction converts into the class-density ratio.
assumptions_latex: The class-conditional input laws are dominated by a common measure.
\(0<P(Z=1\mid X=x)<1\) wherever a finite ratio is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Classification-Based Density-Ratio Estimation
Density-Ratio Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio representation induced by thresholding objective observations into good and bad classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, fix a threshold \(\tau\) and define \(Z=1\) when \(Y\le\tau\). Let \(\ell(x)=p(x\mid Z=1)\), \(g(x)=p(x\mid Z=0)\), and \(\gamma=P(Z=1)\in(0,1)\). Bayes' rule gives \[P(Z=1\mid x)=\frac{\gamma\ell(x)}{\gamma\ell(x)+(1-\gamma)g(x)}.\] Thus ranking points by decreasing posterior promising probability is equivalent, wherever both densities are positive, to ranking them by decreasing density ratio \(\ell(x)/g(x)\). A density-ratio surrogate estimates these class-conditional densities or their ratio rather than the full response law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thresholded observations define good and bad input densities; their ratio ranks inputs exactly as the posterior probability of being promising.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\gamma=P(Y\le\tau)<1\).
The class-conditional input distributions admit densities \(\ell\) and \(g\) with respect to a common measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordering by \(P(Y\le\tau\mid x)\) equals ordering by \(\ell(x)/g(x)\) where the ratio is defined.

notation.meaning: prior probability of a promising response

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bayes-rule identity and induced density-ratio ranking are correct and fit a representation leaf, but no density-ratio optimization source is cited.

children.title: Conditional Quantile Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models targeting selected conditional response quantiles.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact identification condition for a conditional quantile target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), the minimizers of \(t\mapsto\mathbb E[\rho_\alpha(Y-t)\mid X=x]\) are exactly \(\{t:P(Y<t\mid x)\leq\alpha\leq P(Y\leq t\mid x)\}\). The target is unique only when this condition singles out one value; a conditional CDF plateau at level \(\alpha\) can produce an interval of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pinball-risk minimizers are exactly the conditional quantiles satisfying the two-sided probability condition and may be nonunique on a CDF plateau.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[|Y|\mid X=x]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \arg\min_t\mathbb E[\rho_\alpha(Y-t)\mid x]=\{t:P(Y<t\mid x)\leq\alpha\leq P(Y\leq t\mid x)\}.
review_flags: The Builder rationale was corrected: atoms do not by themselves generally create an interval of quantiles; a plateau at the target probability does.
knowledge_statements.title: Pinball-Risk Quantile Identification and Nonuniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quantile Crossing in Separately Fitted Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coherence failure for independently estimated quantile levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conditional quantile function must satisfy \(q_\alpha(x)\leq q_\beta(x)\) for \(\alpha<\beta\). If separately fitted estimates satisfy \(\widehat q_\alpha(x)>\widehat q_\beta(x)\), they cannot jointly be quantiles of one conditional distribution at \(x\). Joint monotonic parameterization, inequality constraints, or rearrangement is then needed for coherence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separately fitted conditional quantiles can cross, in which case they do not represent a coherent conditional distribution.
assumptions_latex: At least two quantile levels are modeled.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantile Crossing in Separately Fitted Surrogates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property of conditional lower quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is strictly increasing and continuous, then the lower conditional quantile satisfies \(q_\alpha(g(Y)\mid x)=g(q_\alpha(Y\mid x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly increasing continuous response transformations carry lower conditional quantiles through the same transformation.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is strictly increasing and continuous.
The conditional distributions exist.

notation.meaning: Lower conditional quantile at level alpha.

knowledge_statements.title: Quantile Equivariance Under Increasing Transformations
Conditional Quantile Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input-dependent quantile function as an asymmetric surrogate target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar response \(Y\), input \(x\in\mathcal X\), and level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the conditional lower quantile is \[q_\alpha(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Y\le t\mid X=x)\ge\alpha\}.\] A conditional quantile surrogate estimates the map \(x\mapsto q_\alpha(x)\), commonly by minimizing empirical pinball loss \(\rho_\alpha(u)=u\bigl(\alpha-\mathbf 1\{u<0\}\bigr)\). At the population level, any minimizer of \(t\mapsto\mathbb E[\rho_\alpha(Y-t)\mid X=x]\) is an \(\alpha\)-conditional quantile, with uniqueness when the conditional distribution crosses level \(\alpha\) strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional quantile surrogate predicts an input-dependent response quantile, naturally learned through asymmetric pinball loss.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is real-valued and the conditional law given \(X=x\) exists.
\(\mathbb E[|Y|\mid X=x]<\infty\) when the pinball-risk characterization is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_\alpha(x)\) is an optimizer of conditional expected pinball loss.

notation.meaning: conditional lower quantile at level alpha

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conditional-quantile and pinball-loss characterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional lower-quantile definition and pinball-risk characterization are standard, precise, and appropriate for this definition leaf, but no authoritative quantile-regression source is supplied.

children.title: Promising-Region Density Models
children.top_down_role: Candidate-space models centered on regions associated with favorable observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct fitting and sampling of a promising-region input density; density-ratio ranking remains sibling-owned.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(D_n=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), a threshold \(\tau\), and \(I_\tau=\{i:y_i\le\tau\}\), fit a normalized density \(\widehat\ell_n\) to \(\{x_i:i\in I_\tau\}\). A direct proposal draws \(X_{n+1}\sim\widehat\ell_n\). To retain exploration, use \(q_n=(1-\varepsilon_n)\widehat\ell_n+\varepsilon_n r\), where \(0<\varepsilon_n\le1\) and \(r\) is an exploration density. Then \(q_n(A)\ge\varepsilon_n r(A)>0\) for every measurable \(A\) with \(r(A)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a density to inputs with favorable outcomes and optionally mix it with an exploration density so regions omitted by the fitted density remain reachable.
assumptions_latex: \(I_\tau\ne\varnothing\), or the estimator supplies smoothing or prior structure.
\(\widehat\ell_n\) and \(r\) are densities under the same base measure.
\(0<\varepsilon_n\le1\).

notation.meaning: indices whose responses meet the promising threshold

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Split Density Fitting
Promising-Region Density Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generative input model conditioned on objective values meeting a promising threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, choose \(\tau\in\mathbb R\) with \(0<P(Y\le\tau)<1\). A promising-region density model is an estimate \(\widehat\ell(x)\) of the conditional input density \(\ell(x)=p(x\mid Y\le\tau)\) with respect to a specified base measure on \(\mathcal X\). Candidate points may be sampled from \(\widehat\ell\) or ranked after comparison with a complementary density \(g(x)=p(x\mid Y>\tau)\). The modeled object is the distribution of inputs associated with favorable responses, rather than the conditional response distribution \(p(y\mid x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A promising-region model estimates the distribution of inputs whose observed objective values pass a favorable threshold.
assumptions_latex: The optimization problem is stated as minimization.
The conditional input law given \(Y\le\tau\) admits a density under the chosen base measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\ell\) models \(p(x\mid Y\le\tau)\) and supports promising-input generation or ranking.

notation.meaning: input density conditional on a promising response

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold-conditioned input-density definition is coherent and correctly distinguishes the modeled object from a response distribution, but it has no specialized source.

children.title: Asymmetric Predictive Targets
children.top_down_role: Predictive targets emphasizing tails, thresholds, or unequal error costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equal Means with Different Tail Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to mean sufficiency for asymmetric tail decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1\equiv0\) and let \(Y_2\in\{-1,1\}\) with equal probabilities. Both means are zero, but at \(\tau=-1/2\), \(P(Y_1\leq\tau)=0\) and \(P(Y_2\leq\tau)=1/2\). A mean-only surrogate therefore cannot generally determine a threshold-risk or quantile decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal conditional means can conceal different tails, so means are insufficient for threshold or quantile decisions.
assumptions_latex: The downstream decision depends on a tail probability or quantile.
knowledge_statements.title: Equal Means with Different Tail Decisions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-aligned predictive functional for an asymmetric binary threshold action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let action \(a=1\) assert \(Y\leq\tau\). If false assertion costs \(C_{10}>0\) and false rejection costs \(C_{01}>0\), the conditional Bayes action is \(a^*(x)=\mathbf1\{P(Y\leq\tau\mid X=x)\geq C_{10}/(C_{10}+C_{01})\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric threshold decision is governed by a conditional tail probability and a cost-derived cutoff.
assumptions_latex: The conditional event probability exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Threshold-Decision Predictive Target

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent normalized loss used to elicit conditional quantiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(u=y-a\) and \(\rho_\alpha(u)=u(\alpha-\mathbf1\{u<0\})\), the asymmetric loss satisfies \(L(y,a)=(c_-+c_+)\rho_\alpha(y-a)\) for \(\alpha=c_-/(c_-+c_+)\). Multiplication by the positive constant \(c_-+c_+\) leaves its Bayes acts unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymmetric absolute loss is a positive multiple of quantile check loss, so both elicit the same conditional quantile.
knowledge_statements.title: Check-Loss Equivalent Formulation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bayes Quantile Under Asymmetric Absolute Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-theoretic characterization of the optimal asymmetric point-prediction target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(y,a)=c_-(y-a)_++c_+(a-y)_+\) with \(c_-,c_+>0\), and set \(\alpha=c_-/(c_-+c_+)\). Conditional on \(X=x\), the minimizers of \(\mathbb E[L(Y,a)\mid X=x]\) are exactly the conditional \(\alpha\)-quantiles \(\{a:F_{Y\mid x}(a-)\le\alpha\le F_{Y\mid x}(a)\}\). If the conditional distribution has a unique \(\alpha\)-quantile, the Bayes act is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under unequal linear under- and overprediction costs, the Bayes-optimal prediction is the corresponding conditional quantile.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[|Y|\mid X=x]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[L(Y,a)\mid X=x]=\{a:F_{Y\mid x}(a-)\le\alpha\le F_{Y\mid x}(a)\}.

notation.meaning: Left limit of the conditional distribution function at a.

knowledge_statements.title: Bayes Quantile Under Asymmetric Absolute Loss
Asymmetric Predictive Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-aligned prediction under unequal costs for over- and underestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a scalar response and let underprediction and overprediction incur unequal linear costs \(c_->0\) and \(c_+>0\). For the loss \[L(y,a)=c_-(y-a)_+ + c_+(a-y)_+,\] every Bayes-optimal point prediction \(a^*(x)\) is a conditional quantile at level \(\alpha=c_-/(c_-+c_+)\). Thus a surrogate intended for an asymmetric downstream decision should target the corresponding conditional quantile rather than the conditional mean. The mean is generally optimal for symmetric squared loss, not for this asymmetric absolute loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal over- and underprediction costs make a conditional quantile, rather than the mean, the decision-optimal surrogate target.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[|Y|\mid X=x]<\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Bayes act for asymmetric absolute loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymmetric absolute-loss Bayes target is correctly identified as the stated conditional quantile, and the principle kind fits the leaf, but an authoritative decision-theoretic citation is absent.

children.title: Tail-Data Scarcity
children.top_down_role: Limits caused by insufficient observations in targeted quantile or promising-region tails.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact i.i.d. sample requirement for controlling the probability of an empty promising class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(N_\tau\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\gamma)\), \(0<\gamma<1\), and \(0<\delta<1\), then \(P(N_\tau=0)\le\delta\) is equivalent to \((1-\gamma)^n\le\delta\). The least admissible integer is \[n_{\min}=\left\lceil\frac{\log\delta}{\log(1-\gamma)}\right\rceil.\] Since \((1-\gamma)^n\le e^{-n\gamma}\), the simpler condition \(n\ge\gamma^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\) is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under i.i.d. tail membership, controlling the chance of no tail observations requires on the order of log one over delta divided by the tail probability samples.
assumptions_latex: \(N_\tau\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\gamma)\).
\(0<\gamma<1\) and \(0<\delta<1\).

notation.meaning: tolerated probability of an empty tail class
least integer sample size meeting that tolerance

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Tail-Observation Sample Requirement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of the empty-tail bound to sequentially selected observations and its failure without a conditional tail-probability floor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_i=\mathbf1\{Y_i\le\tau\}\) be adapted to \((\mathcal F_i)\). If \(P(Z_i=1\mid\mathcal F_{i-1})\ge\underline\gamma>0\) almost surely for every \(i\), then \[P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i=0\right)\le(1-\underline\gamma)^n.\] Hence \(n\ge\underline\gamma^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\) is sufficient for an empty-class probability at most \(\delta\). Without a positive conditional lower bound, no universal finite sample size controls this probability: a policy may assign zero probability to the promising event at every later evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive observations retain a geometric empty-tail bound only when every step has a positive conditional chance of entering the tail; without that exploration condition no universal sample-size guarantee exists.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_i\) is \(\mathcal F_i\)-measurable.
\(P(Z_i=1\mid\mathcal F_{i-1})\ge\underline\gamma>0\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: uniform conditional lower bound on tail-entry probability
number of tail observations through step n

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Tail-Scarcity Boundary
Tail-Data Scarcity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample limitation for learning rare conditional tails or promising regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_i=\mathbf 1\{Y_i\le\tau\}\) for independent observations and let \(P(Z_i=1)=\gamma\). The number of promising observations \(N_\tau=\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\) satisfies \(N_\tau\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\gamma)\), so \(\mathbb E[N_\tau]=n\gamma\) and \(P(N_\tau=0)=(1-\gamma)^n\). Therefore, when \(n\gamma\) is small, a tail-conditioned density or extreme conditional quantile is supported by few observations and may be unidentified by the sample; in particular, no empirical promising-class density can be fitted when \(N_\tau=0\) without smoothing, pooling, or prior structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rare favorable responses yield only about nγ tail observations and can leave a tail surrogate with no direct training examples.
assumptions_latex: \((Y_i)_{i=1}^n\) are independent and identically distributed.
\(\gamma=P(Y_i\le\tau)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[N_\tau]=n\gamma\) and \(P(N_\tau=0)=(1-\gamma)^n\), exposing the rare-tail data limit.

notation.meaning: number of observations meeting the promising threshold
probability of a tail or promising observation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary binomial count establishes the scarcity mechanism

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binomial count identities correctly expose the rare-tail sampling mechanism and fit a failure-boundary leaf. A source is still required for the asserted implications for fitting tail-conditioned surrogate models.

children.title: Structured Surrogate Representations
children.top_down_role: Models adapted to coupled outputs, fidelities, tasks, high dimension, and complex search spaces.

children.title: Cross-Task Output Surrogate Family
children.top_down_role: Models transferring information across correlated outputs or tasks.

children.title: Multioutput Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models coupling multiple response variables observed within a common problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block posterior law for observed and requested input-output pairs in a multioutput Gaussian-process surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_O\) and \(z_*\) collect observed and requested latent output coordinates, with means \(m_O,m_*\), covariance blocks \(K_{OO},K_{**},K_{*O}\), and Gaussian observation-noise covariance \(\Sigma_O\). If \(K_{OO}+\Sigma_O\) is nonsingular, then \[z_*\mid y_O\sim N\!\left(m_*+K_{*O}(K_{OO}+\Sigma_O)^{-1}(y_O-m_O),\ K_{**}-K_{*O}(K_{OO}+\Sigma_O)^{-1}K_{O*}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multioutput Gaussian-process prediction applies Gaussian conditioning to the block covariance over observed and requested output coordinates.
assumptions_latex: The selected latent values and observation errors are jointly Gaussian.
\(K_{OO}+\Sigma_O\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_*\mid y_O\) has the displayed Gaussian mean and covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Multioutput Gaussian Conditioning

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between matrix-valued kernels and scalar kernels indexed by input-output pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^{q\times q}\) and define \(\widetilde k((x,a),(x',b))=K_{ab}(x,x')\) on \(\mathcal X\times\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Then \(K\) has positive-semidefinite block Gram matrices if and only if \(\widetilde k\) is a positive-semidefinite scalar kernel. Under this correspondence, a vector-valued Gaussian process \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_q)\) and \(\widetilde f(x,a)=f_a(x)\) have equivalent finite-dimensional distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional multioutput Gaussian process is equivalently a scalar Gaussian process whose input includes the output index.
assumptions_latex: \(q<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\succeq0\text{ as a matrix-valued kernel}\iff \widetilde k\succeq0\text{ on }\mathcal X\times\{1,\ldots,q\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Domain Equivalence
Multioutput Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued probabilistic surrogates for jointly modeling several outputs at each design point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input domain and \(q\ge 2\). A multioutput surrogate for an unknown map \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^q\) is a probability model on vector-valued functions whose observations satisfy \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\). In the Gaussian-process case, \(f\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,K)\), where \(m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^q\) and \(K:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^{q\times q}\) obey \(K_{ab}(x,x')=K_{ba}(x',x)\) and induce positive-semidefinite block Gram matrices. Posterior prediction returns a joint distribution for all requested input-output pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multioutput surrogate jointly models a vector of responses, using a valid matrix-valued covariance to represent dependence across inputs and output coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty and \(q\ge 2\).
Observation noise has a specified joint distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\mid\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) defines joint predictive laws for vector outputs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, matrix-valued covariance conditions, content kind, and local scope are mathematically appropriate, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator. Authoritative support for multioutput Gaussian-process surrogates is required.

children.title: Multitask Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models transferring information across related optimization tasks or contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Multitask Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Task-indexed surrogate representation permitting observations and predictions at different tasks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T=\{1,\ldots,T\}\) be a finite task set. A multitask surrogate is a probabilistic model for \(g:\mathcal X\times\mathcal T\to\mathbb R\), fitted to data \(D=\{(x_i,t_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) with \(y_i=g(x_i,t_i)+\varepsilon_i\). A multitask Gaussian process specifies \(g\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,k)\) on the augmented domain. A common separable specification is \(k((x,t),(x',t'))=k_X(x,x')B_{tt'}\), where \(k_X\) is positive semidefinite and \(B\succeq0\) is a task-covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multitask surrogate treats the task label as part of the input and uses task covariance to share information across related tasks.
assumptions_latex: \(k_X\) is positive semidefinite and \(B\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is a valid covariance kernel on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The task-indexed formulation and separable covariance construction fit this definition leaf, but no cited source supports the terminology or construction. A specific authoritative section, theorem, definition, or page is required.

children.title: Cross-Output Dependence
children.top_down_role: Representations of correlation or shared latent structure among response channels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why symmetric finite covariance entries do not guarantee a valid joint output covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two standardized outputs at one input, \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}\) is positive semidefinite exactly when \(|\rho|\le1\). Choosing \(|\rho|>1\) gives finite marginal variances and symmetry but an invalid joint covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed cross-correlation larger than one makes the block covariance invalid despite finite marginals and symmetry.
assumptions_latex: Both marginal variances are one.

notation.meaning: proposed cross-output covariance at the common input

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Pairwise Cross-Covariance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence interpretation for jointly Gaussian output values and processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For jointly Gaussian output values, \(K_{ab}(x,x')=0\) is equivalent to independence of \(f_a(x)\) and \(f_b(x')\). If every cross-covariance between the two output processes is zero, their finite-dimensional subvectors are independent and hence the processes are independent under the joint Gaussian prior. Outside the Gaussian family, zero covariance need not imply independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero cross-covariance implies independence for jointly Gaussian outputs, but not generally.
assumptions_latex: The relevant output values or finite-dimensional process vectors are jointly Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_{ab}(x,x')=0\iff f_a(x)\perp f_b(x')\quad\text{for jointly Gaussian values}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Cross-Covariance and Gaussian Independence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coregionalization constructions separating input covariance from output dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each \(k_r\) is a scalar positive-semidefinite kernel and each \(B_r\succeq0\), then \(K(x,x')=\sum_{r=1}^R B_rk_r(x,x')\) is a valid matrix-valued covariance kernel. The separable case is \(K(x,x')=Bk_X(x,x')\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid cross-output kernels arise by combining scalar input kernels with positive-semidefinite output covariance matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(B_r\succeq0\) for every component.
Every \(k_r\) is a positive-semidefinite scalar kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K(x,x')=\sum_{r=1}^R B_rk_r(x,x')\ \text{is a positive-semidefinite matrix-valued kernel}.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable and Summed Cross-Output Covariance
Cross-Output Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for covariance coupling among outputs of a vector-valued Gaussian surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For outputs \(a,b\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), let \(K_{ab}(x,x')=\operatorname{Cov}(f_a(x),f_b(x'))\). The collection represents admissible cross-output dependence exactly when it is symmetric, \(K_{ab}(x,x')=K_{ba}(x',x)\), and positive semidefinite: for every \(n\ge1\), inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), and vectors \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R^q\), \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i^{\mathsf T}K(x_i,x_j)c_j\ge0.\] Nonzero off-diagonal entries encode prior linear dependence between distinct outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-output covariance is valid precisely when its block kernel is symmetric and positive semidefinite; off-diagonal blocks encode dependence.
assumptions_latex: Second moments of all modeled outputs are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is the covariance kernel of a vector-valued Gaussian process precisely under the displayed validity conditions.

notation.meaning: cross-covariance between outputs a and b

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetry and block positive-semidefiniteness conditions correctly characterize a matrix-valued covariance kernel and fit a condition record. The candidate nevertheless lacks an inspectable source for the equivalence and Gaussian-process existence claim.

children.title: Cross-Task Transfer
children.top_down_role: Representations governing information sharing among related tasks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Gaussian certificate that candidate source observations cannot update selected target quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(Y\in\mathbb R^r\) be jointly Gaussian conditionally on \(D\), with \(V=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid D)\succ0\) and \(C=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y\mid D)\). Conditioning on \(Y\) leaves the conditional law of \(Z\) unchanged exactly when \(C=0\). Otherwise its covariance is reduced by the nonzero positive-semidefinite matrix \(CV^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero conditional target-source covariance block exactly certifies no Gaussian transfer.
assumptions_latex: \((Z,Y)\mid D\) is jointly Gaussian.
\(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid D)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional No-Transfer Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prior Relatedness Does Not Guarantee Posterior Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between prior correlation and incremental information after current data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonzero prior covariance between tasks does not guarantee transfer from a proposed source observation after conditioning on current data. Existing observations can make \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y\mid D)=0\), producing no further target update despite nonzero prior dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prior task correlation can be screened off by current data, leaving no incremental transfer.
assumptions_latex: The joint prior and observation model are Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.title: Prior Relatedness Does Not Guarantee Posterior Transfer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of source-observation noise on scalar Gaussian transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With conditional target-source covariance \(c\), source latent variance \(v\), and independent observation-noise variance \(\sigma^2\), the target variance reduction is \(\Delta=c^2/(v+\sigma^2)\). For fixed \(c\ne0\), it decreases strictly with \(\sigma^2\) and tends to zero as \(\sigma^2\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-task variance reduction decreases with source-observation noise and vanishes in the infinite-noise limit.
assumptions_latex: The conditional joint law is Gaussian.
Observation noise is independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Attenuated Transfer Gain
Cross-Task Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-conditioning criterion for information transfer from one task to another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a jointly Gaussian multitask surrogate and two task-indexed latent values \(Z=g(x,t)\) and \(W=g(x',s)\). Given current data \(D\), a noisy observation \(Y=W+\epsilon\), with independent \(\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), updates the target prediction by \[\mathbb E[Z\mid D,Y]=\mathbb E[Z\mid D]+\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W\mid D)}{\operatorname{Var}(W\mid D)+\sigma^2}\bigl(Y-\mathbb E[W\mid D]\bigr).\] Thus cross-task transfer occurs exactly when the conditional cross-covariance is nonzero; its variance reduction equals \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W\mid D)^2/(\operatorname{Var}(W\mid D)+\sigma^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gaussian observation from one task informs another exactly through their conditional cross-covariance, which determines both mean update and variance reduction.
assumptions_latex: The joint conditional law given \(D\) is Gaussian.
Observation noise is independent with variance \(\sigma^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y\) changes the law of \(Z\) only if \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W\mid D)\ne0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional Gaussian update and variance reduction are correct under the stated independent-noise assumptions, and the property fits the Cross-Task Transfer leaf. No source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Negative-Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where weak or misleading relatedness degrades predictions for the target output or task.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-theoretic comparison of a transferred rule with a declared target-only baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_0\) be target-task data, \(D_A\) auxiliary-task data, \(\delta_T(D_0,D_A)\) a transferred decision rule, and \(\delta_0(D_0)\) a specified target-only baseline. Under a fixed joint target-and-auxiliary data-generating regime \(P\) and target loss \(L\), define \(R_P(\delta)=\mathbb E_P[L(\delta,\theta_0)]\). Negative transfer occurs exactly when \[R_P(\delta_T)-R_P(\delta_0)>0.\] Equality is the no-gain boundary, and a negative difference is beneficial transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer is negative when auxiliary-task information makes target risk exceed that of a declared target-only baseline under the same loss and data regime.
assumptions_latex: Both rules are compared under the same joint data-generating regime and target loss.
The relevant risks are finite.
The target-only baseline is fixed before the comparison.

notation.meaning: target risk under the fixed joint regime

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Based Negative-Transfer Boundary
Negative-Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Misspecified cross-task dependence can make auxiliary-task data degrade target prediction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the true target and auxiliary values be independent, \(Z,W\sim N(0,1)\), but let a fitted surrogate impose \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W)=\rho\ne0\). After observing \(Y=W+\epsilon\), where \(\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) is independent, the fitted posterior mean for \(Z\) is \(\widehat Z=\rho Y/(1+\sigma^2)\). Under the true model, its mean-squared error is \[\mathbb E[(Z-\widehat Z)^2]=1+\frac{\rho^2}{1+\sigma^2}>1.\] The separate-task predictor \(0\) has error \(1\); hence any nonzero spurious coupling produces negative transfer in this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When truly independent tasks are fitted with nonzero correlation, auxiliary observations introduce error and strictly worsen target mean-squared prediction.
assumptions_latex: The true variables and noise are mutually independent centered Gaussians.
The fitted model incorrectly uses \(\rho\ne0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and mean-squared-error calculation are correct and constitute an appropriate failure boundary. A cited source is still required to support its placement as a negative-transfer boundary rather than an uncited constructed example.

children.title: Heterogeneous-Source Surrogate Coupling
children.top_down_role: Models coupling observations of differing accuracy, resolution, or cost.

children.title: Multifidelity Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models coupling evaluations across accuracy, resolution, or simulation-fidelity levels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General fidelity-indexed Gaussian-process formulation, without restricting coupling to the autoregressive construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L=\{1,\ldots,L\}\) be a declared fidelity ordering with target level \(L\). A fidelity-indexed Gaussian-process surrogate models \(g:\mathcal X\times\mathcal L\to\mathbb R\) with a positive-semidefinite kernel \(k((x,\ell),(x',m))\); observations at any level condition the posterior for \(g(\cdot,L)\) through the modeled cross-level covariance. The ordering identifies the target and intended accuracy hierarchy but does not by itself require an autoregressive covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifidelity Gaussian process may be represented directly on an input-fidelity domain with an ordered target level and any valid cross-level covariance.
assumptions_latex: \(L\ge2\) and the fidelity ordering is declared.
\(k\) is a positive-semidefinite kernel on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal L\).
Each fidelity level has a specified observation likelihood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\cdot,L)\mid D\) defines the highest-fidelity posterior under the joint fidelity-indexed model.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Fidelity-Indexed Surrogate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latent-component expansion and covariance induced by the seed's ordered autoregressive construction with constant scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \(f_1=\delta_1\) and \(f_\ell=\rho_{\ell-1}f_{\ell-1}+\delta_\ell\), with constant scalars \(\rho_j\) and mutually independent centered processes \(\delta_j\) having kernels \(k_j\), define \(P_{r:\ell-1}=\prod_{j=r}^{\ell-1}\rho_j\), with an empty product equal to one. Then \[f_\ell(x)=\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}P_{r:\ell-1}\delta_r(x),\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(f_\ell(x),f_m(x'))=\sum_{r=1}^{\min(\ell,m)}P_{r:\ell-1}P_{r:m-1}k_r(x,x').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With constant inter-level scaling, every fidelity expands into shared independent discrepancy components, yielding an explicit cross-fidelity covariance.
assumptions_latex: The inter-level scalings are deterministic constants.
The discrepancy processes are centered and mutually independent with valid kernels.

notation.meaning: product of inter-level scalings from level r through level ell minus one
covariance kernel of discrepancy process r

knowledge_statements.title: Induced Autoregressive Cross-Fidelity Covariance

assumptions_latex: \(L\ge 2\) fidelity levels have a declared ordering.
Each \(\rho_{\ell-1}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is deterministic; scalar scaling is included as the constant-function case.
The discrepancy processes have valid covariance kernels and are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f_1,\ldots,f_L)\) has a jointly Gaussian prior and conditioning on observations from the fidelity levels induces a posterior for \(f_L\).

notation.meaning: deterministic inter-level scaling function, possibly constant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autoregressive coupling of ordered fidelity levels with explicit discrepancy processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an input domain, let \(L\ge 2\), and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_L:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) denote simulators ordered from lowest to highest fidelity. An autoregressive multifidelity surrogate represents \(f_1=\delta_1\) and \[f_\ell(x)=\rho_{\ell-1}(x)f_{\ell-1}(x)+\delta_\ell(x),\qquad \ell=2,\ldots,L,\] where \(\delta_1,[200~\ldots,\delta_L\) are mutually independent Gaussian processes and each \(\rho_{\ell-1}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is a deterministic scaling function, including a scalar as the constant-function case. Joint conditioning on observations from the fidelity levels yields a posterior for the designated highest-fidelity response \(f_L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An autoregressive multifidelity surrogate builds each fidelity from a deterministically scaled lower-fidelity response plus an independent discrepancy process.
knowledge_statements.title: Multifidelity Surrogates

children.title: Multi-Information-Source Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models combining heterogeneous simulators, sensors, experts, or experimental channels.

assumptions_latex: \(S\ge 1\), and \(\mathcal S=\{0,\ldots,S\}\) contains the designated target source \(0\).
The augmented-domain covariance kernel is positive semidefinite, and each source has a specified observation likelihood.

notation.meaning: observed input, source, and response triples

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint surrogate over heterogeneous sources without requiring a total fidelity ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\ge 1\), let \(\mathcal S=\{0,\ldots,S\}\) index heterogeneous information sources, and designate \(s=0\) as the target source. A multi-information-source surrogate is a probabilistic model for \(h:\mathcal X\times\mathcal S\to\mathbb R\), conditioned on data \(D=\{(x_i,s_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), where \(n\ge 0\), \(x_i\in\mathcal X\), \(s_i\in\mathcal S\), and \(y_i\in\mathbb R\). It specifies source-dependent means, observation laws, and a valid covariance \(k((x,s),(x',s'))\). Unlike an ordered multifidelity model, it need not place every source on one accuracy hierarchy; prediction and optimization concern \(h(\cdot,0)\), while other sources contribute through modeled cross-source dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-information-source surrogate jointly models observations from heterogeneous sources, designates a target source, and shares information without requiring a total fidelity ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Information-Source Surrogates

children.title: Cross-Source Discrepancy
children.top_down_role: Representations of systematic differences among fidelities or information sources.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Likelihood invariance showing why target and source discrepancies require anchoring information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose observations depend on latent functions only through \(h_s(x)=f(x)+b_s(x)\) for every observed source \(s\), and no observed source is constrained to have zero discrepancy. For any function \(u:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), define \(f'(x)=f(x)+u(x)\) and \(b'_s(x)=b_s(x)-u(x)\). Then \(f'(x)+b'_s(x)=h_s(x)\) for all \(x,s\), so the observation likelihood is unchanged. Consequently, \(f\) and \(\{b_s\}\) are not likelihood-identifiable without a target anchor, identifying constraints, or informative prior restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unanchored additive source model cannot distinguish a common shift in the target from the opposite shift in every source discrepancy.
assumptions_latex: Observed responses depend on \(f\) and \(b_s\) only through their sums.
No target discrepancy is fixed and no other restriction removes the transformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Unanchored Additive Discrepancy Nonidentifiability
Cross-Source Discrepancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive source-bias representation relative to a designated target response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be the target response and let source \(s\in\mathcal S\) return \(h_s\). An additive cross-source discrepancy model writes \[h_s(x)=f(x)+b_s(x)+\varepsilon_s(x),\qquad b_0(x)=0,\] where \(b_s\) is a source-specific systematic discrepancy and \(\varepsilon_s\) is centered observation noise. Assigning a joint prior to \(f\) and \(\{b_s\}_{s\ne0}\) separates uncertainty about the target from persistent source bias; identifiability requires target data, constraints, or informative priors that distinguish \(f\) from the discrepancies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each source is represented as the target response plus systematic source bias and random noise; identifying these components requires anchoring information.
assumptions_latex: All sources are defined on the stated common domain.
Noise is centered conditional on the latent functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_s-f=b_s+\varepsilon_s\) decomposes cross-source error into systematic and random components.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive bias representation and identifiability caveat fit the Cross-Source Discrepancy leaf and are internally consistent. No inspectable citation supports either the representation or the stated anchoring requirements.

children.title: Source-Cost Structure
children.top_down_role: Relative resource demands associated with available fidelity levels or information channels.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-Cost Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost feasibility and budget accounting for source-selective Bayesian optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathcal X\times\mathcal S\to(0,\infty)\) give the known or predicted cost of querying source \(s\) at \(x\). For a remaining budget \(B>0\), a query sequence \((x_i,s_i)_{i=1}^N\) is cost-feasible exactly when \[\sum_{i=1}^N c(x_i,s_i)\le B.\] A cost-aware acquisition may rank feasible queries by \(a(x,s)/c(x,s)\), where \(a(x,s)\ge0\) is expected utility, but this ratio rule is well-defined only where costs are strictly positive and comparable in a common resource unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source-selective optimization must keep total query cost within budget; utility-per-cost ranking additionally requires positive, commensurable costs.
assumptions_latex: Every query cost is finite and strictly positive.
Costs and budget use the same resource unit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i c(x_i,s_i)\le B\) characterizes cost-feasible query sequences.

notation.meaning: cost of querying source s at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The budget-feasibility condition is correct, and the positivity and common-unit qualifications make the utility-per-cost ratio well-defined. The leaf-specific cost-aware Bayesian-optimization claim lacks a source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cost Dominance of Predictively Equivalent Sources
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed one-step policy-pruning result; deferred because its canonical home is one-step value-of-information policy theory, not source-cost representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed information state, suppose two feasible queries \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) induce the same distribution of the updated target belief and have deterministic costs \(c(q_1)<c(q_2)\). For \(U(q)=\mathbb E[V(\Pi^q)]-\lambda c(q)\) with \(\lambda>0\), one has \(U(q_1)>U(q_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a one-step linearly cost-penalized value criterion, the costlier of two informationally equivalent queries is dominated.
assumptions_latex: The queries induce identical updated-target-belief laws.
Costs are deterministic and commensurable.
\(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: target posterior belief after query q

knowledge_statements.title: Cost Dominance of Predictively Equivalent Sources

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the seed's source-query cost function, cumulative budget-feasibility condition, and positivity and commensurability qualifications. The proposed predictive-equivalence dominance result was deferred because it is primarily a one-step policy theorem. General horizon design, value-of-information decisions, and source incompatibility were excluded as adjacent or external scopes.

children.title: Source-Incompatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where source biases or weak relationships undermine useful information transfer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which an auxiliary source has zero Bayesian information value for the target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_0\) denote the latent target, \(D_0\) current target-relevant data, and \(Y_s\) a prospective observation from auxiliary source \(s\). If \[F_0\perp Y_s\mid D_0,\] then \(p(F_0\mid D_0,Y_s)=p(F_0\mid D_0)\) almost surely. Consequently, every posterior functional depending only on the law of \(F_0\), including a Bayes-optimal terminal decision value based on that law, is unchanged by observing \(Y_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary source conditionally independent of the target cannot update the target posterior and therefore has zero target-information value.
assumptions_latex: Regular conditional distributions exist.
The evaluated posterior functional depends on the auxiliary observation only through the posterior law of \(F_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_0\perp Y_s\mid D_0\Longrightarrow p(F_0\mid D_0,Y_s)=p(F_0\mid D_0)\ \text{a.s.}

notation.meaning: latent target response or target-relevant state

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Conditional Independence Boundary
Source-Incompatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of source pooling when systematic discrepancies are excluded from the surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the target be \(f(x)=0\) and an auxiliary source be \(h_1(x)=b\) for every \(x\), with \(b\ne0\). If a misspecified pooled surrogate assumes \(h_1=f\) and estimates a common constant mean from \(n_0\) noiseless target observations and \(n_1\) auxiliary observations, its estimate is \(\widehat f=n_1b/(n_0+n_1)\). Its target squared error is \((n_1b/(n_0+n_1))^2>0\), whereas using target observations alone gives zero error. Thus unmodeled persistent discrepancy makes the auxiliary source incompatible with exact pooling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pooling a persistently biased auxiliary source as if it were the target introduces target error; an explicit discrepancy model is necessary.
assumptions_latex: The fitted model incorrectly enforces a common source mean.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-bias pooling example is algebraically correct and appropriately functions as a source-incompatibility failure boundary. It is uncited, so a source supporting this boundary or an explicitly sourced equivalent result is required.

children.title: High-Dimensional Structural Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Additive, embedded, sparse, and local representations for large input dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Coordinate Exclusion by Zero Relevance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coordinate sparsity in product kernels with relevance weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k_w(x,x')=\sigma^2\prod_{j=1}^d\kappa_j(w_j(x_j-x'_j))\), where \(w_j\ge0\) and \(\kappa_j(0)=1\). If \(w_j=0\), then \(k_w\) is invariant to \(x_j\) and \(x'_j\). With a mean function having the same invariance, the GP prior and posterior cannot distinguish inputs differing only in coordinate \(j\). A positive but small \(w_j\) gives only approximate exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero relevance weight removes a coordinate exactly; a small positive weight only weakens its influence.
assumptions_latex: Each factor defines a positive-semidefinite coordinate kernel.
The prior mean is invariant to coordinate \(j\) when the posterior-invariance conclusion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Coordinate Exclusion by Zero Relevance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process representation through a low-dimensional linear embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) and a positive-semidefinite kernel \(k_r\) on \(\mathbb R^r\), \[k_A(x,x')=k_r(A^{\mathsf T}x,A^{\mathsf T}x')\] is positive semidefinite on \(\mathbb R^d\). It is invariant along every discarded direction: if \(A^{\mathsf T}v=0\), then \(k_A(x+v,x')=k_A(x,x')\). When \(k_r\) is rotationally invariant, replacing \(A\) by \(AQ\) for an orthogonal \(Q\) leaves the kernel unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pulling a kernel back through a low-dimensional projection gives a valid surrogate that ignores the projection's null directions.
assumptions_latex: \(k_r\) is positive semidefinite.
\(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) with \(r<d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_A\text{ is positive semidefinite and invariant along }\ker(A^{\mathsf T}).
knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Pullback Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized nonstationary covariance assembled from regional components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k_1,\ldots,k_L\) be positive-semidefinite kernels and \(w_1,\ldots,w_L:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) deterministic gates. Then \[k_{\rm loc}(x,x')=\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell(x)w_\ell(x')k_\ell(x,x')\] is positive semidefinite. Spatially concentrated gates localize the components; pairwise disjoint hard gates make points in different gated regions uncorrelated under this covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministically gated regional kernels combine into a valid localized covariance model.
assumptions_latex: Each \(k_\ell\) is positive semidefinite.
Each gate is a deterministic real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.title: Localized Gated Kernel

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive covariance over prescribed low-dimensional coordinate groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\), let \(f_j\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,k_j)\) be mutually independent processes on \(\mathcal X_{S_j}\), and set \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j(x_{S_j})\). Then \(f\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,k)\) with \[k(x,x')=\sum_{j=1}^m k_j(x_{S_j},x'_{S_j}).\] Overlapping or redundant groups need not yield identifiable component functions without additional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent low-dimensional GP components sum to a GP whose covariance is the sum of their group kernels.
assumptions_latex: Each \(k_j\) is positive semidefinite.
The component processes are mutually independent.

notation.meaning: Coordinates of x indexed by group S_j.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Gaussian-Process Decomposition
High-Dimensional Structural Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surrogates whose effective representation has complexity below the ambient input dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) with large \(d\). A high-dimensional structural surrogate is a probabilistic approximation whose latent response is restricted to a lower-complexity representation, such as \(f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j(x_{S_j})\) for small coordinate sets \(S_j\), \(f(x)=g(A^{\mathsf T}x)\) for \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) with \(r\ll d\), or a sparse/local model active only on selected coordinates or regions. The structural variables and component functions may be fixed or inferred jointly with predictive uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-dimensional structural surrogate reduces effective complexity through additive groups, low-dimensional embeddings, sparsity, or localized representations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\).
The chosen structural representation defines a valid probabilistic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surrogate depends on structural complexity such as \(m\), \(\max_j|S_j|\), or \(r\), rather than unrestricted \(d\)-variate variation.

notation.meaning: coordinate subset for additive component j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the topic role by covering additive, embedded, sparse, and local representations without conflating them into one theorem. The broad taxonomy-level characterization has no supporting citation, and the listed local low-dimensional value-function source is not attached to the record or clearly sufficient for all four families.

children.title: Structured-Domain Surrogate Family
children.top_down_role: Models respecting categorical variables, combinatorial structure, and conditional parameters.

children.title: Discrete-Domain Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models respecting finite, ordinal, or combinatorial candidate spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covariance construction using graph or combinatorial geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite undirected graph on \(\mathcal X\), with Laplacian \(L=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)U^{\mathsf T}\). For any function \(\phi\) that is nonnegative on the spectrum of \(L\), \[K=\phi(L)=U\operatorname{diag}(\phi(\lambda_i))U^{\mathsf T}\] is positive semidefinite and defines a kernel on the vertices. In particular, \(K=e^{-\beta L}\), \(\beta\ge0\), represents similarity through graph connectivity rather than an arbitrary Euclidean encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative spectral filter of a graph Laplacian gives a valid discrete-domain kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(\phi(\lambda_i)\ge0\) for every eigenvalue of \(L\).

notation.meaning: Graph Laplacian on the configuration set.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Spectral Discrete Kernel

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a nonempty finite or countable set.
Observations have a specified likelihood conditional on \(f\).
The function \(k\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A symmetric positive-semidefinite \(k\) defines a Gaussian-process prior on \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic surrogates defined directly on finite or countable configuration spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a nonempty finite or countable set of feasible configurations. A discrete-domain surrogate is a probability model for \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) whose similarity structure is defined without requiring Euclidean continuity. A Gaussian-process instance uses a symmetric kernel \(k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge 0\] for every \(n\ge 1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal X\), and every \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R\). Conditioning on observations with the specified likelihood produces posterior predictions over feasible configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete-domain surrogate models functions on a finite or countable configuration set using a symmetric positive-semidefinite similarity kernel tailored to that domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Domain Surrogates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nominal-label failure owned primarily by Categorical Similarity Structure rather than this broader discrete-domain leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nominal levels encoded as \(0,1,2\), the Euclidean kernel \(k(u,v)=\exp(-(u-v)^2)\) gives \(k(0,1)=e^{-1}\) and \(k(0,2)=e^{-4}\); permuting the arbitrary codes changes the covariance table.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean kernels on arbitrary nominal codes invent an order and metric that change under relabeling.
assumptions_latex: The levels are nominal.
The numeric codes have no intrinsic metric meaning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is not invariant under relabeling of nominal categories}.
knowledge_statements.title: Label-Encoding Dependence

intermediate_metadata.reason: The seed and graph-spectral construction cover direct PSD modeling and combinatorial geometry on discrete sets. The proposed numeric-label counterexample was deferred to Categorical Similarity Structure. Mixed-domain composition, conditional activity, and invalid-configuration enforcement were excluded as sibling scopes.

children.title: Mixed-Domain Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models jointly representing continuous, integer, categorical, or structured inputs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid alternatives for combining heterogeneous coordinate blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(k_c,k_i,k_g\) are positive-semidefinite kernels on continuous, integer, and categorical blocks, then for \(a_c,a_i,a_g\ge0\), \[k_{\rm add}=a_ck_c+a_ik_i+a_gk_g\] and \[k_{\rm int}=(1+k_c)(1+k_i)(1+k_g)-1\] are positive semidefinite. The additive kernel contains only blockwise main effects, whereas expansion of \(k_{\rm int}\) contains main effects and all cross-block products. Sums and products therefore encode different structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sums of block kernels model main effects, while products add cross-block interactions; both are valid covariance constructions.
assumptions_latex: Each block kernel is positive semidefinite.
\(a_c,a_i,a_g\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_{\rm add}\text{ and }k_{\rm int}\text{ are positive semidefinite}.

notation.meaning: Continuous, integer, and categorical block kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive and Interaction Mixed Kernels
Mixed-Domain Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel representation for continuous, integer, and categorical coordinates in one surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\mathcal X_c\times\mathcal X_i\times\mathcal X_g\), where \(\mathcal X_c\subseteq\mathbb R^p\), \(\mathcal X_i\subseteq\mathbb Z^q\), and \(\mathcal X_g\) is finite. A mixed-domain Gaussian-process surrogate may use \[k(x,x')=k_c(x_c,x_c')k_i(x_i,x_i')k_g(x_g,x_g'),\] where every factor is positive semidefinite on its coordinate domain. Consequently, \(k\) is positive semidefinite on \(\mathcal X\). Observation noise may depend on the discrete coordinates, but posterior conditioning is performed jointly over complete mixed-domain configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-domain surrogate combines valid kernels for continuous, integer, and categorical coordinates into one positive-semidefinite covariance model.
assumptions_latex: \(k_c,k_i,k_g\) are positive-semidefinite kernels.
\(x=(x_c,x_i,x_g)\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=k_c k_i k_g\) is a positive-semidefinite kernel on \(\mathcal X\).

notation.meaning: Continuous, integer, and categorical coordinate domains.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closure of positive-semidefinite kernels under pointwise products; mixed-domain surrogate interpretation needs dedicated source
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The product-kernel construction is mathematically standard and the representation fits the mixed-domain leaf, but no inspectable source supports the mixed-domain surrogate interpretation or the claim about coordinate-dependent observation noise.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acquisition-search failure rather than a mixed-domain surrogate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the feasible integer set \(\{0,1,2\}\), a relaxed acquisition \(\alpha(z)=-(z-1.49)^2\) is maximized at \(1.49\), which rounds to \(1\), while an independently specified feasible acquisition can satisfy \(A(2)>A(1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing an unrelated continuous relaxation and rounding need not preserve discrete acquisition rankings.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation is not required to agree with the feasible acquisition on lattice points.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Relaxation Rounding Failure

children.title: Conditional-Domain Surrogates
children.top_down_role: Models respecting parameters whose relevance depends on other design choices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Naive Imputation Failure on Conditional Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure from treating inactive placeholders as ordinary input values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x\sim x'\), but an encoded kernel satisfies \(k_{\rm enc}(x,z)\ne k_{\rm enc}(x',z)\) for some \(z\). Then the prior covariance depends on a semantically meaningless inactive value, and posterior predictions can differ between encodings of the same configuration. Using one fixed placeholder removes variation among inactive encodings but can still confuse inactivity with a genuinely active coordinate equal to that placeholder unless activity is represented separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary kernels on imputed vectors can depend on meaningless inactive values or confuse inactivity with an active placeholder value.
assumptions_latex: At least one coordinate can be inactive.
The encoded kernel is sensitive to a stored inactive value.

notation.meaning: Kernel applied to the raw encoded vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Naive Imputation Failure on Conditional Domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic invariance for conditionally inactive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_j(x)=0\) mean that coordinate \(j\) is inactive, and write \(x\sim x'\) when two encodings have the same activity structure and agree on every active coordinate. A conditional-domain surrogate respects inactive semantics when its predictive law is constant on equivalence classes of \(\sim\). For a GP model, sufficient prior conditions are \[x\sim x'\Longrightarrow m(x)=m(x')\quad\text{and}\quad k(x,z)=k(x',z)\ \text{for every }z.\] Under a common observation model, these conditions make posterior predictions invariant to arbitrary stored values of inactive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Configurations differing only in inactive placeholder values must receive identical predictions.
assumptions_latex: Activity is determined by the configuration hierarchy.
Inactive coordinates have no response semantics.
Equivalent encodings use the same observation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\sim x'\Longrightarrow \mathcal L(f(x)\mid\mathcal D)=\mathcal L(f(x')\mid\mathcal D).

notation.meaning: Equivalence after ignoring inactive coordinate values.

knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-Value Invariance
Conditional-Domain Surrogates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Masked kernel representation for hierarchically active parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_j(x)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether coordinate \(j\) is active in configuration \(x\). For positive-semidefinite coordinate kernels \(k_j\), define \[\kappa_j(x,x')=\mathbf 1\{a_j(x)=a_j(x')=0\}+\mathbf 1\{a_j(x)=a_j(x')=1\}k_j(x_j,x_j').\] The conditional-domain kernel \(k(x,x')=k_0(x,x')\prod_{j=1}^d\kappa_j(x,x')\) compares coordinate values only when both are active, treats jointly inactive coordinates as matching, and assigns zero covariance when their activity states differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional surrogate uses activity masks so inactive parameters are ignored and configurations with incompatible activity states are separated.
assumptions_latex: \(k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_d\) are positive-semidefinite kernels.
\(a_j(x)\in\{0,1\}\) is determined by the configuration hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\) is positive semidefinite and respects conditional coordinate activity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit positive-semidefinite activity-gated construction; dedicated conditional-parameter source pending
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed activity-gated kernel is positive semidefinite under the stated assumptions and fits the conditional-domain representation leaf. A dedicated source with a specific locator is required to support this conditional-parameter construction.

children.title: Categorical Similarity Structure
children.top_down_role: Representations of similarity or contrast among unordered input levels.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and identifiability boundaries for categorical similarity tables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric table \(S\in\mathbb R^{L\times L}\) defines a covariance kernel on \(\{1,\ldots,L\}\) exactly when \(S\succeq0\). If \(S\) has a negative eigenvalue, some \(a\in\mathbb R^L\) satisfies \(a^{\mathsf T}Sa<0\), precluding covariance validity. A factorization \(S=VV^{\mathsf T}\) enforces validity, but the factor is nonidentifiable because \(VQ\) gives the same table for every orthogonal \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A categorical similarity table must be positive semidefinite; Gram factors enforce validity but are rotationally nonidentifiable.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is a categorical covariance kernel}\iff S\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefiniteness Boundary for Learned Similarities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relabeling-invariant baseline similarity for finite nominal levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal C=\{1,\ldots,L\}\), \[k(c,c')=\tau^2+\sigma^2\mathbf 1\{c=c'\},\qquad \tau^2,\sigma^2\ge0,\] is positive semidefinite, with Gram matrix \(\tau^2\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}+\sigma^2I\). It assigns a common between-level covariance and an additional same-level covariance and is invariant under every permutation of category labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exchangeable categorical kernel combines common and same-level similarity while remaining invariant to label permutations.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau^2,\sigma^2\ge0\).
The category set is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\text{ is positive semidefinite and permutation invariant}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exchangeable Categorical Kernel
Categorical Similarity Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite similarity representation for finite categorical levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a categorical set \(\mathcal C=\{1,\ldots,L\}\), a matrix \(B\in\mathbb S_+^L\) defines the categorical kernel \[k_{m cat}(c,c')=B_{cc'}.\] Conversely, every kernel on \(\mathcal C\) has this form with a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix. Equivalently, there exist vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_L\in\mathbb R^r\), with \(r\le L\), such that \(B_{cc'}=v_c^\top v_{c'}\). Thus learned similarities may be represented either directly by \(B\) or through categorical embeddings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Categorical similarities form a positive-semidefinite matrix, equivalently the Gram matrix of finite-dimensional category embeddings.

children.title: Invalid-Configuration Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for hard validity restriction to return a configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be compact, let \(F\subseteq\mathcal X\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(\alpha:F\to\mathbb R\) be upper semicontinuous. Then \(F\) is compact and \(\alpha\) attains its maximum on \(F\). Thus constrained maximization over \(F\), equivalently masking \(\mathcal X\setminus F\) by \(-\infty\), has a valid maximizer. If \(F=\varnothing\), no validity-preserving selection exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed valid subset of a compact domain and an upper-semicontinuous acquisition guarantee an attained valid maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is compact.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of an uncalibrated finite penalty to enforce a hard boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{x_v,x_i\}\), \(F=\{x_v\}\), and maximize \(\alpha_M(x)=\alpha(x)-M\mathbf1\{x\notin F\}\) for finite \(M\). If \(\alpha(x_i)-\alpha(x_v)>M\), then the invalid point \(x_i\) is the unique maximizer. A finite penalty guarantees validity only when it exceeds a valid upper bound on every acquisition advantage attainable outside \(F\); hard masking requires no such calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any uncalibrated finite invalidity penalty can still select an invalid point.
assumptions_latex: \(M<\infty\).
No acquisition-gap bound ensuring \(\alpha(x_i)-\alpha(x_v)\le M\) is imposed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility masking at structured-domain boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be the encoded search space and let \(F=\{x\in\mathcal X:g_r(x)\le0,\ r=1,\ldots,R\}\) be the set of valid configurations. A validity-preserving Bayesian-optimization step for maximizing an acquisition \(\alpha_t\) uses \[\widetilde\alpha_t(x)=\begin{cases}\alpha_t(x),&x\in F,\\-\infty,&x\notin F,\end{cases}\qquad x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}\widetilde\alpha_t(x).\] Hence every selected configuration is valid whenever \(F\ne\varnothing\) and the acquisition maximum is attained.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational objective and exact KL-gap identity for an inducing family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For likelihood \(p(y\mid f)\) and \(q(f,u)=p(f\mid u)q(u)\), \[\mathcal L(q)=\mathbb E_{q(f)}[\log p(y\mid f)]-\operatorname{KL}(q(u)\|p(u))\le\log p(y),\] and \[\log p(y)-\mathcal L(q)=\operatorname{KL}\!\left(q(f,u)\middle\|p(f,u\mid y)\right).\] Hence maximizing the ELBO minimizes the joint posterior KL divergence over the specified inducing family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inducing ELBO is a certified lower bound on log evidence whose exact gap is a posterior KL divergence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive positive-semidefinite low-rank factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K\in\mathbb S_+^n\), pivoted Cholesky repeatedly selects a largest residual diagonal entry and constructs \(L_r\) such that \[K=L_rL_r^\top+R_r,\qquad R_r\succeq0.\] Consequently, \[\|R_r\|_2\le\operatorname{tr}(R_r)=\sum_i(R_r)_{ii}.\] With dense kernel access, constructing \(r\) columns costs \(O(nr^2)\) time and \(O(nr)\) factor storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivoted Cholesky adaptively constructs a PSD low-rank factor whose residual trace certifies a spectral-error upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
Exact arithmetic is used, or numerical safeguards preserve nonnegative residual pivots.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivoted Cholesky Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear algebra for a stored covariance factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(W\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) and \(\sigma^2>0\), \[(WW^\top+\sigma^2I_n)^{-1}=\sigma^{-2}I_n-\sigma^{-4}W(I_r+\sigma^{-2}W^\top W)^{-1}W^\top,\] and \[\log\det(WW^\top+\sigma^2I_n)=n\log\sigma^2+\log\det(I_r+\sigma^{-2}W^\top W).\] Dense preprocessing costs \(O(nr^2+r^3)\), after which applying the inverse to one vector costs \(O(nr+r^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Woodbury and the determinant lemma reduce regularized rank-r covariance calculations to an r-dimensional system.
assumptions_latex: Dense arithmetic is used for the reduced system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regularized solves and log determinants require factorizing only an \(r\times r\) matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Regularized Solves and Determinants

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best rank-r approximation of a positive-semidefinite matrix in spectral and Frobenius norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^\top\), where \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\), and let \(K_r=U_r\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)U_r^\top\). The Eckart--Young--Mirsky theorem gives \[\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\le r}\|K-B\|_2=\lambda_{r+1},\qquad \min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\le r}\|K-B\|_F=\left(\sum_{j>r}\lambda_j^2\right)^{1/2}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leading-eigenpair truncation is the best rank-r approximation in spectral and Frobenius norms.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Truncated Spectral Approximation
Low-Rank Matrix Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nyström representation of a positive-semidefinite kernel matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb S_+^n\) be a kernel matrix and let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contain \(m\) landmark indices. The Nyström approximation is \[\widetilde K=K_{:I}K_{II}^{\dagger}K_{I:}=WW^\top,\qquad W=K_{:I}(K_{II}^{\dagger})^{1/2}.\] It is positive semidefinite, has rank at most \(m\), and permits matrix-vector products in \(O(nm)\) operations when \(W\) is stored, instead of the \(O(n^2)\) cost of multiplying by a dense matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nyström approximation replaces a dense kernel matrix by a positive-semidefinite factor of rank at most the number of landmarks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the out-of-sample kernel representation induced by m landmark points and its restriction to the training-set Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K_{mm} be the invertible Gram matrix on landmark points x_1,\ldots,x_m, let k_m(x)=(k(x,x_1),\ldots,k(x,x_m))^\top, and let K_{mm}u_i^{(m)}=\lambda_i^{(m)}u_i^{(m)}.
