children.title: Decision-Theoretic Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on the estimated value of further information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite experiment in which individual observations have no value but their combination does.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let independent fair bits \(B_1,B_2\) determine \(\Theta=B_1\oplus B_2\). The terminal action guesses \(\Theta\) under zero-one loss. Query \(i\) reveals \(B_i\) at cost \(0.1\). Before observing either bit, terminal Bayes risk is \(0.5\); after either single query it remains \(0.5\), whereas after both queries it is \(0\). Thus each initial one-step net value is \(-0.1\), but the two-query plan has net value \(0.5-0.2=0.3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Myopic stopping can stop too early when observations are valuable only in combination.
assumptions_latex: \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) are independent Bernoulli\((1/2)\) variables.
Each query reveals its bit without error and costs \(0.1\).
Terminal loss is zero-one error in guessing \(B_1\oplus B_2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Information Defeats Myopic Stopping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multistep stopping-versus-continuation recursion on an information state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the current information state, \(g(D)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E[\ell(a,f)\mid D]\) the risk of stopping, and let querying \(x\) cost \(c(x,D)\ge0\) and produce predictive observation \(Y_x\). For a finite horizon, the optimal value satisfies \[V(D)=\min\left\{g(D),\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\left[c(x,D)+\mathbb E[V(D\cup\{(x,Y_x)\})\mid D]\right]\right\}.\] Stopping is optimal exactly when the stop term attains this minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact decision-theoretic stopping compares terminal Bayes risk with the full continuation value, including all later information decisions.
assumptions_latex: A finite remaining horizon or another well-posed dynamic-programming termination condition is specified.
The displayed risks and conditional expectations are finite.
Admissible queries and predictive observation laws are defined at every reachable information state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(D)\le\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\left[c(x,D)+\mathbb E[V(D\cup\{(x,Y_x)\})\mid D]\right]\iff\text{stopping is optimal at }D.
knowledge_statements.title: Bellman Form of Decision-Theoretic Stopping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Myopic decision-theoretic stopping with a defined predictive observation and nonattainment convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At information state \(D\), let \(g(D)=\inf_a\mathbb E[\ell(a,f)\mid D]\). For query \(x\), let \(Y_x\) have the declared posterior predictive law and define
\[
V_1(x;D)=g(D)-\mathbb E[g(D\cup\{(x,Y_x)\})\mid D]-c(x,D).
\]
Stop when \(\sup_xV_1(x;D)\le0\). If the supremum is positive and attained, query a maximizer; if it is not attained, query any \(\epsilon\)-maximizer with \(0<\epsilon<\sup_xV_1(x;D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The myopic rule stops when no query has positive one-step Bayes-risk reduction net of cost and uses epsilon-maximizers under nonattainment.
assumptions_latex: The posterior predictive law of Y_x is specified for every admissible x.
The displayed risks and expectations are finite.
c(x,D)\ge0.

notation.meaning: Bayes risk of stopping at information state D.
One-step net value of query x.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Step Net-Value Stopping
Decision-Theoretic Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step value-of-information stopping with explicit sampling cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At information state \(D_n\), let \(L_{\mathrm{stop}}(D_n)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A}\mathbb E[\ell(a,f)\mid D_n]\) be the Bayes risk of stopping. For a possible next query \(x\in\mathcal X\), define \[V_n(x)=L_{\mathrm{stop}}(D_n)-\mathbb E[L_{\mathrm{stop}}(D_n\cup\{(x,Y_x)\})\mid D_n].\] With query cost \(c_n(x)\geq0\), one-step decision-theoretic stopping occurs exactly when \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\{V_n(x)-c_n(x)\}\leq0\); otherwise query a maximizer of the net value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when no available query has expected reduction in Bayes risk exceeding its cost; otherwise select the best net-value query.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional expectations and infima are finite.
\(c_n(x)\geq0\) for all \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\{V_n(x)-c_n(x)\}\leq0\) is the one-step stopping condition.

notation.meaning: expected value of information from querying x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits decision-theoretic stopping, but the exact one-step Bayes-risk rule requires source confirmation. The law of Y_x is not introduced, and a maximizer need not exist merely because the displayed supremum is positive.

children.title: Decision-Rule Recommendation Family
children.top_down_role: Recommendation families based on evaluated designs, surrogate beliefs, or risk criteria.

children.title: Incumbent Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Final choices restricted to designs already evaluated.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recommendation restricted to previously evaluated designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, let \(D_n=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) and let \(S_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) be the evaluated designs. Given an incumbent score \(q_n:S_n\to\mathbb R\), an incumbent recommendation is any \[\widehat x_n^{\mathrm{inc}}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S_n}q_n(x).\] In deterministic optimization one commonly sets \(q_n(x_i)=y_i\). With noisy or replicated observations, \(q_n(x)\) may instead be a specified sample-mean or fitted-value score, but the recommendation remains restricted to \(S_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent recommendation minimizes a declared score over designs already evaluated, rather than over the entire search domain.
assumptions_latex: The minimum of \(q_n\) over \(S_n\) is attained.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no citation supports the generalized score-based incumbent convention, particularly for noisy or replicated observations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed failure example is canonically owned by Observation-Based Incumbents rather than this general recommendation-family leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(m\) evaluated designs with equal latent value zero and independent observations \(Y_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\). If \(I_m\in\operatorname*{argmin}_iY_i\), then for every \(a>0\), \[\Pr(Y_{I_m}<-a)=1-[1-\Phi(-a/\sigma)]^m\to1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting the smallest raw noisy observation creates an increasingly extreme observed incumbent without latent improvement.
assumptions_latex: All sites have equal latent value.
Each site receives one independent Gaussian observation.
Selection uses the smallest raw observation.

notation.meaning: Index selected by the smallest raw observation.

review_flags: misplaced: the claim specifically concerns raw noisy observation scoring and belongs under Observation-Based Incumbents
knowledge_statements.title: Raw-Observation Incumbent Selection Bias

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory is recommendation over the evaluated set using a declared incumbent score. The immutable definition is mathematically sound despite its missing locator and is not regenerated. The proposed raw-observation counterexample is deferred as primarily owned by Observation-Based Incumbents; posterior, risk-aware, and recommendation-regret claims remain sibling scopes.

children.title: Posterior Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Final choices based on surrogate beliefs over candidate designs.

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayes-action recommendation derived from the terminal posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi_n\) be the posterior distribution of an unknown objective \(f\) on \(\mathcal X\), let \(a\in\mathcal A\) be a terminal recommendation, and let \(\ell(a,f)\) be its loss. A posterior recommendation is a Bayes action \[\widehat a_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}\int \ell(a,f)\,\Pi_n(df).\] For point recommendation in a minimization problem with loss \(\ell(x,f)=f(x)\), this reduces, whenever the minimum is attained, to \(\widehat x_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[f(x)\mid D_n]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior recommendation is a terminal action minimizing posterior expected loss; posterior-mean minimization is one important special case.
assumptions_latex: The posterior expected loss is finite for admissible actions.
The displayed argmin is nonempty.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is a suitable posterior-recommendation formulation, but the record supplies no authoritative locator for the Bayes-action rule or its posterior-mean special case.

children.title: Risk-Aware Recommendations
children.top_down_role: Final choices reflecting uncertainty or downside preferences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean and CVaR Recommendations Can Differ
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite posterior-loss example separating risk-neutral and upper-tail recommendations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let action \(a\) have posterior loss \(Z_a=0\) with probability \(0.99\) and \(Z_a=100\) with probability \(0.01\), while action \(b\) has constant loss \(Z_b=2\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z_a]=1<2=\mathbb E[Z_b]\), but \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.99}(Z_a)=100>2=\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.99}(Z_b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An action preferred by posterior mean loss can be rejected by an upper-tail CVaR rule.
assumptions_latex: Losses have the displayed posterior distributions.
Upper-tail loss CVaR uses level \(\alpha=0.99\).
knowledge_statements.title: Mean and CVaR Recommendations Can Differ

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust-expectation representation of posterior upper-tail loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n\) be the posterior law and \(Z\in L^1(P_n)\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \[\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(Z\mid D_n)=\sup_{Q\ll P_n}\left\{\mathbb E_Q[Z]:0\le\frac{dQ}{dP_n}\le\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\ P_n\text{-a.s.},\ \mathbb E_{P_n}\!\left[\frac{dQ}{dP_n}\right]=1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior CVaR equals worst-case posterior expected loss over distributions whose density is capped by the CVaR level.

notation.meaning: distribution in the CVaR risk envelope

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior CVaR Risk Envelope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-tail posterior-loss recommendation at a declared confidence level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For posterior loss \(Z_a=\ell(a,f)\in L^1\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define \[\operatorname{CVaR}_{\alpha}(Z_a\mid D_n)=\inf_{\eta\in\mathbb R}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathbb E[(Z_a-\eta)_+\mid D_n]\right\}.\] If the joint minimum is attained, any joint minimizer \((\widehat a_n,\widehat\eta_n)\) yields a posterior-CVaR-minimizing recommendation \(\widehat a_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior CVaR recommendation reduces to joint minimization over the action and an auxiliary loss threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_a\in L^1\) under the posterior for every \(a\in\mathcal A\).
The joint minimum is attained when an argmin is asserted.

notation.meaning: posterior terminal loss for action a

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior CVaR Recommendation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Risk-aware terminal decision with a declared posterior loss threshold and violation level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(L\in\mathbb R\), \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\), and a secondary score \(r_n\), define \(\mathcal A_{n,L,\varepsilon}=\{a\in\mathcal A:P(\ell(a,f)>L\mid D_n)\le\varepsilon\}\). If this set is nonempty and the minimum is attained, then \[\widehat a_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A_{n,L,\varepsilon}}r_n(a)\] is a posterior chance-constrained recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior chance-constrained recommendation minimizes a declared secondary score among actions whose posterior probability of excessive loss is within tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(L\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\) are declared before selection.
\(\mathcal A_{n,L,\varepsilon}\neq\varnothing\).
The secondary-score minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Chance-Constrained Recommendation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal recommendation minimizing a declared posterior loss quantile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Z_a=\ell(a,f)\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), let \(q_\alpha(Z_a\mid D_n)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:P(Z_a\le t\mid D_n)\ge\alpha\}\). If these quantiles are finite and the action minimum is attained, \[\widehat a_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}q_\alpha(Z_a\mid D_n)\] is a posterior-quantile recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posterior-quantile recommendation minimizes a declared generalized loss quantile.
assumptions_latex: Each posterior loss has a finite generalized \(\alpha\)-quantile.
The action minimum is attained.

notation.meaning: lower generalized posterior quantile at level alpha
posterior terminal loss under action a

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Quantile Recommendation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General terminal recommendation under a declared posterior loss-risk functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_a=\ell(a,f)\) be posterior terminal loss for \(a\in\mathcal A\), and let \(\rho_n\) be a declared functional on the posterior laws of these losses. If the minimum is attained, a risk-aware recommendation is
\[
\widehat a_n^\rho\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}\rho_n(Z_a\mid D_n).
\]
The loss orientation, risk functional, level parameters, and tie rule are part of the recommendation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A risk-aware recommendation minimizes a fully specified posterior risk functional of terminal loss.
assumptions_latex: \rho_n(Z_a\mid D_n)\text{ is well-defined for every }a.
The minimum is attained.
Loss orientation and all risk parameters are declared.

notation.meaning: Posterior terminal loss for action a.

knowledge_statements.title: Posterior Risk-Functional Recommendation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative robustness boundary for upper-tail posterior CVaR recommendations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P,Q\) be laws of integrable scalar losses and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Then
\[
|\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(P)-\operatorname{CVaR}_\alpha(Q)|\le\frac{W_1(P,Q)}{1-\alpha}.
\]
Consequently, if two posterior models give CVaR scores differing uniformly by at most \(e\) over actions, a minimizer under either model has CVaR regret at most \(2e\) under the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CVaR sensitivity to posterior-law error grows as the tail level approaches one; uniform score error yields a twice-error recommendation bound.
assumptions_latex: P,Q\text{ have finite first moments}.
\alpha\in(0,1).
For the recommendation statement, the CVaR score error is uniformly at most e over actions and a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein Sensitivity of Posterior CVaR
Risk-Aware Recommendations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior recommendation under a declared risk functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_a=\ell(a,f)\) be the posterior loss induced by action \(a\in\mathcal A\), and let \(\rho_n\) be a specified risk functional on posterior loss distributions. A risk-aware recommendation is any \[\widehat a_n^{\rho}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}\rho_n(Z_a\mid D_n).\] Examples of admissible declared criteria include posterior expectation and upper-tail conditional value-at-risk. The selected functional, its orientation, and its level parameters are part of the decision rule; changing them generally changes the recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A risk-aware recommendation minimizes a declared posterior risk functional of terminal loss, with all tail levels and orientations fixed in advance.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho_n(Z_a\mid D_n)\) is well-defined for every admissible \(a\).
The displayed minimum is attained.

notation.meaning: posterior terminal loss under action a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the broad stochastic-optimization locator does not specifically support a posterior conditional risk functional or the stated CVaR example.

children.title: Recommendation-Regret Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural tradeoffs among recommendation families under finite evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance certificate for a finite recommendation set under two minimized criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite action set \(\mathcal A\), an action \(a\) is Pareto efficient for minimized criteria \((R,C)\) exactly when no \(b\in\mathcal A\) satisfies \(R(b)\le R(a)\), \(C(b)\le C(a)\), and at least one strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite candidate set, absence of a dominating candidate is an exact Pareto-efficiency certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is finite.
Both criteria are minimized and finite on \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\text{ is Pareto efficient}\iff\nexists b\in\mathcal A:\ (R(b),C(b))\le(R(a),C(a))\text{ with one strict inequality}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Candidate Pareto Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of positive weighted sums to recover every efficient recommendation in a nonconvex attainable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the attainable criterion vectors for two minimized criteria are \(\{(0,1),(1,0),(0.6,0.6)\}\). Every displayed vector is Pareto efficient, but \((0.6,0.6)\) minimizes no scalarization \(\lambda R+(1-\lambda)C\) with \(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex attainable set can contain Pareto-efficient recommendations unsupported by every positive weighted sum.
assumptions_latex: Both criteria are minimized.
The three displayed vectors are attainable.
\(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Pareto-Efficient Recommendation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar recommendation rule capable of recovering unsupported efficient criterion vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimized criteria \(R,C\), fix \(c\) and solve \[\min_{a\in\mathcal A}R(a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad C(a)\le c,\] breaking ties by smaller \(C\). Every attained lexicographic solution is Pareto efficient. If \(a^*\) is Pareto efficient, choosing \(c=C(a^*)\) recovers its criterion vector. Thus epsilon-constraint sweeps can recover unsupported points missed by positive weighted sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrain one criterion and minimize the other to recover Pareto points, including unsupported points on nonconvex tradeoff sets.
assumptions_latex: R(a),C(a)\text{ are finite on }\mathcal A.
The constrained lexicographic minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_c\in\operatorname*{lexmin}_{a:C(a)\le c}(R(a),C(a))\Rightarrow a_c\text{ is Pareto efficient}.

notation.meaning: Upper bound on the competing criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Constraint Recovery of Pareto Recommendations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainable Recommendation Tradeoffs and Pareto Efficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-criterion representation of posterior recommendation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal X\) be the admissible recommendation set, \[R_n(a)=\mathbb E[f(a)-\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\mid\mathcal D_n],\qquad C_n(a)\ge0,\] and \(\mathcal T_n=\{(R_n(a),C_n(a)):a\in\mathcal A\}\). An action is Pareto efficient when no admissible action weakly reduces both minimized criteria and strictly reduces at least one. Every attained minimizer of \(\lambda R_n+(1-\lambda)C_n\), \(0<\lambda<1\), is Pareto efficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recommendation tradeoffs form an attainable regret-criterion set; positive weighted-sum minimizers are Pareto efficient.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal X.
R_n(a)\text{ and }C_n(a)\text{ are finite on }\mathcal A.
0<\lambda<1\text{ and the weighted minimum is attained}.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainable Recommendation Tradeoffs and Pareto Efficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Weights for Convex Recommendation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-sum recovery statements for a closed convex upper image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T\subset\mathbb R^2\) contain finite minimized criterion vectors and let \(\mathcal U=\mathcal T+\mathbb R_+^2\) be closed and convex. Every weakly Pareto-efficient \(t\in\mathcal T\) minimizes \(w^\top s\) over \(s\in\mathcal T\) for some nonzero \(w\in\mathbb R_+^2\). Conversely, every minimizer associated with \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^2\) is Pareto efficient. Strictly positive weights need not recover every efficient point without an additional proper-efficiency condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex tradeoff sets admit nonnegative supporting weights for weakly efficient points; positive weights produce efficient points but may not recover all of them.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal U=\mathcal T+\mathbb R_+^2\text{ is closed and convex}.
Both coordinates are finite and minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\text{ weakly efficient}\Rightarrow\exists w\in\mathbb R_+^2\setminus\{0\}:t\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathcal T}w^\top s;\quad w>0\Rightarrow\arg\min w^\top s\subseteq\operatorname{Eff}(\mathcal T).

notation.meaning: Upper image of the attainable set.

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Weights for Convex Recommendation Tradeoffs
Recommendation-Regret Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto formulation of posterior decision quality and recommendation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_n(a)=\mathbb E[f(a)-\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\mid D_n]\) be posterior expected simple regret, and let \(C_n(a)\geq0\) measure a competing recommendation criterion, such as instability or deployment cost. The attainable tradeoff set is \[\mathcal T_n=\{(R_n(a),C_n(a)):a\in\mathcal A\}.\] A recommendation is Pareto efficient when no other action weakly reduces both coordinates and strictly reduces one. For \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), every minimizer of \(\lambda R_n(a)+(1-\lambda)C_n(a)\) is Pareto efficient, provided a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recommendation quality can be represented by an attainable regret-cost set; positive weighted-sum minimizers are Pareto-efficient tradeoff choices.
assumptions_latex: \(R_n(a)\) and \(C_n(a)\) are finite for every \(a\in\mathcal A\).
\(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
The weighted-sum minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}[\lambda R_n(a)+(1-\lambda)C_n(a)]\) contains only Pareto-efficient actions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the tradeoff leaf and the weighted-sum claim is standard, but no source is supplied and R_n(a) evaluates f(a) without specifying that the action space is contained in the objective domain.

children.title: Surrogate Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Failures originating in representation, inference, uncertainty quantification, or numerical conditioning.

children.title: Posterior Uncertainty Collapse
children.top_down_role: Underestimated uncertainty that suppresses necessary exploration.

children.title: Posterior Overconfidence
children.top_down_role: Surrogate beliefs that understate uncertainty relative to observed predictive errors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance-calibration diagnostic distinct from interval undercoverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an assessment pair \((X,Y)\), predictive mean \(\mu_n(X)\), and predictive standard deviation \(s_n(X)>0\), define \(Z=(Y-\mu_n(X))/s_n(X)\). Predictive uncertainty is overconfident in the marginal second-moment sense when \(E[Z^2]>1\). This criterion is not equivalent to nominal-interval undercoverage without additional assumptions on the standardized-error distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal second-moment diagnostic indicates overconfidence when squared standardized predictive errors average above one; it need not agree with interval coverage.
assumptions_latex: \(s_n(X)>0\) almost surely under the assessment distribution.

notation.meaning: reported predictive mean and standard deviation

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Second-Moment Overconfidence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of fixed-level interval coverage from standardized-error second moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nominal 95-percent interval can undercover even though mean squared standardized error is below one.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) has the displayed three-point distribution.
Coverage is assessed by the central cutoff \(1.96\) at nominal level \(0.95\).
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Undercoverage Without Second-Moment Inflation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse separation of standardized-error second moment from fixed-level interval coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean squared standardized error can exceed one while a fixed nominal interval overcovers.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) has the displayed symmetric two-point distribution.
Coverage is assessed by the central cutoff \(1.96\).
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Moment Inflation Without Interval Undercoverage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise, conditional, or marginal undercoverage relative to a declared posterior prediction or credible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an assessment law \(Q\), nominal level \(1-\alpha\), assessment target \(Y\), and reported set \(I_n(x)\). For example, under a central Gaussian predictive convention,
\[
I_n(x)=[\mu_n(x)-z_{1-\alpha/2}s_n(x),\mu_n(x)+z_{1-\alpha/2}s_n(x)].
\]
Marginal overconfidence means \(Q\{Y\in I_n(X)\}<1-\alpha\). Pointwise overconfidence at \(x\) uses \(Q\{Y\in I_n(x)\mid X=x\}<1-\alpha\), and conditional overconfidence conditions on a declared event or sigma-field. These targets are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior interval overconfidence is undercoverage relative to a declared nominal level, target, assessment law, and marginal, pointwise, or conditional calibration notion.
assumptions_latex: \alpha\in(0,1).
The assessment target Y, law Q, and calibration target are declared.
For the Gaussian example, s_n(x)>0 and z_{1-\alpha/2} is the standard-normal quantile.

notation.meaning: Reported prediction or credible set for the declared target.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Posterior Overconfidence
Posterior Overconfidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Miscoverage criterion for an overly concentrated surrogate posterior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the surrogate report posterior mean \(\mu_n(x)\) and standard deviation \(s_n(x)>0\). For a fixed \(z>0\), its nominal pointwise credible interval is \(I_n(x)=[\mu_n(x)-zs_n(x),\mu_n(x)+zs_n(x)]\). Under a data-generating law \(P_0\), posterior overconfidence occurs on \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) when \[P_0\{f_0(x)\in I_n(x)\}<1-\alpha\] for relevant \(x\in A\), despite the interval being reported at nominal coverage \(1-\alpha\). Thus small posterior uncertainty alone does not certify calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate is overconfident when its nominal credible intervals cover the true response less often than their advertised probability.
assumptions_latex: \(s_n(x)>0\) on the assessed set.
The nominal level \(1-\alpha\) and multiplier \(z\) are fixed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no calibration source is supplied. The relation between z and the advertised level 1-alpha is unstated, and 'relevant x' does not give a precise quantifier over A.

children.title: Posterior Variance Collapse
children.top_down_role: Loss of useful predictive variance across insufficiently explored regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Benign Zero Variance at Noiseless Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that zero posterior variance alone is not pathological collapse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact noiseless Gaussian-process interpolator with nonsingular kernel matrix and an observed site \(x_i\), conditioning gives \(s_n^2(x_i)=0\) and \(\mu_n(x_i)=y_i=f(x_i)\). Thus zero posterior variance at an interpolated observation can coincide with zero prediction error and does not by itself establish harmful variance collapse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noiseless GP has zero variance and zero interpolation error at observed sites, so zero variance alone is not a failure certificate.
assumptions_latex: Observations are noiseless.
The Gaussian-process kernel matrix is nonsingular.
\(x_i\) is a conditioned observation site.
knowledge_statements.title: Benign Zero Variance at Noiseless Observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural reason posterior variance need not react to realized prediction errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Gaussian process with fixed kernel \(k\), fixed observation-noise covariance \(\Sigma\), training locations \(X_n\), and responses \(y_n\), the latent posterior variance is \[s_n^2(x)=k(x,x)-k(x,X_n)[K(X_n,X_n)+\Sigma]^{-1}k(X_n,x).\] Hence \(s_n^2(x)\) depends on the design and fixed covariance parameters but not on \(y_n\). Persistent response residuals therefore do not themselves inflate this reported variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed covariance parameters, GP posterior variance depends on locations and the noise model, not on observed response values.
assumptions_latex: The kernel and observation-noise covariance are fixed.
\(K(X_n,X_n)+\Sigma\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_n^2(x)\text{ is independent of the realized vector }y_n.
knowledge_statements.title: Response-Independence of Fixed-Parameter GP Variance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: RKHS Error Certificate for Benign Variance Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic calibration certificate for noiseless fixed-kernel interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be positive definite, let \(X_n\) have nonsingular Gram matrix, and let \(\mu_n\) and \(s_n\) be the noiseless zero-mean GP interpolant and posterior standard deviation. For every \(f\in\mathcal H_k\), \[|f(x)-\mu_n(x)|\le \|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}s_n(x).\] Consequently, if \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B\) and \(\sup_{x\in A}s_n(x)\to0\), then \(\sup_{x\in A}|f(x)-\mu_n(x)|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a correctly specified noiseless RKHS model, posterior standard deviation bounds interpolation error, so uniform variance contraction is benign.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in\mathcal H_k\) and \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B<\infty\).
Observations are exact and the Gram matrix is nonsingular.
The interpolant uses the same fixed kernel \(k\).

notation.meaning: kernel interpolant and posterior standard deviation

knowledge_statements.title: RKHS Error Certificate for Benign Variance Contraction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage Failure Certificate under Noisy Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable local calibration witness when independent validation error bounds are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At validation sites \(z_1,\ldots,z_q\), suppose independent validation estimates \(\bar Y_i\) satisfy simultaneous bounds \(|\bar Y_i-f_0(z_i)|\le e_i\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\). If for some \(i\),
\[
|\bar Y_i-\mu_n(z_i)|-e_i>c\,s_n(z_i),
\]
then on that event \(|f_0(z_i)-\mu_n(z_i)|>c s_n(z_i)\). Vanishing \(s_n(z_i)\) together with a validation discrepancy bounded away from zero therefore certifies harmful local collapse. Failure to detect such a discrepancy at finitely many sites does not certify global calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent validation error bars can certify that latent prediction error exceeds a reported uncertainty band, but finite validation cannot rule out collapse elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: Validation observations are independent of the surrogate-fitting data conditional on their latent values.
The simultaneous validation error bounds have coverage at least \(1-\delta\).
\(c>0\) is the declared posterior-band multiplier.

notation.meaning: Validation error radius for the latent value.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage Failure Certificate under Noisy Validation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational distinction between benign latent-variance contraction and unsupported certainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu_n(x)\) and \(s_n(x)\) be a surrogate's reported latent predictive mean and standard deviation, and let \(f_0\) be the fixed latent response. Harmful posterior variance collapse on a nonempty set \(A\) occurs along a subsequence \(n_j\) when
\[
\sup_{x\in A}s_{n_j}(x)\to0
\quad\text{while}\quad
\limsup_{j\to\infty}\sup_{x\in A}|f_0(x)-\mu_{n_j}(x)|>0.
\]
Variance contraction accompanied by uniform prediction consistency on \(A\) is not harmful collapse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posterior variance collapse is harmful when reported latent uncertainty vanishes on a region while prediction error remains nonvanishing there.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is nonempty.
\(f_0\), \(\mu_n\), and \(s_n\) are defined on \(A\).
The criterion concerns latent predictive variance, not future-observation variance including irreducible noise.

notation.meaning: Region on which collapse is assessed.
Reported posterior mean and latent standard deviation.

knowledge_statements.title: Harmful Posterior Variance Collapse
Posterior Variance Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate uncertainty caused by vanishing fitted posterior variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_n^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(f(x)\mid D_n)\) be the fitted surrogate variance. Posterior variance collapse on a nonempty region \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) occurs when \[\sup_{x\in A}s_n^2(x)\longrightarrow0\] while the true prediction error does not vanish there, for example when \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in A}|\mu_n(x)-f_0(x)|>0\). This separates harmful collapse from legitimate concentration: variance vanishing together with uniformly vanishing prediction error is not, by itself, a failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variance collapse is harmful when fitted uncertainty vanishes on a region while systematic prediction error remains nonzero there.
assumptions_latex: \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) is nonempty.
\(s_n^2(x)\) and \(\mu_n(x)\) are the fitted posterior variance and mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in A}s_n^2(x)\to0\) with persistent error constitutes harmful variance collapse.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits and the distinction from legitimate concentration is sensible, but the proposed uniform asymptotic criterion is an uncited selected definition requiring authoritative support.

children.title: Exploration Suppression
children.top_down_role: Missed evaluations caused by excessively concentrated surrogate beliefs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal sufficient condition for eventual exclusion of a region after its exploratory bonus collapses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_n(x)=g_n(x)+b_n(x)\) be maximized over \(\mathcal X\), with \(b_n(x)\ge0\), and let \(A\subsetneq\mathcal X\). Suppose \(\sup_{x\in A}b_n(x)\to0\) and there exist \(\delta>0\), \(N\), and points \(z_n\in\mathcal X\setminus A\) such that \(g_n(z_n)\ge \sup_{x\in A}g_n(x)+\delta\) for every \(n\ge N\). Then, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_n(x)\cap A=\varnothing\). If \(A\) contains an optimizer or other points whose evaluation is required to correct the surrogate, this exclusion constitutes exploration suppression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region is eventually excluded when its nonnegative exploration bonus vanishes while exploitation retains a fixed disadvantage relative to a point outside the region.
assumptions_latex: a_n=g_n+b_n is globally maximized.
b_n(x)\ge0 for every x and n.
\sup_{x\in A}b_n(x)\to0.
An outside point has an eventual exploitation advantage of at least \delta>0 over every point in A.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive-Bonus Exploration Suppression

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain example in which erroneous variance collapse permanently excludes the true optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{a,b\}\), let \(f(a)=2>f(b)=1\), and suppose a misspecified surrogate reports \(\mu_n(a)=0\), \(s_n(a)=0\), \(\mu_n(b)=1\), and \(s_n(b)=0\) for every \(n\). For any finite \(\beta_n\ge0\), the upper-confidence acquisition \(u_n(x)=\mu_n(x)+\beta_ns_n(x)\) satisfies \(u_n(b)=1>0=u_n(a)\). Thus it always proposes \(b\), and the true optimizer is never evaluated under the stipulated persistent surrogate update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the true optimizer is assigned zero variance and an inferior mean, a UCB rule can select another point forever.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal X=\{a,b\}.
The stated posterior summaries persist after evaluations at b.
The acquisition maximizes \mu_n+\beta_ns_n with finite \beta_n\ge0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}u_n(x)=\{b\} for every n, although a is the unique true maximizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Variance Lockout Counterexample
Exploration Suppression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of exploratory pressure under collapsed posterior uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an acquisition rule \(a_n(x)=g_n(\mu_n(x))+\beta_n s_n(x)\) that is maximized, where \(\beta_n\geq0\) and the second term supplies exploration. Exploration is suppressed on \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) when \[\sup_{x\in A}\beta_n s_n(x)\longrightarrow0\] while \(A\) contains potentially improving points and the exploitation term ranks them below the selected region. If this ranking gap remains positive, then eventually no maximizer of \(a_n\) lies in \(A\), so the acquisition rule cannot correct its error there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collapsed uncertainty suppresses exploration when the exploration bonus vanishes in a potentially improving region that exploitation continues to rank poorly.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta_n\geq0\).
The acquisition rule maximizes \(a_n\).
The exploitation ranking gap against \(A\) remains positive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the leaf, but the source is absent and the undefined 'selected region' and ranking gap are insufficient to ensure that every global acquisition maximizer eventually lies outside A.

children.title: Overconfidence Detection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where available observations cannot reliably reveal uncertainty underestimation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional finite-sample test of marginal undercoverage using validation outcomes independent of surrogate fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_n\) contain the data and randomness used to construct nominal \((1-\alpha)\)-prediction sets \(I_n\). Conditional on \(\mathcal F_n\), let \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m\) be i.i.d. validation pairs and set \(K=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1\{Y_i\notin I_n(X_i)\}\). Under \(H_0:q_n=P\{Y\notin I_n(X)\mid\mathcal F_n\}\le\alpha\) almost surely, reject when \(K\ge k_\gamma\), where \(k_\gamma=\min\{k:P(B\ge k)\le\gamma,\ B\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\alpha)\}\). Then the rejection probability is at most \(\gamma\). The test assesses marginal coverage under the validation distribution, not pointwise or shifted-distribution calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditionally independent held-out outcomes give an exact binomial-tail test for marginal undercoverage, but not pointwise or off-distribution calibration.
assumptions_latex: \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m\) are conditionally i.i.d. given \(\mathcal F_n\).
The validation sample is conditionally independent of interval fitting given \(\mathcal F_n\).
\(q_n\le\alpha\) almost surely under the null.

notation.meaning: information used to fit the surrogate and construct its prediction sets

knowledge_statements.title: Held-Out Undercoverage Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Identical Fitted Summaries with Different Future Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-mechanism witness for the observable-summary detection boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the detector observe only the constant fitted prediction set \(I=\{0\}\), with no assessment outcome. Under \(P_0\), a future binary response satisfies \(P_0(Y=0)=0.95\); under \(P_1\), \(P_1(Y=0)=0.50\). The detector observation has the same law under both mechanisms, but the same nominal 95-percent set has coverage \(0.95\) under \(P_0\) and \(0.50\) under \(P_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same observable fitted prediction set can be calibrated or severely under-covering under two indistinguishable detector inputs.
assumptions_latex: The detector observes only the constant fitted set I=\{0\}.
Future coverage is assessed under the displayed binary-response laws.
The advertised coverage level is 0.95.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_0(Y\in I)=0.95,quad P_1(Y\in I)=0.50,\quad\text{and the detector input has the same law}.
knowledge_statements.title: Identical Fitted Summaries with Different Future Coverage

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Impossibility of detecting future undercoverage from an observable sigma-field having identical laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\) be the sigma-field available to a detector and let \(C(P)\) be coverage under a fixed future assessment experiment and prediction-set rule. If mechanisms \(P_0,P_1\) induce the same law on \(\mathcal O\), while \(C(P_0)\ge1-\alpha\) and \(C(P_1)<1-\alpha\), then every \(\mathcal O\)-measurable detector \(\delta\) has the same alarm distribution under both mechanisms. Hence its power against \(P_1\) equals its false-alarm probability under \(P_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If calibrated and under-covering mechanisms induce the same detector information, no detector using only that information can distinguish them.
assumptions_latex: P_0\text{ and }P_1\text{ induce the same probability law on }\mathcal O.
The future assessment experiment and prediction-set rule are fixed.
Coverage is at least 1-\alpha under P_0 and below 1-\alpha under P_1.

notation.meaning: Information sigma-field observable to the detector.
Coverage under the fixed assessment experiment.

knowledge_statements.title: Observable-Summary Indistinguishability Boundary
Overconfidence Detection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifiability limit for detecting miscalibration from fitted uncertainty alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a detector \(\delta(D_n,\mu_n,s_n)\) observes only the training data and the fitted posterior summaries. If two data-generating mechanisms \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) induce the same distribution of \((D_n,\mu_n,s_n)\), but the nominal intervals are calibrated under \(P_0\) and under-cover under \(P_1\), then \[P_0\{\delta=1\}=P_1\{\delta=1\}.\] Hence no such detector can distinguish calibrated uncertainty from overconfidence uniformly over both mechanisms. Detection requires additional identifying information, such as held-out outcomes, replication, or justified structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overconfidence is undetectable from fitted summaries alone when calibrated and miscalibrated mechanisms generate the same observable distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) agree on the law of \((D_n,\mu_n,s_n)\).
Calibration differs between \(P_0\) and \(P_1\).

notation.meaning: fitted posterior mean and standard deviation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the indistinguishability argument is plausible, but the formal observation model, calibration property, and identifiability result have no cited support.

children.title: Surrogate Regularity Mismatch Family
children.top_down_role: Poor fit to discontinuities, abrupt scale changes, or unmodeled interactions.

children.title: Stationarity Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Poor surrogate fit caused by spatially varying behavior or abrupt scale changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean Nonstationarity Is Not Covariance Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating nonconstant mean structure from stationary residual covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A process may have representation \(f(x)=m(x)+g(x)\), where \(m\) is nonconstant and \(g\) has stationary covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(g(x),g(x'))=\kappa(x-x')\). If the mean is modeled correctly, nonconstancy of \(m\) does not imply stationarity mismatch of the residual covariance. Conversely, subtracting an incorrect mean can make residual dependence appear nonstationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A varying mean does not by itself prove covariance stationarity mismatch; mean structure and residual covariance must be distinguished.
assumptions_latex: The input domain supports the displacement operation used by \(\kappa\).
The process has finite second moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean Nonstationarity Is Not Covariance Mismatch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary second-order condition giving a direct witness against stationary covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a centered second-order process on an additive input domain has stationary covariance \(C(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(f(x))=C(x,x)=\kappa(0)\) is constant in \(x\). Hence unequal marginal variances at two locations rule out stationary covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationary covariance has constant marginal variance, so location-dependent true variance witnesses stationarity mismatch.
assumptions_latex: The centered process has finite second moments.
The input domain supports subtraction.
Stationarity refers to the centered covariance.

notation.meaning: covariance as a function of displacement

knowledge_statements.title: Location-Dependent Marginal Variance Witnesses Nonstationarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating displacement stationarity from the stronger distance-only restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^d\), covariance is stationary when \(C(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\) and isotropic when \(C(x,x')=\varphi(\|x-x'\|)\). Isotropy implies stationarity, but the converse fails: \[\kappa(h)=\exp\!\left(-\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2/\ell_j^2\right)\] is stationary and anisotropic when the positive \(\ell_j\) are not all equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity requires dependence on displacement, not distance alone; anisotropic stationary kernels remain stationary.
assumptions_latex: The input domain is \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(\ell_j>0\) for every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Does Not Require Isotropy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variogram-based necessary condition for stationary second-order covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a second-order process on \(\mathbb R^d\) with stationary covariance \(C(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\). Then \[\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(f(x)-f(x'))=\kappa(0)-\kappa(x-x').\] Hence equal displacements have equal increment variances. If \(x-x'=u-u'\) but the two increment variances differ, the covariance is nonstationary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationary covariance makes increment variance depend only on displacement; a violation witnesses stationarity mismatch.
assumptions_latex: The process has finite second moments.
The input domain is \(\mathbb R^d\).

notation.meaning: stationary covariance as a function of displacement

knowledge_statements.title: Increment-Variance Witness of Stationarity Mismatch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on certifying global covariance stationarity from a fixed finite design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset\mathbb R^d\) be finite and let \(k_s\) be a positive-definite stationary kernel. Choose a nonzero continuous function \(q\) satisfying \(q(x_i)=0\) for every \(i\), and define
\[
k_{ns}(x,x')=k_s(x-x')+q(x)q(x').
\]
Then \(k_{ns}\) is positive semidefinite and agrees with \(k_s\) on \(S\times S\), but it is generally nonstationary because its marginal variance contains \(q(x)^2\). Thus a covariance matrix observed only on a fixed finite design cannot certify global stationarity without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstationary rank-one covariance perturbation can vanish at every sampled site and be indistinguishable from a stationary kernel on a finite design.
assumptions_latex: The input domain contains points outside the finite design.
A nonzero continuous function vanishing on the design exists.
\(k_s\) is a positive-definite stationary kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_{ns}|_{S\times S}=k_s|_{S\times S}\quad\text{although }k_{ns}\text{ need not be stationary}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Design Nonidentifiability of Global Stationarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete covariance-mismatch definition on an additive input group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) lie in an additive group and let the centered true process have finite-second-moment covariance \(C_0(x,x')\). Its covariance is stationary on \(\mathcal X\) when there exists a function \(\kappa\) on the realized displacement set such that
\[
C_0(x,x')=\kappa(x-x')\qquad\text{for all }x,x'\in\mathcal X.
\]
Stationarity mismatch occurs when no such representation exists. Equivalently, there are pairs \((x,x')\) and \((u,u')\) with equal displacement but unequal true covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity mismatch means that the true centered covariance cannot be represented solely as a function of displacement.
assumptions_latex: The input domain lies in an additive group so displacement is defined.
The centered true process has finite second moments.

notation.meaning: Covariance represented as a function of displacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Stationarity Mismatch
Stationarity Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Misspecification caused by fitting a stationary covariance to nonstationary behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fitted Gaussian-process surrogate is stationary when its covariance satisfies \(k_\theta(x,x')=\kappa_\theta(x-x')\). Stationarity mismatch occurs when the true second-order structure cannot be represented in this form; concretely, there exist pairs \((x,x')\) and \((u,u')\) with \(x-x'=u-u'\) but \[\operatorname{Cov}_0(f(x),f(x'))\neq\operatorname{Cov}_0(f(u),f(u')).\] Then no stationary kernel can reproduce both covariances simultaneously. Consequently, fitted length scales and posterior uncertainty must compromise across locations, potentially distorting acquisition scores in regions with different local variability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity mismatch occurs when equal input displacements have different true covariances, which no stationary kernel can represent simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: The true process has finite second moments.
The surrogate covariance has the stationary form \(k_\theta(x,x')=\kappa_\theta(x-x')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal displacements with unequal true covariances imply misspecification of every stationary covariance model.

notation.meaning: stationary covariance as a function of displacement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits stationarity mismatch, but no source is supplied. The displacement formula requires an input space where subtraction is defined, and the claimed effects on fitted uncertainty and acquisition scores are only potential consequences, not consequences of the covariance inequality alone.

children.title: Smoothness Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Poor surrogate fit caused by discontinuities, sharp transitions, or rough responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for a surrogate whose kernel-encoded regularity is incompatible with the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be an objective and let a Gaussian-process surrogate use kernel \(k\). Smoothness mismatch occurs when consequential local regularity of \(f\), such as differentiability, Hölder behavior, or characteristic variation scale, is incompatible with the corresponding regularity assumptions encoded by \(k\). Under such misspecification, nominally small posterior variance need not entail small prediction error, and acquisition values based on the nominal posterior can be miscalibrated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothness mismatch occurs when the objective's consequential local regularity differs from that encoded by the kernel, so confident surrogate predictions and acquisition values may be miscalibrated.
assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\).
The surrogate uses a Gaussian-process prior with kernel \(k\), which encodes regularity assumptions relevant to prediction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A consequential incompatibility between the local regularity of \(f\) and that encoded by \(k\) constitutes smoothness mismatch and can miscalibrate posterior uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical incompatibility between continuous surrogate functions and a jump discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have one-sided limits at an interior point \(x_0\) with jump size \(J=|f(x_0^+)-f(x_0^-)|>0\). For every function \(g\) continuous at \(x_0\), \[\sup_{x\text{ near }x_0}|f(x)-g(x)|\ge J/2.\] Thus a surrogate representation constrained to be continuous cannot uniformly represent the jump with error below \(J/2\), regardless of parameter fitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous surrogate cannot uniformly approximate across a genuine jump more accurately than half the jump size.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0\) is approachable from both sides within the domain.
The stated one-sided limits exist and differ by \(J>0\).
The surrogate function \(g\) is continuous at \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Surrogate Jump Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional variants on a declared common regularity scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\beta(x)\) denote a task-relevant local regularity index of the objective and \(\rho(x)\) the regularity imposed or favored by the surrogate, measured on the same ordered scale. At a consequential location \(x\), \(\rho(x)>\beta(x)\) is oversmoothing mismatch and \(\rho(x)<\beta(x)\) is undersmoothing mismatch. Equality removes only this directional mismatch, not possible length-scale, stationarity, likelihood, or structural mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oversmoothing assumes more regularity than the objective has; undersmoothing assumes less, and matching the index does not exclude other mismatches.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta(x)\) and \(\rho(x)\) use the same ordered regularity scale.
The location is consequential for the optimization task.
knowledge_statements.title: Oversmoothing and Undersmoothing Variants

children.title: Structural Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Poor surrogate fit caused by missing interactions, constraints, or latent organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-class failure caused by omitted objective structure rather than parameter error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed function space on \(\mathcal X\), let \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal F\) be a closed effective surrogate model class, and let \(f\in\mathcal F\). Structural mismatch occurs when \(f\notin\mathcal M\) because the model excludes a consequential feature such as nonstationarity, discontinuity, anisotropy, or known composition. Then the task-relevant approximation distance \(d(f,\mathcal M)=\inf_{g\in\mathcal M}\|f-g\|\) is positive. Additional observations may reduce estimation uncertainty within \(\mathcal M\) while leaving this approximation bias, so nominal posterior confidence can increase without correcting acquisition-relevant error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural mismatch occurs when a closed surrogate class excludes a consequential feature of the objective; more data may reduce estimation uncertainty while leaving positive approximation bias.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F,\|\cdot\|)\) is a normed function space on \(\mathcal X\).
The effective surrogate class \(\mathcal M\subseteq\mathcal F\) is closed, and the objective satisfies \(f\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(f\notin\mathcal M\), then \(d(f,\mathcal M)=\inf_{g\in\mathcal M}\|f-g\|>0\), and concentration within \(\mathcal M\) does not remove this approximation bias.

notation.meaning: distance from the objective to the surrogate model class

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences
source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.2 Sequential design and nonstationary surrogate modeling p. 34

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing why closedness is required to infer positive distance from model-class exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=C([0,1])\) with the uniform norm and let \(\mathcal M\) be the polynomial functions. For \(f(x)=e^x\), one has \(f\notin\mathcal M\), but the Weierstrass approximation theorem gives \(\inf_{p\in\mathcal M}\|f-p\|_\infty=0\). Thus exclusion from a nonclosed surrogate class does not by itself imply positive irreducible approximation bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function can lie outside a nonclosed model class yet be approximated arbitrarily well, so nonmembership alone does not establish structural bias.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F=C([0,1])\) uses the uniform norm.
\(\mathcal M\) is the nonclosed class of polynomial functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmembership Without Irreducible Approximation Bias

children.title: Mismatch-Induced Search Bias
children.top_down_role: Systematic proposal errors caused by unsuitable surrogate assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Mismatch-Induced Search Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential-design consequence of surrogate regularity or structural mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), let \(U\subseteq\mathcal X\) be a neighborhood of \(x^\star\), and suppose \(x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_t(x)\). Mismatch-induced search bias occurs when systematic posterior error yields a region \(B\subseteq\mathcal X\setminus U\) and an iteration \(T\) such that every acquisition maximizer belongs to \(B\) for all \(t\ge T\). The resulting policy allocates all later evaluations to \(B\) and does not sample \(U\); absent an independent exploration mechanism, its evaluation sequence need not approach a true optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent surrogate error induces search bias when every later acquisition maximizer lies in a wrong region, preventing evaluation near the true optimizer unless an independent exploration mechanism intervenes.
assumptions_latex: The policy selects \(x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_t(x)\), and these maximizers exist.
The acquisition \(a_t\) is computed from a misspecified surrogate posterior.
A neighborhood \(U\) of a true optimizer \(x^\star\) is disjoint from the persistently favored region \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}a_t(x)\subseteq B\subseteq\mathcal X\setminus U\) for every \(t\ge T\), then no evaluation after \(T\) enters \(U\), and the evaluation sequence need not approach \(x^\star\).

notation.meaning: systematically favored region disjoint from the optimizer neighborhood

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition preventing permanent mismatch-induced exclusion of optimizer neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((z_j)_{j\ge1}\) be dense in \(\mathcal X\), and suppose a sequential policy evaluates every \(z_j\) through an infinite forced-exploration subsequence independent of acquisition maximization. Then every nonempty open set \(U\subseteq\mathcal X\) is evaluated at least once. If every tail of \((z_j)\) is dense, every such \(U\) is evaluated infinitely often. Consequently, no \(B\subseteq\mathcal X\setminus U\) contains every sufficiently late evaluation, although mismatch may still bias unforced evaluations and recommendations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense forced-exploration schedule prevents permanent exclusion of open optimizer neighborhoods but does not remove surrogate bias elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \((z_j)\) is dense in \(\mathcal X\).
Every scheduled forced-exploration point is executed.
For infinite visitation, every tail of \((z_j)\) is dense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U\ne\varnothing\text{ open}\Rightarrow\exists t:x_t\in U;\quad\text{tail density implies infinitely many such }t.
knowledge_statements.title: Forced-Exploration Exclusion Boundary

children.title: Observation-Process Mismatch Family
children.top_down_role: Unreliable inference under heteroscedasticity, heavy tails, censoring, or replication imbalance.

children.title: Noise-Structure Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Inference failures caused by heteroscedastic, correlated, or otherwise misspecified noise.

assumptions_latex: Observations obey \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\mid x_i]=0\).
The fitted surrogate assumes conditional variance \(v_0(x)\) and independence across observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the true conditional covariance is not \(v_0(x_i)\mathbf 1\{i=j\}\), the surrogate has noise-structure mismatch and its posterior variance is generally miscalibrated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch in heteroscedasticity or dependence of additive observation noise.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(y_i=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\) with \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_i\mid x_i]=0\). A surrogate assuming \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j\mid x_i,x_j)=v_0(x_i)\mathbf 1\{i=j\}\) has noise-structure mismatch whenever the true covariance \(\Sigma_\varepsilon\) differs materially through heteroscedasticity or cross-observation dependence. Because Gaussian-process conditioning uses the matrix \(K+\Sigma_\varepsilon\), replacing it by \(K+\operatorname{diag}(v_0(x_i))\) changes posterior means and variances. Consequently, nominal credible intervals and exploration bonuses need not have their intended calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise-structure mismatch occurs when assumed variances or independence differ from the true observation process, distorting posterior predictions, uncertainty, and exploration bonuses.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Structure Mismatch

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact calibration gap for a Gaussian-process linear predictor using the wrong noise covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the latent training vector have covariance \(K\), covariance vector \(k_x\) with \(f(x)\), and true observation-noise covariance \(\Sigma_\star\). A surrogate using \(\Sigma_0\) forms \(w=(K+\Sigma_0)^{-1}k_x\) and reports \(s_0^2(x)=k(x,x)-k_x^{\mathsf T}w\). If the mean and latent covariance are correct, then the true mean-squared prediction error of \(w^{\mathsf T}y\) is \(\operatorname{MSE}_\star(x)=s_0^2(x)+w^{\mathsf T}(\Sigma_\star-\Sigma_0)w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact variance-calibration error from using the wrong noise covariance is the predictor-weight quadratic form of that covariance mismatch.
assumptions_latex: The latent covariance and mean model are correctly specified.
The fitted and true noise covariances are \Sigma_0 and \Sigma_\star.
K+\Sigma_0 is invertible.

notation.meaning: linear prediction weights under the assumed covariance

knowledge_statements.title: Predictive-MSE Error from Noise-Covariance Mismatch

children.title: Likelihood Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Inference failures under heavy tails, censoring, discreteness, or unsuitable observation models.

assumptions_latex: Conditional observations have true density \(p_\star(y\mid f(x),x)\).
Inference uses likelihood family \(\{p_\theta(y\mid f(x),x):\theta\in\Theta\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(p_\star\notin\{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), the likelihood is misspecified and its posterior uncertainty need not be calibrated under the true observation law.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observation-law failure beyond variance or correlation misspecification alone.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_\star(y\mid f(x),x)\) be the true conditional observation density and let inference use \(p_\theta(y\mid f(x),x)\), with \(\theta\in\Theta\). Likelihood mismatch occurs when \(p_\star\notin\{p_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), for example because Gaussian tails, symmetry, censoring, or support are incorrectly imposed. The posterior is then formed from likelihood ratios different from those of the data-generating process. Even when a pseudo-true parameter minimizes \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\star\|p_\theta)\), nominal posterior variances and tail probabilities need not be calibrated for acquisition computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Likelihood mismatch means the fitted observation family excludes the true law, so posterior tail probabilities and uncertainty used by the acquisition may be miscalibrated.
knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood Mismatch

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular asymptotic uncertainty boundary under a misspecified likelihood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) be i.i.d. from \(p_\star\), and let \(	heta^\star\) uniquely minimize \(\operatorname{KL}(p_\star\|p_	heta)\) in a regular parametric family. Define \(H=-\mathbb E_\star[
abla_	heta^2\log p_{	heta^\star}(Y)]\) and \(J=\mathbb E_\star[
abla_	heta\log p_{	heta^\star}(Y)
abla_	heta\log p_{	heta^\star}(Y)^{\mathsf T}]\). Under the standard consistency and central-limit regularity conditions, \(\sqrt n(\widehat	heta_n-	heta^\star)\Rightarrow N(0,H^{-1}JH^{-1})\). Inverse-curvature uncertainty \(H^{-1}/n\) agrees with this sampling covariance only when \(J=H\), which need not hold under mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under regular likelihood misspecification, estimator uncertainty has sandwich covariance rather than generally having inverse-curvature covariance.
assumptions_latex: Observations are i.i.d. and satisfy regular misspecified maximum-likelihood conditions.
The KL minimizer \theta^\star is unique and interior.
H is nonsingular and the required score moments exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic covariance is H^{-1}JH^{-1}/n, not generally H^{-1}/n.

notation.meaning: expected negative likelihood Hessian at the pseudo-true parameter
score outer-product matrix at the pseudo-true parameter

children.title: Replication Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Unreliable uncertainty assessment caused by inadequate or imbalanced repeated evaluations.

assumptions_latex: At design site \(x_j\), observations \(y_{jr}=f(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jr}\) are collected for \(r=1,\ldots,n_j\).
Conditional replicate errors are independent with variance \(\sigma^2(x_j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Treating \(\bar y_j\) as having variance other than \(\sigma^2(x_j)/n_j\), or treating all replicates as one raw observation, constitutes replication mismatch.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to represent how repeated observations change effective noise precision.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At site \(x_j\), let \(y_{jr}=f(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jr}\) for \(r=1,\ldots,n_j\), where the errors are conditionally independent with variance \(\sigma^2(x_j)\). Then the replicate mean \(\bar y_j=n_j^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{n_j}y_{jr}\) has conditional variance \(\sigma^2(x_j)/n_j\). Replication mismatch occurs when the surrogate assigns \(\bar y_j\) a variance inconsistent with this scaling, or collapses unequal replication counts without preserving their precision. Posterior uncertainty and the acquisition's valuation of further replication are consequently distorted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication mismatch ignores how replicate counts alter mean precision, causing incorrect posterior uncertainty and distorted choices between resampling and sampling new sites.
knowledge_statements.title: Replication Mismatch

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of independent Gaussian replicates to a mean with count-adjusted variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fixed site, let \(y_r=z+\varepsilon_r\), \(r=1,\ldots,m\), with independent \(\varepsilon_r\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) and known \(\sigma^2\). Since \(\sum_{r=1}^m(y_r-z)^2=\sum_{r=1}^m(y_r-\bar y)^2+m(\bar y-z)^2\), the first term is independent of \(z\). Hence the likelihood for \(z\) from all replicates is proportional to that from \(\bar y\mid z\sim N(z,\sigma^2/m)\). Replacing replicates by \((\bar y,m)\) with variance \(\sigma^2/m\) therefore preserves inference on \(z\) conditional on \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Gaussian replicates can be replaced exactly by their mean only when their count is retained through the reduced variance.
assumptions_latex: Replicates share one latent site value z.
Errors are conditionally independent Gaussian variables with common known variance \sigma^2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For inference on z, the replicate likelihood is equivalent to \bar y\mid z\sim N(z,\sigma^2/m).

notation.meaning: latent response at the replicated site

knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Preserving Replicate Aggregation

children.title: Noise–Replication Confounding
children.top_down_role: Regimes where sparse replication prevents reliable separation of signal from observation variation.

assumptions_latex: At one site, \(y_r=\mu+\varepsilon_r\) for \(r=1,\ldots,n\).
The errors are exchangeable with variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The replicate mean identifies only \(\sigma^2[1+(n-1)\rho]/n\); without additional information, noise magnitude and dependence are confounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability between marginal noise and within-site replicate dependence.

source_refs.locator: 2 Applications to Learning, Repeated Games, State Dependent Noise, and Queue Optimization p. 29
source_refs.source_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exchangeable replicates \(y_r=\mu+\varepsilon_r\), suppose \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_r)=\sigma^2\) and \(\operatorname{Corr}(\varepsilon_r,\varepsilon_s)=\rho\) for \(r\ne s\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar y)=\sigma^2[1+(n-1)\rho]/n\). Thus an observed effective variance of the replicate mean can be explained by multiple pairs \((\sigma^2,\rho)\). Without raw replicate contrasts, multiple replication levels, or an identified dependence model, marginal noise and replicate correlation are confounded; assuming \(\rho=0\) can falsely attribute dependence to large noise or understate uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate-mean variability combines marginal noise and within-site dependence; without additional replication information, these components cannot be separately identified.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise–Replication Confounding
